papers.abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT
authors: Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang, Jinze Bai, Bo Wang, Xiang Bai
bullets: Introduces Mixture-of-Loops Attention, which uses keys and values as reusable memory across depths and loops.
MoLT-KV removes same-position cross-loop dependence and supports single-traversal decoding beyond the training loop horizon through loop forcing.
U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout, skipping unnecessary decoder traversals without changing predictions.
Across multiple model scales and settings, U-MoLT improves token efficiency, perplexity, and task accuracy while matching non-looped inference latency in one evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer with KV memory reuse directly targets LLM architecture efficiency and inference memory.
papers.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
papers.tldr: MoLT improves the efficiency–expressivity trade-off of looped Transformers by selectively reusing key-value memories across loops, enabling efficient training and decoding without sacrificing quality.

papers.abstract: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.
authors: Jiachen An, Sijie Zhao, Le Li, Hongyu Liu, Zhiyuan Li, Tianyu Yang, Xiaoyu Kong, Xunliang Cai, Yong Zhang, Chi-Man Pun, Xiaoming Wei, Xiaodong Cun
bullets: Existing video VAEs are latency bottlenecks, especially for encoding, due to heavy convolutions or global spatiotemporal attention.
Effective receptive-field analysis shows that VAE patches depend mainly on nearby spatial and temporal neighbors.
Causal window attention reduces per-frame computation and keeps the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming.
Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation and joint finetuning enable drop-in replacement with the original VAE.
On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE delivers 5.2–6.2× faster encoding and 3.0–3.3× faster decoding with higher PSNR; infrastructure raises speedup to 13.4× with nearly no quality loss.

papers.title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
papers.tldr: LiveVAE accelerates both streaming video VAE encoding and decoding using causal local-window attention while preserving quality and compatibility with the pretrained latent space.

papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
authors: Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi, Lin Niu, Runzhi Fan, Zhaojing Zhou, Haodi Lei, Jiebin Zhang, Saiyong Yang, Junqiang Zheng, Zhenghai Xue, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu
bullets: Targets the memory, prefill, cache-hit, and concurrency costs of maintaining a drafter-side context cache.
Shares each target layer’s cached KV states and selected context positions with its paired drafter layer.
Uses block-parallel drafting without independently scoring or caching context positions.
Across DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Hy4~flash, accepts more tokens per step than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark.
Reported gains are larger on long-context and agentic workloads; at high concurrency on two 64K DS-V4.1-Flash sets, throughput is 62% and 81% higher at matched per-user decode speed.

papers.selection_reason: Shares the target's sparse attention selection and cache to speed up speculative decoding, directly addressing token selection and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.tldr: DFly2 accelerates speculative decoding for sparse long-context models by reusing the target model’s KV cache and query-specific sparse attention selections, avoiding a separate drafter cache and scoring pass.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
authors: Cui Yakun, Tiantian Geng, Huixiang Kong, Xingqun Qi, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets the gap between offline video QA evaluation and real-time, context-dependent streaming scenarios.
Introduces 4,983 questions across 462 videos with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations.
Uses the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation.
Presents EviStream, a causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget.
Experiments show current VLMs remain substantially short of realistic streaming video reasoning requirements.

papers.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
authors: Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses accuracy gaps between integer precisions and severe degradation at 2-bit quantization.
Uses coded bit-planes with extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks, shared row-level lookup tables, and joint multi-precision encoding.

papers.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
papers.tldr: Any-Rate enables one LLM checkpoint to support 2–8-bit inference, including half-bit steps from 2–4 bits, with improved low-bit accuracy and potentially lower energy use.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
authors: Alessio Devoto, Avinash Vem, Tara Safavi, Sanjay Kariyappa, Yu-Hsuan Tseng, Paul Furgale, Ricardo Silveira Cabral
bullets: Replaces harness-triggered summarization with a context API that lets models decide when and what to compact.
Evaluated on document research and machine learning engineering across 8K–512K-token budgets.
Effective API use improves performance at tight budgets: GPT 6.1’s OfficeQA Pro v2 score rose from 21% to 56% at 32K tokens, while Kimi used up to 41% fewer input tokens.
Models vary widely in compaction frequency, aggressiveness, and timing; prompt changes also affect when compaction begins.
KV-cache reuse after context edits reduced prefill compute by up to 15% per request without measurable accuracy changes.

papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.tldr: Model-driven context management can substantially improve agent accuracy and token efficiency under tight context budgets, especially when inference engines support efficient KV-cache editing.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in visual reasoning, but extended generation over large visual contexts remains computationally expensive. During autoregressive decoding, visual attention is recomputed for every generated token, even when consecutive tokens rely on similar visual evidence. We introduce VAPOR (Visual Attention Persistence with On-demand Refresh), a training-free framework that reduces this redundancy by reusing visual attention outputs across decoding steps and refreshing them when needed. VAPOR caches the visual attention output while continuing to update textual attention at every step, helping reduce visual grounding drift during extended reasoning. To decide when to reuse cached outputs, VAPOR estimates visual attention mass using a low-rank approximation. It also uses prefill-based attention consistency and cache age to make independent Persist and Refresh decisions for each attention head. VAPOR retains the full visual key-value (KV) cache, so all visual tokens remain available when new evidence is needed. Experiments on eight image and four video reasoning benchmarks across two MLLM families show that VAPOR improves accuracy over dense attention on nearly all benchmarks while achieving 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups. Compared with the strongest state-of-the-art acceleration baseline in each setting, VAPOR further improves accuracy by 0.35-2.15 percentage points while achieving comparable or lower decoding latency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Su-my/VAPOR.
authors: Mingyu Su, Wei Wu, Erle Zhu, Chengxing Xie, Deyao Hong, Hongning Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of recomputing visual attention for every generated token in long visual-context reasoning.
Uses a training-free cache of visual attention outputs while continuing to update textual attention at each step.
Makes per-head Persist/Refresh decisions using low-rank visual attention estimates, prefill consistency, and cache age.
Retains the full visual KV cache so all visual tokens remain accessible when new evidence is needed.
Across image and video benchmarks, improves accuracy over dense attention while delivering 1.11–1.21× decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.
authors: Jiankun Zou, Daixing Chen, Tongtong Yuan
bullets: Addresses cache-eviction decisions made before future decoding queries are available.
Extends FTQ-8 by adjusting seven repeated first-token embeddings with learned additive offsets.
Trains offsets to match the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation.
Computes all eight probe queries in one causal forward pass, avoiding extra autoregressive drafting steps.
On LongBench, matches the performance of eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget.

papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
bullets: Addresses the linear growth of standard attention’s key-value cache by learning context-dependent memory retention.
Uses a learned scorer to rescore memory chunks as new context arrives, while a standard attention reader accesses retained representations.
Trains retention jointly with reading using either gradual soft-to-hard selection or hard retention from the outset, aided by generated recovery supervision.

Across retrieval, variable tracking, reasoning, and language modeling, SSA substantially outperforms equal-budget bounded attention and can match or exceed attention with roughly four times its readable budget on retrieval tasks.
Its main remaining gap to full attention at small model scale is on RULER; the approach is evaluated across different training and inference context/model scales.

papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
authors: Ahmed Alajrami, Ondrej Bohdal, Seokwoo Song, Taegeon Um, Peyman Hosseini, Savas Ozkan, Mete Ozay, Taha Ceritli
bullets: Addresses persona-attribute inference from a single day of mobile logs for personalization.
Introduces a synthetic benchmark containing 1,600 persona–log pairs.
Filters semantically similar logs while retaining behaviorally distinct events.
Reduces memory use by up to 39% across nine models and more than halves prefill time without hurting prediction quality.
Results suggest behavioral diversity matters more than retaining redundant log entries.

papers.abstract: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
bullets: Generic-text calibration often loses downstream accuracy at very low bit widths.
FragCal-DC adds training documents from task families that retain little full-precision accuracy under two-bit quantization.
Across six dense models and ten tasks, SignRound V2 improved mean accuracy by 1.83 percentage points at two bits over generic-text calibration.
Benefits depend on the quantizer and bit width: iterative methods improved at two bits, while GPTQ and AWQ showed small mean responses at three bits.
Accuracy recovery concentrated on task families represented in calibration, and reconstruction error did not consistently predict gains.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.
authors: Wentao Zhu, Ziao Sheng, Peng Deng, Huiqi Hu, Xuan Zhou, Xing Wei, Zhuang Wang
bullets: Compresses BF16 KV caches to 0.71× and FP8 caches to 0.85–0.87× of raw size using a calibrated per-head 3-bit code.
Supports external-tier compression with unchanged storage, eviction, and prefetch behavior, plus GPU-pool compression with in-place decode-attention.
On AgentX, tier mode delivers 2.7–3.6× raw goodput across the cache-capacity cliff and reduces mean TTFT by 1.9–3.1×.
Pool mode fits 1.31–1.34× more GPU tokens; under joint tier and pool constraints, goodput increases by 1.24×–1.59×.
Compression is lossless/bit-exact for tier mode, matches FlashAttention-3 accuracy in pool mode, and costs at most 2.2% throughput when capacity is sufficient.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.
authors: Natalia Frumkin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Kristof Denolf, Eric Dellinger, Stuart Biles
bullets: The study evaluates MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4 across six LLMs while varying rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale selection.

Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection method, reduces clipping from power-of-two block scales and improves most tested MXFP4 configurations.
Using MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most 4-bit accuracy loss and matches or exceeds an in-house BF16 baseline on Llama-3.1-8B.
Adding a per-tensor macroscale does not improve average MXFP4 accuracy, indicating global rescaling does not resolve block-scale limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies quantization techniques (MXFP4) for LLM inference, providing practical guidance on combining numerical formats and scale selection for memory efficiency.
papers.title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
papers.tldr: Accurate MXFP4 LLM inference depends on format-specific combinations of rotation, PTQ, and scale selection rather than directly transferable quantization recipes.

papers.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang, Yanzhao Li, Hui Dong, Sifan Cheng, Mingen Zheng, Hui Wang
bullets: Addresses suboptimal HiF4 scale representations caused by conventional rounding and fixed extension thresholds.
Calibrates the Level-1 E6M2 rounding bias and optimizes Level-2/3 scale-extension thresholds using empirical magnitude distributions.
Calibration parameters are fixed offline, while block-level hierarchical encoding remains deterministic and adaptive.
Reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%–23.50% across five activation distributions, including 13.00% on real Qwen3-8B activations.
Improves average end-to-end benchmark scores by 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively.

The three components highlighted in red—the E6M2 rounding rule and the Level-2 and Level-3 magnitude thresholds—are the parameters calibrated in this work; all other operations follow the original HiF4 procedure.

papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses the slowdown, accuracy loss, and context-window limits of one-pass long-context inference.

Employs a stair position schedule to keep spans within the model’s trained position range.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity generation, but inference is expensive because every denoising step evaluates a large transformer over all spatiotemporal tokens of the video. Temporal caching accelerates them by reusing intermediate features across denoising steps. However, retaining dense feature tensors introduces a persistent storage cost that grows with video length, resolution, and cache coverage, reaching 109-346 GiB per video for the predictive caches we evaluate. Such states exceed the memory of a single GPU, so native caches must either be offloaded to the CPU, which slows generation, or be sharded across several GPUs, e.g., with sequence parallelism, so that the cache rather than the compute sets the number of GPUs. We instead shrink the cached state itself, exploiting its redundancy: a few channel patterns shared across tokens capture much of the energy of each cached feature. Based on this observation, we propose LRQ-Cache, a training-free method that combines low-rank approximation and quantization for feature-cache compression. LRQ-Cache represents each cached feature with a small set of factors, quantizes them before storage, and reconstructs the feature at reuse time, leaving cache mechanisms unchanged. Across three caching mechanisms on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, LRQ-Cache reduces the persistent state of predictive caches by 42-71x, to 2.3-4.9 GiB per video. VBench stays within 0.25 pp of the native cache for TeaCache, and the larger drops of the Wan2.1 predictive caches, up to 3.5 pp, shrink at higher ranks. As a result, predictive caches that exceed the memory of a single 80 GB H100 GPU fit on it with LRQ-Cache, making generation 2.7-5.9x faster than with CPU-offloaded native caches.
authors: Ruizhe Yao, Zhen Huang, Songpan Gao, Danyi Liu, Zijian Cao, Weijie Zheng, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Video diffusion caches can require 109–346 GiB per video, forcing CPU offloading or multi-GPU sharding.

Quality remains within 0.25 percentage points for TeaCache; Wan2.1 predictive-cache drops reach up to 3.5 points but improve with higher ranks.
Previously oversized predictive caches fit on a single 80 GB H100 and run 2.7–5.9× faster than CPU-offloaded native caches.

papers.selection_reason: Low-rank and quantization compression of video diffusion feature caches directly targets memory efficiency during inference, fitting the KV-cache/memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: LRQ-Cache: Compressing Feature Caches in Video Diffusion via Low-Rank Approximation and Quantization
papers.tldr: LRQ-Cache compresses video diffusion feature caches with low-rank approximation and quantization, greatly reducing memory use while largely preserving generation quality and improving speed.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ
authors: Minchan Kang, Kyeonghye Park, Seoyoung Cho, Junhee Lee, Daeshik Kim, Yucheol Cho
bullets: PTQ degradation is traced to outliers that dominate shared quantization ranges, causing many typical values to collapse to zero.
The work shifts attention from increasingly complex calibration strategies to the underlying quantization representation.
RRQ combines local Hadamard transforms, group quantization, and group-aware execution.
Across 8 multimodal tasks, RRQ improves performance over prior baselines while reducing inference time and memory use.
At W4A4, it retains over 96% of full-precision performance for 8B models and over 99% for a 32B model; baselines retain less than 8%.

papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
authors: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
bullets: Linear attention avoids growing key-value caches but can lose information through fixed-size memory collisions.
The method uses a delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of past delta states.
An adaptive readout combines both states to retrieve information across multiple timescales.
A chunkwise parallel formulation supports hardware-efficient training.
Experiments report improved performance across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, alongside evaluations of efficiency and memory use.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.
authors: Xiaoling Zhou, Haopeng Li, Yufa Zhou, Rui Ding, Yu Li, Jun Lin, Enze Xie, Chunhua Shen, Xuan Shen
bullets: Addresses spatial and visual inconsistency when revisiting locations, while reducing the latency and memory cost of growing KV histories.
Uses geometric grounding and query-conditioned draft relevance to retrieve the most useful historical KV cache blocks.
Introduces tile-wise streaming attention with CPU offloading to overlap KV transfers and computation under bounded GPU memory.
Reports 3.27× end-to-end speedup and 42.2% lower peak GPU memory than other CPU-offloaded retrieval methods.
Supports high-quality historical-KV world generation on a single H100 GPU with SolarWM-33B.

papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
authors: Jian Yang, Zhizhuo Kou, Qiyuan Zhu, Han Chen, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Persistent clean-KV updates can dominate runtime once denoising is accelerated, while stale-cache reuse increases later denoising work.
SAMR combines motion-aligned historical KV with in-flight KV, using calibrated affine correction and selective true $t=0$ refreshes.
Tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels implement the reconstruction efficiently without retraining the frozen video DiT.
On LongLive-1.3B, it cuts DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7%, while improving final-quarter PSNR over token reuse.
It transfers to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, reducing reuse-induced step inflation and improving late-stage PSNR, with calibration further recovering diagnostic quality.

(a) Streaming loop: denoising block b yields latents, in-flight KV, and exit steps s; SAMR then writes the cache Mb read by block b+1, so memory fidelity sets future early exits and closes the loop of Eq. (1). (b) One-time offline calibration fits the exit-step-conditioned Pre-RoPE affine maps (Wℓsh, bℓsh), the readout-risk table ρ, and the KV-update + Step-1 latency model T̂ ; nothing is fitted at test time. Per block, online control runs register-resident local patch matching (π(i), di), a readout-risk lookup by exit step, distance, and action a with staleness, and single-wave scoring of the 21 tile-aligned plans Pb (kernels 27.6× and 11.7× faster than PyTorch). The KV update applies phase-aligned reuse on Ub, t = 0 refresh on Rb, and Pre-RoPE reconstruction on Gb; refresh rows share one tile-aligned pass with Step 1 of block b+1. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.
authors: Yuanhong Chen, Yiping Ji, Cameron Gordon, Emily Hackett-Jones, Hemanth Saratchandran, Anton van den Hengel
bullets: Addresses the rising memory and inference costs of accumulating retrieved content in RAG KV caches.
Learns to selectively consolidate layer-wise native KV states without access to future queries.
Uses anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement alongside a frozen generator LLM.
Processes new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimization.
Maintains competitive performance on retrieval-augmented QA and synthetic long-context benchmarks under constrained memory.

papers.abstract: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.
bullets: Repeated planner prefill accounted for 89.5% of executed planner prompt tokens in default overload conditions, motivating KV reuse.
The authors add host-DRAM KV restoration through public runtime copy calls and a scheduler-aware event model.
SLO attainment rose from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in two tested overload conditions.
Endpoint tests indicated conservative load gains of 11.8% for chain workflows and 18.2% for fork workflows; mixed and bursty workloads were seed-sensitive.
The model stayed within 15% of median and P99 latency in 24 common-load conditions, but misordered some policy comparisons and overestimated a cheaper transfer path’s benefit.

papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.

Right: On-Policy Codec Distillation provides the tokens removed by codec pruning to the frozen teacher as privileged information and compares the student’s prediction with the teacher’s.

papers.title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
papers.tldr: CodecOPSD uses video-codec redundancy detection and on-policy self-distillation to prune conditioning tokens, accelerating all-in-one video generation with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Samuel Xu, Ivy Gu, Nathan Huang, Siqi Zhang
bullets: Addresses costly full-history re-prefill and the incompatibility of reusing KV caches across adapter versions.
Uses frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections to preserve base projections and low-rank coordinates.
Migrates the final-block cache by reconstructing K/V, reevaluating the latest token, and atomically committing the adapter, cache, and logits.
Proves continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under its model assumptions.
Reports 68.98× median paired publication speedup at 32 sessions with 8K-token histories, about 4.8% decoding overhead, and 3.42× lower additional storage than retained-boundary replay at 8K.

papers.abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.
authors: Anindya Roy Chowdhury, Atanu Barai, Nandakishore Santhi
bullets: Targets predictive-fidelity loss in low-bit LLM weight quantization.
Randomized orthogonal mixing makes residuals more Gaussian-like, improving sign-based reconstruction.
Progressive residual stages independently normalize and analytically calibrate reconstruction without codebooks, CDFs, or trellis optimization.
On GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B, five stages achieve perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73 versus full-precision 29.89 and 11.07.
Ablations show benefits from orthogonal mixing and activation-aware scaling, with reduced-precision statistics lowering storage overhead at negligible perplexity cost.

papers.abstract: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.
bullets: Targets Transformer inefficiencies, especially associative recall and context-length extrapolation.
Uses a tree-graph architecture and incorporates synthetic key-value retrieval tasks into language-model training.
Evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints.
On WikiText-103, achieves perplexity 19 and 100% KV retrieval accuracy when extrapolating from context length 512 to 16,384.
Reports perplexity 13 on PG-19 with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

(b) During the top-down pass, the global root hroot modulates mid-level subtree slots Hmid through a multiplicative bilinear gate before a secondary convex tree sweep produces the global summary htd.

papers.abstract: Repeating rows then selecting originals retains layout-dependent drift despite equal encoding counts. We measure when existing checks fail to establish preservation contracts in fixed quantized KV-cache implementations. In four-bit HQQ axis zero at sixteen cycles, median paired relative-L2 increases over same-shape re-encoding are 7.22 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B and 11.59 for SmolLM3-3B. Matched encoded states cover sixteen shared questions per model at one and sixteen cycles. Axis one matches the shape-preserving control; lazy reorders preserve the initial state. On one known input, fixed update counts retain the difference; preserving group members removes it. Our prefix-view extension passes current-prefix checks yet changes history and next logits in six model/codec settings at residual capacities four and 128. Public lookup reaches this boundary, including one of four precommitted project-new GPU inputs; fixed query swaps isolate a conditional old-history effect. Checkpoint/dense rollback is exact. An explicit delayed lookup client admits a supported 129-token path excluded by native AR on one known context. Failed task-harm expansion precludes population failure-rate or general answer-degradation claims. Native MLX-LM fixtures expose stale caller caches; synchronization restores the tested in-place contract with native computations preserved. In rejection tests, stale callers change logits but not greedy tokens.
bullets: Layout-dependent drift appears after repeated four-bit HQQ axis-zero updates, while axis-one and lazy-reorder controls match shape-preserving behavior.
Prefix-view checks can pass even when history and next logits change across six model/codec settings and residual capacities 4 and 128.
Preserving group members, checkpoint/dense rollback, or synchronized callers prevents or restores the tested state; stale callers can change logits without changing greedy tokens.
A delayed-lookup client supports a 129-token path excluded by native autoregressive handling on one known context.
Task-harm expansion failed, so population-level failure rates and general answer-degradation claims are not established.

papers.selection_reason: Quantized KV-cache maintenance and preservation directly concern memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Testing Quantized KV-Cache Maintenance: Encoding Layout and Historical Restoration
papers.tldr: Quantized KV-cache updates can silently alter historical states and next-token logits despite passing shape-based checks, while explicit restoration and synchronization preserve the tested in-place contract.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.
authors: Huan Xu, Maosen Zhao, Pengtao Chen, Tao Chen
bullets: Deployed parallel decoders, rather than fixed-step samplers, determine where quantization hurts dLLM accuracy and efficiency.
Most quantization-induced prediction flips arise from forced commitments when no position reaches the confidence threshold.
Quantization compresses top-logit gaps, causing extra forward passes even when predictions remain mostly unchanged—a parallelism tax.
DECAL reweights layer calibration using deployed-decoder commitment risk and applies an argmax-preserving commit temperature.
On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL achieves the best average W4A4 accuracy among evaluated methods with lower run-to-run variance than the closest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of DECAL and the commit temperature. Top left: a W4A4 student is calibrated layer by layer against the full-precision teacher with a hidden-state MSE weighted by w[p], and decodes with the commit temperature Tmatch. Bottom: how w[p] is obtained. Under the deployed parallel decoder, positions committed above τ are safe (low flip risk π), whereas forced commitments at small logit margins may flip (high π); positions committed early are read by more later passes (high reach a); w[p] follows from r[p] = E[π · a]. Top right: dividing the logits by Tmatch restores the top-logit gaps that W4A4 compresses, and with them the full-precision commit rate.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization of diffusion LLMs under parallel decoding; memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
papers.tldr: DECAL improves W4A4 quantization for diffusion LLMs by targeting commitment-risk errors and reducing quantization-induced decoding slowdowns.

papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.
authors: Marco Pichler, Patrick Podest, G\"unter Klambauer, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Edge forecasting requires fast refreshes, bounded latency and memory, and stable accuracy as observations accumulate.
Causal recurrent models support fixed-size state updates, unlike non-causal models and KV-cache approaches whose costs grow with history.
The authors persist recurrent states across refreshes and verify equivalence with full recomputation.
Nine TSFM configurations are evaluated on univariate forecasting across a GPU and three edge devices.
Most models lose accuracy beyond their trained context; only TiRex-2 meets all requirements, including constant resource use over one million steps.

papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with concurrency and context length, the regime in which existing self-speculation gains least.
bullets: Looped language models require multiple sequential passes per token, and existing self-speculation loses efficiency as concurrency increases.
The key bottleneck is speculative-work layout: separate rows repeatedly reread the same loop-specific KV caches.
PackLoop packs deep-loop and context-copy proposals into already-used rows, with an economic-order-quantity rule controlling accumulation.
It is token-for-token exact in FP32, including sampling and early exit.
Across 164 load points, it beat the best existing schedule at 161 points, with a median 1.25× and maximum 1.76× speedup, without significant slowdowns.

papers.selection_reason: Row-packed self-speculative decoding for looped LLMs under concurrency; strong efficient-inference contribution via KV-cache scheduling.
papers.title: PackLoop: Row-Packed Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models under Concurrency
papers.tldr: PackLoop preserves exact self-speculative decoding while improving throughput under concurrent GPU workloads by packing speculative positions into rows that are already being read.

papers.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.
authors: Tianqi Li, Xin He, Xue Geng, Le Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between smaller quantized models and actual deployability, where temporary tensors, latency, and action-sensitive errors matter.
Chooses layer-wise bit assignments and GPU execution routes under memory, latency, and task-evaluation budgets.
Uses calibration-guided candidate proposals, optional language-model assistance, and full-model GPU profiling before costly task trials.
Across 15 workloads and four model families, achieved a median 99.2% of FP32 task score, 2.36× speedup, and 71.5% lower peak allocated memory.
Scope: results focus on fixed GPU replays; code release is forthcoming.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents enable automated interactions with mobile, web, and desktop interfaces. However, their large memory footprint and repeated model calls hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining. Quantization can degrade GUI response accuracy and distort the instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations needed for GUI target selection. Small coordinate errors can cause missed clicks, while early action errors can alter subsequent interface states and disrupt task execution. Local reconstruction error alone does not directly assess whether these responses and relations are preserved. We propose GUI-Q, a PTQ framework that targets response and relation preservation with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16). Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation (TSGA) allocates finer groups under a scale-byte budget by combining response sensitivity with the measured reduction in activation-weighted distortion. Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection (RPSS) then selects symmetric or asymmetric grids to preserve instruction-vision affinities and local spatial relations in GUIs. Across three GUI-capable models, GUI-Q improves mean grounding TargetHit by 8.04 to 12.55 points over the strongest evaluated 4-bit configurations, while reducing static peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory by 49.9% to 56.2% relative to bfloat16 (BF16). Fixed-output replay with packed 4-bit execution provides 1.7 to 2.8 times model-call speedups. The code will be released.
authors: Tianqi Li, Yang Wang, Xin He, Le Zhang, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses GUI-agent deployment constraints from large memory use and repeated model calls.
Uses Task-Sensitive Granularity Allocation to assign finer quantization groups where response-sensitive distortion is reduced most.
Uses Relation-Preserving Symmetry Selection to retain instruction–vision affinities and local spatial relations.
Across three GUI-capable models, improves grounding TargetHit by 8.04–12.55 points over evaluated 4-bit baselines.
Reduces peak GPU memory by 49.9%–56.2% versus BF16 and achieves 1.7–2.8× model-call speedups with packed 4-bit execution.

papers.abstract: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
authors: Zikang Wen, Yuning Zhang, Dong Yuan
bullets: Shared-GPU inference reduces the cost of deploying many task-specific VLA policies, especially with LoRA adapters sharing a frozen backbone.
MotionExec triggers observations using motion structure in predicted action chunks to overlap inference with buffered execution.
SlackBatch uses per-robot slack and estimated GPU workload to decide when to wait, batch requests, or dispatch them.
With up to 96 simulated robots, it reduces mean episode stall by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points across evaluated settings.
Backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
