papers.abstract: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.
bullets: Existing Hopper 4-bit KV kernels underuse memory bandwidth because decoding and matrix operations are serialized and exceed instruction capacity per byte.
The proposed kernel overlaps TMA loading with computation, stores the cache for register-fed tensor-core inputs, and avoids padding for small query groups.
It reaches 67–75% of peak H200 bandwidth and is 1.12–1.49× faster across 11 tested shapes than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4’s proposed native FP8 path.
In vLLM, it is 1.12–1.64× faster per decode step than FlashInfer FP8 at batch sizes ≥8 and supports 1.63× as many tokens; prefill-heavy workloads lose 7% speed.
K mean removal, rotation, BF16 sink tokens, and retaining layer 0 in BF16 preserve accuracy across tested models, including Qwen variants that degrade with FP8 KV.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a fast 4-bit KV-cache decoding kernel with memory-efficiency and inference-speed improvements, directly fitting the KV-cache and memory-efficiency subtopic.

papers.tldr: A Hopper-optimized 4-bit KV-cache decoder fixes software-decoding bottlenecks, achieving near-bandwidth performance and higher throughput than FP8 while preserving accuracy with targeted safeguards.

papers.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can remain stable while individual graded answers change.
Across nine feature configurations, seven exact features flipped 1.47%–1.78% of requests, no higher than the 1.72% scheduling floor.
FP8 KV caching flipped 3.36% of graded outcomes, comparable to FP8 weights, and 3.91% with batch-invariant kernels.
Batch-invariant kernels made all seven exact features, including speculative decoding, reproduce reference text on every request.
Certification should use batch-invariant kernels or a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas; single-replica comparisons can reject unchanged configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM serving efficiency shortcuts including FP8 KV cache compression and prefix caching, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency research.
papers.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
papers.tldr: Most exact serving features cause answer flips no more often than request-reordering noise, but FP8 KV caching produces substantially more changes unless batch-invariant kernels are used.

papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
authors: Tiwari Ankit Satyaprakash, Adamya Shyam, Vikas Kumar, Bharti Rana, Venkateswara Rao Kagita
bullets: Targets inefficient fixed-depth computation in transformer-based sequential recommenders.
Uses a shared transformer backbone with learned routing to assign item-wise recursion depths.
Employs cascade-based key-value sharing for efficiency and gated attention for adaptive context regulation.
Outperforms strong transformer baselines across three benchmarks, with average gains of 2.28% Recall@5, 2.50% NDCG@5, and 2.0% MRR@5.
Gains remain consistent at top-10 and top-20 cutoffs; efficiency is demonstrated against vanilla transformers.

papers.abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.
authors: Patrick Pynadath, Nicolas Perez-Nieves, Bobak Shahriari, Jean Tarbouriech, Ruqi Zhang, Ivan Lobov
bullets: Immediate commitment harms quality when the entropy bound is relaxed, whereas leaving tokens revisable maintains accuracy.
Committing entire blocks wastes computation because tokens typically converge in a left-to-right order.
RES commits a contiguous accepted prefix after it reaches a minimum length and keeps later positions open for revision.
Across seven benchmarks, RES raises tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, with macro accuracy decreasing from 80.7% to 78.8%.
RES requires no training and extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier beyond entropy-bound tuning alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Columns in the top and middle rows show LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, and Natural2Code. Top row: Spearman 𝜌 and Kendall 𝜏 between the acceptance order of the DiffusionGemma EB sampler and the AR generation order; across all tasks the sampler is strongly biased towards left-to-right order. Middle row: Percentage of wasted denoising slots averaged across canvases for LCB v6, GPQA Diamond and Natural2Code. For a given sampling step, a slot is wasted if it belongs to a contiguous prefix that has already converged to its final token. By denoising step 20, the mean fraction of wasted canvas slots exceeds 50% on all three tasks. Bottom row: Accepted tokens are revised more often at higher entropy bounds (in both argmax and sampled-token stability), independent of renoising.

Figure 4 | Three passes of the rolling sampler. Every pass spends a fixed budget of ten positions (dashed frame), split between an encoded prefix of the tokens committed on the previous pass and the remaining denoising window; the mask panel on the right is exactly that block of ten. Left: positions keep their column, so each slot can be read down its column. Out-of-order acceptances wait for a contiguous prefix (w at 𝑡) and unaccepted slots stay mutable (column ten: r→ o). The prefix completing at 𝑡+1 is four slots long, so four slots must be encoded at 𝑡+2: the block advances by however many positions graduated into the KV cache, and the split is 0+10, then 2+8, then 4+6. Right: rows are queries, columns are keys; a coloured cell means the query attends to the key. The encoded prefix is causal, so its KV-cache entries depend only on committed tokens and are never revised, while denoising positions are bidirectional among themselves and attend fully to the prefix. Committing more positions per pass therefore moves the KV cache forward faster, but leaves fewer positions to denoise on the next pass. Every query additionally attends to the whole KV cache (white cells), which the panels omit for space.

Brick marks a slot spent re-denoising a position that was already accepted but is still waiting for its prefix, that is, wasted work. (a) The block sampler appends only once the block is fully resolved, so converged positions idle and each block re-pays warm-up. (b) The rolling sampler appends the accepted prefix immediately and admits fresh positions in its place, wasting far fewer slots.

papers.selection_reason: Rolling entropy sampling accelerates diffusion language models via KV cache commitment; efficiency contribution.

papers.abstract: The decay exponent $\alpha$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-\alpha}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $\alpha$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $\alpha$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.
bullets: Frames H2O and StreamingLLM as endpoints of a shared score: cumulative attention weighted by token age via exponent α.
Calibrating α on WikiText produces model-consistent ranges that also align with perplexity-based optimal regions across five models.
Achieves the lowest perplexity on WikiText, PG19, and arXiv without per-dataset tuning, outperforming H2O and StreamingLLM.
Matches or exceeds StreamingLLM on all evaluated QA task–budget cells; QA results are treated as corroborating because per-cell tests are not significant.
The approach is scoped to calibrated model-specific exponent ranges and is accompanied by a calibration script and drop-in scorer.

papers.selection_reason: Unifies KV cache eviction frameworks into a power-law family; directly relevant to KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
papers.tldr: NoHairCache unifies attention- and recency-based KV-cache eviction with one power-law exponent calibrated once per model and transferable across domains.

papers.abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.
authors: Qiuyu Ren, Sudipta Paria, Aritra Dasgupta, Swarup Bhunia
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in small-batch LLM decoding, where bits per weight determine weight traffic.
Bins channels by sensitivity and applies variable precision within each quantization group, without codebooks or fine-tuning.
BITSHARE-U uses a fixed layout for simple decoding; BITSHARE-N selects layouts per group under the same bit budget.
At 2–3 bits, both modes achieve lower WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity than GPTQ at matched storage; BITSHARE-N also outperforms reported SliM-LLM and GPTAQ baselines.
A verified SkyWater 130 nm decoder reconstructs weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.
authors: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
bullets: Top-$p$ selection adapts computation to attention distributions, avoiding top-$k$’s fixed-budget waste or context loss.
Integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM with scheduler-decoupled block selection and a two-stream pipeline that overlaps selection with layer computation.
Uses a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel to reduce selection cost.
Relocates tokens based on prefill attention scores to reduce intra-block sparsity and inflated selection budgets.
Reports 1.17×–1.80× faster sparsity analysis, negligible accuracy loss, and up to 8× larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
bullets: Targets serialization cost, repeated schema prefill, and decoding that is unaware of live catalogs and MVCC.
Uses an in-process Rust runtime with Python, Rust, and OpenCypher models ranging from 16.8M to 1.07B parameters.
Introduces epoch-invalidated schema KV caching, catalog/source-span logit masking, and an MVCC gate for read-only queries.
Reports 4.91–13.68× faster warm CPU time-to-first-token, 0.0% hallucination leak, and 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool-planning tasks.
Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation recovers 13.61 MBPP points while operating without VRAM for the distillation verifier.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
bullets: Large-model computation is most valuable at the rollout’s beginning and when video content changes; reversing the model order largely loses the semantic benefit.
BigSmall is a training-free planner–renderer sampler: the 14B model plans the opening and selected transition chunks, while the 1.3B model renders the rest.
An approximate, windowed, lazy cross-model KV cache enables the large planner to leave and re-enter generation efficiently.
On VBench, BigSmall is 3.02× faster than the 14B model with unchanged semantic score and motion; a faster variant reaches 3.77× speedup with a 10% motion trade-off.
On minute-long videos, BigSmall is 3.14× faster and scores 1.78 points higher than the 14B model.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BIGSMALL on a real rollout (“a teddy bear and a frisbee”). Top: a zero-cost change score decides, chunk by chunk, whether the 14B planner is called. The planner generates the plan chunk c0 with all four denoising steps and only the first step t1 of each sketch chunk; the 1.3B renderer takes all other steps (squares: denoising steps t1–t4; orange: 14B, blue: 1.3B). Bottom: each model reads its own KV cache; dashed arrows write a finished chunk into a cache, solid arrows read from it. The renderer’s cache is exact: every chunk is written. The planner’s cache is windowed: a planner call reads only the sink c0 and the previous chunk. It is lazy: that previous chunk is written only when the planner needs it (c1 when c2 is sketched, c4 when c5 is sketched), and other chunks are never written. It is approximate: a chunk is re-encoded sparsely, only its moving tokens, while the others copy K/V from the previous frame with re-rotated RoPE; it is re-encoded densely if the chunk before it was never written, as for c4. Right: inside sketch chunk c5, the planner’s first step from noise already fixes the layout (x̂(1) 0 ); it is re-noised to σ2, keeping 6% of the signal, and the renderer completes the chunk from its own cache.

papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.
authors: Haibin Tong, Liangliang Xin, Yamei Zhu, Jiang Yu
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and throughput bottlenecks in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling.
Uses explicit state bottlenecks and independently trainable one-step transition objectives with distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses.
Introduces a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances states, while an inner recurrent loop adaptively computes each transition with shared weights.
Integrates three-region caching, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and transition-centric evaluation.
Scope is reasoning tasks where the next step depends on a sufficient Markovian state rather than the full history.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Dual-loop Transformer architecture with transition-centric pretraining. With a fixed-size sufficient-state interface and bounded step length, cross-step memory does not grow with the number of completed steps k.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes specialized LLMs for Markovian reasoning using a dual-loop transformer and structural cache compression to decouple memory footprint from reasoning length.
papers.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
papers.tldr: A specialized LLM design treats Markovian reasoning as state transitions, reducing KV-cache growth from sequence-dependent storage to constant-size state transfer.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.

Fig. 2. Direction-aware trajectory propagation. DATP advects instructionconditioned semantic relevance along signed optical flow over multiple future horizons and merges them into a future-critical interaction corridor.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient VLA inference via flow-guided visual token pruning and action caching with KV-cache compression, directly relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
papers.tldr: FlowPAC uses task-aware optical flow to dynamically prune visual tokens and cache actions, achieving faster VLA inference while preserving control performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.
A compiler VLM processes the video once and a decoder generates interpreter LoRA weights plus optional prefix tokens, without seeing questions.
Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter improved over full in-context reading by 1.7 points alone and 4.3 points with a 9B compiler.
Compression reduces up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens and uses 5.5× less memory than the video’s key-value cache.
Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone; their roles differ depending on whether prefix tokens are used.

papers.selection_reason: Compiles video into LoRA weights and prefix tokens for a frozen VLM, combining video understanding, memory efficiency, and inference-time adaptation.
papers.title: Video-as-Weights: Compiling a Video Once into Parametric and Token Memory
papers.tldr: Video-as-Weights compiles a video into LoRA weights and a few prefix tokens, enabling small VLMs to answer questions with far less memory while benefiting from larger models.

papers.abstract: Repeatedly accessing the full key--value (KV) cache is a major bottleneck in long-context language model decoding. We find that small query-specific subsets can accurately approximate full attention, yet their union covers nearly the entire cache, motivating query-adaptive access for the KV cache. A natural approach is to split the KV cache into clusters, using compact representatives for clusters that incur negligible error while expanding the rest to their original KV entries. We derive a selection criterion from an upper bound on attention-output error, which reveals two complementary factors governing the error: importance measures the impact of a cluster, while distortion measures how faithfully the cluster can be represented. Based on this criterion, we propose RefineKV, a decoding-time query-adaptive KV compression method. Experiments on two models and three benchmarks demonstrate that RefineKV retains near-full-attention quality while achieving up to 7.6x speedup in the attention phase and 1.66x faster decoding, establishing a new quality-latency Pareto frontier.
authors: Kewei Lian, Jiayi Zhai, Anji Liu
bullets: Full KV-cache access is a major long-context decoding bottleneck, and query-specific relevant subsets can be much smaller than the full cache.
The method clusters KV entries and represents low-error clusters with compact summaries while expanding higher-error clusters to their original entries.
An attention-output error bound guides selection using two factors: cluster importance and representation distortion.
Across two models and three benchmarks, RefineKV achieves up to 7.6× attention-phase speedup and 1.66× faster decoding while retaining near-full-attention quality.
The approach targets decoding-time KV compression and its reported evaluation covers the stated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Quality-latency trade-off of REFINEKV and existing KV-cache compression baselines. Experiments are evaluated across two models (Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5) on three longcontext benchmarks (LongBench, RULER, and HELMET), with results averaged across all tasks. We present a conservative threshold τ = 0.01, which matches full attention performance across all settings while achieving up to 1.56× decode speedup as measured by Time Per Output Token (TPOT). Our method extends the quality–latency Pareto frontier.

Figure 3: REFINEKV Pipeline. Prefill phase: The KV cache is partitioned into contiguous clusters, and a representative key-value pair together with auxiliary metadata is computed for each cluster. Decode phase: Each query qt uses the cached summaries to calculate risk score RC . Clusters with RC > τ are expanded, while clusters with RC ≤ τ retain only their representatives. The resulting mixed KV sequence is used to compute the output ot. The color depth of each block indicates attention score.

Figure 2: Left: Cluster selection is jointly determined by importance and distortion. Each point represents a cluster positioned by its global importance p̂C and local distortion δboundC . Background color encodes the risk score RC , with the dashed line denoting the decision boundary at RC = τ . The tilted boundary captures their trade-off: important clusters tolerate only small local distortion, whereas low-importance clusters can tolerate larger distortion. Point colors indicate the error incurred on approximating cluster. Three cases show the within-cluster attention-score patterns. Right: Risk score RC strongly correlated with approximation error. These figures illustrate the correlation between Risk Score and cluster approximation error ∥oC − ôC∥2, where oC and ôC denote original output and approximate output for cluster C.

Figure 1: Left: Each query needs only a small KV subset, but together these subsets cover nearly the entire cache. For each query, we select the highest-weight KV entries needed to retain p% of its total attention weight. The figure compares sizes of these per-query subsets and their union across queries, alongside the resulting attention output error. At roughly 10% output error, each query needs only a small subset of the cache, yet their union covers most KV entries. Right: Queryadaptive methods surpass query-independent methods. Oracle query-adaptive top-k attention achieves a markedly better perplexity–access trade-off than representative eviction baselines. Our method recovers a substantial portion of this advantage without oracle access.

papers.selection_reason: Query-adaptive KV cache compression with attention-error bounds, directly fitting KV cache and memory efficiency topic.
papers.title: RefineKV: Query-Adaptive KV Cache Compression via Attention-Error Bounds
papers.tldr: RefineKV accelerates long-context decoding by adaptively accessing only the most important and faithfully representable KV-cache clusters while preserving near-full-attention quality.

papers.abstract: Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
authors: Hyunwook Kang, Junoh Park, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
bullets: Targets failures in existing memory methods, including wrong appearances, identity mixing, and unrequested background retention.
Stores tracked-object KV features, selectively retains background KV using attention scores, and attaches readable scene/appearance records.
Uses an LLM to select requested memories, then integrates their KV into a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator.
Introduces a six-scene evaluation covering selective attribute edits, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition.
More reliably preserves identities and requested past appearances under explicit references and natural-language cues than existing memory methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of our framework. (a) Memory formation keeps the full-box KV of tracked objects and selects sparse background KV by attention. (b) Scene records pair this KV with readable metadata, so a new look never overwrites an earlier one. (c) An LLM selects records from the catalog, and the generator attends to their KV together with the ongoing scene’s KV under the current prompt. Frames and boxes come from our runs, whereas grids and the tracking sketch are schematic.

papers.selection_reason: Object-aware KV memory framework for selective recall in interactive autoregressive video generation; relevant to memory efficiency and autoregressive video models.
papers.title: Choose What Returns: Object-Aware KV Memory for Selective Recall in Interactive Video Generation
papers.tldr: An object-aware KV memory framework enables more precise selective recall of people, appearances, and backgrounds in interactive long-video generation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. Project page: https://minar09.github.io/scenetether/
authors: Matiur Rahman Minar, Seunghun Oh, Ganghyeon Jeong, Unsang Park
bullets: Targets accumulated appearance drift in static scene regions without disrupting evolving materials such as water, smoke, or fire.
Uses a training-free attention-read policy: retains the newest latent’s keys, blends low-activity values with co-located source-image values, and leaves active values unchanged.
Freezes an activity map estimated from early generated latents; adds no denoising evaluations and does not alter cache updates.
Improves source-support PSNR over framewise and spatial Echo baselines, with additional gains from value anchoring alone.
A small blinded study favored SceneTether for preserving natural scene appearance and motion; evaluation covers two seeds and a preselected four-minute subset.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models on commodity CPUs is often constrained not only by computational throughput but also by the resident memory required to execute quantized models within fixed system budgets. We present MemVanta, an experimental C++20 inference runtime for quantized GGUF language models that treats memory residency as a first-class systems objective. MemVanta combines memory-mapped model access, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution paths, paged key-value state, and explicit memory-pressure validation. We evaluate MemVanta against a pinned llama.cpp baseline using the same OpenLLaMA 7B v2 Q4_0 GGUF under CPU-only execution. Across five measured runs following warm-up, MemVanta records a peak resident set size of 3,983,412 KiB compared with 7,586,960 KiB for llama.cpp, corresponding to a 47.50 percent reduction in peak RSS. This memory reduction involves a substantial throughput trade-off: MemVanta achieves 3.15 +/- 0.04 tokens/s for prompt processing and 1.52 +/- 0.02 tokens/s for token generation, compared with 45.82 +/- 0.96 and 7.76 +/- 0.09 tokens/s, respectively, for llama.cpp. In a separate Linux cgroup-v2 experiment with swap disabled, MemVanta completes execution at a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling, while llama.cpp is OOM-killed at that ceiling and first succeeds at the tested 3840 MiB level. These results position MemVanta as a memory-efficiency research prototype rather than a throughput competitor. We analyze the architectural mechanisms underlying this trade-off and discuss reproducibility, correctness, limitations, and opportunities for memory-constrained CPU and edge inference.
authors: Saurav Singla, Aarav Singla, Advik Gupta, Parnika Gupta
bullets: Targets memory-constrained deployment of large language models on commodity CPUs.
Uses memory mapping, bounded tensor caching, quantized execution, paged key-value state, and memory-pressure validation.
In the reported OpenLLaMA 7B Q4_0 comparison, peak RSS is reduced by 47.50% versus llama.cpp.
Runs under a tested 3584 MiB memory ceiling where llama.cpp is OOM-killed, but is much slower for prompt processing and generation.
Presented as a memory-efficiency research prototype, not a throughput competitor.

papers.abstract: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
bullets: Targets activation-cache memory, complementing checkpointing and lossy compression.
Uses custom Triton kernels fused with autograd for GPU-resident compression and exact reconstruction.
Supports BF16 and FP8 activations, with optional sign-bit packing for higher compression.
Reduces per-token VRAM by 31% in Modded-NanoGPT and 30% in Nemotron-H, with up to 1% overhead at practical sequence lengths.
Introduces preallocated buffers to avoid host synchronization for variable-size tensors.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu, Yiqing Hu, Caifeng Shan
bullets: Addresses the linear GPU-memory growth and quadratic computation of Transformer KV caches, while preserving more detail than fixed-size state compression.
Uses a memory encoder-decoder to store selected final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstruct attention KV caches.
Applies sparse attention that retrieves relevant memories once per input and shares the sparse indices across layers.
Reports substantial efficiency gains, including 1313× lower memory-state cache, 6.9× lower prefill latency, and 3.5× higher throughput at 1M context in one adaptation setting.
Generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks with competitive performance against specialized models.

This enables a constant active memory state for continual inference, alongside an Lr× cache compression across both depth and time dimensions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces scalable memory architecture for LLMs with KV-cache reduction and long-context efficiency.
papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MemOnce enables LLMs to retain long-term, fine-grained memories with compact states, reducing memory and computation costs for long-context continual inference.

papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.
authors: Zunhai Su, Keyu Fan, Ruishan Guo, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jingzehua Xu, Bohan Sun, Hansen Feng, Ruihan Hu, Yik-Chung Wu, Ngai Wong
bullets: Streaming geometry transformers face growing KV caches and sensitivity to quantization across cache locations, causing cache–geometry mismatch.
Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization preserves sensitive cross-view evidence.
Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads using quantized history.
Across five benchmarks and two backbones, it achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings and can outperform unquantized inference.
The optimized backend reaches 5.05× physical KV compression, 23.1% lower latency, and up to 5.4× larger batch size under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Layer skipping can reduce large language model inference costs, but a request budget does not specify how to allocate layer execution across generated tokens. We introduce \method{}, which allows tokens to execute different numbers of layers while matching each request's mean executed depth to a continuous budget. At each routed layer, a router reads the current token state and its request's budget and decides whether to execute the Transformer block. Tokens that skip the block pass through a lightweight residual adapter and write no key/value (K/V) entry at that layer. A single checkpoint serves requests with different budgets in the same batch. Across three LLaMA backbones, six quality metrics, and 13 budgets, AVERT is best or tied for best in 206 of 234 comparisons. Across single- and mixed-budget batches, the mean absolute per-request budget error is at most 1.15 percentage points. When grouping requests by budget leaves batches underfilled, mixing budgets reduces decode time per output token (TPOT) by 4.3--21.2%.
authors: Pengjie Zheng, Mengwei Xie, Huan Yang, Si Wu, Pengfei Hu, Feng Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of allocating a request-level layer-execution budget across generated tokens.
A router uses each token’s state and request budget to decide whether to run each Transformer block.
Skipped tokens use a lightweight residual adapter and do not write K/V entries at that layer.
One checkpoint supports different budgets within the same batch.
Across three LLaMA backbones, six metrics, and 13 budgets, it was best or tied in 206/234 comparisons; mixed-budget batching reduced TPOT by 4.3–21.2%.

papers.abstract: Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.
authors: Fabian Isensee, Jakob Wasserthal, Lalith Kumar Shiyam Sundar, Maximilian Rokuss, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Stefan Michael Happold, Klaus H. Maier-Hein
bullets: Standard inference materializes per-class logits on multiple grids, causing extreme memory use for whole-body CT segmentation.
The method streams intermediate features through a one-patch ring instead of storing class logits, while preserving exact outputs.
It applies to models with a pointwise affine classification head and requires no retraining.
A single all-class model matches or slightly exceeds specialist-toolkit quality, runs 5.8–15× faster, and uses 3.2–7.6× less RAM with under 8 GB VRAM.
The approach is provided as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, and MOOSE.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming inference method that removes the memory wall for many-class 3D segmentation, directly relevant to memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
papers.tldr: An exact streaming inference method removes the class-dependent memory bottleneck in many-class 3D segmentation, enabling one unified model to run substantially faster with much lower memory.

papers.abstract: Serving engines treat the ways of running a greedy language model as interchangeable: cached or not, padded or not, alone or batched, one token or several verified at once (speculative decoding). In finite precision they round differently. We measure how often the greedy text of Qwen3-0.6B (bfloat16, 128 new tokens, GSM8K and ARC prompts) differs from a reference that decodes one token per pass. Verifying 4 guessed tokens per pass changes 60% of 150 prompts and padding changes 68%; every first divergence has a top-1 minus top-2 logit gap of 0.375 or less. A split of the noise shows that cache entries written by multi-token passes are about as noisy as the multi-token pass itself. A margin gate (fall back to one token when the gap is below a bound calibrated on separate GSM8K prompts) whose fallback reads that cache does not help: 58 of 100 prompts differ, against 61 of 100 for plain verification. Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes leaves 0 of 100 different but costs 7.2 model passes per token, against 1.0 for the reference. Fixed-width decoding makes drafted and plain decoding identical (0 of 100 prompts differ) at 0.75 passes per token. On shifted MMLU and HellaSwag prompts the rebuild gate leaves 0 of 60 different, plain verification 48 of 60. On 138 further and shifted prompts the bound was exceeded at 0.6% of positions and missed 0 of 309 flips. One GPU, one drafter, small models.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R
bullets: Multi-token verification changed outputs on 60% of prompts, while padding changed 68%; divergences occurred only when the top-1/top-2 logit margin was at most 0.375.
Cache entries written during multi-token passes were a comparable source of noise to the passes themselves.
A margin-based fallback that reused the noisy cache barely helped: 58/100 prompts differed versus 61/100 with plain verification.
Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes eliminated observed differences, but increased cost to 7.2 model passes per token versus 1.0 for the reference.
Fixed-width decoding matched plain decoding on all tested prompts at 0.75 passes per token; scope was limited to one GPU, one drafter, and small models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes rounding noise and cache effects in speculative decoding for LLM inference, directly contributing to efficient inference and cache management.
papers.title: Vega-Fafnir: Is Greedy Decoding the Same Decoding? Where Rounding Noise in Speculative Verification Comes From and What Removing It Costs
papers.tldr: Finite-precision rounding makes supposedly equivalent greedy and speculative decoding produce different text, but fixed-width decoding removes the mismatch more efficiently than rebuilding the cache.

papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.
authors: Omkar Shewale, Deepak Kumar, Divakar Kumar Yadav
bullets: Across eight reward models, three generative judges, and four quantizers, quantization changed 1.1–12.3% of RewardBench pairwise preferences while aggregate accuracy sometimes shifted by only 0.03 points.
Decision flips concentrate in a vulnerability window where full-precision margins are small relative to quantization noise; this window shrinks from 25% to 7% as model size increases.
Under adversarial pressure, some quantizers produced strongly harmful flip patterns, while benign best-of-16 evaluation often kept churn within noise.
Downstream, 14.6–65.7% of best-of-64 selections changed, versus 2.6–9.6% of final answers; benchmark churn tracked this change better than benchmark accuracy.
Margin-based predictors identified flips well (AUC 0.927), but directly measured churn was most useful in-distribution and was matched by plain top-k routing.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes decision instability caused by 4-bit quantization of reward models, relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: The Vulnerability Window: Decision Instability in Quantized Reward Models
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can substantially alter reward-model and LLM-judge decisions despite nearly unchanged benchmark accuracy, especially for small-margin cases and downstream candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Michael Pellauer, Hyoukjun Kwon, Sitao Huang
bullets: Addresses prompt-specific dominant activation directions that fixed, offline-calibrated subspaces may miss.
Extracts dominant components during prefill, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer’s GEMM.
Reuses each prompt’s low-rank basis throughout decoding, avoiding weight modifications.
At comparable mixed-precision bit width, outperforms the referenced state of the art across six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters.
Recovers up to 46% of perplexity lost by 4-bit activations, with 4% prefill and 8% decoding overhead on Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PLoQ at one layer input, on an activation example (6 tokens, 12 channels; color: magnitude). Steps 1–3 and the INT8 GEMM are the offline mixed-precision method: a calibrated basis U , folded into the weights, gathers the directions that are large in every prompt into a block kept at 8 bits. PLoQ (dashed box) handles the remaining 4-bit part Xc, whose dominant direction depends on the prompt. Once per prompt, during prefill, it estimates that direction V from a sample of the prompt’s tokens (4). Each token’s component along it, C = XcV ⊤, is subtracted (5, 6); the remainder R has a smaller range and is quantized to 4 bits with clipping, and C to 4 bits on its own scale (7). C is restored through k extra rows VW⊤ c of the 4-bit GEMM (8). V and VW⊤ c are kept for decoding.

Figure 4. Activation magnitudes |X| over tokens and channels (max-pooled to a 128× 128 grid) for one WikiText-2 prompt on Llama3.2-1B, layer 15. From left to right: the original input; after QuaRot’s Hadamard rotation, all at 4 bits; what a calibrated 8-bit block leaves at 4 bits; and what PLoQ leaves at 4 bits after subtracting the prompt’s own 32 leading directions. The last two share one scale. Each title gives the mean per-token range, which sets the token’s 4-bit step. PLoQ narrows the calibrated block’s range by 12% at the attention input and by 47% at the down-projection input, where a few tokens carry very large values; averaged over all 16 layers, by 10% and 27%.

papers.selection_reason: Prompt-adaptive low-bit quantization of LLM activations and KV cache for memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.tldr: PLoQ improves 4-bit LLM activation quantization by adapting a low-rank protection subspace to each prompt without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.
authors: Kartikeya Bhardwaj, Mohammed Almousa, Chaitanya Mullapudi, Ananth Balasubramanian, Nithin Ramesan, Tuc Nguyen, Harris Teague
bullets: Targets flat quantization loss surfaces and optimization difficulties in 2-bit and sub-2-bit channelwise quantization.
Introduces a continuous relaxation of the quantization-aware training process with dynamically changing bitwidth.
Provides theoretical and empirical insights into why gradual bitwidth changes can improve QAT.
Reports up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision tasks and 7.7% on natural language tasks versus leading QAT methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) An example of our proposed RelaxQAT bitwidth schedule which gradually and smoothly reduces the bitwidth. The gradient of the schedule 0 whenever it is approaches 2-bits; this helps to ease into the 2-bit precision instead of an abrupt change. (b) Prior progressive quantization methods reduce the bitwidth suddenly during training like UPQ, or (c) keep it the same throughout.

Figure 7. (a) ParetoQ SEQ simulation for a 1-d optimization problem. QAT gets stuck near the minimum point around step 2000 and stays there until the end of training (10000 steps). (b) RelaxQAT (with just a half cycle bit schedule) converges within the first 2000 steps.

Figure 6. (a-d) Clip-then-Round operation in the existing SEQ (Eq. (2)) creates integers at the extremes (see vertical red dotted lines) since the round operation follows the clip. As the bitwidth reduces, the extreme integers are suddenly lost (e.g., from {−15, 15} to {−13, 13} and so on). This means that a training assumes that the previous range of integers (say {−15, 15}) was available until k = 2b−1 reduces sufficiently; once k is sufficiently small, the round abruptly moves on to the new range of integers (i.e., {−13, 13}). The sudden change in integer ranges can cause loss spikes (similar to UPQ (Lee et al., 2025)) and unstable training behavior. (e-h) RelaxSEQ employs the Round-then-Clip operation (Eq. (3)) which keeps the extremes in floating point as the k reduces. The range of the distribution changes slowly and the extremes stay floating point until the end of the schedule. This causes the loss to change smoothly as the bitwidth shrinks.

Figure 3. (a) A simple 1-d function to minimize. (b) The 1-d function above results in a highly complex 2-d, 2-bit quantization loss surface (generated using LSQ) where the width of the hyperplanes (defined as the flat regions between integer changes) increases with larger scales. Red line shows the QAT trajectory.
Figure 4. RelaxQAT converges significantly faster than ParetoQ.

Figure 2. ParetoQ SEQ with a bitwidth schedule loses extreme integers as k = 2bt−1 decreases with a shrinking bitwidth. RelaxSEQ shows a smooth change in extreme values which results in a smoothly changing loss.

Figure 5. Existing SEQ (Clip-then-Round) with a bitwidth schedule shows an unstable training behavior with sudden loss spikes as predicted by Fig. 2. The new RelaxSEQ with Round-the-Clip has a smooth transition in loss with changing bitwidth. Although, the final loss after the end of schedule was similar for both Clip-thenRound vs. Round-then-Clip, we found that RelaxSEQ resulted in better benchmark scores (see Table 10).

papers.selection_reason: Continuous relaxation of quantization-aware training reduces model memory footprint, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
papers.tldr: RelaxQAT improves difficult low-bit quantization-aware training by gradually changing bitwidth during training instead of fixing or abruptly switching it.

papers.abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
bullets: Agent execution histories grow over time, driving shared GPU KV-cache demand and limiting throughput.
Tool-operation provenance identifies earlier outputs and turns superseded by later operations; 64% of final-history tokens are removal candidates.
Contexture separates the complete harness history from the model’s execution context and evicts context based on supersession, cache residency, and GPU pressure.
Across two models, harnesses, and benchmarks, it improves SLO-constrained throughput by 20–73% versus the strongest baseline and reduces GPU energy per session by up to 11%.
Live-agent accuracy improves by 1.4 percentage points on average versus unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points.

papers.selection_reason: A runtime context eviction framework for high-throughput LLM agent serving that uses tool-execution information to manage KV cache and improve memory efficiency.
papers.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
papers.tldr: Contexture improves high-throughput LLM-agent serving by evicting superseded conversation context at runtime while coordinating with shared KV-cache state.

papers.abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.
authors: Vinnam Kim, Seong Hoon Seo, Junhan Kim, Jaeseong You, An Chen
bullets: Addresses the gap between sub-4-bit memory savings and decoding speed on mobile NPUs, where unsupported formats may require costly conversion.
Executes 3-bit and symmetric 2-bit weights directly with native integer operations, avoiding wider weight expansion during decoding.
Assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-grained mixed precision without disrupting execution.
On a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 Hexagon NPU across Qwen3 models, it matches or exceeds llama.cpp sub-4-bit accuracy at equal bits per weight.
Reports 1.16–1.41× faster decoding and 1.5–4.3× higher tokens per joule than the llama.cpp Hexagon backend.
