papers.selection_reason: Sub-4-bit mixed-precision quantization and output-channel grouping for memory-efficient LLM inference on mobile NPUs.
papers.title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
papers.tldr: MixFold enables efficient sub-4-bit LLM inference on mobile NPUs by combining native 2-/3-bit execution with tile-aligned output-channel mixed precision.

papers.abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.
authors: Soheil Zibakhsh, Pedram Aghazadeh, Farinaz Koushanfar
bullets: Local LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, leaving compute capacity unused for safety checks.
ToRA runs a guard model as an extra decode row, sharing generator weights and KV cache through dual-row kernels.
On Qwen3-0.6B, it matches or outperforms a dedicated streaming guard, achieving higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks.
It detects 11.8 percentage points more unsafe responses than a cheap hidden-state probe at similar cost.
Scope: results are reported for Qwen3-0.6B and 17 benchmarks.

papers.title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
papers.tldr: ToRA adds a second safety-checking model to each local LLM decode step with under 4% per-token overhead by sharing weight and KV-cache reads.

papers.abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
authors: Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon
bullets: Addresses the costly need to re-embed an entire corpus when changing embedding models, without query logs.
Selects informative anchors using Cosine Farthest Point Sampling from the existing target index.
Trains a lightweight adapter with Manifold Alignment Loss and orthogonal regularization to align representations without collapse.
Uses a deterministic router to escalate rare, difficult queries that most affect retrieval quality.
Across five BEIR datasets, achieves up to 35% relative nDCG@10 improvement on Arguana and reduces latency from roughly 160 ms to 38–86 ms at a 20% nominal escalation budget.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval using lightweight adapters and routing, addressing test-time adaptation and memory efficiency in retrieval systems.
papers.title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
papers.tldr: ERA enables cold-start retrieval with a new encoder by adapting embeddings from a small informative anchor set and routing only difficult queries for re-encoding.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of re-encoding long video histories when escalating from a continuously running small VLM to a large VLM.
Distills a label-free, per-layer linear map from the large model’s answers, using only the current frame to transform the small model’s KV cache.
The useful transfer is concentrated in one direction across the middle third of the large model’s layers; faithfully reproducing the large model’s cache does not improve performance.
On RoboMME, Baton outperforms the small model alone, pruned or shortened re-watching, and text memory, while matching re-watching with 28–47% less compute.
The approach transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA and scales with the large model’s capability across eight model pairs from four families.

papers.selection_reason: Hands off visual KV memory between VLMs for embodied agents; fits KV-cache efficiency and embodied memory.
papers.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
papers.tldr: Baton lets a large VLM reuse a small VLM’s visual KV memory during escalation, preserving re-watching quality while substantially reducing compute.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.
authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu, Song Han, Qinghao Hu
bullets: Targets heterogeneous cache demands in hybrid models under long contexts and concurrent requests.
Uses a transparent cache pool to redistribute GPU pages without changing cache layouts or backend interfaces.
Streams global-attention prefixes layer by layer during bounded-state computation while keeping generated KV resident.
A scheduler selects resident versus streamed execution and adjusts capacity based on request size and queue state.
Across seven configurations on GB300 and GH200, it achieves up to 2.04× more agent turns, 20–59% lower P50 per-token latency, and 1.40–3.05× better agent P50 TTFT than SGLang with HiCache.

papers.selection_reason: Hybrid LLM serving cache management and layer-wise streaming, directly targeting KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.tldr: TideCache improves hybrid LLM serving by dynamically sharing and streaming cache memory between GPU and host memory, increasing throughput and reducing latency.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
authors: Ryan Lucas, Petros Prastakos, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Temporal KV-cache reuse creates memory bottlenecks, while distant-token quantization suffers from large ranges and errors.
TRQ rotates temporally adjacent cache vectors to flatten per-channel means before quantization.
It uses gradient-free, online-fitted trees of 2-bit planar rotations followed by a shared Hadamard transform.
A greedy fitting procedure is proven globally optimal for the mean-flattening objective, with efficient fused Triton inference kernels.
At matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG on LongCat-Video-13B and HY-WorldPlay-8B, while also improving other metrics.

Figure 4. Figure 1 shown for an additional 10 channels. There exist differences across channels, but within a channel adjacent frames tend to have similar values.

Figure 1. Structure of video-diffusion KV cache. Each panel overlays key and value magnitudes (|K| and |V |) on the corresponding video frame. We observe that (i) Within a video, nearby frames share persistent spatial patterns and (ii) the final two panels show that these patterns differ across videos, even at the same frame index and channel. Together, these observations motivate fitting rotations online to each video’s cache and sharing them within local temporal blocks. For other channels, see Section 7 of the appendix.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ) to improve KV-cache efficiency in Video Diffusion Transformers, directly addressing a bottleneck in long video generation and improving subject consistency.
papers.title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: TRQ enables accurate 2-bit KV-cache quantization for long video diffusion by learning lightweight, video-specific temporal rotations online.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
bullets: Targets the mismatch between short-text quantization calibration and 100K+-token, tool-using agent sessions.
Uses trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on tokens generated by the BF16 model during agent sessions.
At 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight, matches BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA.
The 2.0-bit checkpoint performs worse than the higher-bit versions.
Releases Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF and a supporting llama.cpp fork for inference.

The model-token step also adds the two-standard-error margin, so it does not isolate masking alone. Dashed: GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS.

papers.selection_reason: Sub-3-bit quantization of a Qwen LLM for long-horizon agentic tasks, directly relevant to efficient AI and LLM foundation models.
papers.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
papers.tldr: NariQ enables 2.5–3.0-bit quantization of Qwen3.8-27B while preserving BF16-level performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
authors: Alper Kalle, Theo Rudkiewicz, Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli, Mohamed Tamaazousti
bullets: Targets post-training low-rank compression that preserves input-output behavior, not just layer weights.
Linearizes the network and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce compression to a closed-form weighted SVD.
Estimates the otherwise intractable output-side factor unbiasedly with random probes, requiring K backward passes per sequence.
On WikiText-2 calibration, it reports the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity across matched uniform-rank settings and at ratio 0.7 with LEMS allocation.
KL-SVD usually improves calibration perplexity and downstream accuracy but increases cross-corpus perplexity; Complete-SVD improves IFEval accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
papers.selection_reason: Output-aware low-rank SVD compression for LLMs; reduces model memory while preserving logit behavior.
papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.tldr: Complete-SVD compresses LLMs by minimizing equal-weighted changes to the model’s output logits, achieving strong perplexity and instruction-following performance in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.
bullets: Targets hybrid models whose recurrent states can only be reused from exact saved positions.
Predicts checkpoint frontiers such as chat turn ends and search branch points, avoiding mid-prompt prefill cuts.
Logs recurrent-layer inputs and uses a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to construct checkpoints 6–37× cheaper per token than full recomputation.
A frontier-aware policy prioritizes active and proven branches while reallocating unused checkpoint capacity to attention KV caching.
Across architectures and workloads, it reduces median TTFT by 16–89%, increases SLO capacity by up to 1.73×, and improves goodput by up to 4.26× while preserving exact accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 5: FrontierReplay architecture. The host scheduler maintains a prefix index over 16-token pages and manages checkpoint placement, retention, and dead-slot reclaim. 1⃝ The index returns the deepest checkpoint c on the cached prefix. 2⃝ The worker copies it into the request’s state slot. 3⃝ The uncut prefill over [c,n) writes KV pages and stages recurrent-layer inputs for [c, t) in a temporary log. 4⃝ State-only replay starts from the saved state at c and writes the checkpoint at t into a free slot. 5⃝ The scheduler publishes the checkpoint after the GPU event completes. Solid arrows show data and execution flow. Dashed arrows show control flow, including the reassignment of dead checkpoint slots to the KV pool.

papers.selection_reason: Exact prefix caching for hybrid LLMs; directly improves inference memory efficiency and cache reuse.
papers.title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: FrontierReplay enables efficient exact prefix caching for hybrid language models by creating checkpoints at predictable structural boundaries without interrupting prefill.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
authors: Filippo Galgani, Ziwei Ji, Omri Homburger, Ganesh Jawahar, Michelle Ramanovich, Ivan Korotkov, Luciano Martins, Utku Evci, Edouard Yvinec, Pooja Consul, Vivek Kumar, Tal Schuster
bullets: Addresses the need for lightweight, accurate draft generation in speculative decoding.
Uses a shared drafting head with target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
Evaluated with the Gemma 4 family, achieving reported speedups of up to 3.1× on server-side setups and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU.
Introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that require up to 1.83× fewer target-model forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
Scope: results are reported for Gemma 4 models and the specified hardware environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Architecture of the optimized Multi-Token Prediction (G-MTP) module. The input to the drafter is constructed by concatenating the token embedding (𝑒(𝑥)) with the backbone hidden state (ℎ(𝐿)), both of dimension 𝑑target, and reducing to the drafter dimension 𝑑draft. The draft tokens are then propagated through the MTP layers, utilizing cross-attention against the backbone’s frozen KV Cache to bypass prefill computations before recursively triggering the next forward step. For subsequent drafting steps, the drafter’s output state is up-projected (𝑊up), concatenated with the embedding of the sampled draft token, and down-projected (𝑊down) to form the next input (Equation 3).

Figure 2 | The autoregressive G-MTP drafter (blue blocks) is initialized with activations from the main model (gray blocks) and cross-attends to its KV cache. Across successive drafting steps, the positional encoding (𝑝1) remains constant, as the drafter repeatedly queries a static, pre-computed KV snapshot.

Figure 3 | Empirical scaling of theoretical Block Efficiency (BE) and speculative wall-clock throughput across varying lookahead horizons (𝛾). While longer draft sequences monotonically increase token acceptance, throughput degrades for some models (e.g., 26B MoE) as drafting and verification costs exceed generation gains.

Table 6 | Batch size scaling performance: Gemma 4 26B MoE (𝛾 = 4, measured on 2×H100)

papers.selection_reason: Optimized multi-token prediction drafting accelerates LLM inference and reduces KV-cache memory overhead.
papers.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: G-MTP is an optimized multi-token drafter that accelerates speculative LLM decoding across server and mobile hardware while remaining efficient and adaptable under domain shift.

papers.abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.
authors: Haowen Hua, Sen Lin, Yaokun Huang, Zeyi Shao, Hao Zhang, Wei Sui, John See, Zeyd Boukhers, Cong Yang
bullets: Targets accurate W4A4/W5A5 recovery when only synthetic calibration data is available.
Functional Grid Calibration selects activation scales and integer offsets using full-precision responses from the student’s current block input.
Progressive inversion refines the same synthetic images through increasingly deep DeiT/ViT teacher prefixes.
With 1,000 images, the pipeline surpasses reported MimiQ accuracy across all 18 settings and nine backbones.
With 256 images, it achieves 68.20% top-1 on DeiT-S and 66.90% on ViT-S at W4A4; gains also persist on ImageNetV2.

papers.selection_reason: Data-free low-bit quantization for vision transformers; memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Calibrate in Context: Efficient Data-Free Quantization from Small Synthetic Pools
papers.tldr: Calibrate in the student’s block context and progressively refine synthetic images to achieve accurate data-free low-bit quantization from very small image pools.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu
bullets: Addresses privacy risks in remote LLM inference, where sensitive user queries are exposed to the service provider.
Hides the real query among dummy queries and randomly shuffles the set before server-side inference.
Uses shared-prefix transformer KV-cache reuse to reduce the efficiency cost of processing augmented queries.
Evaluated on classification, generation, and QIA, EIA, and GPT-based privacy attacks.
Reports strong inference-time privacy, near-plaintext utility, and improved inference efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference method that reuses shared-prefix KV caches to improve efficiency while maintaining privacy.
papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.tldr: DP-SPD protects LLM queries by mixing them with client-generated dummy queries, shuffling them, and reusing shared-prefix KV caches to preserve utility and efficiency.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
authors: Yichen Guo, Yanlong Chen, Xinyue Zhang, Mohan Liu, Song Zhang, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets W4A4KV4 deployment of world action models on onboard robot computers.

Adds gaze-guided refinement, giving action-relevant tokens a second 4-bit quantization pass in the denoising loop and cache.

papers.abstract: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $\beta_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-\beta_1)\|G_t\|_F + \gamma\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $\Theta(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}\eta_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.
bullets: The buffer bound depends on gradient norms and decay, not matrix dimensions or approximation rank.
The proof applies to metric projections onto closed cones, covering top-$k$ selection and truncated SVD without singular-value separation assumptions.
In standard two-stage analyses, a dimension-dependent factor of order $p^2/r^2$ improves to order $1$.
Rate transfer incurs a leakage term controlled by the step-weighted gradient mass, producing an additive $O(log^2 T)$ floor rather than a slower rate.
On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$, feedback decay reduces validation $F_1$ by under $0.008.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Targets redundant, low-utility tokens in long reasoning traces, which can nevertheless receive high attention scores.
Uses uncertainty-guided pruning: retains more cache during uncertain phases and prunes more aggressively when confidence is high.
Uses redundancy-aware selection to favor informative and diverse tokens over content similar to recent reasoning.
Co-designs the method with vLLM through fused CUDA decode kernels while preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
Across three benchmarks and two reasoning models, improves accuracy under constrained cache budgets; for one 8B model, reports up to 1.43× speedup and 45% higher throughput versus Full-KV.

papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.
authors: Anish Khazane, Alex Saad-Falcon, Guanchu Wu, Marcio Porto, Jasper Shan, Fei Yu, Eugene Shulga, Intaik Park, Yongzhe Zhang, Xiaoyu Deng, Sheng Luo, Xiaoya Wang

papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context LLM inference.
Propagates token importance across attention-induced transition graphs beyond recency or immediate attention.
Evaluated on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning across multiple LLM families.
Maintains competitive task performance under moderate to aggressive compression, including up to 90%, with low end-to-end overhead.
Scope: performance is demonstrated across the reported tasks and model families, with a favorable accuracy–memory trade-off rather than universal superiority.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free KV cache eviction method based on global importance estimation, directly targeting memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: PRKV uses Personalized PageRank to estimate globally important tokens for training-free KV-cache eviction, enabling substantial memory savings while preserving long-context performance.

papers.abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan, Bob Kamma, Michael Ge, John Xin Zhou, Andrea Olgiati
bullets: Addresses stale fixed dispatch rates caused by changing fleet capacity and unpredictable output lengths.
Uses fail-fast capacity checks, durable priority queues, and a stateful controller that probes upward and backs off based only on refusals.
Production A/B testing served a classifier with 43% fewer H100s, though lower-priority work waited longer during backfill peaks.
In replay, it achieved within 1% of tuned fixed-rate goodput with about one-quarter the refusal share.
Deployed at Meta for post and live-video understanding, processing over 300 million requests and hundreds of terabytes of media daily.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The traffic shaper implements CAP-AND-TRACK. (a) One enqueue interface feeds online and batch queues. TRACK runs in the online workers and dispatches each queue through the gateway at its learned rate. A refusal from any of the four kinds of CAP (model-server cap, provider admission, per-caller quota, or engine queue-depth aware router) returns as HTTP 429. Other failures stay outside the feedback loop. (b) Each worker paces each queue at the rate the leader pushes. A 429 returns the request to the front of its ready queue with media staged. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a system for optimizing LLM inference request dispatch and capacity management, addressing memory and latency efficiency in serving.
papers.title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
papers.tldr: Cap-and-Track adaptively dispatches LLM inference requests to shifting capacity using refusal signals, reducing required GPUs while maintaining near-fixed-rate goodput.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
authors: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
bullets: Problem: Standard early exit leaves past-token key-value caches incomplete, while full recurrence increases sequential decoding latency.
Method: New tokens enter directly into the final K recurrent steps; Wake verification checks projected states using a logit-margin tolerance τ within a static CUDA graph.
Modes: τ=0 provides greedy-exact decoding, τ>0 enables margin-gated verification, and τ=∞ gives non-rollback lossy late entry.
Results: On Ouro-2.6B, K=2 achieved 5.2× exact and 6.8× lossy speedups; scaling recurrence on Huginn-3.5B reached up to 8.4× exact and 12.5× lossy speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for looped LLMs that reduces latency and cache-related overhead; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Late entry accelerates looped language-model decoding by letting new tokens skip early recurrent passes while preserving configurable exactness or accepting controlled approximation.

papers.abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.
authors: Oana Balmau, Saurav Banka, Jiaxuan Chen, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Ramya Narasimha Prabhu, Rafael Pires, Mathis Randl, Martijn de Vos
bullets: MoE expert parallelism creates 8–13% prefill-time bubbles because GPUs receive uneven token loads.
BubbleTea predicts each GPU’s bubble at every layer and schedules short fine-tuning chunks during that idle time.
Compiler passes automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM without requiring model-specific training-engine ports.
Across three MoE models on four A100 GPUs, BubbleTea achieves 1.9–6.2× higher fine-tuning throughput than LLMStation.
It keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads and performs strongly on bursty production traces.

papers.abstract: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.
authors: Lei Yang, Dayan Wu, Yiliang Zhu, Xinze Liu, Hengjie Zhu, Zihao Zhang, Ding Wang, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin
bullets: Active visual reasoning accumulates crop and reasoning tokens, causing KV-cache growth and higher memory and inference costs.
Existing compression criteria may discard earlier views that remain useful for future exploration, especially when crops replace only local evidence.
CanopyKV uses parent–child crop relationships and tool metadata to retain complementary history, stabilize retained tokens, and protect ongoing reasoning state.
It avoids additional attention-based scoring and reduces subsequent attention costs through compact KV storage.

Across four evaluated benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the compared KV-compression methods; on MME-Lite, it retains about one-quarter of Dense’s KV, improves accuracy by 10.5 percentage points, and speeds reasoning by 1.64×.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.
authors: Zizhuo Fu, Haochen Huang, Shengxuan Qiu, Linye Wei, Ziyu Tang, Runsheng Wang, Meng Li
bullets: Existing wave-style methods waste computation by drafting at fixed loops and following stale predictions.
They can also amplify memory traffic by loading KV caches from multiple loops per decoding step.
LoopCache uses confidence-guided draft updates across intermediate loops to improve speculative trajectories.
A cyclic loop KV-cache strategy limits each step to one loop’s KV traffic while enabling lossless verification; selective shallow-layer caches further improve acceptance.
It reports average speedups of 10.25× over WFD and 14.56× over LoopSpec.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.
authors: Pengyu Li, Zhitao Gao, Lingling Zhang, Heng Wang, Chengqian Ma, WenHao Wang, Wenxuan Huang, Chen Zheng, Jun Liu
bullets: Long-video dependence is concentrated early in the response, so continued video access is often unnecessary.
The method first creates question-focused, timestamped notes before withdrawing the video from inference.
On Qwen3.6-27B, notes preserve accuracy better than unrestricted reasoning at the same withdrawal point; substituted notes hurt, while retaining the video adds no significant benefit.
Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy at 0.12–0.13× the modeled decode cost.
With fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model withdraws after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.

papers.title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang, Hongxia Wang
bullets: Separates content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights for context billing.
Context ablations find relevance dominates position; distance-decay weighting does not beat a relevance-only baseline.
Serving measurements show cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute costs by over 100× at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends limit discounts.
Calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31–42%, but revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs produce similar reductions and increase median charges.
The work offers bounded per-token accounting and deployment constraints, not a validated utility estimator.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Zhang, Bing Hu, Guangmin Song, Chenyi Zhang, Li Wang
bullets: Problem: KV-cache pruning lets growing reasoning tokens evict image tokens, causing larger accuracy losses in later conversational turns.
Method: Keep all visual entries in CPU memory and dynamically swap query-relevant visual entries into slots occupied by low-scoring text entries.
Training-free and compatible with existing retention policies, including DBTrimKV.
Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV improves DBTrimKV by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points when DBTrimKV has twice the memory.
It outperforms a fixed visual reserve in conversational settings without reducing standalone-question accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.
authors: Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman, Ammar Mohanna
bullets: Early-step-weighted cross-step training improves acceptance by 15–24% over uniformly weighted detached training, while proxy cross-entropy does not reliably predict acceptance.
Under a fixed 256-node budget, confidence-guided candidate allocation raises speedup from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval and from 1.31× to 1.75× on MT-Bench.
Allocation gains also transfer to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify them.
Host-thread settings can nearly remove speedups without changing acceptance, highlighting the need for controlled end-to-end latency evaluation.
The study uses a lightweight feature-prediction drafter, a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target, and greedy decoding.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes FACT for speculative decoding, optimizing draft token allocation and training to reduce latency in language model generation.
papers.title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FACT shows that speculative decoding speed depends jointly on drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions—not acceptance alone.

papers.abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.
authors: Abdul Qadir Ibrahim, Martin Burger, Abel Maviano Jonathan
bullets: Calibrated rules bound the probability of exceeding the error budget under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, abstaining when calibration is infeasible.
Mode selection reduces active Fourier support but not measurable latency because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate runtime.
Channel narrowing reduces Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection requires the dense prediction first.
An input-only width selector runs at 0.52–0.95× dense latency, yet often misses its 90% coverage target and is generally slower or less covered than matched static widths.
Adaptive methods should be evaluated by coverage and complete runtime against calibrated static baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces adaptive computation in neural operators using conformal calibration to select Fourier modes and channel widths, addressing inference efficiency.
papers.title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
papers.tldr: Conformal calibration can enforce error-budget coverage for adaptive neural-operator computation, but adaptive selection often fails to reduce end-to-end latency or outperform calibrated static widths.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the time-consuming, model-specific redesign of post-training quantization recipes.
The agent iteratively builds and evaluates candidate recipes using output KL divergence on hidden reasoning traces, with long-generation checks for failures.
A compatible library of public PTQ methods speeds recipe construction across model architectures.
Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.
For GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy; checkpoints run on existing serving kernels without inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 4. System architecture of QDA. QDA has three components: the composable library (§ 5.1), the isolated evaluator (§ 5.2) and the harness (§ 5.3), which runs the agent in a sandbox and schedules its GPU jobs. From the sandbox, the agent can reach the rest of the system only through four commands: (1) qda builds a recipe in the library and returns its checkpoint, (2) kl sends a checkpoint to the evaluator and returns its KL, (3) qsched submits other jobs, such as long-generation checks, to the scheduler, and (4) handin submits the final checkpoints, which are evaluated on the test benchmarks after the search.

papers.selection_reason: Fits efficient AI via memory-reducing quantization and language foundation models via LLM serving.
papers.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
papers.tldr: QDA uses an LLM agent and fast evaluation to automatically design effective, deployable quantization recipes for each model and precision.

papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
bullets: Separate per-layer n-gram tables are memory-intensive, while naïve sharing limits layer-specific preferences.
Chorus lets each layer adapt shared embeddings using a layer-specific projection and hidden-state-conditioned rescaling.
With 1.2B table parameters, Chorus outperforms FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram using 9.6B parameters.
It outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram across the compared table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters.
Combined with Ember, Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory by 99.2% versus AdamW without degrading training performance.

papers.selection_reason: Shared n-gram embeddings with layer-wise adaptation improve LLM capacity while substantially reducing memory use.
papers.title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
papers.tldr: Chorus shares n-gram embedding tables across all layers while allowing layer-specific adaptation, achieving comparable or better quality with substantially lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).
authors: Zhen Gao, Xiao Yin, Kexin Liang, Pedro Reviriego, Shanshan Liu, Fabrizio Lombardi
bullets: Binary Transformers are evaluated for dependability under approximate-memory errors using BERT as a case study.
Significant accuracy degradation occurs primarily at high bit-error rates, such as 5%–10%.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces memory and power requirements for binary Transformers using approximate memory with selective protection, relevant to efficient model memory.
papers.title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.
authors: Shing Wai Pun, Kai Wu, Pengfei Xia, Hui Zang, Wei Guo, Yong Liu
bullets: Targets GR inference with long prompts, wide beam search, and short fixed outputs.
Uses Tree Attention to share prompt-prefix computation and avoid redundant KV-cache accesses across beams.
Reduces overhead with pre-generated masks, static KV allocation, loop-unrolled dispatch, graph compilation, operator fusion, and constrained decoding.
Achieves latency comparable to a state-of-the-art custom-kernel solution.
Shows that end-to-end pipeline optimization can precede custom-kernel development.
