papers.abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank
bullets: Represents each quality-resource frontier using effective active channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=s^2/\kappa$, versus remaining log-error depth.
Separates intrinsic frontier shape from the scale and origin of each resource axis, with bounds from complete monotonicity and divisibility.
For $N$ active resources, recommends operating where $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$ in delivered units.
Derives minimax prices $\lambda_i^\star=\alpha_i/(N+1)$ and worst-case regret $\ln(N+1)$ nats.
Evaluates the theory on 117 published frontiers and provides the open-source nn-rank package for pricing and ranking candidates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The paper in one picture, and where each part is proved. The object is a Laplace transform of a task’s difficulty law evaluated at what the resource buys; the theory is the plane curve it traces; the two structural hypotheses are two differential inequalities on that curve, and the two walls that bound every frontier are those inequalities integrated from the floor. Everything in the dashed box is a consequence of the figure above it.

Figure 8: The rules actually in use, scored against the derived price on the same frontiers. (a) Regret of each selection rule, one point per frontier, bars at the median; the dashed line is the 0.05-nat band inside which the recommendation does not change. The canonical rule lies inside the band on almost every frontier, while the comparison quantifies the cost of alternative choices. (b) The bits gained against the extra resource spent past the canonical point: the median frontier buys 0.99 bits at 44× the cost, which is the price of not knowing where to operate. (c) The floor read from three models against the floor from a full fit. Detail in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

Figure 2: The theory as one curve. (a) The primitive is Neff against the depth still available, with Neff(0) = 0 at the floor. The axiom bounds its growth by ˙Neff ≤ Neff +1 and the hypothesis by ˙Neff ≤ 1; integrated from the same initial condition those two inequalities are the two charts, so the tangency at the origin is a property of one initial-value problem. The shaded wedge is the whole divisibility question, and the dotted rays represent the admissible constant-slope chart family. (b) The working statistic c3 ≥ 0 is ˙Neff ≤ 2: it cannot see the band between the two slopes, which D̂1 ≥ 0 closes at no extra measurement cost. (c) In the gaugefree coordinates of Proposition 6 the single-channel regret is − ln sinφ identically, the rule is the right angle, and the axiom states that φ is 1-Lipschitz with respect to arc length—whence L ≥ π over the complete sweep. (d) What the stronger rung is worth on clean charts at matched level; on this corpus both statistics stay at their nominal level.

Figure 3: The theory is one plane curve. (a) Channels remaining against depth remaining. The axiom confines every completely monotone frontier below e∆S −1 and the hypothesis below that curve’s own tangent at the origin, ∆S; the two bounding solutions are charts, the two-atom chart and the cure chart, and each is the unique frontier saturating its wall (Proposition 1(iii)). Every constant-σ chart is a ray whose slope is |σ| and whose intercept is the floor, so the admissible charts form a pencil (Corollary 4). The operating point is the height Neff = 1/t; where it meets a wall is the recommended depth, one bit on the axiom’s extremal against one nat on the hypothesis’s. (b) The gap between the walls closes quadratically at the origin, and the origin is the floor: a second-order test is powerless at the deep end by theorem, not by accident of this corpus. (c) The admissible arc is a functional of the same curve, so the walls bound it from below; with the covering law the right-hand axis reads the number of operating points a benchmark needs, and the hypothesis bound passes the axiom’s limiting value π at λ = π2/4. (d) The archive’s 117 frontiers, read with three accuracies per point and no bandwidth. The curve is noise-dominated: the median straightness is R2 = 0.22 and against a design-matched null no statistic read from it has power (Section 10).

Figure 4: (a) The regret law (30): the fraction of a complete frontier within ϱ nats of the canonical point, with the 0.900√ ϱ form, and (inset) the 35 panel cells’ observed inband fractions against the prediction conditional on each cell’s own arc. (b) The mean regret (32) of an operating point placed uniformly in arc length: exactly one bit for a single reducible channel, rising to γ+ ln 2 and never beyond. This is the cost of not knowing where to operate, and it is bounded. (c) The microfoundation comparison: measured pairwise co-failure rates for the three mechanisms on the per-item panel of the technical report in the archive, § “What the item level says”.

Figure 6: The floor is not a parameter. (a) A two-atom fit to a frontier whose floor is exactly zero returns a floor that is a large fraction of the best observed error, monotone in the shape index, and the curve sweeps the whole of (0, 1) as the index does; the archive’s own median fitted share, 0.96 of the best observed error, is what a floorless frontier with β = 0.10 produces. (b) The shape index from three independent routes—a direct floorless fit, the bandwidth-free three-point chord arc, and the collapse coordinate ζ—on the frontiers where each is defined. (c) The arc predicted from β against the measured chord arc; the increasing-hazard frontiers, which have no arc at all, are the three distribution-shift evaluations. Statements, proofs and scripts in the Appendix, § “Proofs: The floor”.

The three-parameter law plateaus well above the measurement noise (shaded); the whole completely monotone class, fitted nonparametrically, plateaus with it; the one shape parameter β of the stretched-exponential form removes most of the gap. (b) Agreement on the 2 025 pooled interior leave-one-out predictions. (c) The fitted β, with one point per frontier and a bar at the corpus median: corpus-specific and, on these windows, weakly identified. Details are provided in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

Figure 5: (a) The complete sweep of a single-channel frontier is the same arc of Fisher–Rao length π, from the pure power law at φ = π to the floor at φ = 0; a frontier with a floor reaches only 2 arccos √ ε∞ of it at or below chance level. The shaded segment is the 0.05-nat band, the open circles are the five checkpoints of Theorem 15, and the inner curves are the 12 of the 18 archived ImageNet single-resource windows that have a measurable chord arc, median 0.39π, drawn on the same absolute scale and centered on the right angle so that their lengths can be compared—the chord returns a length and not a position, and the positions the jet does return sit deep, at a median Neff = 0.465 and hence φ = 1.20 < π/2. (b) Regret from the reference is minus the log sine of arc position, (29); the shaded cells are the five checkpoints’ covering neighborhoods. (c) Checkpoints the arc needs against Pareto points measured, one point per frontier; crosses are the six frontiers whose log-convexity defect is non-positive, on which the chord returns no arc and the law fails.

Table 3: Held-out prediction, scored per frontier. Interior is leave-one-out on each interior measurement; forward trains on the least expensive two-thirds and predicts the most expensive third; backward trains on the most expensive two-thirds and predicts the least expensive third. The error is | ln εpred − ln εobs|, summarized per frontier and then across frontiers, with intervals bootstrapped over the 117 frontiers—never over the 2 025 dependent prediction events. The lower panel is the paired comparison on the same frontiers. The law is better than the floorless power law on a majority of frontiers in all three regimes; it loses the interior to a model-free interpolator and wins the backward extrapolation against every baseline. Script 169, from script 68’s per-frontier output.

Table 5: Where each reported number comes from. The archive’s scripts are numbered and run in order; each writes a CSV under results/, so every figure below can be checked without typesetting a table. Three of the 163 scripts reach the network and none is needed to reproduce a number in this paper.

Table 1: What refutes the divisibility hypothesis, what it costs, and where it can be read. “Order” is the lowest derivative of S the test involves. In the derivatives of S alone the axiom and the hypothesis coincide at every order ≤ 2, so without a floor the discriminating content begins at order three; the order-2 rows buy their discrimination with a floor instead, which is the second of the two currencies named below.

Table 4: Selection rules on the 26 attainable single-resource frontiers of the archive, scored against the derived price. Regret is in nats; the tolerance is 0.05 nats inside which the recommendation does not change. Each rule is implemented directly on a discrete measured frontier. This explains why the knee row is not zero even though the knee and the canonical point coincide on the chart. The ratio of accuracy to log10 cost is the “efficiency score” of Prucs et al. (2025), whose limitations are discussed by Dehghani et al. (2022); the knee is Das (1999); Satopää et al. (2011); the budget is the rule of Sun et al. (2026) at the geometric midpoint of each frontier’s own range. The fixed-exponent row is the soft objective of Tan et al. (2019), ACC · (LAT/T )w, whose target enters only through the constant T−w

Table 2: The admissible-ceiling test of Corollary 3, read against a null in which each frontier is the three-parameter form (4) fitted to it, drawn on its own nodes at its own residual scale. “False” is the per-frontier rate at which the procedure declares a violation when none exists, and power is measured against the deformed wall Neff = θ(e∆S − 1) at θ = 2, a floor at twice its admissible value. The incumbent statistic minimizes ε/(1 + Neff) over every triple and is not calibrated under the null at any precision reported here. The two pre-registered readings are at their nominal level and have no power on these windows, which is what Corollary 3(iii) predicts. Precision is not the binding constraint: the incumbent’s false-violation rate is 1.000 at every precision down to 2 milli-nats, a factor 25 below the archive’s own residual scale, and the two pre-registered readings never leave [0.01, 0.10] in power. The constraint is depth, not noise—see the text.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a differential theory for quality-resource trade-offs in AI model selection, providing a framework for optimizing resource usage.
papers.title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
papers.tldr: A differential framework turns multi-resource AI quality frontiers into price-independent geometry and derives minimax resource prices and regret for model selection.

papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
authors: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
bullets: Targets prompt responses for video-based agents operating over bounded histories.
Caches each frame’s recurrent-state transformation and composes transformations associatively as the window advances.
Uses a specialized data structure and GPU kernels to limit caching and composition overhead.
Across five hybrid VLMs and four benchmarks, it achieved the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 tests.
Reduced p95 time-to-first-token by 6.6× on average versus the faster of two vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of the hybrid VLM. Multiple input frames are converted into visual tokens by a vision encoder and passed alongside text tokens into a unified backbone. This backbone interleaves recurrent layers, which update a fixed-size state for each token, with attention layers, which retain per-token key–value entries.

Figure 8. Mean GDN state error. Relative Frobenius error averaged over each model’s GDN layers, comparing Spool with Spool without reconstruction against the vLLM reference. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions.

Figure 1. Spool maintains a sliding video window without replaying retained frames. (a) Shifting the window retains four of five frames. (b) Prefix-cache invalidation forces the retained context to be rebuilt. (c) Spool composes cached recurrent transformations and reclaims key–value slots by moving surviving tail entries into holes left by eviction.

Figure 4. Efficient recurrent-state reconstruction with cached transformations. Spool caches each block’s affine state transformation and then replays them without the effect of a given block. A segment tree composes consecutive transformations, enabling reconstruction of the active window in O(logW ) operations. In this example, frames 5–8 occupy cyclic slots 1–3 and 0, with frame 8 wrapping around to slot 0. Spool first applies F5, then the combined transformation F6,7, and finally F8 to the prefix state Sp. This recovers the window state using only three cached transformations, without reprocessing video tokens or updating the tree during reconstruction.

Figure 5. KV tail filling and RoPE rebasing. Top: surviving tokens 11 and 12 fill holes in slots 1 and 2, releasing the final page; P denotes the fixed prefix. Bottom: filling changes storage slots while preserving position coordinates. A separate rebase shifts all cached positions by a common offset (−100 here) and rotates cached keys consistently.
Figure 3. Cost of window rebuilding. Here we plot time for a frame to be processed by Qwen3.5-9B on 1 A100. Every time the window must be rebuilt from scratch, a 29.2x latency cost must be paid.
Figure 6. Component ablation: latency per ingested frame (ms, ↓) as caching components are added, from a naive cache to the segment tree cache and KV filling.

Figure 7. Effect of state reconstruction on output fidelity. (a) Output KL divergence from vLLM-Omni remains near 0.04 through 1024 expired frames with reconstruction, but accumulates without it. (b) Accuracy gain (points) from reconstruction on PhoStream’s backward questions, which target earlier video content, grouped by expired frames relative to window size. Both variants perform identically before expiration; reconstruction gains 2.4 points after half a window expires and 3.8–4.7 points beyond two windows.

Figure 9. Per-layer GDN state error for Qwen3.5-9B. Relative Frobenius error against the vLLM reference for all 24 GDN layers, averaged over questions within each expired-frame bin. The evaluation uses all 9,000 Beyond3D questions and a 64-frame retained window.

Figure 10. Empirical CDFs of online TTFT. Rows correspond to Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Nemotron-VL Nano-12B, and Qwen3.5-27B. Columns correspond to PhoStream, StreamingBench, FastBench, and BEYOND3D.

Table 1. Online p95 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool can maintain real-time performance as live video streams in, achieving the lowest tail latency in all 20 model–benchmark tests: a geometric-mean speedup of 6.6× over the faster baseline and 33.8× over vLLM-Omni. Gains are largest on smaller models (0.34 s vs. 12.22 s on PhoStream with Qwen3.5-9B, 35.7×) and remain clear at the largest scale (0.33 s vs. 1.99 s on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B). (Parentheses are speedup over the faster baseline.)

Table 3. Offline accuracy (%, ↑). Spool’s windowed state maintenance preserves the backbone’s answer quality: without timing pressure, it stays within −1.6 to +1.8 points of the more accurate baseline in each of the 24 tests and has the highest mean accuracy, 54.4% vs. 54.1% for vLLM-Incremental and 53.7% for vLLM-Omni. Combined with the large online gains (Table 2), this shows that Spool’s online advantage comes from answering on time, not from changing what the model sees. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 4. Peak GPU memory (GiB, ↓). Each of Spool’s components has a modest memory cost: the segment tree trades 2.3– 4.4 GiB for 4.7–14.8% lower per-frame latency (Figure 6), and KV filling recovers 0.38–1.77 GiB of it while lowering latency further. Overall, the full system uses 9.2% more memory on average than the naive cache.

Table 2. Online accuracy (%, ↑). By answering on time, Spool drops fewer questions under live load and answers more correctly than both baselines where they fall behind. On BEYOND3D, it improves over the more accurate baseline by 3.6–18.4 points (mean 9.5), such as 30.32% vs. 11.94% with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B. On the other benchmarks, it stays within −2.5 to +3.6 points. Averaged over all tests, Spool reaches 52.8%, compared with 50.3% for vLLM-Incremental and 45.4% for vLLM-Omni. Questions dropped while the server is busy count as incorrect. (Parentheses are percentage points change over the more accurate baseline.)

Table 5. Online p50 TTFT (s, ↓). Spool’s latency advantage is concentrated in the tail: vLLM-Incremental answers typical questions quickly but stalls on a minority, which dominates its p95 (Table 1). Spool still has the lowest or tied-lowest p50 in 18 of 20 tests (1.9× geometric mean over the faster baseline, 32.2× over vLLM-Omni), with the largest gap on FastBench with Nemotron-VL Nano-12B (0.14 s vs. 2.66 s). vLLM-Incremental is marginally faster on StreamingBench with Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, by 0.01– 0.02 s. Parentheses: speedup over the faster baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Low-latency streaming inference for hybrid VLMs via state transformation caching.
papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Spool enables exact, low-latency sliding-window inference for hybrid vision-language models by efficiently removing expired video frames without replaying the full window.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
authors: Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Existing autoregressive video diffusion models are too slow for fluid interactive experiences.
Profiling shows VAE decoding and KV-cache updates contribute over half of end-to-end inference latency.
FastFrames replaces these components with lightweight alternatives in a family of fast models.
The 1.3B model achieves 36 ms per frame on a single B200 GPU while matching a much slower state-of-the-art model’s quality.
The 14B model achieves 45 ms per frame on an 8×B200 node with significantly better visual quality and realism, enabling real-time camera- and physics-conditioned generation.

Given a single keypress, FastFrames is 16× faster to respond. Right: generation latency of officially released implementations and our optimized implementations. papers.abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.
bullets: Gemma 4’s key is a scaled value, allowing one 640-value row to replace separate 1,024-value key and value rows.
The implementation uses two overlapping strided cache views, leaving the paged attention kernel unchanged.
In a vLLM prototype, outputs were bit-identical to arithmetic emulation; 2 of 432 final answers differed from the stock engine, within run-to-run noise.
With a 15 GiB decode pool, throughput increased by 1.38× for 16K-token prompts and 1.24× for 8K prompts; the block-pool model predicted both within 1%.
The approach adds 4–9% eager-step latency at equal batch and does not yet combine with default-scale 8-bit KV caching.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.
authors: Daniil Li, Mars Davletshin, Vadim Klyzhenko, Artem Danilishin, Valery Sandul, Daniil Ryazanov, Ekaterina Muravleva
bullets: Addresses severe distortion from aggressive quantization, especially in highly sensitive channels.
Uses random preconditioning to regularize weights before quantization.
Separately quantizes weight directions and magnitudes in polar coordinates.
Employs an E8-lattice codebook for compact directional representation.
Preserves highly important channels identified by a proxy Hessian at an additional 0.16 bits, with empirical accuracy improvements.

papers.abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Haoran Li, Yi Yue, Tak L. Fung, Quan Chen
bullets: Targets the quadratic attention cost caused by reference tokens, which comprise roughly half of the sequence.
Ranks tokens using latent redundancy and VLM-derived importance, assigning them to prune, cache, or keep tiers.
Pruned tokens are removed before generation while preserving rotary positions; cached tokens reuse their keys and values.
Achieves 1.57× and 1.49× end-to-end speedups on two benchmarks with only 0.24% and 0.17% VBench quality drops.
Combines with existing acceleration methods, reaching up to 2.15× speedup in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.
authors: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang
bullets: Addresses inference-induced stalls caused by blocking action-chunk generation.
Uses an action-conditioned predictor to forecast next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state.
Precomputes a speculative KV cache and action chunk with a frozen VLA, then accepts or repairs them based on predicted–real differences and task conditions.
On LIBERO, reports 2.67× and 1.27× query speedups over synchronous π0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT baselines while maintaining competitive success rates.
Under target-motion perturbations, retains baseline-comparable success with 1.52×–1.93× query speedup.

papers.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair

papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.
authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan
bullets: Targets two serving bottlenecks: discarded vocabulary-wide scores and repeated prompt attention across beams.
Trie-Head stores the identifier trie in validated GPU tensors, reducing Python callbacks, CPU–GPU coordination, and memory traffic.
Scores compact codebook candidates while streaming the full-vocabulary normalizer to preserve the model’s valid-token scores.
Shared-context attention reuses prompt key/value blocks while keeping beam-specific decode tails.
Implemented in SGLang; the combined system achieves up to 5.57× throughput over CLP and 2.63× over BF16 FlashRec at beam width 200 on one workload.

papers.title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
papers.tldr: Trie-Head and shared-context attention make wide-beam generative retrieval substantially more efficient without retraining or changing valid-token scores.

papers.abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra generation cost in text-based communication between multimodal language models.
Provider models observe complementary video frames and transfer projected, aligned visual KV states to a carrier model via gated residual updates.
The injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while adding provider and communication-module computation.
Experiments on MLVU and Video-MME report modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-based baseline.
More provider-side frame coverage helps selected tasks, but some categories are unchanged or worse; computation budgets remain an open consideration.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal KV-state communication between MLLMs for video understanding while preserving carrier cache length, touching both video understanding and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
papers.tldr: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection enables multimodal LLMs to communicate complementary video information through aligned visual KV states, yielding modest task-dependent gains and lower latency than text communication.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.
authors: Yijun Sun, Xudong Liao, Zhuobin Huang, Kai Chen, Nikita Lazarev, Zhizhen Zhong
bullets: Problem: GPU HBM capacity limits serving concurrency because hot KV buffers and fully resident K-index caches consume substantial memory, even with scale-up memory pools.
Method: Dynamically selected KV entries use TMA-based retrieval fused with attention in a tile-level pipeline, while predictable K-index pages use GPU-initiated DMA prefetching.
Contribution: A sparse-attention offloading system implemented atop SGLang for scale-up memory expansion.

Results: On emulated scale-up memory, it achieves up to 4.98× and 4.52× higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, and up to 1.34× over naive same-platform integration across 16K–1M contexts.
Scope: Evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool.

papers.abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

papers.abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets memory-bound attention caused by repeatedly reading growing historical KV caches.
Builds shared read plans from seed queries using exact priority and recovery tiers, while recomputing attention with fresh queries and current-block KV.
Protects potentially useful history from permanent eviction and amortizes sparse-support construction without modifying the backbone or decoder.
On DreamReasoner-8B, it preserves comparable task performance and reports up to 5.53× attention speedup at 128K context.
Across eight settings and three models, it decodes faster than tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.
authors: Zewen Huang, Xiangwen Zhuge, Yingkun Hu, Zheng Yang, Qiang Ma
bullets: Targets underutilized cloud-GPU decoding and the limited concurrency of edge FPGAs.
Assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding based on accelerator capacity, queue load, prompt length, and network state.
Reduces offloading overhead using pipelined layer transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV-cache compression.
On a V100–Alveo U280 prototype, achieves up to 4.11× request goodput and 61.1% lower mean latency than cloud-only vLLM at 500 Mbps.
Benefits are strongest for communication-intensive workloads and include lower per-request energy, with performance dependent on network conditions.

papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of independently rounded INT4/FP4 values and the large tables or restricted decoders of prior trellis codes.

Comes within 0.07 bits of the information-theoretic ideal at 4 bits and matches a random-permutation trellis code with a table thousands of times larger.
Achieves the lowest reported KL divergence across tested bit widths for Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP codebooks, by up to 27%.
Runs at native FP4/FP8 throughput on AWS Trainium 4 with negligible systolic-array area; scope is tensor quantization without fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a low-bit quantization method for LLM weights, reducing memory requirements and improving efficiency.
papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.tldr: CPTC delivers near-optimal low-bit tensor quantization using two multiplications and a 64-byte lookup table, with efficient decoding and strong LLM weight-quantization results.

papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra derivation between stored conversations and assistant queries.
Restores cached sessions and appends the question, while retaining raw text as the authoritative fallback.
Defines budget-based retention, append-only reads, bounded aggregation, and a cost model for storage and querying.
Estimates substantially higher cache storage than text, with costs varying by model architecture and retention scenario.
Introduces logical QA evaluation via session prefill plus a separate real-cache replay test for numerical equivalence and runtime cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Published system-level comparisons under two different benchmarks and source evaluation protocols: (a) LongMemEval’s 97-question subset with 3–6-session histories [1, Fig. 4a]; (b) LoCoMo J scores from Mem0’s vendor-authored evaluation [2]. Full-history reading scores highest among the selected systems shown in each panel, not across all evidence. Zep’s separate vendor-reported LongMemEval-S comparison favours its retrieval system over a full-context baseline averaging about 115K tokens and is not plotted here (§3.2, §8.1). These comparisons do not isolate a memory mechanism, and scores depend on evaluation labels and judges (§9.1). L1–L4 are our descriptive memory modes; KV-LTM has no measured accuracy bar (§8). Costs are modelled separately (§7).

Figure 2: KV-LTM write flow (once per session): canonical per-session prefill creates the stored state at session end; session text, metadata with integrity digests, and native reader state are retained under the §4.8 storage and latency policy, which may evict or invalidate state — the text is always kept. Valid state is read from a request-local working copy; when policy allows, invalid or evicted state is rebuilt from the verified text (§4.3), otherwise the session is counted as not cached and delegated to the §4.8 text fallback, outside the depicted cache-read path. papers.selection_reason: Proposes persistent per-session KV caches as long-term memory for LLM assistants, directly addressing LLM memory and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.tldr: KV-LTM proposes storing each conversation session’s raw text and model KV cache to preserve long-term memory while accelerating future question answering without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
bullets: Packed INT2/INT3 kernels execute natively, but all tested INT2 configurations degenerate during generation.
Module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive, with Korean and reasoning tasks showing different sensitivity patterns.
The final recipe uses 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head.
On the untouched FINAL-81 set, it uses 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory, retains 0.904 Korean teacher-correct accuracy, and reaches a 0.939 TPOT ratio versus BF16.
It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by 1.4 percentage points, though the roles of activation precision and INT8 allocation are not isolated.

papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.tldr: A deployment-constrained mixed-precision recipe for Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 passes memory, Korean-quality, and latency gates, outperforming NVFP4 W4A4 while revealing major risks in ultra-low-bit quantization and candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: Repeated profile-text prefills dominate ranking inference because profiles appear after varying prompt prefixes, preventing effective prefix caching.
Lightweight LoRA writers, trained by self-distillation, generate reusable profile KV caches during profile updates.
A KV scheduler overlaps host-to-GPU cache transfers with computation for the next batch.
On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill across memory updates.
Under saturated load, throughput improves 4.0–4.5× for scoring and 1.4–1.9× for profile updates.

papers.selection_reason: Reusable KV caches as persistent user memory for LLM recommenders; fits KV cache efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.tldr: KVUse accelerates LLM recommendation serving by storing user profiles as reusable KV caches instead of repeatedly prefilling their text.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
bullets: High-concurrency VLM serving becomes compute-bound, while long image-token contexts make draft prediction expensive.
The method identifies sparse cross-modal information flow: only a few draft KV heads need visual features, primarily from the target model’s top layers.
VisHead-Spec-8 routes image features to 8 of 40 KV heads and restricts the rest to text features.
On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, accepted length stays within 0.3% of the DSpark baseline.
At batch size 64, throughput gain reaches 16.0% versus 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, performance remains comparable.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.
bullets: Addresses VLMs’ difficulty in exploiting critical evidence already present in visual representations.
Builds a compact associative memory during a single visual prefill, avoiding repeated image encoding.
Progressively retrieves evidence to guide attention queries and hidden representations without explicit reasoning traces.
Experiments report consistent gains in general visual understanding and fine-grained perception.
Achieves faster inference than reasoning-intensive approaches, though specific benchmarks and quantitative results are not given.
