papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets quality degradation beyond the training horizon, self-generated history, and increasing KV-cache costs.
WinTF builds a multi-step base using window-wise denoising with local bidirectional attention and causal access to prior history.
HieraKV reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality by adapting retained history across layers.
CuLT-DMD enables efficient long-rollout distillation by aggregating gradients across temporal positions while keeping one local computation graph.
On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30 seconds, while MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods through 60 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains a few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise a rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at a history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising.

Figure 3 WinTF learns rolling generation through parallel supervision of windows with progressive noise levels. Phase offsets expose the model to both short prefill windows and full decoding windows. Within each window, later chunks receive higher noise levels. The attention mask combines bidirectional interactions within a noisy window with access to clean preceding history, while isolating noisy windows from one another. This allows multiple windows to be trained in parallel, each conditioned on its own event prompt and preceding clean history.

Figure 5 CuLT-DMD combines supervision across a long rollout in each generator update. The top panel shows local distillation supervision from teacher and critic predictions. LongLive-style training updates the generator from individual windows while carrying detached history forward. CuLT-DMD instead keeps parameters fixed throughout the rollout and averages the local gradients before updating. This incorporates supervision from multiple temporal positions while retaining one local computation graph at a time.

Figure 6 AnnealCFG reduces the late-denoising extrapolation produced by constant guidance throughout 30s generation. Across prefill and early, middle, and late decoding, the left plots show the additional latent-update magnitude induced by guidance. The right plots show its share in the final 20% of denoising steps. Annealing lowers both the late-step peaks and their contribution to the total update. Results aggregate 32 paired prompts, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown by bands and whiskers.

Figure 7 KV recomputation refreshes historical context for generation beyond the training horizon. Fullhistory caching expands the context as video length grows, while sliding-window caching retains dependencies on evicted chunks. At the history threshold, recomputation selects sink, intermediate, and recent chunks and causally re-encodes them into a fresh cache. This bounds the retained context and removes cached dependencies on discarded chunks before generation continues.

Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within a per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer.

Figure 1 MovieRoll generates a minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with a new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt.

Figure 4 Layer-dependent attention patterns motivate hierarchical history retention. In the WinTF-trained model, shallow layers distribute attention broadly across historical chunks, while deeper layers place relatively more attention on the sink and most recent chunks. The heatmap and lower entropy and coverage plots show this shift with depth. HieraKV follows these patterns by retaining full historical context in shallow layers and restricting deeper layers to the sink and most recent chunks.

Figure 9 The Parallel Streaming Variational Autoencoder (PS-VAE) supports continuous video decoding through temporal caching and spatial parallelism. The upper panel shows how cached decoder states carry temporal context across arriving latent chunks, allowing each chunk to be decoded as it becomes available. The lower panel distributes high-resolution decoding across GPUs through row partitioning and boundary exchange. Together, these designs support streaming output and reduce per-GPU decoding cost.

Figure 10 Qualitative comparison of 10s single-event video generation. Under the same prompt of a mermaid combing her hair on a seaside rock, MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled retain recognizable subjects and consistent surroundings as poses and waves change. Rows compare methods evaluated under the same prompt, and columns show successive temporal intervals within each 241-frame video.

Figure 11 Qualitative comparison of 30s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled preserve the facial features, clothing, and surroundings of a man eating at a bar as the action continues. Rows compare methods under the same prompt, and columns follow the 721-frame sequence, showing how subject and background consistency evolve during generation.

Figure 17 Memory and latency comparison across full-history and sink--recent attention allocations. The left plot shows slower cache-memory growth when fewer layers retain full history. At 18 cached chunks, the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local layers reduces memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB and peak denoising-step latency from 33.8 to 15.8s relative to all-global attention. Measurements use MovieRoll-Base with CFG on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Each timed denoising step includes both conditional and unconditional DiT evaluations. Timing excludes KV recomputation and VAE encoding/decoding.

Figure 16 Ablation of long-horizon extrapolation strategies. All three strategies use the same Stage 1 MovieRollBase checkpoint to extend generation from 10s training clips to 30s videos. Full-history and sliding-window caching produce increasingly washed-out backgrounds, whereas KV recomputation preserves clearer subject and street details through the end of the sequence.

Figure 12 Qualitative comparison of 60s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves the diver and underwater environment with relatively stable colors as generation continues. Rows compare methods under the same diver-and-wreck prompt, and columns follow successive 10s intervals of the 1441-frame videos.

Figure 26 Examples of multi-event video generation with sequential prompts. The upper examples show threeevent, 30s videos from MovieRoll-Base, and the lower examples show six-event, 60s videos from MovieRoll-Distilled. Prompts change every 10s, with one frame representing each event. Both models retain recurring characters and settings as new interactions develop, such as a cat reacting to a robotic vacuum and a keeper responding to a seagull.

Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of 30s multi-event video generation. The sequence progresses from sketching a flower to observing a frog and raising a camera, with a prompt change every 10s. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts these action changes while retaining the botanist and rainforest setting. Each row shows one method, and each pair of columns corresponds to one event.

Figure 14 Qualitative comparison of 60s multi-event video generation. The sequence develops from paddling to successive interactions with an otter, including surfacing beside the kayak, handling a rock, and approaching the hull. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts this event progression while maintaining a consistent lake setting. Rows compare methods under the same six sequential prompts, and each column represents one 10s event.

Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise progression and temporal advances at a fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt.

Figure 24 Examples of 60s single-event videos generated by MovieRoll-Distilled. This first set of six examples includes miniature ships, an origami dragon, and underwater performances. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves subject appearance as waves, steam, and gestures evolve. Each two-row group follows one 1441-frame video from left to right and then top to bottom, with frame indices overlaid and its prompt below.

Figure 18 Ablation of HieraKV attention allocations. The comparison varies the allocation of 54 transformer blocks between full-history and sink–recent attention. With the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local blocks, the rider and horse remain recognizable throughout the sequence. All-global attention progressively crops the subje ts, while all-local attention shifts toward a close rear view.

Figure 22 User preference comparison for multi-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled wins a majority of judgments against every evaluated baseline, with win rates from 62.3% to 81.9%. Each bar reports win, tie, and loss rates from the MovieRoll-Distilled perspective under the same prompt sequences, pooling judgments across 30s three-event and 60s six-event videos with ties included in the denominator.

Table 8 Shared architecture and history-cache configuration of the MovieRoll models. Both variants use an 8.3-billion-parameter backbone with text conditioning, a causal video VAE, and a five-chunk active window. The first six transformer blocks retain full history, while the remaining 48 retain the sink and most recent chunks, preserving broad historical context through a small subset of layers.

Table 2 Comparison of video decoding speed, memory use, and reconstruction quality. Single-GPU PSVAE outperforms the tested tiling methods in runtime and reconstruction PSNR. Spatial parallelism further reduces decoding time and per-GPU memory. With eight GPUs, PS-VAE achieves a 3.97× decoding speedup over its singleGPU version while preserving high numerical agreement. Measurements decode 1441 frames at 480× 864 on NVIDIA H20 GPUs in FP16.

Table 9 Inference settings of MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled. Distillation reduces sampling from 50 steps to 5 while preserving the shared rolling-generation pipeline. MovieRoll-Base uses guidance annealed from 4 to 1, whereas MovieRoll-Distilled operates without CFG. Both use the same chunk and window sizes and rebuild their KV caches at the same history threshold. Denoising passes are counted per output chunk, with the conditional and unconditional CFG branches contributing separately to the reported count.

Table 1 Efficiency comparison of block-causal attention implementations. The comparison evaluates fullhistory attention with three or five windows on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. FBCA achieves the lowest forward and backward runtimes across fixed and varying input shapes, with preparation taking less than 0.1s when shapes vary. In multiple-shape tests, it also reduces peak memory relative to FlexAttention, supporting efficient training across inputs with different spatial resolutions.

Table 10 Training stages and hyperparameters of MovieRoll. The two base-model stages introduce single-event and multi-event streaming generation. ODE initialization then transfers the base model to a few-step student, and CuLT-DMD trains it on self-generated rollouts. The columns summarize the data and optimization settings supporting this progression. The two distillation phases are denoted by P1 and P2, while G and F identify the generator and fake-score critic in the optimization settings for each phase.

Table 6 Single-GPU inference efficiency for 60s video generation. The table compares denoising and endto-end costs across methods at the listed resolutions for 1441-frame videos on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Switching from FlashAttention-3 to SageAttention increases MovieRoll-Distilled end-to-end throughput from 1.52 to 2.04 FPS. Single-GPU throughput remains below the 24 FPS playback rate required for real-time generation.

Table 5 Quantitative ablations of training and inference designs. WinTF outperforms chunk-wise formulations, while the selected HieraKV allocation, KV recomputation, long-rollout CuLT-DMD, and AnnealCFG schedule achieve the highest total scores within their respective comparisons. Shaded rows identify these choices. Autoregressive formulations are evaluated at 241 and 721 frames, and the remaining comparisons use 721 frames. Higher ratings indicate better quality and less drift.

Table 14 Comparison ofGPT-5.2 andGemini-2.5-Proas video evaluators. Both evaluate the same 30s single-event videos and rank MovieRoll-Distilled first and MovieRoll-Base second. Method rankings agree closely, with Spearman correlation ρ = 0.930. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro because it provides greater score separation between methods, as shown by the statistical measures in the lower section.

Table 11 Rollout settings for the two CuLT-DMD training phases. Phase 1 uses single-event, 241-frame rollouts lasting 10s. Phase 2 extends training to two-event, 721-frame rollouts lasting 30s. Both phases average local gradients across each rollout, allowing one update to incorporate supervision from multiple temporal positions. Bounded score clips keep distillation supervision local as the generated sequence grows.

Table 15 Distribution of user-study judgments across baselines and video durations. The study collects 2616 preference judgments across single-event and multi-event comparisons. Each cell counts individual judgments for MovieRoll-Distilled versus the listed baseline at a given duration. Judgments are pooled across durations to calculate win, tie, and loss rates for each baseline, separately for single-event and multi-event generation. Each judgment contributes one vote, including ties.

Table 13 Conversion of HeliosBench quality and drift metrics to a common rating scale. The listed intervals map raw metric values to ratings from 1 to 10 for weighted aggregation. Higher quality scores and lower drift scores receive higher ratings, so higher converted ratings consistently indicate better performance.

Table 7 Inference scaling across GPU counts and attention backends. Increasing the GPU count improves MovieRoll-Distilled throughput with both backends, and SageAttention is faster at every tested count. On eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, the best setting generates a 60s video in 152.2s, reaching 9.47 FPS. Real-time generation at 24 FPS remains a limitation even with eight GPUs. Videos contain 1441 frames at 480× 864.

Table 12 HeliosBench metrics, evaluators, and aggregation weights. Five full-video metrics cover aesthetics, dynamics, motion smoothness, semantic alignment, and naturalness. Four drift metrics measure changes between the beginning and end of a video. The aggregation weights give greater emphasis to semantic alignment and naturalness while retaining contributions from all four metrics of temporal drift.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video generation with KV-cache compression and distillation.
papers.title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
papers.tldr: MovieRoll is a framework for generating long-form videos by combining streaming fine-tuning, compressed context caching, long-rollout distillation, and stabilized long-horizon inference.

papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of generating textual guidance with a large model before small-model generation.
Uses a trainable bridge to convert frozen sender hidden states into attention keys and values for the receiver.
Supports periodic review, where the sender updates guidance from the receiver’s partial output while preserving the receiver’s KV cache.
Improves reasoning and coding performance across independently trained model families, with gains comparable to a stronger sender pairing.
Transfers from math and coding training to general-knowledge tasks without domain-specific retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of POND. A frozen sender prefills the input, and a trainable bridge compresses its last layer hidden states into a shared latent message, which layer-specific adapters project into KV entries for the receiver. The receiver, fine-tuned jointly with the bridge, generates the full response. At review boundaries, the sender prefills the newly generated segment and the resulting entries are appended to the latent memory, leaving the receiver’s KV cache untouched.

Figure 2: Accuracy gains and sender compute savings. Left: Math and code scores for the receiver (Qwen3.5-4B), the receiver with POND, and the sender (GLM-5.3); labels give the gain in points. Center: Estimated sender FLOPs for GLM-5.3 (40B active) with 1k input and 10k output tokens. Prefill-only guidance reduces sender compute from 880 to 80 TFLOPs. Right: Fraction of sender compute saved, T/(L + T ), as a function of output length T with L = 1k. Estimates use 2Pactive FLOPs per token and exclude attention, routing, communication, and bridge or receiver inference. The panels are not a matched end-to-end comparison of accuracy and cost.

Table 1: Math and code results. Senders are frozen and prefill-only. POND uses one latent transfer; +Review adds periodic prefill updates. Acc.: accuracy/pass@1 (%, higher is better); Token: total decoded receiver tokens, including both thinking and final-response tokens (thousands per 100 runs, lower is better); Speed: end-to-end latency (s/run, lower is better). Bold marks the better of POND and +Review for each metric, including ties. Improve compares the bold value with the receiver alone: accuracy gain in percentage points, or relative reduction in tokens/latency; an upward latency arrow indicates an increase. Avg averages the five tasks.

Table 2: Knowledge benchmark results. Configurations, metrics, and metric-wise bolding follow Table 1. Improve reports accuracy gains (percentage points) or relative token/latency reductions (%) against the receiver; upward latency arrows denote increases. Avg averages all four tasks. Differences and reductions are computed before rounding.
Table 3: Training and review controls. Suite-average accuracy. Receiver-only training uses math/code data; POND uses Qwen3.8-Max as the sender.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes POND, a 'prefill-only, no-decode' method using a latent bridge to transfer representations from large to small models, improving efficiency and model collaboration.
papers.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
papers.tldr: POND lets a small model benefit from a large model’s hidden representations without paying the cost of large-model autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.
authors: Ofir Gordon, Lior Dikstein, Paul Balanca, Idan Achituve, Douglas Orr, Hai Victor Habi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth growth from longer contexts and larger batches.
Combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats as a drop-in codebook-quantization replacement.
Uses beam search for large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks.
Introduces MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX format.
Reports lower WikiText perplexity, higher GSM8K accuracy, and the best NVFP4 LongBench average on Llama3 and Qwen3 among evaluated baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1. MicroScaling trellis quantization overview. (a) Inputs are scaled blockwise before beam search on the bitshift trellis. (b) Trellis-state bits are mixed and mapped through the scale-dependent inverse CDF to form MX-Gaussian reconstruction values. The distribution diagrams are schematic.

Figure 2. MiSTiQ parameter analysis with standard Gaussian inputs, consistent with the MX Gaussian hash derivation. (a) Vector length: beam search and Viterbi. (b) Trellis length: both methods with bstart = 8 (S8) or bstart = 0 (S0). (c) MX block size with fixed UE8M0 scales, T = 1024, V = 8, and beam widths 128 and 1024, at approximately matched effective rates. The ordinate is RMSE · 2beff ; beff counts payload, scale, and start-state bits per scalar.
Figure 4. WikiText-2 perplexity comparison for decreasing bit rates between MiSTiQ and NSNQuant (Son et al., 2026).
Figure 5. WikiText-2 perplexity versus vector length for MiSTiQ with UE5M3 scales, dmx = 128, and T = 128 and a trellis payload of 1 bit per element.
Figure 3. Comparison between the standard Gaussian distribution and the MX-Gaussian marginal distribution for a block size of 32 with E2M1 scaling.

Figure 6. WikiText-2 perplexity versus K/V payload allocation for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with UE5M3 scales, dmx = 128, and T = 1024. Upper and lower x-axis labels show K/V bits per transition for V = 4 and V = 8, respectively.

Table 1. WikiText-2 perplexity, mean LongBench score, and GSM8K accuracy (%) for MX KV-cache quantization. Effective bits include payload and stored quantization metadata. Blue marks the best quantized result, including ties, per model and metric within each rate and format group.

Table 2. WikiText-2 perplexity (↓) across quantizer designs at approximately 1.30 effective bits per element with a UE5M3 scale format, providing a comparison at similar storage budgets. Blue cells mark the lowest perplexity for each model.

Table 4. Below-1-bit MX KV-cache quantization perplexity. Effective Bit denotes mean effective bits per element using dynamic storage accounting. Within each block-scale format and model, dark blue cells mark the lowest perplexity and light blue cells mark the second-lowest perplexity among the displayed quantized methods.

Table 6. LongBench task scores for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (↑). Bold marks the best per scale and bit section, excluding historical BF16.

Table 7. LongBench task scores for Qwen3-8B (↑). Bold marks the best per scale and bit section, excluding historical BF16. UE8M0/UE5M3 VecInfer uses MX-unaware quantization; NVFP4 retains the original setup. All MiSTiQ rows use beam 128.

papers.selection_reason: Novel KV-cache quantization combining trellis coding with microscaling formats for extreme compression in LLM inference.
papers.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
papers.tldr: MiSTiQ compresses LLM KV caches to about 1.25 bits per element while enabling low-precision computation and improving quality over evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
authors: Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu
bullets: Targets the remaining inference bottlenecks in long-video generation: repeated denoising and KV-cache operations across video chunks.
Uses Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations.
Applies Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical KV-reading budgets across layers and attention heads.
Uses Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to select informative spatial tokens while preserving coverage.
Achieves up to 2.28× speedup on Self-Forcing and 1.86× on LongLive, with consistently improved quality and no pretrained-parameter changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The top shows the overall inference pipeline, integrating denoising acceleration and KV cache optimization. The bottom illustrates three components. (a) CDR estimates clean latent updates from noise variations and shallow feature changes. (b) ORHR allocates historical KV reading budgets based on attention output perturbations. (c) CCSC reduces cache construction costs through content and coverage guided spatial token selection.

(c-e) Effects of shallow feature projection dimension rs, staleness threshold A, and regularization scale λ/m on generation quality and speedup using Self-Forcing.

Figure 9. Analysis of historical KV reading effects on generation quality. (a) Consecutive reference frames and spatial changes in previousframe bias after restoring omitted historical KV reads. Blue and orange indicate increased and decreased bias, respectively. (b) Distribution of bias changes on Self-Forcing and LongLive, with percentages indicating the proportion of videos showing increased bias.
Figure 10. Additional qualitative comparison of video generation results.

(b) Attention output errors under uniform reading and ORHR with the same budget of 720 frame accesses. (c) Output NMSE across subsequent video chunks using the early calibrated allocation, demonstrating consistently lower errors without recalibration.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free acceleration of few-step autoregressive video diffusion via KV cache and denoising optimizations.
papers.title: ScoutCache: Efficient Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Conditional Readout and Selective Caching
papers.tldr: ScoutCache is a training-free framework that accelerates few-step autoregressive video diffusion by reducing denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction costs while improving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
bullets: Speculative decoding normally stores target and draft KV caches, creating substantial extra memory use.
The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, preserving the target model’s correction rule.
The proposed K4V4 scheme uses per-channel keys and per-token values, co-designing precision with quantizer layout.
Across six model pairs, draft-cache memory falls 66.20% and total cache memory 23.95%.
Mean acceptance decreases only slightly, from 57.93% to 57.14% (1.36% relative).

figures.caption: Figure 3: Memory and acceptance. (a) K4V4 total KV saving and paired acceptance change across six target/draft pairs. Error bars are paired 95% CIs; the star is the equal-model macro. (b) Actual bit-packed draft cache storage, including quantizer metadata and the BF16 residual window. The absolute saving grows with retained context.

Figure 2: Quantizer geometry changes the K/V conclusion. (a) Each line follows one model pair while models and bit budgets remain fixed. Positive values favor more key bits. (b) On 192 paired Qwen2.5 passkey examples, grouped per-channel keys recover most of the failure of K2V4 and sharply reduce the apparent key-bit advantage.
Figure 1: Quantizer geometry. Draft keys share scales by channel, while draft values share scales by token. K8V4 and K4V8 allocate equal average payload precision.
Table 3: Acceptance contrasts in pp. “Shift” is grouped per-channel minus per-token. Brackets give paired 95% CIs for each within-pair contrast.
Table 9: Measured compute for major experiment families. GPU-hours equal wall time multiplied by allocated GPUs, including model loading. The experiments of Appendix E are not included.
Table 10: Upstream licenses and terms for reported third-party assets.
Table 1: Primary speculative-decoding model pairs (Hugging Face checkpoint identifiers).
Table 2: Cross-family K4V4 generalization. Acceptance changes are differences in pp from the BF16 draft cache. BF16 and K4V4 are acceptance rates in %.

papers.abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.
authors: Yuanhang Gao, Xiangrui Yang, Lingyuan Meng, Yuanfeng Chen, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Generic latent KV compression requires costly reconstruction before RoPE and attention during decoding.
Exact execution requires the latent map to preserve RoPE rotations, allowing mixing only among coordinates with shared frequencies.
GaugeRoPE combines a RoPE-compatible carrier with an approximate position-independent residual key–value correction.
The training-free method achieves 5.85× KV compression on Mistral-7B with quality close to the full-cache baseline.
Direct latent execution provides up to 2.48× the decode throughput of the uncompressed baseline; results also extend to MHA.

papers.abstract: Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. However, its multi-input multi-output (MIMO) computation, exponential-trapezoidal discretization, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) introduce dense, element-wise, and sequential operations. Despite kernel fusion, conventional GPUs execute these operations inefficiently. Our characterization of Mamba-3 hybrid models reveals numerous kernel launches, substantial data movement, and increased register pressure that reduces warp occupancy and memory-latency hiding. We propose RescuCore, a specialized GPU execution unit for Mamba-3 inference that retains other hybrid model layers on existing GPU resources. Integrated alongside CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) sub-partition, RescuCore shares the register file, shared memory, and warp schedulers. Dense projections remain on conventional GPU resources, while RescuCore pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO computation, recurrent state updates, and output gating to reduce kernel fragmentation and intermediate data movement. We select BF16 after evaluating multiple numerical formats, preserving model accuracy with an estimated area overhead of 5.9% of an A100 die for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4. We evaluate RescuCore using cycle-accurate Accel-Sim simulation, RTL synthesis, and synthesis-informed AccelWattch power modeling. Compared with conventional GPU execution, RescuCore achieves 1.4-9.4x speedup and 1.4-5.0x energy reduction during prefill, and 1.3-2.8x speedup and 1.2-2.6x energy reduction during autoregressive decoding. These results demonstrate the potential of GPU-integrated specialized execution for SSM-based hybrid models.
authors: Shiva Raja, William Desueza, Ajay Joshi
bullets: Mamba-3’s MIMO computation, discretization, RoPE, and recurrent updates cause kernel fragmentation, data movement, and register pressure on conventional GPUs.
RescuCore integrates alongside CUDA and Tensor Cores, while leaving dense projections on existing GPU resources.
It pipelines discretization, normalization, RoPE, MIMO, state updates, and output gating to reduce intermediate data movement.
Using BF16, the design estimates 5.9% A100 die-area overhead for state size 32 and MIMO rank 4.
Simulation and synthesis-based evaluation reports 1.4–9.4× prefill speedup and 1.3–2.8× decoding speedup, with corresponding energy reductions.

papers.abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.
authors: Benhao Huang, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Hector Liu
bullets: Feeds each token’s top-layer state into the next token’s input and is compared with a vanilla Transformer at matched compute.
Across model sizes and data regimes, it generally improves the value of both FLOPs and unique tokens, except when data is very scarce relative to model size.
With fixed unique data, it reaches a target loss using less compute; with fixed epochs, it reaches the target using less unique data.
A shared scaling law models latent feedback as equivalent to using a larger Transformer and generalizes accurately to a held-out model size.
Reported maximum savings are 48% compute and 47% unique data; downstream tasks show the same trend.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that latent feedback (feeding top-layer states to the next token) acts as a compute and data amplifier, effectively reducing the need for multiple training epochs.
papers.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
papers.tldr: Latent feedback makes language-model training more compute- and data-efficient than spending equivalent compute on repeated epochs, especially when unique data is plentiful.

papers.abstract: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.
authors: Yuyang Tian, Desen Sun, Shuncheng Jie, Lishan Yang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Problem: Uncompressed activation caches impose high memory and bandwidth costs, while post-edit compression may require buffering over 100 GB per request.
Method: Compresses reusable activations during serving and supports selective reuse for masked edits.
Method: Uses a scheduler designed to balance faster cached edits with initial generation requests.
Result: Sustains over 2× the baseline request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment.
Result: Speeds up edits by 2.4–4.5× and initial generations by 1.3–2.2× while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.
authors: Moshe Kimhi, Idan Kligvasser, Yotam Intrator, Regev Cohen, Ehud Rivlin
bullets: Caches a full-depth appearance representation as a read-only temporal anchor and combines it with selected partial features from the current frame.
A lightweight controller selects encoder exits before processing, using shallow computation for stable scenes and deeper computation when visual conditions change.
Separates temporal appearance reuse from geometric alignment: current calibration defines geometry, while a motion-conditioned adapter handles ego motion.
On nuScenes, achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP with 2.16× lower latency than dense DETR3D; StreamPETR sees a 1.92× speedup with similar accuracy.
Scope: the method targets temporally redundant driving sequences and relies on policy-based recognition of semantic driving regimes.

papers.title: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection
papers.tldr: EvoMem3D accelerates multi-camera 3D detection by adaptively reducing image-encoder depth and reusing temporally stable appearance features while preserving current-frame geometry.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.
authors: Shi Bin Hoo, Magnus Buehler, Omar Swelam, Frank Hutter, Lennart Purucker
bullets: GPT-6 Astra programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving mean ROC AUC 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline.
It diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic data while largely preserving benchmark performance.
It writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, including reversing linear trends and approximating square waves from sine waves.
The results suggest LLM-driven programming can complement optimization and provide tools for probing and intervening in TFM computations.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that LLMs can program tabular foundation models via weight-space reasoning and KV-cache editing, offering a novel method for model intervention and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: LLMs can directly program, repair, and steer tabular foundation models by manipulating weights or KV caches without gradient-based optimization.

papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in on-device LLM deployment, large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models remain impractical on resource-constrained devices, as sparse expert activation still requires all expert weights to be memory-resident. To address this, we identify three key observations for on-device MoE inference: (a) cache hit rates are fundamentally bounded even under Belady's optimal policy; (b) these bounds are insufficient for low-latency on-device inference; and (c) prior cache-aware routing based on binary cache presence can induce routing instability. Based on these insights, we propose CECAR (Cache & Expert Co-Aware Routing), a MoE inference system that jointly considers expert routing and cache management. Unlike prior cache-aware routing methods, CECAR uses an ML-based cache policy to predict the expected reuse distance of each expert and prioritizes routing and execution toward experts with smaller predicted reuse distances. On the Qwen3-30B-A3B model, CECAR achieves 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer-grade GPU with only 16 GB of VRAM, where non-resident experts are fetched from SSD, delivering a 4.5x speedup over conventional MoE inference and exceeding the decode speed of baselines that keep the entire model fully resident in DRAM. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/CECAR.
authors: Byeongju Kim, Hoonki Lee, Byungjun Kim, Inyul Ra, Yongjin Kim, Yongseong Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: On-device MoE inference is constrained because all expert weights cannot fit in memory, requiring SSD transfers for non-resident experts.
Cache hit rates are fundamentally limited, and binary cache-aware routing can cause unstable expert selection.
CECAR predicts each expert’s expected reuse distance with an ML-based cache policy and favors experts likely to be reused soon.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it reaches 12.5 tokens/s on a consumer GPU with 16 GB VRAM and outperforms fully DRAM-resident baselines in decode speed.

papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.
authors: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
bullets: Long-output reasoning requests can suffer KV thrashing, repeatedly losing and recovering state while producing little output.
Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in CPU memory and transfers them efficiently using fused gather/scatter kernels with double buffering.
Age-based readmission and protected decoding turns prevent repeatedly stalled requests; hidden-state length estimates guide preemption victims.
On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request waited over 50 seconds, while p99 time per output token decreased 50.7% versus recomputation.
The full replay finished 10.7% sooner, with 12.0% higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.
bullets: Large vocabularies impose a measurable deployment memory tax, especially on small edge models; for Thai–English deployments, the median tax is 4.4% below 0.5B parameters.
Retaining tokens from a deployment’s writing systems is exact, while retaining tokens observed in user text removes substantially more vocabulary rows.
Naive text-based trimming breaks BPE tokenization by removing intermediate merge tokens; merge closure repairs this with only 5.9% more rows.
A Good-Turing trim certificate estimates tokenizer shift and required text from trimming data alone, closely matching observed behavior across languages and settings.
Across six models and 11 languages, certified trims removed a median 89.7% of rows, with bits-per-character increasing by at most 2.0% while predictions were preserved.

papers.abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.
authors: Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, Nehal Kathrotia, Priyanka Tiwari
bullets: Targets prompt bloat, excessive token consumption, and error-prone loops in reflective multi-turn agents.
Uses a two-stage process: penalty-free skill discovery followed by accuracy-guarded pruning and code offloading to workspace utilities.
Evaluated across four models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench.
Reduced output tokens in 11 of 12 configurations, by up to 80% versus unconstrained EvoSkill, while improving mean accuracy on every benchmark.
Lowered total token usage and serving cost across all configurations, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.
authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Uses shared initial and final layers around independently parameterized parallel branches, with Wide-Shallow, Narrow-Deep, and Balanced variants.
Balanced branching improves validation quality and remains effective as the number of branches grows.
Joint-KV shares key-value caches across branches to reduce long-context inference memory and improve decoding throughput.
Across controlled pretraining scales, branching provides gains beyond width and depth changes and works across fusion functions.
The approach is most effective in middle layers and is evaluated within the reported pretraining and single-GPU inference settings.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.
bullets: Session-local drafters require no training and make drafting nearly free while a verifier reuses its KV cache.
Most-recent prompt lookup improves speedup by up to 0.09 over earliest-match lookup; session-memory weighting and backoff add no measurable benefit.
On medical and legal text, selective abstention saves 3–4 J per 100 tokens, whereas unselective drafting is faster but uses similar energy to plain decoding.
Drafted outputs match greedy decoding in 94% of generations; divergences occur only at numerical near-ties.
Repetition penalties reduce long-generation speedups to 1.1–1.2×, though recency remains beneficial and a minimum match-length floor consistently saves energy.

papers.selection_reason: Session-local drafting for speculative decoding with KV-cache verification; directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
papers.tldr: Recency-based session-local drafting delivers most of the speed benefit in speculative decoding, while confidence-based abstention is key to reducing energy use.

papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.
authors: Lucia Licakova, Niklas Schmidinger, Lukas Hauzenberger, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Depth recurrence increases effective depth but normally grows autoregressive KV memory with each iteration.
The authors evaluate looped Transformer hybrids using recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks plus periodic attention anchors.
A Parcae-style recurrent workspace and stabilising adapter are tested to constrain recurrence and improve stability.
Recurrent KV replay trains later iterations to reuse KV states written by selected earlier iterations.
Hybrid quality depends on sufficiently frequent attention anchors and the choice of recurrent mixer; KV replay retains near-baseline performance while reducing cache sharing overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Depth-recurrent language model architectures with KV replay reduce memory, relevant to LLM architecture and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
papers.tldr: The study reduces depth-recurrent language-model decoding memory by sharing key-value (KV) caches across recurrence iterations, with recurrent KV replay preserving performance close to separate-cache baselines.

papers.abstract: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.
bullets: Targets the large energy gap between unavoidable token-generation arithmetic and general-purpose GPUs, where memory movement and programmability dominate.
Keeps model weights and all users’ KV caches on-chip, with a datapath specialized to one loadable model architecture.
A pre-silicon design reaches 0.52 mJ per token—1.8× its co-designed arithmetic floor—and supports up to twelve users on-chip.
Compared with a measured NVIDIA B300 serving twelve users, it reports 110× higher per-user decoding speed and 690× lower energy.
Polyglot-DC extends the fixed architecture to distilled drafting, multilingual guarding, agent, and financial-reasoning models, with reported latency and benchmark gains.

On the Exstill design, the architecture is fixed in the silicon, the weights and every conversation are kept on the die beside the arithmetic, and only tokens enter and leave, a few bytes each (Section 3.2). papers.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
papers.tldr: Exstill co-designs a fixed-function 5 nm chip and language models to approach the arithmetic energy floor, achieving dramatically faster and more energy-efficient token generation while supporting multiple specialized workloads.

papers.abstract: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.
authors: Felipe A. Louza, Giovanni Manzini, Guilherme P. Telles
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth bottlenecks in repeated matrix-vector products by reducing stored and transferred data.
Partitions CSRV matrix data between RePair grammar compression and ans-fold entropy coding.
Further improves compression through row sorting, delta encoding, and contiguous alphabet remapping.
Experiments on word embeddings and transformer hidden states show greater compactness and lower peak multiplication memory than mm-RePair, with competitive multiplication times.
Combining the method with column reordering improves compactness on sparse matrices but substantially increases compression time; thread scaling remains comparable to mm-RePair.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the partitioning scheme. The integer sequence Sint is partitioned into two components: SA is compressed with RePair as in mm-RePair, and SB is encoded with ans-fold, while V is stored unchanged.

Figure 5: Compression pipeline of hybrid mm-RePair. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), and S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2). When criterion (1) holds, the identifiers of Sint are replaced by their ranks and the reverse mapping wcode is produced (step 3). The remapping is computed once on the whole sequence, so a single wcode serves both components, and it does not affect the partition, which depends only on digram frequencies. The sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), and SA is compressed with RePair into RA and CA (step 5). The rows of CA and of SB are sorted and delta encoded (ole) and entropy coded with ans-fold, as is wcode, while RA is stored as a packed array (step 6). The five blocks on the right form the compressed representation (RA, CA, SB, V ), plus wcode.

Figure 3: Compression pipeline of mm-RePair in its re-ans variant. The matrix is converted into its CSRV representation (V, S) (step 1), the sequence S is encoded as the integer sequence Sint (step 2), Sint is compressed with RePair, modified so that no rule contains the delimiter 0, into the rule set R and the final sequence C (step 3), and R is stored as a packed array while C is entropy coded with ans-fold (step 4). The compressed representation is the triple (R, C, V ), with V stored uncompressed.

Figure 6: The compression pipeline of hybrid mm-RePair on the matrix of Figure 1. To keep the example small, an incident digram occurring twice is enough here to keep an entry in SA. The CSRV sequence is encoded as Sint (steps 1–2). Criterion (1) holds, since |Sint| = 36, |Σ| = 12 and b = 4 give 36 · 28 > 32 · 12, producing wcode (step 3). The remapped sequence is partitioned into SA and SB (step 4), SA is compressed with RePair (step 5), and the rows of SB are sorted and delta encoded (step 6).

Figure 7: Relative improvement in compression ratio of re-pc, re-hybd and re-hybd-pc over reans, computed as (co − cr)/co, where co and cr are the compression ratios of re-ans and of the compared method.

Figure 2: The mm-RePair representation of the matrix of Figure 1. The top part shows the integer sequence Sint with m = 6, obtained by encoding $ as 0 and each pair ⟨ℓ, j⟩ as ℓm+ j+1, and the numbers above the cells are positions. The bottom part shows the rule set R and the final sequence C produced by RePair. Since no rule may contain 0, every delimiter remains in C, which also contains terminals, such as 10 in the first row and 1 in the second.

Figure 1: A matrix M (left) and its CSRV representation (V, S) (right). The array V holds the distinct nonzero values of M , and S is a single sequence of t+n symbols, obtained by scanning M row by row: each nonzero M [i, j] becomes the pair ⟨ℓ, j⟩ with V [ℓ] = M [i, j], and the delimiter $ closes each row. In S the pair ⟨2, 5⟩ of the second row denotes the value V [2] = 6.0 in column 5, while the same value in column 4 of the first row is the different pair ⟨2, 4⟩, since a pair identifies a value in a given column.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes hybrid compression strategies for matrix-vector multiplication to reduce memory footprint in iterative ML algorithms.
papers.title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
papers.tldr: A hybrid grammar–entropy compression scheme makes compressed matrix-vector multiplication more memory-efficient, especially for dense matrices with many distinct values.

papers.abstract: Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at https://github.com/brian030128/flipquant.
authors: Jian-Jia Chen, Brian J. Chan, Wen-Hung Lee, Yi-Ting Li, Po-Shen Chen, Kuan-Te Kuo, Hsien-Cheng Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Chi-Chih Chang, Mohamed S. Abdelfattah, Kai-Chiang Wu
bullets: Targets the accuracy gap of native 4-bit W4A4 NVFP4 inference versus BF16.
Learns a binary format map for each MMA weight tile using gradients from a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher.
Keeps both quantized candidates fixed while re-evaluating tile-format choices after each update.
Uses native 16×64 tiles on SM120 and 256×64 tiles on SM100, with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%.
Across six language models and two corpora, closes 42.5% of the NVFP4–BF16 PPL gap on average, versus 13.3% for FourOverSix.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hardware-native quantization method for efficient LLM inference, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
papers.tldr: FlipQuant learns hardware-compatible per-tile choices between E2M1 and E0M3 formats, substantially reducing NVFP4’s perplexity gap to BF16 with minimal GEMM overhead.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.
authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and inference-latency bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and packs indices into standard data types to remove redundant bits.
Shares codebooks across attention heads to reduce codebook storage while preserving accuracy.
Reaches sub-4-bit compression, down to 1 bit, with comparable perplexity.
Reports 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than prior VQ methods at comparable perplexity.
