papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression via variable-bit vector quantization for long-context LLM serving, directly fitting KV cache efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
papers.tldr: MeltKV compresses long-context LLM KV caches to as little as 1 bit while reducing memory use and decoding latency through alignment-aware variable-bit packing and shared codebooks.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but preserving accuracy with efficient training remains challenging. Scalar quantization encodes weights independently, while explicit-codebook vector quantization introduces costly search during training. We propose E8-QAT, a 2-bit quantization-aware training framework that uses the $E_8$ lattice as an implicit eight-dimensional codebook. It jointly quantizes weight groups through arithmetic projection without storing or searching an explicit codebook during the training forward pass. A 2-bit core encoding and sparse extension preserve the selected lattice points exactly, adding less than 0.1\% to core index storage. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, E8-QAT matches the performance of the full-precision model in terms of the average score across the four tasks. E8-QAT improves over the state-of-the-art baseline by 2.03\% on IFEval and by 1.51\% on LiveCodeBench, under the same data, schedule, and bit width. The 2-bit representation reduces peak memory by 80\% and supports a $4\times$ larger batch. At each representation's largest feasible batch, E8-QAT reaches $1.97\times$ the decoding throughput of BF16.
bullets: Uses arithmetic projection to jointly quantize weight groups without storing or searching an explicit codebook during training.
Employs a 2-bit core encoding with a sparse extension that adds less than 0.1% to core index storage.
On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, matches the full-precision model’s average score across four tasks.
Outperforms the stated baseline on IFEval and LiveCodeBench under matched training conditions.
Reduces peak memory by 80%, enables a 4× larger batch, and achieves 1.97× BF16 decoding throughput at maximum feasible batch size.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization-aware training for LLM memory reduction fits Efficient AI and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
papers.tldr: E8-QAT enables efficient 2-bit quantization-aware training by using the E8 lattice as an implicit codebook, preserving model performance while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
authors: Dayoon Ko, Yichuan Wang, Soyeong Jeong, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Gunhee Kim, Sewon Min
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but information-limited OCR indexing and slow full visual encoding for continuously arriving screenshots.
Uses pixel differences to prune redundant spatial tokens and reuse cached temporal key-value representations for unchanged regions.
A learned adapter preserves similarity to full-screenshot embeddings despite pruning and reuse.
On ScreenMemEval, it achieves up to 3.7× faster encoding without accuracy loss and up to 6.3 Recall@10 points over OCR at matched latency.
A memory-efficient index stores a simulated year of screenshots using 0.13 GB of RAM, supporting local visual screen-history assistants.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces StreamEmbed for real-time visual embedding using spatial token pruning and temporal KV reuse to handle screen history efficiently.
papers.title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval

papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
bullets: Targets agent sessions where context edits invalidate cached KV and delay decoding.
Uses invalidated KV to generate speculative drafts, then verifies them against the correct post-prefill KV before committing tokens.
Schedules speculation during underutilized decode capacity and preempts low-value speculation.
On a two-GPU testbed across three model families, achieved 1.05–1.19× all-request speedups over vLLM at moderate load.
Cluster-level simulations using real-world traces indicate the gains can extend to larger-scale deployments.

papers.selection_reason: LLM serving optimization that reuses invalidated KV cache for speculative decoding; fits KV-cache and inference-efficiency interests.
papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.tldr: Callo reduces cache-miss latency in disaggregated LLM serving by speculatively decoding with invalidated KV states and verifying drafts after exact prefill.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.
bullets: The 6.2 MiB recurrent state exceeds the FPGA’s 0.87 MiB on-chip memory, requiring external-memory paging.
Paging adds 26.0 MB of traffic per token, but accounts for at most 11.2% of calculated total cost; the state phase takes 13% of measured layer time.
The tile computes a complete layer of a 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model at 75 MHz, with one token taking 11.15 ms using synthetic weights.
Fixed-point hardware matches a fixed-point reference bit for bit; state logic also agrees across all 18 recurrent layers in simulation and all reported board tests.
The conclusion is scoped to this model and memory interface: weight delivery remains the decoding bottleneck.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware-efficient linear-attention LLM inference with paged recurrent state; directly fits efficient attention and memory-efficiency topics.
papers.title: The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon
papers.tldr: For this edge-FPGA Gated DeltaNet tile, paging the recurrent state is practical because weight delivery—not state paging—limits token-decoding performance.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.
authors: Haoyi Hu, Gaoyang Guo, Yunjia Xi, Wen Chen, Weiwen Liu, Jian Wu, Yuning Jiang, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the growing cost of directly processing long interaction histories in generative recommendation.
Uses bifurcated encoder-decoder compression with slot-wise forget-gated recurrent updates.
Trains memory with recommendation supervision and stream-consistency objectives for sequential-versus-packed processing.
Provides a horizon-independent discrepancy bound under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency.
On MerRec, 16 memory slots plus a 216-token context retain 87.9% of HSTU-1200’s Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200; archived distant history remains predictive.

papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
authors: AI Training Platform Team, Bingwei Zhang, Jing Li, Amir Abdullin, Sihang Chen, Xin Chen, Liangjun Feng, Yingmeng Gao, Tao Guo, Junjie Huang, Dongfang Li, Zhanglian Lin, Jiajun Liu, Zekun Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Xiaodong Luo, Jian Meng, Ivan Nosov, Linyuan Qiu, Weijian Sun, Wanrui Yan, Binfan Zheng, Zhicheng Zhou, Baotian Hu, Min Zhang, Haizhou Li, Zhiquan Luo

Supports evaluation of both trained models and custom optimization agents through model and model-harness modes.
Reproduces practical Ascend kernel execution pipelines and includes search orchestration with experience accumulation for model evaluation.
Introduces Speedup-Token Score (STS), combining performance gains and token cost under a budget.
Scope: the initial benchmark targets Ascend NPUs and kernel optimization rather than kernel generation.

papers.abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
authors: Yavuz Yetim, Bor-Yiing Su, Zhe Wang, Arthur Liu, Pranav Sharma, Ying Wang, Randy Shuai, Luke Pfister, Ruichao Xiao, Bill Zhao, Zihao Liu, Liyuan Li, Jiangyuan Li, Gaoxiang Liu, Nathan Yan, Geonhwa Jeong, Jatin Chhugani, Elias Ellison, Uladzimir Pashkevich
bullets: R&R models need very high throughput but tolerate almost no quantization-induced quality loss: NE must stay within 0.01% of baseline.
The study evaluates MXFP8 and 6-bit MXFP6 on AMD MI350X, including native MXFP6 GEMMs that quantize weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements.
Selective MXFP6 achieves end-to-end throughput gains of 1.5–5.3% on Model A and 7.6–14.3% on Model B relative to FP8 configurations.
Across supported linear layers, MXFP8 GEMMs are 1.33–1.55× faster than FP16, while MXFP6 reaches 1.73–1.99× and up to 2.90× on individual layers.
MXFP8 provides accuracy nearly equivalent to row-wise FP8, allowing the faster format to be selected by GEMM shape.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces microscaling formats for quantized inference, reducing memory and compute.
papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.tldr: Microscaling MXFP8 and MXFP6 enables substantial inference acceleration for production recommendation and ranking models while maintaining the strict required quality margin.

papers.abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting
bullets: Targets document QA, labeling, and evaluation workloads with many independent questions sharing one context.
Uses independent parallel decode streams plus a stream-ID attention mask so each answer attends only to the document and its own question.
Implemented in SGLang with lightweight code changes, dense-mask-free attention, and fixed-shape CUDA graphs.
For CodeLlama-7B workloads, it achieved 3.7× speedup on an A100 and 5.9–6.0× on an RTX A6000 versus stock SGLang.
Evaluation covered 144 identical-input runs across two GPUs, two SGLang releases, six workloads, and six input sets; it was faster in every run.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three ways to answer several questions about one document, shown at one decode step (dark: the token generated in this step). A serving engine such as SGLang or vLLM runs a batch of requests, and every decode step adds one token to each request. Batched requests with prefix caching store the document’s KV once but use one request per question, so every step reads the document once per question. Batch prompting (Cheng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024) puts all questions and answers in one sequence: it reads the document once, but the answers are generated one after another, and later answers attend to earlier ones. Parallel Prompting decodes the questions as streams of one request: every step adds one token per stream and reads the document once for all of them, and a stream mask (Figure 2) keeps the answers independent. The batch still has room for other requests, for example for other documents (Figure 6).

papers.selection_reason: Parallel decoding with shared context reduces memory bandwidth and inference cost, fitting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: Parallel Prompting accelerates multi-question LLM inference over the same long document by decoding all questions together while reading the shared KV cache only once per step.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache of autoregressive transformers grows linearly with context length and dominates memory at long context. Most training-free remedies evict low-importance tokens, an irreversible choice along the sequence axis. We instead keep every token and store it more cheaply along the "feature" axis. We therefore propose AttSVD, a new "interpretable" low-rank compression whose basis is derived from each prompt's own attention geometry: an online, per-prompt truncated SVD that keeps only the directions attention actually reads, cutting persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to the retained rank. We propose two decode-time caching strategies, accumulating and streaming, for short and long generation regimes. Furthermore, we propose two refinements that make compression adaptive. A per-matrix energy rule sizes the logit space and the attention mass independently. An attention-aware basis truncates only in the spaces attention actually reads, preserving both the attention logits and the attention output. The same factors also provide free, per-head interpretability insights into the effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. Across multiple models, on both an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite AttSVD stays on par with the dense cache while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache memory growth of long-context autoregressive transformers without evicting tokens.
Derives an online, per-prompt SVD basis from attention geometry and retains only attention-relevant feature directions.
Introduces accumulating and streaming decode-time caching strategies for short- and long-generation settings.
Uses independent energy-based rank selection and attention-aware truncation to preserve attention logits and outputs.
Matches dense-cache performance across multiple models, an agentic benchmark, and LongBench, with up to 50% KV-memory reduction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: AttSVD keeps a thin, compressed side cache of attention-aware factors A,B plus a small exact cache of recent tokens, cutting persistent memory to a fraction of dense while retaining all token positions. At decode, accumulating keeps every token exact (small decoded tokens); streaming compresses tokens leaving a sliding window, keeping the exact buffer bounded.

(a) At 50% cache the attention-aware keys (blue) lie almost on the full-attention target (black), while SVD on raw KV (red) distorts it. (b) Query-relevant logit error vs. cache size: attention-aware stays below SVD on raw KV at every budget (0.013 vs. 0.141 at 50%). Real-model analogue of Table 8.

papers.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
authors: Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
bullets: Targets memory capacity and bandwidth limits on resource-constrained edge devices.
Tunes GPTQ code distributions, then applies lossless Huffman coding in interleaved lanes.
Uses a small DRAM-to-L2 decoder, preserving existing deployed weight formats and GPU execution.
Across tested models, achieves 5.7–31.4% smaller weights within stated perplexity budgets.
Reports up to 36% lower latency and 38% lower energy per token on Orin, with larger gains under prompt-lookup speculation; also improves Nano performance and energy use.

papers.abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
authors: Wei Feng, Meiling Chen, Boxiao Chen, Lu Liu, Bin Zi, Libin Ye, Xingyu Lu, Lei Xu, Jun Zhou
bullets: Targets agent workloads that alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction.
Uses workload-based GPU-memory allocation, reference concurrency, and trajectory-aware routing to improve parallelism and cache reuse.
Introduces CAAS to prioritize progressing long chains when environment capacity is constrained.
Controlled replay enables ablation of the proposed optimizations.
Live evaluations report 10.4%–65.0% makespan reductions across four benchmarks, with aligned evaluation scores.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.
authors: Saehun Chun, Wonje Choi, Jinwoo Jang, Taeyoon Kwack, Honguk Woo

Tracks memory contents across action decisions and preserves KV states for unchanged information.
Reconciles only KV states affected by updates, supporting stable inference as task context evolves.
Evaluated on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments.
In the real-world setting, achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds versus MemRL.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.

Uses query-guided memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query.
Applies contrastive compressor learning with same-document, multi-query hard negatives to distinguish differing evidence needs.
Enables bidirectional attention among memory slots to improve information flow despite causal masking.
Outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
bullets: Addresses limited latent capacity for modeling fine details in complex 3D objects.
Uses continuous coordinate-based scene representations to tokenize arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference.
Explores trade-offs among compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality through ablations.
Achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits.
Also supports high-quality generative modeling with an autoregressive 3D generator.

papers.abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.
authors: Xuan Luo, Zhiyuan Wang, Hanzhong Cao, Xifeng Yan
bullets: Motivation: KV representations for the same token across neighboring layers share information and exhibit correlated changes.
Method: Store a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, then generate compact delta KVs for subsequent layers.
Variants: KVPath-Residual uses residual additions; KVPath-Rolling updates feature dimensions progressively.
Result: Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68% for GQA and 55% for MLA while maintaining or improving performance.

papers.title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers
papers.tldr: KVPath reduces Transformer KV-cache storage by representing later-layer KVs as low-dimensional updates to a shared base KV while preserving layer-specific states.

papers.abstract: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.
authors: Pierre-Luc Bacon, Diego Calanzone, Jean-Maxime Larouche
bullets: MoE offloading keeps most expert weights in CPU memory and transfers requested experts to the GPU.
Reducing routing switches is not a reliable proxy for reducing real transfer cost: faster fixed-set policies increased next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats.
When eviction is necessary, evicting the expert needed farthest in the future outperforms LRU.
The approach achieves 2.1× fewer copies than LRU, with no quality loss, and comes within 3.5% of the minimum possible copies.
Future demand from the next 16 tokens recovers 96% of the reduction; past-request counts recover only 27%.

Points at ∆NLL = 0 preserve every routing decision. papers.title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
papers.tldr: Expert eviction based on predicted future use can cut MoE CPU-to-GPU expert transfers by 2.1× versus LRU without changing routing or model quality.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.
VPR shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing.
The training-free method works directly on the KV cache without attention-map extraction or extra forward passes.
Static VPR improved 97 of 100 model–task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
It increased attention to answer-relevant image regions with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.

papers.abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
authors: Zahraa Selim, Menna Hamed, Wesam Ahmed, Sohyla Said, Sara Basheer, Rami Zewail
bullets: Addresses VRAM and bandwidth constraints that prevent co-locating models, vector indices, and KV caches on edge GPUs.
Finds GPTQ offers higher throughput but becomes unstable for contexts of 2048+ tokens, while NF4 provides more reliable long-context behavior.
Integrates Florence-2 vision processing with only 430 MB of additional VRAM.
Structured prompting reduces latency by 47% and improves quantization-affected mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
The complete architecture uses 8.37 GB of memory, targeting 12–16 GB GPUs, with evaluation focused on Turing hardware such as the Tesla T4.

papers.title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
papers.tldr: An edge-optimized multimodal RAG system combines NF4 quantization, decoupled vision processing, and structured prompting to fit robustly within 12–16 GB consumer GPUs.

papers.abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.
authors: Igor Sadalski, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Jones, Wojciech Matusik
bullets: Recasts algorithms as proof graphs whose assumptions are explicit and auditable.
Uses an LLM to relax one assumption, re-derive and re-prove the algorithm in Lean, then generate code.
Formalizes 89 algorithms spanning KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, and speculative decoding.
Improved on every evaluated published algorithm in KV-cache eviction and weight pruning.
Matched OpenEvolve within a point at equal budget, with lower repeat-to-repeat variability.

papers.selection_reason: Directly proposes algorithms for KV-cache eviction and weight pruning via assumption search, fitting efficient-AI methods for token/memory reduction.
papers.title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
papers.tldr: AutoAssumption searches over explicit algorithmic assumptions, using checked proofs to discover new ML-systems algorithms and achieve state-of-the-art results in KV-cache eviction and weight pruning.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$\mu$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).
authors: Anish Saxena, Hritvik Taneja, Christos Kozyrakis, Aamer Jaleel
bullets: HBF offers much higher capacity than HBM but its roughly 20× higher read latency can severely slow on-demand LLM inference.
SlipStream profiles repeatable weight-page demand order and uses a staging warp to prefetch pages through a producer-consumer pipeline.
Hardware retires tracking entries when demand first accesses a page, keeping prefetching closely paced with consumption and limiting lead distance.
Across seven dense models, SlipStream reaches 92.4% of ideal HBM-latency HBF performance with a 40 MB buffer, versus 43.1% for H3 with 320 MB.
A 16 MB buffer remains within 4% of the 40 MB configuration; SlipStream also reaches 91.2% of ideal performance on Mixture-of-Experts models.

papers.selection_reason: Targets LLM inference memory and latency overheads using prefetching and buffer management, fitting efficient memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
papers.tldr: SlipStream makes high-latency High-Bandwidth Flash practical for GPU-based LLM inference by using demand-paced, software-hardware co-designed prefetching with small, latency-independent buffers.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.
authors: Tek Raj Awasthi (Friedrich-Alexander-Universit\"at Erlangen-N\"urnberg), Babita Awasthi
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth-limited, one-token-at-a-time LLM decoding on Apple-silicon edge devices.
Uses Metal kernels that stream 2:4 compressed weights and expand them in registers, plus a fused decoder.
Achieves 3.6× over PyTorch-MPS and 1.52× over MLX on tested Qwen2.5-1.5B configurations; dense performance matches MLX.
Sparsity realizes 97% of the speedup theoretically enabled by reducing weight bytes, while prompt processing does not accelerate.
Combines Wanda pruning, block-wise reconstruction, and jointly trained 4-bit low-rank adapters to reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 3.01× to 1.34× dense.

papers.abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Logesh L, Aliyas Ahmad Misri
bullets: The approach stores 8-bit weights, initially decodes with the top 4 bits, and escalates uncertain steps using entropy or top-two margin thresholds.
In 36,724 replayed steps, low-precision uncertainty predicted argmax flips well (AUC 0.93); the margin gate caught 94% of flips at a 15% escalation rate.
On 150 live problems, the entropy gate scored 62.7% at 87% of all-high weight-byte cost, versus 64.0% all-high and 55.3% all-low.
Live paired differences did not clearly distinguish the entropy gate from either precision endpoint.
Quantization was simulated on Qwen3-0.6B and GSM8K; several controls and evaluations, including a second model and live KL, were not run.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic weight-bit escalation at uncertain decoding steps for efficient local LLM inference; relevant to memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model
papers.tldr: An uncertainty-triggered gate selectively reruns low-precision decoding at 8-bit, but on GSM8K its live accuracy was statistically indistinguishable from always-low or always-high precision.

papers.abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Logesh L, Aliyas Ahmad Misri
bullets: The study tests whether lower weight precision increases sensitivity to answer-option ordering under a fixed inference budget.
It evaluates simulated 8-, 6-, 4-, and 3-bit round-to-nearest quantization on two Qwen3 models across four multiple-choice benchmarks.
Six-bit quantization matches or slightly exceeds fp16 accuracy, while 4-bit quantization substantially increases answer-slot skew.
Averaging four cyclic option orders recovers 12.6 points at 4 bits for the 0.6B model, compared with 5.3 points at fp16.
Cost-matched comparisons favor extra orders over extra bits only at 6 bits or higher; findings are limited to two small models and a simple simulated quantizer.

papers.title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models

papers.abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.
authors: Haolin Jiang, Weihang Li, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jinwen Pan, Santosh Pandey, Hang Liu
bullets: Linear-attention queries, keys, and values concentrate in a stable low-dimensional subspace, making recurrent states effectively low-rank.
Dense state updates create substantial memory traffic that grows with batch size and can dominate decoding cost.
SinkState uses buffered updates, local SVD over the top subspace, and asynchronous CPU consolidation.
Across four hybrid models using Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet layers, it reduces recurrent-state peak memory by up to 2.6× and speeds decoding by up to 1.58× while maintaining accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.
authors: Zhikun Tao, Fangyong Jin, Junping Zhao
bullets: Across four updates, cache reuse retained useful task information but produced highly variable retrieval accuracy.
With source caches available, reuse delivered median time-to-first-token speedups of 2.10–5.08× on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks.
Functional Cache Divergence measures differences between next-token distributions from reused and native caches.
Reuse better preserved native behavior for natural-text continuation, while compatibility worsened with longer prefixes in single-token retrieval.
Matching the first generated token did not guarantee matching answers or stopping behavior.

papers.abstract: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.
authors: Linru Zhang, Xiangning Wang, Jun Jie Sim, Zhicong Huang, Jiahao Zhong, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam
bullets: Targets the computational overhead of secure LLM inference over encrypted inputs.
Uses a consistent column/diagonal packing evaluation flow to avoid expensive format conversions.
Introduces rotation-free Softmax and LayerNorm algorithms, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference.
Uses column packing and interleaved batching to reduce rotations in plaintext–ciphertext and ciphertext–ciphertext matrix multiplications.
Reports 52.8% lower evaluation time than THOR, 55.7% lower than Powerformer, and extension to LLaMA-3-8B.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek-V4.1's 203 GB of Engram n-gram tables sit in host DRAM today, taking 190 of the 223 GiB a 4-GPU serving process uses. Row indices depend only on input tokens, so reads can start with each step and overlap earlier layers. V4.1's two Engram layers have windows that differ by 30x (0.3 vs. 9.3 ms). We show that this deadline, together with session reuse and contention on a shared device, decides which tier each table can use and which layers need cache, and we give a model that predicts the resulting slowdown from measured read times. Agent and chat traffic reuse rows within sessions, and static hot sets transfer poorly. We build SlackTier, a table tier for SGLang that issues all lookups at step start. It reads the short-window layer first and splits a small GPU row cache across layers. The path runs inside the decode CUDA graph and is bit-exact with the original gather. Layer 14's table can go to NVMe uncached with no measurable decode cost. With both tables on four NVMe disks, mean time per output token on agent and chat replays rises at most 1.4% over unmodified SGLang, and host memory falls from 212 to 34 GiB. Both tables need no cache when read over RDMA (remote direct memory access) from another node's memory; one copy serves two instances. On a KV-constrained agent workload, using the freed memory as host KV cache at the same memory budget raises median throughput by 36% and cuts median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 s.
bullets: Engram table reads can begin at each decoding step and overlap earlier-layer computation, but layers have very different deadlines (0.3 ms versus 9.3 ms).
The proposed model accounts for deadlines, session reuse, and shared-device contention to select storage tiers and cache requirements.
SlackTier prefetches all lookups at step start, prioritizes the short-window layer, and partitions a small GPU row cache across layers within SGLang’s CUDA graph.
With both tables on four NVMe disks, agent and chat replays slow by at most 1.4% while host memory drops from 212 to 34 GiB.
Freed memory used for host KV cache improves median throughput by 36% and reduces median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 seconds on a KV-constrained agent workload.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces host memory and manages cache tiers for LLM serving, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Placing LLM Lookup Tables by Per-Layer Prefetch Deadlines
papers.tldr: SlackTier places LLM lookup tables according to per-layer prefetch deadlines, preserving near-baseline decoding while greatly reducing host-memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. We show that this makes prefix-cached agent serving metastable. With an identical base workload, a few minutes of extra arrivals leaves a vLLM server in a degraded regime--a ~10% hit ratio, about half the throughput, and a backlog that grows for the remaining 70 minutes--while its no-burst twin stays healthy (9 of 12 pairs; none in the reverse direction). The regime appears at loads the cache-warm server sustains, is absent without prefix caching, and also appears with Qwen3-32B on SWE-bench agent trace shapes and on SGLang, which tolerates larger triggers. Slower service keeps more sessions in the system, their working set outgrows the KV pool, and every turn becomes a recomputation; a first-order workload-balance condition, calibrated independently, brackets when the regime can drain. Getting out is the harder problem: throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 matched collapsed runs, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity-based limit recovered all of them within minutes. A CPU offload tier delays the collapse but does not prevent it. A budgeter that bounds the resident KV demand of active sessions to the pool, with thresholds that need no per-workload tuning, prevented the failure in every run we tested.
bullets: Closed-loop agents make cache misses expensive because growing contexts require recomputing 10–40K tokens instead of incremental prefill.
Brief arrival bursts can push vLLM into a metastable state with roughly 10% cache hits, half throughput, and persistent backlog; this occurred in 9 of 12 workload pairs.
The collapse arises when slower service retains sessions whose working set exceeds the KV-cache pool, making subsequent turns recompute their contexts.
Suspending admitted sessions recovered all tested collapsed runs, whereas throttling new admissions recovered only 1 of 7; CPU offload delayed but did not prevent collapse.
A workload-agnostic budgeter limiting active sessions’ resident KV demand to pool capacity prevented failure in every tested run and generalized across models and serving systems.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, yet caching full-context key-value (KV) states across layers and rounds severely bounds serving batch size. We design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) that achieves recurrent depth with zero round-wise KV growth, addressing where and how to loop an asymmetric stack in which only sparse encoder layers generate global KV. We find that recurrence must be placed in the encoder to iteratively refine global KV representations rather than re-reading static decoder projections, which both drives language-modeling gains and preserves long-context scaling. Furthermore, training the encoder loop under stochastic recurrence depth induces a fixed-point equilibrium where every round losslessly shares the last round's KV cache. Compounding cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing, the resulting Looped CED matches an unlooped CED's minimal memory footprint and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. To test serving at production scale, we loop the 552B-parameter DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node: with per-layer and per-round KV the loop cannot fit a single 128K-token request, whereas Looped CED holds 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 such requests (as many as the unlooped model), and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.
authors: Jiaqi Leng, Minshen Zhang, Zhaofeng Sun, Yu-Yang Qian, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang
bullets: Problem: Standard looped Transformers grow KV caches across layers and rounds, limiting batch size and long-context serving.
Method: Place recurrence in sparse encoder layers to iteratively refine global KV representations, and train with stochastic recurrence depth to encourage KV sharing across rounds.
Contribution: Cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing yields recurrent computation without round-wise KV growth.
Results: Looped CED recovers 86–93% of a looped Transformer’s gain using one-sixth the global KV, while matching an unlooped CED’s memory footprint.
At production scale, it uses 36.8× less KV per token, fits 38 128K-token requests on one node, and delivers 3.6× higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Looped causal encoder-decoder with recurrent depth and zero round-wise KV growth; directly targets KV-cache and memory-efficient LLM serving.
papers.title: Looping Deeper Without Growing the KV Cache: Recurrent Depth for Causal Encoder-Decoders
papers.tldr: Looped CED adds recurrent depth while keeping KV-cache memory effectively unchanged, enabling long-context serving at substantially higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.
authors: Susav Shrestha, Brad Settlemyer, Narasimha Reddy
bullets: Motivation: Existing data, tensor, and decode context parallelism approaches trade off KV-cache capacity, attention scalability, and cross-node communication.
Method: TKNP places one model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks, uses intra-node tensor parallelism for dense layers, and assigns each node’s requests to local KV-cache attention.
Communication: Only current-token activations cross nodes; dense all-reduces stay within NVLink domains, and attention avoids cross-node partial-result aggregation.

Evaluation: In vLLM experiments on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B using up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP achieved up to 1.7× the completion throughput of DCP and 2.06× that of data parallelism at matched GPU counts.
Scope: Results target long-context, high-concurrency decoding workloads.],

papers.selection_reason: Decode-pool architecture that shards KV cache and avoids cross-node attention aggregation, directly improving memory efficiency and LLM decoding throughput.
papers.title: Decode Token Parallelism: Memory-Efficient Distributed Attention Parallelism for Scalable LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP) improves long-context, high-concurrency LLM decoding by separating dense-layer weight placement from request-local attention ownership.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
bullets: The study compares REAP expert pruning with REAM expert merging across five web-hosting production tasks and two 30B-parameter MoE models.
At 25% expert removal, REAP preserves 93.6% of Qwen3-30B’s generative quality, versus 62.5% for REAM.
Across 20 matched comparisons, REAP performs significantly better in 16, while REAM does so in 2.
Most quality loss in email generation comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts, and runaway generation—not loss of content.
Cross-perplexity, logit divergence, and repetition-loop rates track production quality; n-gram diversity does not.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates expert compression methods for MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and memory optimization.
papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
papers.tldr: On multilingual production tasks, one-shot expert pruning substantially outperforms expert merging for compressing MoE LLMs, mainly by preserving required output formats and behavior.

papers.abstract: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.
bullets: Extends KV-Lingo beyond GQA to MLA latents, recurrent linear-attention states, and sparse-attention indexer keys.
Uses token-wise linear maps for MLA, corrected or replayed recurrences for linear-attention states, and predicted keys for sparse attention.
Across several 16–48B hybrid model pairs, transfers generally reach native or re-prefill quality in both directions.
Decoding token identities from MLA latents restores long-range needle recall, reaching 0.99 at 2–32K tokens and 0.83–1.00 at 64K.
At 64K context, transfer reduces time to first token by 18.7–46.8× versus re-reading; naive repeated translation fails.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering diverse, multi-level, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks.
Evaluates six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours.
Further improvements occurred in 135 of 150 runs during the second half of evaluation, showing shorter tests may miss progress.
Agents discovered solutions surpassing human-designed baselines; Claude Opus 5.5 improved mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86× on one task.
Trajectory analysis highlights task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained optimization.
