papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.
bullets: Targets the compute-heavy prefill phase and memory-bandwidth-limited decoding phase with different model sizes.
Uses a lightweight KV-stitching module with local layer mixing and separate nonlinear key/value mappings to reconcile cache differences.
Trains the translation module with both models frozen; optional low-rank adapters support further task adaptation.
Across six model pairs and five datasets, it outperformed matched-budget fine-tuned small-model baselines in all 30 settings and closed up to 80% of the quality gap to the large model.
Reported serving gains include 3.0× faster requests for an 8B-to-1B pair and simulated gains up to 33.86× faster with 27.5% lower energy for a 70B-to-1B pair.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache translation for heterogeneous prefill/decode; directly targets memory efficiency in LLM inference.
papers.title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
papers.tldr: BridgeKV accelerates LLM serving by using a large model for prompt prefill and a small same-family model for decoding, translating the large model’s KV cache between them.

papers.abstract: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and attention costs from long visual histories and candidate rollouts.
Uses planner-extracted constraints and text cross-attention to group relevant queries, then selects a single top-k set of high-value cache entries.
Training-free, operates independently per candidate, and preserves retained keys, values, and positions without extra video generation.
Across four backbones and three benchmarks, it supports 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation; on Causal Forcing, it reports a 1.22× speedup and 3.35× lower KV-cache memory.
At 0.7 compression on Causal Forcing, it reports a VBench score of 84.10 versus 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic KV cache compression for agentic autoregressive video generation; directly targets KV-cache memory and video generation efficiency.
papers.title: Semantically Aligned KV Cache Compression for Efficient Agentic Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: SemanticKV compresses KV caches for agentic autoregressive video generation by preserving entries most relevant to planner-specified semantic constraints, reducing memory and improving speed with minimal reported quality change.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd
bullets: Quantization, weight staleness, and injected noise introduce mismatch, but OPD quality degrades meaningfully only beyond an empirical mismatch budget.
Mismatch tolerance and quantization sensitivity vary across models and layers, with some layers especially vulnerable to reduced precision.
OPD stays stable under rollout settings that destabilize reinforcement-learning methods.
Weight noise can alter generated prefixes, causing errors that per-token corrections cannot fix.

A lightweight admission check screens rollout configurations; model-specific FP8 recipes support at least 1.93× more KV-cache tokens, while FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches equivalent quality 1.62× sooner than synchronous BF16.

figures.caption: Figure 8. REINFORCE broke under all three rollout configurations that OPD tolerates, and GRPO under two by step 200. Training accuracy (for GRPO and REINFORCE, mean 0/1 reward), smoothed over 11 steps. Each method uses different prompts, so compare it only with its own dashed standard-engine baseline.

Figure 7. At a memory-bound rollout batch, FP8 benefits from faster generation and saved KV-cache memory. The 7B student with 1,536 responses per step, 24 times the training batch. The lighter Model Optimizer FP8 bar is not decomposed. Values: App. Table 9.

papers.title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation remains robust to substantial training–inference mismatch, enabling faster and more memory-efficient rollout systems until a model-specific tolerance budget is exceeded.

papers.abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.
bullets: Targets long-context inference where the KV cache exceeds GPU HBM and host-memory transfers dominate latency.
Keeps query-agnostic pivotal tokens and a token-level sketch on the GPU, while storing the full cache in CPU memory.
Uses PoissonComp for pivotal-token sampling and KVFetch to verify attention error against a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance.
Fetches additional CPU-resident tokens only when the tolerance cannot be met locally.
Reports 90–100% of dense quality at 32K context, with 8–32× lower GPU memory use and 2–23% cache fetched per generated token across the evaluated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VERKV. The GPU holds query-agnostic pivotal tokens (deterministic and stochastic) and a sparse attention indexer (sketch), while the full KV cache resides in CPU memory. An error-estimation module uses the pivotal tokens and sketch to decide whether the approximation already meets a user tolerance (ϵ, δ); if not, a query-aware fetch recovers additional tokens from the host so that the final attention is guaranteed to have error (ϵ, δ).

Figure 3. Quality vs. compression rate. Average quality of different compression setups across the RULER and LOFT benchmarks at context lengths of 32K and 128K for three models. We observe that (1) POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) consistently outperforms KVzip, and (2) VERKV(C=KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) = POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) + KVFETCH improves upon POISSONCOMP under all settings. (3) Relative to dense attention, quality is better preserved at shorter context lengths for a given compression rate, for the Qwen family compared to Ministral, and on RULER compared to LOFT. In particular, VERKV recovers near-dense quality on RULER-32K across all three models. Our algorithm currently uses a naive 2-bit sketch to bootstrap its estimates; improving sketch accuracy is a promising direction for further quality gains as can be seen with VERKV(C=KVzip, A=perfect sketch) which matches Dense in nearly every setting. Host traffic for these runs is reported per generated token in Table 1 and per forward pass in Table 2.

Figure 7. Decode throughput, time per output token and time to first token vs. batch size in vLLM (Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K and RULER-128K, 16×, δ = 0.05). At 32K, VERKV stays ahead of Dense (offload) at every batch size, and its throughput grows from 13.8 to 20.6 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.05 and from 26.8 to 42.4 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.5, while Dense (offload) is bound by PCIe and stays near 9 tokens/s. The gain from batching is small because the decide kernel saturates shared memory and runs the requests of a batch one after another. At 128K, VERKV at ε0 = 0.05 approaches Dense (offload) as the batch grows, whereas ε0 = 0.5 keeps a 4–5× advantage. Fast KVzip is fastest throughout but loses most of its quality (Table 1).

Figure 6. Quality vs. speed in vLLM. VERKV(C=Fast KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K at 16×, sweeping ε0 at δ = 0.1 against dense attention with the cache offloaded to host memory. At the default ε0 = 0.05, VERKV decodes 1.6× faster and cuts end-to-end latency by 5 s at near-dense quality; larger ε0 trades a few points of quality for up to 3× throughput, with gains flattening once fetching becomes negligible.

papers.title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive action generation on resource-constrained robots.
Uses a lightweight retrieval-augmented draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without an additional neural draft model.
Reduces verification overhead through kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention.
Introduces the Zora core to accelerate irregular memory access during retrieval.
On four VLA models using LIBERO, it retains comparable accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× software-only and 7.6× hardware-supported speedup over GPUs.

Partial similarity scores are accumulated and then consumed by either the reduction unit for greedy search in upper HNSW layers or the comparison units for top-k selection in the bottom layer. Lastly, the neighbor index fetch unit updates the search frontier for unvisited nodes.

papers.abstract: Small hand-tracking networks are deployed as 4- and 8-bit codes, and they should keep adapting to a user's camera after deployment, on the device and within roughly the memory of the model itself. Quantization-aware training cannot do this cheaply, because it keeps a 32-bit master copy of every weight together with its optimizer state, about 96 bits per weight. Training the codes directly with stochastic rounding needs no copy but injects rounding noise at every step, and the methods that remove this noise keep a residual buffer for every weight. We introduce sensitivity-gated accumulator caching (SGAC), which keeps residual state for only a small and changing set of weight groups. A set-associative cache of 8-bit accumulators collects the sub-step updates of the groups with the largest Fisher-weighted squared code step and writes them into the codes as whole steps; an evicted line is flushed by stochastic rounding, and a group without a line does not move until it is admitted. We prove that the write-back is unbiased and show, under a local quadratic model, that rounding a sub-step update costs loss of the same order as the update's own gain, so that rounding pays only where the expected gradient is large relative to the curvature. On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, SGAC trains with 8.1 bits of state per weight. Scored on the 4/8-bit network that the device runs after adaptation, it has the highest mean accuracy of nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras. On twelve ImageNet-C corruptions it has the highest average of corrupted and clean accuracy of seven deployed methods, ahead of the PEQA-style, ECO-style and direct low-bit baselines with confidence intervals that exclude zero, and it matches an 8-bit accumulator kept for every weight with 56% of that state.
bullets: Targets post-deployment learning within roughly the model’s memory budget, avoiding full-precision master weights and per-weight residuals.
Uses an 8-bit set-associative cache guided by Fisher-weighted squared code steps; cached updates are written back as whole steps, while evictions use stochastic rounding.
Theoretical analysis shows unbiased write-back and that sub-step rounding costs are controlled by update gain relative to local curvature.
On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, it uses 8.1 state bits per weight and achieves the highest mean accuracy among nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras.
Across twelve ImageNet-C corruptions, it has the highest combined corrupted/clean accuracy among seven methods and matches a full 8-bit accumulator with 56% of its state.

papers.abstract: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.
bullets: Static collective-communication heuristics work well without contention but degrade under background traffic.
A detector uses an LSTM classifier with a sequential probability ratio test to distinguish sustained contention from transient spikes.
A selector uses Dueling Double DQN with Conservative Q-Learning to adapt communication configurations.
Implemented over NCCL, the method reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over fully converged AutoCCL on an isolated Chameleon Cloud cluster.
Across six AI workloads, it achieves up to 65% speedup on a Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 networking.

papers.abstract: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.
bullets: The work addresses the inefficiency of using the same number of iterative computations for every decision.
AIC jointly learns action selection and when to stop refining, using an expected-depth penalty and intermediate value predictions.
With up to eight refinement steps, it averages 3.3 steps across twelve benchmark tasks.
On four control and robotics tasks, AIC reduces per-decision latency by 31–44% versus a fixed eight-step policy.
AIC beats the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four; stopping and value supervision contribute differently across tasks.

papers.tldr: Adaptive Internal Computation lets reinforcement-learning policies spend more reasoning on difficult states and less on easy ones, reducing latency while often preserving or improving reward.

papers.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM. Code is available at https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ .
bullets: Targets low-precision weights and activations to reduce neural-network inference memory and compute costs.
Uses per-channel scaling and online block-Hadamard activation transforms, with inverse transforms absorbed into weights.
Introduces Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent method that adjusts individual FP4 codes beyond round-to-nearest quantization.
Adds 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM and matches competing methods’ best Llama-3-8B perplexity using 11× less quantization time.
Its layer-local design supports streaming quantization, diffusion models, and a 122B-parameter model using 32.5 GB GPU RAM in 64 minutes.

papers.abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.
bullets: Offline, it fits key normalization and K/V codebooks to preserve the frozen model’s projected attention output.
It estimates channel sensitivity from squared gradients of a reference next-token loss, then scores KV states by sensitivity-weighted reconstruction error.
Online, it stores the highest-scoring token key-value states at FP16 under per-layer, per-KV-head budgets.
With 56 extra FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, d8b8 outperforms evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines across seven benchmarks and three models.
The d8b10 variant narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90–2.01 points at a nominal 1.25 bits per channel; the theory bounds selection risk under exact restoration.

(b) During inference, sensitivityweighted reconstruction errors rank historical KV states for FP16 retention, with up to N anchors per layer and KV head. Attention combines decoded history, restored anchors, and unquantized recent and live K/V. The nominal 1-bit rate refers to codeword indices.

papers.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
bullets: Targets unified-memory systems-on-chip, which existing datacenter and local inference engines do not fully exploit.
Uses model surgery to reduce model memory footprint and data movement.
Preserves agent state across turns, enabling instant resumption without recomputation.
Applies adaptive speculation to generate multiple tokens per decoding step.
On a DGX Spark with models up to 125B parameters, achieves up to 3.4× more agentic tasks per hour and 3.9× higher decoding throughput than established frameworks.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
bullets: Targets memory overhead from concurrent environments and delays from slow tool calls.
Combines shared environment state, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution.
Introduces BunshinFork, which supports live whole-workspace forks with copy-on-write memory, preserved state, and rollback.
Implemented via Linux kernel-module and CRIU modifications.
Reports up to 43% lower peak memory, 51% lower total memory, and 23% lower end-to-end rollout latency.

figures.caption: Figure 4. BunshinFork architecture. A brief freeze captures a consistent workspace state. The live fork path reconstructs isolated clones that share unchanged pages copy-on-write and allocate private pages on writes. Retained snapshot holders support asynchronous serialization, allowing the source to resume without waiting for disk writes.

Figure 3. Illustration of BunshinRL. Right shows two samples in a simplified rollout step; left shows the on-disk and in-memory workspace snapshot stores for tool call prefix. Reasoning steps’ generated tool call signatures are matched with the tool prefix tree. All initial matched tool calls are skipped until the first miss in tool signature (Tool 3 for R1 and Tool 4 for R2), at which point the corresponding snapshots are used to reconstruct the workspaces. As C3 is not cached in memory, Tool 3 is replayed for R2 and its delta write is added to the C0+C1+C2 snapshot. The samples execute actual Tool 3 for R1 and actual Tool 4 for R2, creating new delta CoW pages. After these calls finish, speculation starts from the resulting workspaces: Tool 4 for R1 and Tools 5 and 6 for R2. The Spec Tool Selector selects tool calls that are likely to happen from previous tool call history. When a reasoning step finishes, its output tool signature is compared with the speculative tool signature. For failed speculation, the system rolls back to the workspace snapshot before speculation.

Figure 5. Linux Process Fork vs. BunshinFork Process-Tree Fork. Left: native fork() duplicates one process as a child of the source process. Right: BunshinFork creates a sibling container and reconstructs the whole process tree inside an independent namespace.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

papers.abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is constrained by GPU memory. This constraint is mitigated by expert offloading, which stores part of the model's weight in host memory and executes on demand. Though MoE architecture has computation sparsity, more GPUs are needed for serving increasingly larger frontier models. However, existing expert offloading systems overlook this need and fail to scale performance with additional GPUs. We present AdaOffload, a general and efficient multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework that effectively handles heterogeneous hardware and workloads. We co-design GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation that adapts to different hardware, workload, and batch size heterogeneity. We evaluated AdaOffload on five different platforms with varying GPU capability (L4, Pro6000, B200), number of GPUs, CPU capability, and NUMA topology on three different frontier open-weight models (284B to 753B). AdaOffload achieves $1.9\times$ to $15.5\times$ throughput speedups across different models over state-of-the-art systems.
bullets: Targets GPU-memory limits and poor scalability of existing expert-offloading systems as models and GPU counts grow.
Uses a multi-GPU hybrid execution framework that adapts online to hardware, workload, and batch-size heterogeneity.
Co-designs GPU–CPU parallelism and co-execution for both decode and prefill phases.
Evaluated across five hardware platforms and three frontier open-weight models ranging from 284B to 753B parameters.
Reports 1.9×–15.5× throughput speedups over state-of-the-art systems across evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
authors: Dayou Du, Woon Yee Ng, Guangming Sheng, Nick Lau, Jianyi Cheng, Luo Mai
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Uses dual-residual query quantization, underflow-aware probability scaling, and outlier-aware key quantization to reduce FP4 accuracy loss.
Removes softmax overhead with transposed softmax, fused probability quantization, and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches.
Stays within 0.5 accuracy points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 and within 1 point with MXFP4 across dense and MoE models.
On NVIDIA B300, achieves 2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV for Qwen3 models.

papers.abstract: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
authors: Donglin Zhuang, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Xiaoxia Wu, Shuaiwen Leon Song, Zhongzhu Zhou
bullets: Targets decode attention, where quantized KV caches reduce memory traffic but can remain latency-bound by dequantization overhead.
Uses affine folding tailored to token-wise or channel-wise quantization, preserving the exact dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic.
Employs bit manipulation and warp-specialized Hopper/Blackwell GPU pipelines to efficiently feed quantized operands to Tensor Cores.
Reports substantial kernel speedups on H100 and B200 against BF16, FP8, and, in some cases, NVFP4 baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves peak aggregate throughput on long-context serving workloads by up to 170% versus 2-bit and 341% versus 16-bit baselines.

papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.
authors: Kazi Hasan Ibn Arif, JinYi Yoon, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Hans Vandierendonck, Deepu John, Bo Ji
bullets: Prefix caching accelerates multi-turn LLM serving by reusing key-value states, but reuse is difficult to predict.
User intent correlates with conversation continuation probability and inter-turn delay.
IAC classifies requests, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent logs, and applies an oracle-inspired online eviction policy.
On WildChat and ShareChat, IAC achieves a 34.6% cache hit rate versus 18.8% for a prior learning-based method and 12.2% for LRU.
IAC reduces average serving latency by up to 46.1%.

papers.abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.
bullets: Runs lower layers normally, predicts later-layer inputs, and fills their caches while preserving selected rows, recent tokens, and all decoding steps exactly.
Fits each prediction map once in closed form from calibration text, making the approach training-free and applicable to models not designed for cache filling.
Evaluation finds that keys dominate error on Llama-3.1-8B, while values and recurrent state matter more on Qwen3.5-9B.
On evaluated systems, prefill speed improves 1.25–1.31× at 16K–120K tokens and 1.50–1.60× at 9K–32K tokens.
Quality changes are generally small but uncertain: reported benchmark shifts include roughly 1–1.4 point decreases, while some needle tasks remain near exact performance.

Figure 4. Why the correction matters only on layers that remember. A prompt row’s weight in a Gated DeltaNet layer’s final state is the product of the gates after it; tan is the filled prefix and blue the exact tail. (a) With gates of 0.90, the filled rows’ share of the final state is about 0.005. (b) With gates of 0.995 it is 0.65. Illustrative: 200 rows, the last 50 exact. The share shown is the share of the state the tail ends with, not ρ at the end of the prefix (§2.3).

Figure 5. The two-sweep prefill on Qwen3.8-27B, split at layer 16. (1) The first sweep runs layers 0 to 15 for every row and writes the prefix rows’ late attention caches from the maps; the tail and the late Gated DeltaNet layers are not yet computed. (2) The probe: the last 256 rows run the exact late layers over the filled cache, with the Gated DeltaNet layers starting from an empty state, and every prefix row is ranked by the attention it receives from them. (3) The second sweep runs the late layers for the chosen rows and the tail, and carries the Gated DeltaNet state once over every prefix row; the other rows keep their filled attention caches.

Figure 1. Speculative decoding and RidgeFill each spend the resource their phase has spare. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so a draft head spends the spare compute guessing tokens and the full model verifies every guess. Prefill reuses each weight read across hundreds of prompt rows, so it is limited by arithmetic. RidgeFill spends the spare bandwidth on extra reads, the fill maps from VRAM or host memory, and in return skips most of the late layers’ arithmetic. A filled cache has no affordable verifier, so the rows most likely to matter are kept exact instead (§2.4).

Figure 6. How the probe’s budget is set. The base rules, the rarer half of the protected-class matches, every digit token, and the top 20 % of the prefix by lower-layer question attention, are used only to count E, the number of exact prefix rows. The probe fills E with the rows that receive the most late-layer attention from the last 256 rows; lexical-net rows are reserved inside E, at most 5 % of the prefix. Special tokens are added on top, and the 4,096-token tail is outside the count. On the 27B timing prompts E came to 28 to 31 % of the prefix.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free late-layer cache fill accelerates prefill and reduces computation, fitting memory/cache efficiency.
papers.title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
papers.tldr: RidgeFill accelerates long-context prefill without retraining by using a one-pass ridge-regression map to predict late-layer cache inputs, delivering up to 1.6× speedups with modest, uncertain quality changes.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
bullets: Targets the memory–computation tradeoff in large language model training.
Uses information from the original forward pass to guide approximate rematerialization.
Selects components via greedy selection or randomized sketching.
Ablations find gradients closely match exact gradients.
In a Llama-488M model, recomputing two-thirds of feed-forward, attention, or both layer components raises perplexity by 1.7%, 1.2%, or 2.5%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
authors: Andras Szecsenyi, Thomas L. Lee, Vaisakh Shaj, Elliot J. Crowley, Amos Storkey
bullets: Targets the memory bottleneck of long-context inference on local consumer devices, where KV caches can exceed model weights.
Replaces standard key/value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck and stores packed, metadata-free integer codes.
Adapts pretrained transformers by retraining only the key/value projections using 0.25 tokens per original parameter.
Across 0.6B–8B models, it is the most accurate evaluated method on RULER at 12×–97.5× compression.
A fused Triton decoder reaches near-native SDPA throughput at 32× compression and 1.54× native throughput at 97.5× on Qwen3-8B-Base.

papers.title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
papers.tldr: Transformer-FSQ enables extreme KV-cache compression by storing each token as discrete integer codes while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy and near-native decoding speed.

papers.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
bullets: Targets single-stream inference, where weights must be streamed from memory for each generated token and batching is unavailable.
Introduces dtANS-LLM, which exploits non-uniform weight distributions that remain after quantization.
Auto-tunes tensor- and GPU-specific parameters to balance compression ratio and decoding latency under a memory budget.
Integrates with vLLM and reports speedups on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint on two GPUs.
Scope: results focus on single-stream inference and the evaluated Llama checkpoint/GPU configurations.

Figure 2: Overview of the performance-critical mvm kernel. Compressed data is fetched and decoded into weights which are used in place for fused matrix-vector multiplication with activations.

Figure 3: Evaluation of MINE (blue) and other inference engines on checkpoints of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and two GPUs (left and right half). Columns state quantization method, checkpoint (CP), size of dequantization side streams, entropy bits per weight, achieved bits per weight, and single-stream (batch 1) steady-state decode throughput.
