papers.selection_reason: Entropy-coded memory-efficient LLM inference directly reduces model memory requirements and speeds up deployment.
papers.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MINE accelerates memory-bound single-stream LLM inference through GPU entropy coding that compresses and decodes weights losslessly.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.
authors: Siyuan Yan, Shen Gu, Xiaoxing Ma, Chun Cao, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets two inference costs: growing historical-prefix attention and repeated processing of mostly unchanged generation positions.
Uses prefix KV sparsity by selecting a compact, cross-step-stable subset of historical keys and values.
Uses early query sparsity to predict which positions will update, then runs only their queries through deeper Transformer layers.
Training-free and evaluated at 32K context length.
Reports end-to-end/per-step speedups of 1.34×/2.83× on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41×/4.72× on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Duet. (A) Block-level prefix selection: After the first dense step, Duet selects a compact historical prefix subset for each sparse suffix layer and reuses the resulting KV cache within the generation block. (B) Step-wise query selection: in subsequent denoising steps, Duet identifies active query rows at an early selection layer and propagates only these rows through the remaining Transformer layers, reducing redundant computation in both attention and FFN/MoE. Active and bypassed states are then recombined for the next denoising step.

Figure 4: Inference speedup across context lengths. End-to-end and stable-step speedups over dense inference on LLaDA2.1-mini and SDAR-8B at 8K, 16K, and 32K context lengths. Stable-step latency averages all denoising steps except the first step, highlighting the execution efficiency of sparse decoding. Duet achieves increasingly larger speedups as the context grows and consistently provides the strongest stable-step acceleration among the compared methods.

Figure 3: LongBench quality–throughput trade-off. Five-task Macro-F1 relative to each model’s dense score (100%) versus 32K end-to-end throughput. Absolute Macro-F1 scores are reported in Table 1; task-wise results appear in Appendix Table 4.

Figure 1: Illustration of different sparsity patterns in BDLM inference. FOCUS only reduces computation along the query dimension, whereas LoSA only sparsifies the historical prefix. Our method is designed around the two orthogonal computation dimensions, selectively reducing both the query rows propagated through deep layers and the historical prefix KV states they attend to.

Figure 5: Two sparsity opportunities in BDLM inference. (a) A compact prefix subset selected at the beginning of a generation block continues to cover most of the prefix-attention mass throughout denoising. (b) Intermediate representations can identify, with high recall, the positions selected by the final-layer decoding policy. Results are shown on LLaDA2.1-mini as a representative example.

Table 4: Task-wise results on LongBench. We report F1 (%) on five long-context tasks and Macro-F1, the unweighted average across tasks. For LoSA, parentheses give the measured average number of attended prefix KV tokens per task; the Macro-F1 column gives the mean of these five KV counts. Higher F1 is better.

Table 2: Generation quality on short-context benchmarks. We report accuracy (%) on GSM8K, MMLU, and MATH-500, and pass@1 (%) on HumanEval. For LoSA, parentheses give the average number of selected KV tokens per task. Higher is better.
Table 1: LongBench Macro-F1 (%). Column headings give nominal prefix budgets. For LoSA, parentheses give measured prefix KV counts, which can exceed those budgets. Higher is better.

Table 3: Detailed inference efficiency results. E2E is end-to-end latency in seconds; Step is stable-step latency in milliseconds; Steps is the mean number of decoding steps per sample. Lower latency is better.

papers.selection_reason: Directly targets efficient inference for diffusion language models via prefix KV sparsity and query sparsity.
papers.title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Duet accelerates block diffusion language model inference by sparsifying both historical attention and current-step query computation while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
authors: Chiang Qin Zhi, Ranjan Satapathy, Erik Cambria, Joyjit Chattoraj
bullets: Targets finance-specific challenges including low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and costly autoregressive decoding.
Uses a lightweight 2.68M-parameter backbone with grouped-query attention to reduce Key-Value cache memory-bandwidth overhead.
Reports inference acceleration of up to 48.1% compared with existing state-of-the-art time-series foundation models.
Across multi-asset, multi-resolution benchmarks, matches larger baselines’ predictive fidelity and is more resilient during high-volatility periods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TailDART architecture. Each decoder block applies pre- and post-RMSNorm with a residual add around a grouped-query attention sublayer and a feed-forward sublayer. The dense model uses a GeLU-gated MLP; the MoE variant routes each token to one of three experts (top-1).
Figure 2: Scaling behavior of dense andMoETailDART. Lower validation NLL is better in all panels.
Table 3: Asset-level comparison of TailDART and Lag-Llama. Δ is the percentage change from Lag-Llama to TailDART.
Table 2: Performance of TailDART against baselines.
Table 1: Base and continued-pretraining datasets

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight financial time-series foundation model with grouped-query attention reduces KV cache memory and inference latency, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
papers.tldr: TailDART is a compact financial time-series foundation model designed to deliver competitive forecasting with substantially lower inference latency.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CascadeRec architecture. Tier-1 reranks every request and emits a confidence signal. The router accepts the Tier-1 ranking or escalates the request to Tier-2.
Figure 2: Production request path. The router escalates a minority of requests to the Tier-2 pool. Any LLM failure falls back to the best earlier ranking (dashed red). Orange boxes are LLM inference.
Figure 3: Cost and quality on MovieLens-1M: aggregate NDCG@10 against average tokens per user, with values from Table 2. The dashed line marks B0.
Table 2: Aggregate results (1,000 users per dataset). Bold: best NDCG@10 per dataset. Underline: best within each LLM group. Esc.: share of escalated users. Tok: average tokens per user.
Table 1: NDCG@10 by cold-start bin (200 users per bin). ∗: the 95% paired-bootstrap CI of the delta vs. B0 excludes zero. CR uses τ=5, so bins with k ≤ 5 are escalated.
Table 4: Output-compliance failure rates in the offline matrix: the share of requests whose LLM output had no parseable ranking. Such requests fall back silently.
Table 3: First-stage retrieval quality on MovieLens-1M (iALS fold-in). R@10 bounds what head-10 reranking can change. R@100 bounds any reranker on this candidate set.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a cascade architecture for LLM reranking that reduces inference cost by routing requests based on user history, demonstrating a practical efficiency strategy.
papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.
bullets: The study tests compression by evaluating both a frozen SAE on compressed activations and an SAE retrained on them.
Feature retention after retraining has no clear universal scale: compression effects can be smaller or larger than changing the random seed.
Frozen-SAE correlation broadly follows codec precision, but simple L2 distance gives nearly the same ranking and does not transfer consistently across sites.
The authors calibrate each site using identical-byte retraining as a ceiling and reseeding as a floor, requiring four training runs and two evaluation passes.

At research-scale budgets, naive per-token int4, PCA, and random projection can underperform reseeding; channel standardization improves int4, while bf16 can lose slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Retrained agreement against perturbation size. Blue: calibrated isotropic noise, fp32 on both sides; orange: real codecs; star and diamond: one ulp on one scalar and on a millionth of them; the shaded band marks fp32’s own precision, below which no dense fp32 noise can go. Retraining barely responds to the size of tiny perturbations but separates the real codecs clearly. GPT-2 L6, seed 0; the fp16-scale noise and the millionth-of-values change were each run three times and are plotted at their original run.

Figure 3: Agreement as a multiple of each site’s own seed floor, against measured bits per dimension, 1× budget (33M token-visits on GPT-2, 24.6M on Pythia). Filled markers: fp16 and the rotated codecs; hollow: naïve per-token at the same rate. The dotted riser is the effect of standardizing and rotating at identical bytes (on GPT-2, standardizing alone gives the same, Table 18), and at 4 bits it spans the floor at every site. Read the ordering, not the levels: at 10× budget rot-int4’s ratio is 1.09×. Pythia’s fp16 is its own bf16 master, so it is omitted there.

Figure 4: Agreement on a fixed-size stable set (N = 774, the 1× tier’s stable-feature count, taking the top N by cross-seed stability at each budget) against training budget; error bars are binomial standard errors. fp16 is flat; the rotated codecs improve, so the gap does not widen.

Figure 5: The frozen-SAE reading against the retraining it stands in for, at three sites; the x axis is frozen disagreement 1 − r, log scale, improving rightward. Every series is monotone (the frozen SAE ranks codecs correctly), but the series are offset from each other (the same reading corresponds to different retained percentages at different sites); the viable codecs crowd into a span a linear axis would collapse to a point. Dotted lines are each site’s seed floor. Pythia’s fp16 point is omitted: the bf16 master makes it bit-lossless.

Figure 1: GPT-2 layer 6, seed 0: one ulp on a millionth of values already costs three quarters of fp16’s loss, so the count needs a floor. Bars: alive features a retrained SAE recovers at best match r > 0.9 (grey: control; blue: tiny perturbations; orange: real codecs); dashed line: seed floor.

Table 1: Full GPT-2 codec panel. ± rows are three-seed means (± half the range), bare cells seed 0, so fp16 reads 59.3 ± 1.1 here and 60.6 (seed 0) in the text. survived: best match above r = 0.9 against fp32 at the same seed; FVU: fraction of variance unexplained; mean r: the retrained SAE’s best-match correlation, averaged over alive features (not the frozen reading); stable: survival among the 774 features reproduced in both other fp32 seeds; Hung. cos: mean matched encoder and decoder cosine over all latents, dead ones included; frozen: the thresholded reading through the frozen fp32 SAE. FVU is flat across every viable codec (0.1355 to 0.1361) while seed-0 agreement falls from 60.6 to 37.6%. The floor row’s FVU is the fp32 reference’s own, and its Hungarian cosine averages the two seed-0 pairs.
Table 13: Ratio to floor as the counting threshold moves. Levels change with the threshold; the ordering and the below-floor verdict for naïve int4 do not.

Table 14: The noise levels and sparse changes (seed 0; pp/decade is the change in agreement per decade of relative L2 to the next row): isotropic noise at an exact relative L2 and one-ulp changes to a fixed count of values, all stored in fp32 on both sides. Everything from n = 77 to 15,335 is flat; the one-value change also differs in when it reaches training (Appendix J). The fp16-scale noise and the millionth-of-values change were re-run twice with fresh randomness (60.6/60.4/60.8 and 70.5/69.7/71.6%); the table prints the original runs.

Table 16: How far the two smallest perturbations sit above the seed floor at each counting threshold. The margin is positive everywhere (11–43 pp dense, 12–47 sparse) but its size is thresholddependent.

Table 22: Predicting per-feature survival from fp32 statistics. CV AUC: a logistic model on all three, 5-fold cross-validated; the other columns are single-statistic AUCs. Mean activation is the strongest single predictor, unlike the peak activation reported for weight quantization.

Table 28: The frozen-SAE test explained by TopK margins (GPT-2 layer 6, the frozen test’s own SAE and tokens). model: Spearman correlation, over alive features, between predicted and measured frozen disagreement 1 − r; the prediction uses only the second moment of the codec’s error, estimated on held-out tokens, and the SAE’s margins on clean activations. statistic: the largest |ρ| of log firing rate, log mean or log peak activation with 1− r. crossing %: median share of a degraded or damaged feature’s squared error that comes from tokens where it is active on one side only (–: not reported for the noise-like codecs, which have at most 6 degraded or damaged features each). Below the rule, codecs that remove part of the signal rather than add noise. Sources: geom_margins.json, geom_summary.json.

Table 29: Predicting from one SAE which features retraining recovers (GPT-2 layer 6, AUC). Above the rule the target is seed stability (best match r > 0.9 in both other seeds); the logistic model is fit once on the 1×, k = 32 SAE (its row is cross-validated) and applied unchanged to the other regimes’ own SAEs. Below the rule, the same seed-fit model predicts which features survive retraining on each codec. positive %: seed-stable or retained share of alive features. statistics: log firing rate, log mean and log peak activation. geometry: co-firing share with the best partner, decoder coherence, co-firing of the nearest decoder atom, TopK margin relative to the activation, encoder-decoder cosine. Predictors use held-out eval tokens. Source: geom_identifiability.json.

Table 8: The alive cut, swept. Tightening it raises agreement and the floor together and lowers rotint4’s ratio monotonically (1.63 to 1.13× on GPT-2); our 0.001 cut is the loosest of the five. rot-int4 only, so this bounds a ratio, not an ordering; the floor here averages the two seed-0 pairs at each site (23.1 against the three-pair 23.0 on GPT-2).

Table 7: Linear probes: accuracy change against the fp32-trained probe, and learned-direction cosine, each scored against a seven-split resample floor (0.008/0.002 accuracy and 0.80/0.77 cosine on sst2/ag_news, mean over splits, with cosine minima 0.788/0.759; probe_floor.json). Accuracy resolution is one validation example, so read the deltas as counts. PCA-256 keeps accuracy on sst2 but not on ag_news (its drop there is outside the floor) while its directions collapse to about 0.5 on both; int4-o16 fails the sst2 direction floor (0.778 against a floor minimum of 0.788) on a test the retraining test passes. The two other codecs with probe runs, int8 and rot-int6, clear both floors on both tasks (0.991/0.995 and 0.998/0.998 cosine) and are omitted for width.

Table 2: Pythia-1.4B layer 8, same construction as Table 1. Codec runs are seed 0 only, so gaps under the 2 pp tie band are unresolved; the bracketed intervals resample features against the seed0/seed-1 floor pair, not seeds. fp16 is bit-lossless under the bf16 master, so its row is a same-seed ceiling.

Table 4: Frozen-SAE mean r beside retrained agreement at three sites. Within a site the frozen SAE ranks the codecs as retraining does; across sites the same reading carries no level (rot-int8 reads within 0.00005 everywhere and retrains to 2.09–2.73× the local floor). Codec rows are seed 0; floors are three-pair means.
Table 3: Pythia-1.4B layer 16. Identical construction, interval convention and bit-identical fp16 ceiling reading to Table 2. Source: runs_m4_L16/eval.

Table 5: JumpReLU panel (GPT-2, calibrated λ = 8.68). The viable codecs land within a few points of the floor (fp16 26.4, rot-int4 26.1, rot-int8 25.3 against 23.7 to 24.2), too close together for a graded verdict. mean r: the retrained best-match correlation averaged over alive features. The fp32 and viable-codec runs end with about a third of latents dead (the naïve int4 run about a quarter), and the naïve int4 run converged to L0 = 38.2 against fp32’s 18.6, so its row is shown but excluded from any verdict as confounded.

Table 10: A treatment that is not a storage codec: computing the cache with a bf16 forward (stored in fp32) beside the storage codecs. Over three seeds the bf16 forward retains 49.7–51.2% against rot-int8’s 51.6–53.8, disjoint but with n = 3 (a sign test cannot go below p = 0.25; within-seed deltas −2.7, −1.8, −3.0 pp). At 3× budget the comparison reads 44.4 against 45.3% (one seed each), inside the tie band. It runs 2.21× faster.

Table 12: Serial loader throughput per store (prefetch = 0, warm page cache, one Apple M5). The 1× training run consumes 10,017 tokens/s, so even the slowest store (int4-o16, 55k tokens/s) outruns training; the standardize-and-rotate decode path costs real time (rot-int8 reads at 64% of int8’s rate). One-machine numbers. In a paired idle-machine measurement (two interleaved runs each), std-int4 decodes at 88 MB/s against rot-int4’s 89; our std-int4 keeps the rotation matmul with an identity matrix, so this does not isolate the rotation’s own cost.

Table 11: Lossless zstd-3 over the quantized payloads, measured on one shard per codec. Rotated codecs compress only 1.04–1.26× further; naïve scaling leaves headroom that zstd recovers. Standardization without the rotation lands with the rotated codec (303.8 against 307.5B/token).

Table 17: The causal test: a difference-in-means steering vector injected into the residual stream, scored against the variation between two disjoint halves of the same data (the half-versus-half floor runs about twice a full-data comparison, so it is conservative only for a fail; the like-for-like referent is half the floor). Naïve int4 fails at least 399 of 400 resample splits on both tasks; PCA-256 passes on average but fails 51 of 400 ag_news splits against the like-for-like referent; task-matched prompts and a strength sweep leave every verdict unchanged.

Table 15: The noise levels and codecs on the seed-stable stratum (n = 774) beside all alive features. The response is flatter still on the stable stratum (0.35 pp per decade from noise 10−7 to 10−4, against 2.6 from fp16 to rot-int4), and the ratio of the two rates depends on the window, so we quote no single ratio.

Table 27: Training throughput on an A100 (thousand tokens/s, full 1× run, mean of two fresh containers) by cache format and where the loader decodes; busy is the share of training time the loader spent reading, decoding and shuffling. Every decode path of a format trains bit-identical weights. Best std-int4 over best fp32: 1.09 from local disk, 1.04 from the network volume, under the pre-registered 1.10 for a material gain. Volume reads varied 60–840 MB/s between runs.

Table 30: In this run, when a perturbation reaches training decides its cost (GPT-2 layer 6, seed 0, one run per row). Each perturbed run is a copy of the reference run, which reproduces Table 1’s fp32 seed-0 SAE bit for bit, that receives the change at the listed step(s) and trains on the same batches. agreement: the paper’s retained percentage against the reference. distance: relative Frobenius distance of the decoder from the reference’s, at the end and 2,000 steps after the change. The one-ulp row replays the one-scalar experiment (its altered value enters training twice; the weights are bit-identical to the reference at every logged step from 130 until the second entry; optimizer moments were not compared) and reproduces that SAE bit for bit. The last row is not a copy: it is the separately trained noise7 SAE of Table 14, where every batch carries the change, scored against the same reference. Sources: geom_summary.json, pair_geomdyn_*.json.
Table 9: Sparsity moves the floor without touching a byte: over a 1.95× swing in the floor, rot-int8’s ratio spreads 1.72–3.23× while its survival among seed-stable features spreads only 92.8–97.1%.

Table 6: Budget scaling on a fixed stable set (N = 774 features at every tier, binomial SE about 1.1 pp). fp16 is flat, the rotated codecs improve. fp16’s count is 741 of 774 at all three tiers by coincidence: the three pairs are distinct runs whose all-alive agreement is 60.6, 49.2 and 50.6%. Budget was scaled by re-reading one 20M-token cache (up to about 16 passes over the same tokens), so this isolates optimization from data diversity but not from convergence on a fixed corpus; at 3×, fresh text gives the same floor (Table 25).

Table 18: Which step repairs 4-bit. std-int4 is byte-identical to rot-int4 with the rotation set to the identity, so the two differ by exactly the rotation: standardization alone gives 38.0 ± 0.9%, adding the rotation 37.7 ± 0.3%, inside the tie band. All three arms are three-seed means over same-seed pairs. The ablation keeps the rotation matmul, so it isolates the rotation’s effect, not its decode cost.

Table 19: Is codec damage a shared bias or seed-like noise? On the fp32 seed-stable set (n = 774), losses are enriched above independence for every codec, so a shared component exists, but under rot-int8 only 0.13% of seed-stable features are lost in all three seeds against 24.2% under naïve int4. Recomputed from released pair files; no training.

Table 20: Survival among seed-stable / seed-unstable features under four definitions of stability: activation-space matching at three thresholds, and weight-space Hungarian matching on encoder+decoder cosine. Under every definition the viable codecs keep far more of the stable features than of the unstable ones (stable 62.9 to 98.8%, unstable 19.9 to 57.9%), and naïve int4 is lowest on both; the levels move with the definition, so a stratified percentage is only interpretable with its definition attached. On Pythia the viable codecs keep 18.6 to 38.3% of the unstable features (runs_m4_L8, runs_m4_L16 stability files). GPT-2 L6, seed 0. Sources: stability_fp32_s0_t0p*.json, stability_hungarian.json.

The 15 GPT-2 conditions are the 13 storage codecs of Table 1 plus the bf16 forward and the std-int4 ablation. None of the three needs a retrained SAE, and none ranks better than the others.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses memory-efficiency in AI by studying activation-cache compression for SAE training, fitting the efficient-AI and memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
papers.tldr: A calibrated evaluation framework shows that activation-cache compression can severely alter SAE features, while channel-standardized int4 preserves more features than naive int4 at the same storage cost.

papers.abstract: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Direct in-place convolution removes the dual-buffer cost, but the memory-optimal formulation of Gural and Murmann assumes valid padding, unit stride, unit dilation, and odd square kernels, and needs a non-sequential traversal costing $2\times$ inference time in transposes. We identify two regimes in which their published closed form does not hold: (1) an under-allocation of exactly $(k-1)C_{in} \bmod (C_{out}-C_{in})$ scalars, active on every convolutional layer of their own deployed network and manifesting as a silent corruption of still-live input; (2) an unbounded overestimate, up to $2{,}432\times$, once the critical leg leaves the output grid. We correct both and generalize to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. We then propose Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a bit-identical operation in which every layer reads its input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes its output left-aligned from index zero. The debt is piecewise affine in the output pixel index, so evaluating its breakpoints in $O(1)$ yields the minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid, with row-major access preserved. Across $10{,}000$ random layers RiP produced no corruption, and across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures it matches the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Written into TinyEngine's kernels and deployed to a Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it cuts peak activation memory across eleven MCUNet models by 12.5 to 33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising the number of models that fit the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.
bullets: Addresses activation-memory limits caused by dual-buffer CNN inference on microcontrollers.
Corrects flaws in prior memory-optimal formulations and generalizes them to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels.
Uses right-aligned inputs, left-aligned outputs, and O(1) breakpoint analysis to find the minimum safe workspace gap while preserving row-major access.
Matches the exact herringbone workspace on 58 of 84 layers and comes within 5% on 81; it uses 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average.
On Raspberry Pi Pico devices, it reduces peak activation memory by 12.5–33.3% with unchanged cycles and bit-identical outputs, increasing fitting models from 6 to 9 on the Pico 1.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on memory-efficient CNN inference (RiP convolution) to reduce activation memory on constrained hardware, directly addressing a key challenge in Efficient AI.
papers.title: Right In-Place (RiP) Convolution: A Simple, General, and Near-Optimal Strategy for Memory-Efficient CNN Inference
papers.tldr: RiP convolution enables safe, near-minimal in-place CNN inference for constrained devices while preserving speed and bit-identical outputs.

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
bullets: Targets the high latency and cost of maintaining diverse populations in iterative LLM-based program evolution.
Uses hundreds of low-cost agents organized into swarms, with each swarm exploring a different perspective.
Promotes diversity through hidden-state distance filtering and combines ideas by aggregating agents’ KV caches for a summarizer.
Across 21 mathematical discovery and scientific computing problems, it reaches benchmark best scores in a median of 3–8 minutes versus 60 minutes for other frameworks.
Qwen3 8B sometimes improves solutions initially found by AlphaEvolve using frontier LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Minutes that SwarmEvolve needs to reach the best score that OpenEvolve (left), ShinkaEvolve (middle), and CodeEvolve (right) reach in 60 minutes. All frameworks use Qwen3 8B and run for three seeds. Hollow circles mark problems where SwarmEvolve does not reach the target within 60 minutes. On most problems, SwarmEvolve reaches in a few minutes what the baselines reach in one hour.

Figure 2: Workflow of SwarmEvolve. In each round, SwarmEvolve launches 10 swarms of 45 latent agents. Each swarm draws parent programs from the archive and gets a focus prompt to refine, hybridize, explore, or start fresh. In each swarm, the agents take 40 latent reasoning steps, a novelty filter removes the 15 most similar agents (hollow circles), and the summarizer reads the KV caches of the rest to write one new program. The new programs are evaluated and added to the archive. A parameter tuning agent tunes the hyperparameters of the best program.

Figure 5: Mean hidden states of the latent agents for a circle packing problem with Qwen3 8B, projected onto their first two principal components: the 450 latent agents of all 10 swarms with the swarm centers (left), and the 45 latent agents of one exploration-focused swarm, each reading different parent programs (right). The swarms occupy distinct regions, and the novelty filter keeps latent agents from every cluster.

Figure 3: Latent reasoning and communication in a swarm. Each latent agent reasons recursively in the embedding space without decoding to text. Its latent reasoning steps are stored as KV cache. The summarizer then reads the concatenated KV caches from all agents and writes a new program in text.

Table 1: Best score within 60 minutes, averaged over three seeds (scores defined in Section 4 and Appendix D). For each model, bold marks the best score and underline marks the second best. SwarmEvolve (ours) has the highest average score with every model.

papers.selection_reason: Latent-space agent communication via shared KV caches is a technically meaningful efficiency contribution for LLM-based search.
papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.tldr: SwarmEvolve accelerates LLM-guided evolutionary program search by using large latent-space agent swarms that share KV caches instead of repeatedly generating long text.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–memory/bandwidth tradeoff in 2–4-bit weights and 2–3-bit KV-cache quantization.
Co-designs precision representation, selection, and delivery, overlapping transfers with computation and reusing fetched precision across decoding steps.
On 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while retaining 95.4% of quantized-base throughput on an RTX 5090.
With 2-bit weights and KV cache, improves Qwen3-8B AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use.
At 128K context, 3-bit weights plus 2-bit KV matches the reported perplexity and speed of 4-bit AWQ plus 8-bit KV while using approximately half the GPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit LLM inference with selective precision streaming and KV-cache quantization; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.tldr: StrataFlux recovers much of the accuracy lost by ultra-low-bit LLM quantization by streaming selective higher-precision data from host memory and storage without sacrificing most inference speed or GPU-memory savings.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation from low-bit quantization in resource-constrained edge MLLMs, especially small models.
Uses self-relabeling to better align limited fine-tuning data with the pretrained data distribution.
Introduces progressive block activation to recover multimodal understanding before language-modeling capabilities.
Employs a vision-sensitive factor to identify layers critical to multimodal understanding.
Across 2B–8B models and multiple benchmarks, W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct gains 6.6% average accuracy and remains about 1% below full precision.

papers.abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.
bullets: Model switching in long conversations normally repeats context prefill, while hybrid models additionally maintain recurrent and convolution histories.
HST transfers all three state types using structured recurrent-state maps and order-preserving convolution-history alignment.
Adapters are calibrated against the frozen target model’s continuation outputs; full-attention cache updates are merged offline.
Across five benchmarks, reported task retention is 89.88% for 4B→27B and 94.11% for 9B→27B transfers.
On synthetic 16K inputs with source caches available, handoff body speedups are 21.66× and 21.91×.

papers.abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
bullets: Targets mobile deployment under compute and memory constraints without additional training.
Decomposes grouped-layer weights into shared SVD-derived dictionaries and sparse, layer-specific coefficients.
Uses Hessian-aware sparsification, dictionary refinement, and factor-specific quantization.
On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, it outperforms existing post-training low-rank methods.
Compresses LLaMA-7B by 5.1× with a 2.9-point WikiText-2 perplexity increase; the abstract reports a 3.6× higher compression ratio than the prior low-rank state of the art.

papers.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A natural way to estimate this is a learnable gate: give each cached entry a gate on its attention weight and train the gate on the model's own objective. The gate belongs inside the normalizing softmax, where suppressing one entry hands its mass to the others rather than discarding it. That same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op, and a near-constant score ranks nothing. The no-op is not a floor the gate improves from but what its objective asks for. A second obstacle survives once the gate moves, since the same gradient charges the gate for errors the frozen model already makes, which no reweighting of positions separates out. Much of the machinery in learnable eviction, from sparsity penalties to relaxations of the discrete decision, works around the first obstacle rather than removing it; both are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate's reach and making the dense model's predictions its target. Under these two conditions capacity is never the missing ingredient: neither a larger scorer, nor explicit access to the past, nor a trainable backbone helps. The same holds for what eviction unavoidably discards, which is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it, since the mass they must return is a share of that normalizer and available nowhere else. At 75\% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.
bullets: A gate inside the attention softmax reallocates suppressed entries’ probability mass instead of discarding it; constant gates exactly reproduce dense attention.
Language-modeling loss on a frozen dense model favors this no-op, leaving gate scores nearly constant and unable to rank entries.
Even after gates move, gradients conflate eviction decisions with errors already present in the frozen model.
The proposed setup gives the gate a target beyond dense attention and uses parameter-free centroids inside the softmax to recover discarded information.
At 75% KV-cache compression, it scores 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, within 3.72 and 1.36 points of full-cache inference.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes gating mechanism for KV cache eviction, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: Learnable KV-cache eviction fails when trained only against a frozen dense-attention model, but succeeds when dense attention is kept outside the gate and discarded information is restored within the same softmax.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.
bullets: Addresses the memory bottleneck caused by tens of thousands of vision tokens in 3D CT/MRI volumes.
Applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform, reverse-water-filling bit allocation, and fixed scalar quantization without calibration.
Exploits spatial frequency concentration to preserve high-energy KV components more effectively.
Achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate in 11 of 12 medical VLM–benchmark comparisons.
The three-axis approach also generalizes to video VLMs; results are reported across four general-purpose VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TACT-KV pipeline. A medical VLM encodes a volumetric CT scan and a clinical prompt into visual and text embeddings ev, et. Inside each decoder block, visual keys/values Kv, Vv enter the four-stage pipeline below, while text Kt, Vt bypass at bf16. Reverse Water-Filling: a per-layer bit budget is allocated above water level λ, with bins below dropped (bar color = bit width 4/2/1/0). papers.abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.
bullets: Targets joint selection of model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and layerwise mixed-precision recipes without exhaustive search.
Uses RMQD, based on next-token distribution divergence, as an inexpensive proxy for downstream generation quality.
Combines a quality surrogate, Few-shot Median Calibration for more accurate latency estimates, and BandPareto for structured configuration search.
Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 and Jetson Thor show improved feasibility and small RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations.
Scope is evaluated across the model sizes and precisions included in the study, with quality estimated using a small calibration corpus.

papers.abstract: Linear attention reduces the quadratic sequence-length complexity of softmax attention by maintaining fixed-size recurrent states. However, these states scale quadratically with the representation dimension and require repeated data transfers during decoding, creating a substantial GPU memory bottleneck. Recent studies have revealed significant low-rank redundancy in recurrent states, suggesting opportunities for more efficient representations. We introduce SPARE (State Projection for Accelerated Recurrent Execution), a training-free method that exploits this redundancy through fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation. By performing recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states, SPARE reduces memory traffic without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction. SPARE achieves 2.55x full-model decoding speedup, 7.49x lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31x lower peak GPU memory, while preserving better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.
bullets: Addresses quadratic-in-representation-dimension recurrent states and repeated GPU data transfers in linear attention.
Uses fixed low-dimensional subspaces, heterogeneous rank allocation, and lightweight write compensation.
Performs recurrent reads and updates directly on compact states without online decomposition or dense-state reconstruction.
Reports 2.55× faster full-model decoding, 7.49× lower recurrent-kernel DRAM traffic, and 3.31× lower peak GPU memory.
Preserves better associative-retrieval accuracy than structured pruning at matched memory budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Ablation studies of the key design choices in SPARE. All panels report associative retrieval accuracy on 512 four-choice prompts, with 256 prompts each at retrieval depths of 64 and 128. (a) Heterogeneous rank allocation. We compare SPARE with Uniform SPARE at matched recurrent-state budgets of 6, 9, and 12 MiB. Both methods use the same Key-PCA basis construction and write-compensation mechanism, differing only in how ranks are distributed across layers and heads. Heterogeneous allocation consistently achieves higher retrieval accuracy. (b) Subspace construction. We compare Key-based, State-based, and Value-based PCA projections under a fixed 12 MiB state budget, matched calibration data, and identical per-head rank allocations. Key and State PCA use right-side projections, whereas Value PCA uses a left-side projection. Key-side write compensation is disabled for this comparison and is not applicable to the Value-side formulation. Key PCA achieves the highest retrieval accuracy among the evaluated subspaces. (c) Write compensation. We compare SPARE-H32 and SPARE-H64 with and without projected-Key write compensation, holding their respective rank allocations and projection bases fixed. Enabling compensation improves retrieval accuracy at both compression budgets. All state budgets refer to persistent recurrent-state storage per request rather than peak GPU memory.

papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
bullets: Long-context inference can exhaust HBM because KV-cache usage grows with sequence length and concurrency, limiting concurrency.
The architecture fully offloads KV caches for both prefill and decode while optimizing cache access across the serving pipeline.
Key techniques include rolling HBM and hot decode caches, a reverse sparse index, and compute–load overlap.
On GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding, it improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38× and decode throughput by up to 1.91× under a 30 ms TPOT SLO.
The system is integrated into the open-source vLLM-Ascend serving framework.

papers.abstract: Parallel block drafting accelerates speculative decoding by predicting multiple future positions in a single backbone pass, but on-device deployment constrains both drafter capacity and context storage. Under tight memory budgets, drafters must model long-range dependencies and fine-grained draft-position interactions without the growing KV-cache overhead of full-context attention. We propose HyFlash, a compact parallel drafter that introduces a prefix-memory prior to separate long-range context modeling from fine-grained draft-position interactions with limited capacity. Local attention captures recent context and draft-position interactions, while recurrent memory compresses historical target features into fixed-size states. This inductive bias enables effective local and long-range modeling with bounded draft-side memory. Experiments show that HyFlash achieves higher acceptance than full-context attention with substantially less KV storage and with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.
bullets: Targets on-device speculative decoding under limited drafter capacity and context-storage budgets.
Uses local attention for recent context and draft-position interactions, plus recurrent memory for compressed long-range target features.
Maintains bounded draft-side memory through a fixed-size prefix-memory state instead of growing full-context KV storage.
Experiments report higher acceptance than full-context attention, with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant
bullets: Addresses uneven within-column weight sensitivity and the decoding overhead of runtime outlier detection.
Uses training-free, offline calibration with activation-aware or gradient-informed tile scoring.
Retains top-scoring tiles at 16-bit within a budget and quantizes the rest to 8-bit.
Employs compact weight buffers and local accumulation for efficient mixed-precision execution.
Reports 2.66× original-model generation throughput while preserving or improving quality across several task types.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TileQuant framework for calibration-driven mixed-precision linear layers. The input-activation-aware route (top left) combines forward activation statistics with weight magnitudes, while the gradient-informed route (bottom left) accumulates weight-gradient importance over calibration batches. Per-layer top-k selection converts either tile-score map into a 16-bit/8-bit decision map. Retained tile IDs and grid metadata guide load-time reconstruction (right). The reconstructed layer supplies the selected weights to two arithmetic paths, whose tile products are combined through output-local 32-bit floating-point accumulation.

papers.selection_reason: Tile-based mixed-precision PTQ reduces LLM memory footprint and boosts throughput, fitting efficient inference and memory-efficiency interests.
papers.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: TileQuant improves LLM PTQ efficiency and quality by assigning 8- or 16-bit precision to hardware-aligned weight tiles rather than entire columns.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth, which limits context length, batch size, and decoding throughput.
Amortises values using lightweight per-head predictors, storing residuals only for poorly reconstructed tokens; this provides 4× near-lossless value compression.
Combines value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression in an asymmetric pipeline.
Reconstructs only selected KV pairs during decoding, achieving up to 5× higher peak decode throughput at 4× compression.
Composes with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LowRAM, a test-time KV cache compression method using value amortization and low-rank keys, directly addressing memory efficiency and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
papers.tldr: LowRAM compresses KV caches by separately exploiting low-rank keys and predictable values, enabling aggressive, composable memory savings with near-lossless decoding.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates LLM agent context compaction via speculative verification, directly relevant to long-context and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
papers.tldr: SpecCompact speeds up LLM-agent context compaction by speculatively generating summary slots in parallel and having a target model verify and repair them.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
authors: Chenyang Le, Pei Zhang, Yuxiang Chen, Bing Han, Derek F. Wong, Baosong Yang, Yanmin Qian
bullets: Targets the quality–latency trade-off in LLM-based SimulST and avoids redundant KV-cache recomputation.
Uses an end-to-end interleaved read-write architecture with an omni-modal LLM, supporting full KV-cache reuse and unbounded streaming.
Introduces an Actor-Critic pipeline: an RNN-T Actor samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM Critic scores semantic and latency rewards.
Evaluations on sentence- and document-level benchmarks show improved quality–latency Pareto frontiers over cascaded and static-alignment baselines.

Figure 7: Translation timing visualization for a sample from the FLEURS EN-ZH test set. Figure 2: Structural details of the RNN-T aligner and the Refiner layer.

The Refiner loss Lrefiner is computed at every text position, and the two losses are summed; the same ground-truth token is thus the target of two prediction heads over one sequence, not duplicated in it.

papers.title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.tldr: CRESiST enables segmentation-free, low-latency simultaneous speech translation by combining interleaved speech-text processing with self-enhancing policy learning.

papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.
authors: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
bullets: Reuse loses 19–100% of context-dependent questions answered by full prefill, with greater losses when distractors resemble the target chunk.
Damage is distributed across other chunks, so repairing a few distractors recovers little; repairing the target is more effective.
Recomputing the target against the reused cache outperforms inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven tested settings, despite remaining different from full-prefill KV.
Question attention identifies the target in at most 18.8% of development questions; retrieval finds it more often.

At the same 5% budget, retrieving, moving, and recomputing the top chunk beats InfoFlow-style reordering in six of nine QA/API-documentation settings, but not dialogue memory versus its token-level selector.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reuse cuts each chunk off from the chunks before it, and similar chunks then mislead the model. papers.selection_reason: KV-cache reuse and repair-budget allocation directly fits KV-cache and memory-efficiency interest.
papers.title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
papers.tldr: For non-prefix KV-cache reuse, a small repair budget is usually best spent recomputing the answer-bearing chunk—ideally after retrieving and placing it near the question—though this advantage depends on the task.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.
authors: Jiacheng Lu, Haoyi Zhu, Sipei Yi, Enze Xie, Cheng Zhuo, Yu Li
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory and historical-attention costs in long video generation.
Uses cluster centers and low-bit joint head-channel residual coefficients to exploit token and head redundancy.
Fits Key and Value compression differently: Keys preserve downstream block outputs, while Values prioritize reconstruction through quantization.
Across three video backbones, it improves the quality–storage trade-off; on HY-WorldPlay, it reaches 26.09× effective compression and improves PSNR by 1.0 dB over KVTC.
NanoKV-Fast enables mixed-dimensional attention, retaining 20.53× compression and delivering an approximately 1.15× end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of NanoKV for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. (b) The encoder compresses residuals into INT4 coefficients; the decoder reconstructs them and adds back centers. (c) Key decoders use block-output alignment; Value encoders and decoders use quantizationaware fitting. (d) A fixed policy routes history to full- or low-dimensional attention. The latter reduces Queries and restores output dimensions before LSE merging.
