papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
bullets: Targets MoE expert parameters, which dominate the memory footprint of multimodal large language models.
Separates expert importance for vision and language in a single forward pass using redistribution-aware output change and low-attention vision tokens.
Uses text-side importance for preservation, vision-side importance for pruning, and globally ranks experts across layers.
Across three MoE-MLLMs, outperforms modality-agnostic pruning on most multimodal benchmarks and remains competitive on text-only tasks.
Reduces the BF16 expert footprint by about 27 GB, enabling an approximately 58 GB model to fit on one 40 GB GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Pipeline of MAEP. Text and low-attention vision tokens are scored separately via ∆H(l,j), layer-wise normalized, combined with asymmetric signs—text preservation (+) and low-attention vision pruning (−); see Eq. 4—and ranked globally.

papers.selection_reason: Modality-aware expert pruning for MoE-based multimodal LLMs, reducing memory footprint and fitting both efficient AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MAEP is a training-free, modality-aware expert-pruning method that substantially reduces MoE-MLLM memory while preserving multimodal and text performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
authors: Geng Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, Cong Xie, Tiantian Fan, Yang You
bullets: Diffusion drafters use compact draft queries to attend over much longer, block-sparse contexts.
Split-KV keeps key/value shards local and communicates only query-sized tensors, making attention communication independent of context length.
A global query view enables longest-processing-time-first scheduling to balance sample-dependent attention costs.
At context-parallel size 64, Split-KV achieves 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and up to 3.67× speedup over the fastest baseline.
LPT reduces load imbalance to below 1% and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best compared balancer.

papers.tldr: Split-KV efficiently parallelizes diffusion-drafter training by exploiting short queries, local key/value shards, and cost-aware load balancing.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
bullets: Problem: Early workspace errors can corrupt later queries and reinforce incorrect eviction decisions.
Method: Bootstrap a feedback-compatible workspace, use early decode queries to recover it, then continue lookahead-based eviction.
Efficiency: Matches LAQ’s number of workspace forward passes and adds tensor re-scoring for workspace repair.
Results: Improves several LongBench evidence-intensive tasks, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long-document comprehension, across budgets and two model backbones.
Scope: Gains are selective, while performance remains comparable on other LongBench subsets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EchoKV overview. papers.selection_reason: Self-corrective KV cache eviction via iterative query feedback; directly addresses KV cache efficiency and token eviction.
papers.title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback
papers.tldr: EchoKV improves query-driven KV-cache eviction by iteratively repairing the workspace used to generate eviction queries, especially when relevant evidence is dispersed across long contexts.

papers.abstract: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
authors: Hengjie Zhu, Dayan Wu, Xinze Liu, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin, Weiping Wang
bullets: Addresses prediction reuse errors caused by indexing only the last token, especially at image-sensitive states.
Combines request-local one-, two-, and three-token memories with persistent token-level memory to balance specificity and coverage.
Uses entropy-confidence weighting, best-first candidate-tree construction, suffix continuations, and one target pass for greedy verification.
Reports mean speedups of 1.66× on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 1.56× on LLaVA-1.6-7B across seven single-turn benchmarks.
Outperforms the cited Token Recycling baseline, which achieves 1.51× and 1.37× respectively; results are scoped to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.title: RECAP: Context-Aware Prediction Recycling with Request-Local and Persistent Memories for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: RECAP accelerates multimodal speculative decoding by recycling context-aware target-model predictions without training or a draft model.

papers.abstract: Visual autoregressive generation spans two dominant paradigms: next-scale prediction for images and video, and next-frame prediction for video. Both decode block-by-block rather than token-by-token, yielding KV caches whose statistics diverge from those of language models. At scale, KV memory exceeds the weights and limits large-scale deployment caused by a large amount of visual tokens. Our analysis of these caches reveals three findings. First, a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load: ablating these outlier channels collapses generation, whereas ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact. Second, the outliers organize along two axes, feature and block, with magnitudes persistent within each cell and shifting across cells. Third, this structure arises from two independent mechanisms: projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering. Guided by these findings, we propose VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework that groups along the same two axes. The generation loop provides block boundaries for free, removing the need for outlier detection or calibration. Paired with bit-packing kernels for runtime memory reduction, VAR-Q delivers low-bit quantization across nine models spanning both paradigms, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enabling 6x larger inference batches.
authors: Boxun Xu, Jiaji Lu, Yuxuan Yin, Zihu Wang, Ziyue Liu, Yu Wang, Zirui Liu, Peng Li
bullets: Visual autoregressive models decode in blocks, creating KV-cache statistics that differ from language models and can make KV memory exceed model weights.
A small set of persistent outlier channels is functionally critical, with outliers structured across feature and block axes.
VAR-Q groups cache values along these two axes and uses naturally available block boundaries, avoiding outlier detection and calibration.
Bit-packing kernels reduce KV memory by up to 78.5% across nine models and enable inference batches up to 6× larger.
The approach targets next-scale and next-frame image/video generation; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond these paradigms.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
bullets: Uses a normalized Transformer with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, divided into input, recurrent, and output blocks.
Variable loop counts provide elastic inference compute, with harder prompts routed to deeper loops during post-training.
More loops yield the largest accuracy gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks.
With at least two loops, it outperforms several larger models across 12 benchmarks, according to the abstract.
Caching only the final loop’s keys and values keeps KV-cache memory comparable to a non-looped model; quantized checkpoints are released.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.
bullets: Looped transformers reduce parameter memory, but their KV caches grow with the number of loop steps and become the main bottleneck.
LoopVQ jointly vector-quantizes channels across multiple loop steps and fine-tunes codebooks to match full-precision outputs.
At 0.5 bits per element, it outperforms existing KV-cache quantization methods across general, long-chain-of-thought, and long-context retrieval tasks.
Combined with TaSQ, it retains much of BF16 accuracy at 0.25 bits per element.
In SGLang, it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and increases peak throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on the evaluated Ouro models.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LoopVQ. Each loop step of a looped LM writes its own KV cache. LoopVQ codes G/Tc channels across Tc loop steps, so one index serves all of them at the same bitwidth as coding each loop step separately, and fine-tunes the codebooks against the full-precision output through the loop. At inference, each loop step reads the shared indices through its own slice Bt of the codebook.

Figure 1. Looped LMs trade parameter memory for KV cache. (a) Parameter memory versus KV cache per token, both in bf16, for standard LLMs and the looped Ouro models with four loop steps. Figure 5. Serving LoopVQ in SGLang. The KV cache keeps the sink and recent tokens in bf16 at every loop step, and all other tokens as codebook indices shared across loop steps. At loop step t, the LoopVQ attention kernel loads Bt, the slice of the codebook entries for loop step t, into shared memory once and looks up the keys and values of each token from its indices in registers; the bf16 kernel reads the bf16 keys and values of loop step t directly. Both attend with the query q(t) of the new token, and their outputs are merged. The key and value of each new token are written in bf16, and after every 8 generated tokens the oldest recent page is encoded into indices.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.
authors: Yining Wei, Tianyuan Wu, Gu Gong, Yuechen Tao, Yinghao Yu, Xiaowen Chu, Wei Wang
bullets: NVFP4 W4A4 can degrade rollout quality and amplify training–inference mismatch, destabilizing RL post-training.
The method targets concentrated errors with TIM-aware filtering of drifted trajectories and sparse BF16 compensation for outlier activation channels.
A fused SpliceGEMM kernel reduces the runtime cost of these protections across prefill and decode.
It maintains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality, improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76–2.60× while remaining within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $c\mu$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $\mu$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.
authors: Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
bullets: Models LLM inference as an online multiclass queue with heterogeneous prompts, outputs, computation, KV-cache access, and memory occupancy.
Derives effective service rates that jointly account for compute speed, memory bandwidth, and KV-cache capacity.
Proves the $c\mu$ rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model, while also minimizing finite-workload completion time and maximizing full-run output-token throughput.
Constructs a feasible policy for the finite system and proves convergence of its scaled dynamics to the optimal fluid policy.
Experiments on an NVIDIA H800 show lower average latency while maintaining high throughput compared with existing scheduling policies.

papers.abstract: A team serving a 9B-20B open-weight language model on vLLM or SGLang must choose a quantization recipe, and needs two numbers: the speedup over BF16 and the accuracy given up. We assemble every public measurement of these numbers that we could verify and find that the record supplies them only in pieces. Only two checkpoints, both INT4 builds of Gemma 3 12B, have both a vLLM timing and an accuracy score, and that score covers a single MMLU subject, one that the AWQ build was calibrated on. The batch-1 timings predate current engine releases, AMD and Intel Gaudi have no timing in this band at all, and FP4 has none against BF16. The timings that do exist follow one rule. Decoding a small batch is limited by memory bandwidth, so 4-bit weights roughly double speed (2.12x for Qwen2.5-14B on an A100), but the gain vanishes once a large batch makes the GPU compute-bound (1.02x for Gemma 3 12B at batch size 256), where FP8 is the recipe that can still help. Many published accuracy deltas, including every HumanEval delta, lie within benchmark sampling noise. We close with a seven-item reporting checklist for future measurements.
authors: Smit Kadvani, Kriti Faujdar, Spurthi Tallam
bullets: The literature lacks complete, directly comparable measurements of speedup over BF16 and accuracy loss for 9B–20B open LLMs.
Only two checkpoints—both INT4 Gemma 3 12B builds—combine vLLM timing with an accuracy score, and that accuracy evidence is narrowly scoped.
Small-batch decoding is memory-bandwidth-limited, producing roughly 2× speedup in one reported case; large batches can reduce the gain to about 1×.
FP8 may remain beneficial when large batches make the GPU compute-bound.
Many reported accuracy differences, including all HumanEval deltas, fall within benchmark sampling noise; the paper proposes a seven-item reporting checklist.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on quantization techniques for LLM serving, a core topic in Efficient AI, specifically addressing memory bandwidth and compute-bound bottlenecks.
papers.title: Twice as Fast, Until It Isn't: Quantized Serving of Mid-Size Open LLMs
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can nearly double decode speed for small batches, but its benefit largely disappears at large, compute-bound batches, while reliable accuracy trade-offs remain underreported.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

Figure 2. Layer-wise contribution of each branch to long-context retrieval. ∆CE (nats) on AR-32k when the TTT (top) or SWA (bottom) branch is removed at a single layer, broken down by the distance between a query and its target. Warm cells indicate degradation, that is, a larger increase in loss when the branch is removed. The TTT branch contributes almost nothing across the interior layers (ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) but dominates at the boundary layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}), whereas SWA contributes broadly at every depth. The color scale is symmetric-log with a linear region below 0.01, and both panels share one scale.

Figure 3. Improved Attention Transfer in Stage-1 Linearization. Held-out attention-transfer loss LMSE (left) and perplexity (right) during Stage 1. (a) Training on LMSE alone matches the teacher’s attention outputs closely, reducing the loss by over 25×, yet perplexity rises from 5.3K to 236K: the student reproduces each layer’s output while losing the ability to model language. (b) Adding next-token supervision LCE resolves this, lowering both losses together and reaching a perplexity of 34, which provides a stable initialization for the TTT parameters.

Figure 10. Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Accuracy across context lengths (1K–8K) and needle depths for Llama-3.1-8B, a LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention), and the ANCHOR 3:1 hybrid. ANCHOR reaches a mean accuracy of 0.95 (baseline 1.00), whereas the LoLCATs hybrid (18.75% SoftMax Attention) (0.33) retrieves reliably only at 1K or when the needle lies near the end of the context.

Figure 6. Study on Performance–efficiency trade-off. ANCHOR evaluated on reasoning (MMLU) and recall (SWDE, FDA, SQuAD) benchmarks, together with end-to-end throughput and recurrent state size. (a) Reasoning accuracy of the ANCHOR series against LoLCATs; targeted placement of the cross-layer recurrent state improves reasoning. (b) Throughput (tokens/s) against reasoning accuracy; ANCHOR attains 4.3× higher throughput than the baseline at comparable accuracy. (c) Recall accuracy against recurrent state size; ANCHOR improves recall over LoLCATs by 2.3–3.1× while using a 10.2× smaller state.

Figure 4. Representational similarity of TTT states on (a) PG-19 and (b) WikiText. Each point is one layer pair, plotted as debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity on cross-window targets, that is, those whose source lies beyond the local window. Interior pairs ( , ℓ ∈ {2, . . . , 27}) are drawn separately from anchor pairs (▲, ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}). Anchor pairs are more strongly aligned than interior pairs on both corpora (0.97 versus 0.82 on PG-19, 0.92 versus 0.49 on WikiText). High CKA with near-zero cosine indicates closely related information encoded in different bases.

Figure 1. Recurrent states across layers are redundant, so one shared state suffices. Left: Debiased CKA between the TTT states of every pair of layers in Llama-3.1-8B, measured on WikiText for targets beyond the local window. The anchor layers (ℓ ∈ {0, 1, 28, . . . , 31}, dashed boxes) are strongly aligned with one another (mean CKA 0.92), whereas the interior layers are not (0.49). Right: Number of recurrent states per block as the ratio of hybrid to softmax-attention layers grows. A per-layer design keeps one state per hybrid layer; ANCHOR keeps a single shared state, reducing the count by 3–6×.

Figure 8. The learned reader rotation is concentrated in a few planes. Rotation angles of Q’s planes, ranked (log scale), at L31; median over 32 heads, whiskers show the IQR. Shaded bands span from the learned profile to a random rotation with equal total squared angle (dark: learned above null; light: below). The learned map exceeds the null only in the leading planes (up to plane 5 for Llama-3.1-8B and plane 3 for Mistral-7B), and its top 5 planes carry 82% and 92% of the squared rotation versus 26% for the null.This holds in all 128 reader-layer heads of both backbones.

Points are readout vectors projected onto the layer’s dominant rotation plane and coloured by position in the sequence; arcs trace the rotation step, which preserves the radius within the plane. Panel titles give the rotation angle θ in that plane and the share of readout energy it carries. Both backbones follow the same pattern, with the rotation concentrated in a few planes (Figure 8). Head 0 of 32; axes are scaled per layer.

papers.selection_reason: Uses test-time training with recurrent memory for efficient long-context retrieval, fitting TTT, memory efficiency, and long-context models.
papers.title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Anchor improves long-context retrieval and efficiency by storing TTT memory only in a few anchor layers and sharing it across layers through learned read transformations.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.
authors: Tianle Zhou, Yang Zhang, Tianyu Wu, Zhuohan Wang, William Nixon, Juncheng Yang
bullets: Looped transformers keep separate KV caches per loop, creating substantial memory pressure during serving.
An offline profile estimates quantization and sharing sensitivity for each (loop, layer) cell.
A planner selects 4-bit, 2-bit, or final-loop KV reuse under damage and storage budgets.
Runtime decoding fetches low bits only when attention requires 4-bit precision, using a fused vLLM kernel.
On Ouro-1.4B, LoopKV-M stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit KIVI-4 and achieves 1.7–2.2× higher goodput under the stated latency objective, without significant benchmark degradation versus BF16.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
authors: Kunming Shao, Xijie Huang, Jierun Chen, Jiaqi Shao, Yanli Wang, Jiangnan Yu, Qiwei Li, Wei Zhang, Kwang-Ting Cheng, Chi Ying Tsui
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks by making 2-bit quantization more reliable.
For each 32-channel key piece, chooses between rotation and no rotation using calibrated attention error.
Rotates queries at read time to match each stored key representation.
Decision frequency follows the cache axis: per head for per-channel caches and per key for per-token caches, using existing sign bits for storage.
At 2.5 bits per value, reduces KIVI’s twelve-model KL divergence from 18.7 to 12.4 × 10⁻³ and improves long-context benchmark scores in affected models.

papers.abstract: Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.
bullets: Targets the tight SRAM and Flash limits of microcontrollers while avoiding interpreter dispatch and framework dependencies.
Compiles .tflite or .safetensors models into complete C sources, including kernels, weights, memory layout, and RTOS integration.
Uses MLIR-based specialization to generate model-specific inference code without linking a pre-written kernel library.
On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, it uses 38% less SRAM and 15% less Flash than MCUNet TinyEngine.
Demonstrates 1-token/s interactive GPT-Neo generation on a Cortex-M7 using quantization, an int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning.

papers.abstract: We introduce ShamAN-Q, a sub-1-bit post-training quantization method that extends NanoQuant by replacing each its diagonal reconstruction geometry with a tractable dense curvature metric, using a general paradigm popularized by the Shampoo optimizer. For each linear weight, ShamAN-Q fits a Kronecker product to the empirical Fisher information matrix of a small calibration set by Kullback--Leibler minimization, forming a Mahalanobis reconstruction loss from the result. The continuous ADMM updates from NanoQuant become solutions to Sylvester equations, while its discrete projection and deployment format remain unchanged. Because the curvature is local to a given set of weights, ShamAN-Q re-measures the input curvature statistic for each layer immediately before layer factorization, periodically refreshing all statistics on the partially quantized model. ShamAN-Q also redistributes the uniform rank from NanoQuant across layers at the same total number of bits. On Qwen3-Base, ShamAN-Q lowers WikiText-2 perplexity at $\approx$1 bpw from 27.56 to 22.96 (0.6B), 19.21 to 16.72 (1.7B), and 14.29 to 13.80 (4B) while matching or improving zero-shot accuracy on the Eleuther LM Evaluation Harness. On 0.6B, ShamAN-Q at $\approx$0.8 bpw matches the published perplexity of NanoQuant at $\approx$1.0 bpw.
bullets: Extends NanoQuant with a Shampoo-inspired Kronecker-factored approximation of empirical Fisher curvature.
Uses KL-fitted curvature to define a Mahalanobis reconstruction loss; continuous ADMM updates solve Sylvester equations.
Refreshes layer-local input curvature during quantization and reallocates rank across layers without increasing total bits.
On Qwen3-Base near 1 bpw, reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 27.56 to 22.96 (0.6B), 19.21 to 16.72 (1.7B), and 14.29 to 13.80 (4B).
At about 0.8 bpw on the 0.6B model, matches NanoQuant’s published perplexity at about 1.0 bpw while matching or improving zero-shot accuracy.

The transported statistics alter only the continuous U/V optimization component; Euclidean consensus leaves SVID, dual updates, scale extraction, and sign extraction unchanged from NanoQuant.

Figure 2: ShamAN-Q end to end. Phase 1 runs the calibration set through the frozen teacher, fits and shrinks the curvature statistics (Aγ ,Gγ) of every linear layer, and allocates ranks at bit parity. Phase 2 processes decoder blocks in order. The factorized prefix and the untouched full-precision suffix are frozen while block b is tuned (TUNEFP), factorized layer by layer by Kron–LB–ADMM under the transported statistics (A,G) (Figure 3), and refined by latent STE. The statistics of the unfactorized layers are refreshed on the partially quantized model after every ∆ blocks. Phase 3 distills only the scale vectors against the teacher, with the sign matrices frozen. papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: https://github.com/Tianyu9748/ReelCache
bullets: Addresses the large memory cost and regeneration delay of KV caches in autoregressive video diffusion.
Combines online low-rank, video-coded intra-chunk compression with inter-chunk basis sharing and tree-based cache management.
Supports efficient cache restoration for resume, rewind, and fork generation branches.
Across five video generation models, reduces KV storage by 14.46–21.13× and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25–3.36×.
Reports less than a 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics.

papers.abstract: Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.
bullets: Addresses the need for expert-quality plant disease and insect pest diagnosis without cloud connectivity.
Combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and offline on-device serving with chat-based interaction.
Evaluated two VLM backbones, four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.
Eight-bit quantization has minimal impact on answer quality; 4-bit AWQ retains 98.6% of full-precision quality while reducing 2B model weight memory by 49%.
The compact configuration uses 2.01 GiB of weight memory, produces its first token in about 0.12 seconds, and completes 64-token responses in 0.78 seconds.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs without per-LLM fitting, and no law names the factors that set it. From closed-form expressions of LLM inference's computational and memory-access complexity, we derive the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache and next-token computation cost. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from several families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. SIMPLE explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and higher GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy linearly relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; accuracy rises but energy rises faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x range. Moving to agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x, as both prefill and KV-cache terms grow with input length; prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), but not KV-cache cost, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.
bullets: Derives energy scaling from inference computation and memory-access complexity, separating prefill from decode costs.
Evaluated on 13 dense LLMs across NVIDIA H100 traces, achieving R² = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE without per-LLM fitting.
Shows prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, while higher GQA grouping linearly lowers per-token energy versus MHA.
Longer reasoning budgets can exceed the energy-minimizing output length: accuracy improves, but energy rises faster and Intelligence per Joule declines.
Agentic serving greatly increases request energy; prefix caching removes most prefill cost but leaves substantial KV-cache cost.

papers.selection_reason: Directly models and analyzes LLM inference energy costs, explicitly separating prefill, decode, and KV-cache contributions, fitting the KV-cache and memory efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
papers.tldr: SIMPLE is a calibration-free, four-parameter law that predicts and explains the non-linear energy cost of LLM inference across prefill, KV-cache, and next-token computation.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.
bullets: Targets quality degradation from aggressive token pruning in long-form, open-ended generation.
Uses Structure-Aware Token Consolidation to merge structurally redundant video and audio representations.
Uses Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation to assign lower or higher value precision based on estimated attention-output sensitivity.
Achieves a 5.0× average memory-footprint reduction, 97.98% of baseline generation quality, and a 1.48× end-to-end speedup.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on long-form generation benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces structural and precision redundancy in omni-LLMs via token consolidation and KV-cache precision allocation.
papers.title: R$^2$-Omni: Reducing Structural and Precision Redundancy in Omni-LLMs for Long-Form Generation
papers.tldr: R²-Omni reduces redundant multimodal tokens and their numerical precision to make long-form Omni-LLM generation substantially more memory- and time-efficient while retaining most baseline quality.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Chunk-indexed sparse attention retrofits dense models, reducing KV reads for long-context inference.
papers.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: CISA retrofits pretrained dense-attention LLMs with chunk-level sparse attention, achieving substantially faster million-token inference while keeping quality close to dense attention without retraining.

papers.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
bullets: Addresses information dilution in deep Pre-LN language models without adding substantial cross-layer computation or memory access.
Uses stride-aligned shallow–middle source pairs to reconstruct deep-layer keys and values.
KV-sharing edges provide non-local gradient paths that sharpen key retrieval directions and enrich value representations.
Evaluated on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters under GQA and MLA, with consistent downstream gains.
On a 16B MoE model, reports improvements of 7.0% on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical KV-sharing LLM architecture that reduces KV cache by a third while improving downstream performance, fitting both efficiency and LLM architecture interests.
papers.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DepthGraft hierarchically reuses KV projections across layers to regularize deep representations, reduce KV-cache memory by roughly one third, and improve language-model performance.

papers.abstract: Block-scaled lookup-table (LUT) formats, which represent weights as indices into a small value set (the grid), have become standard for low-bit LLM quantization, ranging from NF4 and BOF4 to the 3-bit LUT instruction in NVIDIA Rubin. While these formats leave the grid definition flexible, existing implementations rely on fixed grids derived either from numerical data types (INT, FP) or assumed weight distributions (NF, BOF). We demonstrate that no single fixed grid is universally optimal; the best fixed grid varies with bit-width: BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and INT at 6 bits. We introduce SHq, a closed-form family of grids parameterized by two critical degrees of freedom: a companding strength α that interpolates level spacing from uniform to floating-point-like, and an offset c that introduces asymmetry. This offset allows the sign bit of the FP8 block scale, otherwise unused, to select between the grid and its mirror image, up to doubling the number of distinct values available per block. SHq modifies only the lookup table contents and serves as a drop-in replacement for the grid in any such format. Across five models ranging from 3B to 35B parameters, including a mixture-of-experts architecture, evaluated at 2-6 bits using RTN and GPTQ, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in every setting at 3 and 4 bits and in most settings at 2, 5 and 6 bits. It outperforms the best fixed grid by up to 34% and remains superior under mixed-precision configurations. At 4.5 bits per weight, the SHq format reduces the KL divergence of NVFP4 by 41-67% while improving downstream accuracy. Grid families incorporating both spacing and offset parameters perform comparably, whereas those lacking an offset exhibit clearly higher error, confirming that these two degrees of freedom drive the observed gains. We therefore propose SHq as the standard grid for block-scaled lookup-table formats.
bullets: Fixed grids are not universally optimal: the best choice varies with bit-width.
SHq uses companding strength α and offset c to control spacing and asymmetry; the offset can exploit the FP8 scale sign to select mirrored grids.
It is a drop-in replacement for lookup-table grids in block-scaled formats and supports 2–6-bit quantization with RTN or GPTQ.
Across five 3B–35B models, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in all tested 3- and 4-bit settings and most other settings.
SHq improves KL divergence by up to 34% over the best fixed grid and reduces NVFP4 divergence by 41–67% at 4.5 bits while improving downstream accuracy.

papers.abstract: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^dσ(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.
bullets: A function formed by d two-atom heads uses 2d head-atom terms but needs exactly 2^d atoms in any equivalent single-head representation.
The 2^d lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below 1/2 on all of R^d and for exact equality on any nonempty open query domain.
The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; the bound is tight for fixed head counts when the count divides d.
A normalized construction preserves the exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls.

Cache experiments on two disjoint 64-context banks show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects; a classical affine-rank bound and certified instance rule out exact preservation at a specified atom count.

papers.abstract: On-device multimodal agents are limited by two deployment mismatches: pretrained attention structures may not divide evenly across the compute cores of an edge accelerator, causing irregular partitions; and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, whose capacity grows with the number of rounds. We present PARC, which combines parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization. At the model level, it uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection to make attention dimensions divisible by the target core count while preserving the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension. At runtime, it separates the system prompt, persistent text history, and transient visual observations by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so that historical images leave the persistent cache and more interaction rounds fit a fixed budget. On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, hardware-aligned pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%; a parameter-matched control confirms that the speedup stems mainly from core alignment rather than parameter reduction.
bullets: Addresses uneven attention partitioning across edge-accelerator cores and cache growth from multi-round visual interactions.
Uses Taylor-based, grouped-query-attention-aware structured pruning while preserving key attention dimensions and target-core divisibility.
Reorganizes KV-cache contents by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so past images do not remain persistent.
On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression; recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and coordinate hit rate to the original level.
With seven cores, pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, raises decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap memory high-water usage by 12.7%.

papers.title: Parallelism-Aligned Pruning and Round-Aware Context Reuse for On-Device Multimodal Agents

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. We make two observations: (i) tensor-parallel communication is an important cost when deploying low-rank KV-cache compression in distributed inference; and (ii) Value compression can be associated with the output projection, allowing the same low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and tensor-parallel communication. Based on these observations, we propose BasisKV, a low-rank KV-cache compression method for communication-intensive, long-context LLM inference. BasisKV jointly optimizes the low-rank factors across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output, rather than fitting each partition in isolation. The compressed Value cache is further reused to help identify which Key pages should be accessed: it predicts part of the Key information needed for routing, while a Key-specific residual stores what cannot be recovered from Value. The original Keys are then retrieved only for the selected pages to compute exact QK scores. Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV achieves a better quality--efficiency tradeoff than existing low-rank baselines, reaching up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexz949/BasisKV
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth and communication overhead in distributed, tensor-parallel inference.
Jointly optimizes low-rank factors across GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output.
Uses compressed Values to predict routing-relevant Key information, with a Key residual for unrecoverable details.
Retrieves original Keys only for selected pages to compute exact query–key scores.
Reports a better quality–efficiency tradeoff than low-rank baselines, with up to 1.42× end-to-end speedup in 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.
bullets: Eviction quality depends strongly on scoring-layer depth: it is poor near the input, peaks around 40–75% depth, and declines at the final layer.
The pattern reflects when layers have incorporated the question enough to identify answer-relevant tokens; a top-k survival model reproduces the observed curve.
Calibration prompts with known answers select an effective scoring layer, improving on the default in 16 of 18 per-layer-cache models and significantly in 7.
Using the selected layer to score all heads beats per-head SnapKV by 18–43 points on five models up to 14B, including financial filings at 32K context, without extra forward passes.

The benefit is model- and task-dependent: larger models often have near-optimal defaults, shared-cache writers can be substantially worse, and no mid-depth advantage appears on LongBench open-book QA.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates which layer should score KV-cache eviction, directly improving cache efficiency.
papers.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: Mid-depth transformer layers are generally the best judges for KV-cache token eviction, improving long-context retrieval when a single selected layer scores caches.

papers.abstract: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.
bullets: Scalar Lipschitz and Hessian measures miss how responses vary with perturbation size, direction, and location.
A finite-difference roughness spectrum unifies global sensitivity and directional curvature across scales, grounded in Besov theory.
The analysis shows that larger output shifts can sometimes cause less task damage than smaller shifts, and local curvature can overlook vulnerable blocks.
Roughness Source Control improves noise robustness across 80 image-classification checkpoints spanning four model–dataset combinations.
For post-training quantization, spectrum-guided mixed precision achieves lower perplexity than HAWQ-V2 in all 14 tested settings across seven held-out language models.

papers.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.
bullets: Targets the gap between capable but oversized medical LLMs and compact models that struggle on knowledge-intensive healthcare tasks.
Uses synthetic medical data, teacher-generated chain-of-thought targets, two SFT stages, and two RL stages with hard-sample mining.
Across seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B and matches MedGemma-27B; MedPsy-1.7B also exceeds MedGemma-1.5-4B.
MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B on HealthBench-Hard while using far fewer parameters.
Shorter outputs, quantization, and edge testing yield lower latency, energy use, and storage needs, with peak RAM below 5 GB in tested configurations.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.
bullets: Recurrent models require separate treatment of extra-state weights/activations and the recurrent state itself.
Decayed recurrences develop fewer residual outlier channels than softmax attention, reducing the need for incoherence processing.
LoReS combines value-axis scale grouping, decay-aware mixed precision, and stochastic rounding to control recurrent-state quantization error.
It supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower precision for shorter decode horizons across several large models.
A vLLM implementation demonstrates end-to-end decoding speedups.
