papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: We present FloodDiffusion 2 (FD2), an efficient and controllable framework that builds upon FloodDiffusion (FD1), a state-of-the-art streaming motion generation model. While FD1 produces plausible motion, it suffers from low efficiency and limited controllability, as its attention design requires repeated computation over the entire history, and it lacks precise trajectory control for real-world applications. To address these limitations and improve generation quality, FD2 introduces three advances. First, Partial Attention makes finalized history representations independent of the active window, enabling KV-cached inference and shared-history packing for efficient training. Second, we establish a necessary-and-sufficient Bregman criterion for regression losses to preserve diffusion's conditional-mean velocity field. This criterion guides an FK-induced quadratic loss that incorporates motion geometry without online FK evaluation. Third, FD2 introduces precise path conditioning to control the character's root trajectory while preserving natural body motion. Experiments show that FD2 reduces training computation by 4.6$\times$ and accelerates denoising by 11.29$\times$, reaching 2.303 ms per update on long sequences. Alongside these efficiency gains, FD2 improves motion quality over FD1 and achieves state-of-the-art FID scores among streaming methods, with 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.
bullets: Targets FD1’s repeated-history computation and limited trajectory control.
Uses Partial Attention for KV-cached inference and shared-history packing during training.
Introduces a Bregman-based criterion and FK-induced quadratic loss to incorporate motion geometry without online forward-kinematics evaluation.
Adds precise root-path conditioning while preserving natural full-body motion.
Reports 4.6× lower training computation, 11.29× faster denoising, and improved FID over FD1, including 0.048 on SEED and 0.053 on HumanML3D.

papers.abstract: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
bullets: Fixed partitions for model weights and attention states waste memory and limit concurrency under changing workloads.
Rimuru uses a shared page pool with tensor-specific memory views and page tables to support different layouts and allocation granularities.
A multi-level allocator enables page splitting, merging, and cross-tensor capacity reuse, while a fused MoE kernel accesses non-contiguous expert weights without copying.
A workload-aware adjuster reallocates pages at runtime based on demand and is implemented in vLLM.
The system reports up to 19.03× baseline throughput and an average 98.1% reduction in time to first token (TTFT).

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.
bullets: Uses a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score passages from one shared prefilling of the cached context.
A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, decision-making, and reranking with about 0.1 GiB extra memory per decision skill.
After brief MS MARCO fine-tuning, it reports higher nDCG@10 than bge-reranker-v2-m3 on SciFact and NFCorpus.
On 300 HotpotQA questions, Glance-selected context improves answer F1 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same generator.
Reranking quality continues improving to 200 candidates, but evaluation is limited to two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset, and one backbone family.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.
authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Targets the limitations of independently optimized, local reconstruction objectives that overlook downstream prediction sensitivity.
Approximates output changes from joint weight and activation quantization using a Hessian and tractable Fisher approximation.
Jointly optimizes quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under one output-sensitivity objective.
Designed to remain practical for modern large language models.
Consistently outperforms existing transformation and rounding methods across channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

papers.abstract: Linear attention stores historical information in a recurrent state of fixed size, providing a compact memory representation for long-context inference. Reducing state precision further lowers per-request storage requirements, but quantized writeback errors enter subsequent recurrences, degrade prediction quality on long-reasoning tasks, and can be accompanied by repetitive generation and excessively long outputs. We propose Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) and the Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) to address precision allocation and recent-information maintenance. GGA combines candidate quantization residuals with gradient sensitivity to future prediction loss to allocate head bit widths under a model-wide mixed-precision budget. PW independently maintains recent pure writes as FP8 vector pairs, propagates them through the full GDN state transition, and merges them into the low-bit historical state only after they leave the window. Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, GGA allocation alone improves over STEPQuant@4 by 19.48/29.84 percentage points. Adding PW-S8 yields seven-task macro-averages of 69.83%/78.63%, improving over STEPQuant@4 by 38.39/41.21 percentage points, respectively. Both precision reallocation and window maintenance improve task scores while mitigating excessively long outputs: at @6, GGA reduces mean generation length, averaged equally across tasks, by 10.45%/14.65% relative to STEPQuant; adding PW-S8 to GGA@4 further reduces mean generation length by 32.32%/36.77%. Comparisons at similar storage budgets further show that using additional capacity to maintain recent writes yields higher task scores and shorter mean outputs than solely increasing the bit width of the accumulated state.
authors: Qinghang Huang, Xuchu Huang, Xunzhao Yin
bullets: Low-precision writeback errors accumulate in linear-attention recurrent states, harming long-context reasoning and causing repetitive or excessively long outputs.
Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) assigns mixed-precision head bit widths using quantization residuals and sensitivity to future prediction loss.
Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) keeps recent writes as FP8 vector pairs, then merges them into the low-bit historical state after they leave the window.
Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, GGA and PW improve task scores over STEPQuant@4 and substantially shorten mean generation length.
At comparable storage budgets, reserving capacity for recent writes outperforms using it only to increase accumulated-state bit width.

papers.abstract: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TRACE and dLLM-KVQ. TRACE reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. dLLM-KVQ uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, dLLM-KVQ achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.
authors: Yan Tai, Yunan Ding, Guangzhao Li, Siqi Luo, Chaoyang Zhang, Guangtao Zhai, Guodong Guo, Xiaohong Liu
bullets: Diffusion language models reuse KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional representations can change as masked tokens are revealed.
The study adapts KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse.
TRACE reconstructs reveal trajectories from prompt–answer pairs to produce calibration states that better match iterative decoding.
dLLM-KVQ selectively keeps important K-cache entries in high precision while quantizing values to low bitwidth.
Across LLaDA and Dream on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, it achieves the highest average score among evaluated quantized methods at 4-bit and 2-bit cache settings.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.
authors: Neehal Tumma, Philipp Nazari, Rohan Cherukuri, Daniela Rus, T. Konstantin Rusch
bullets: Targets the underdeveloped problem of low-precision inference for linear recurrences, especially during chunkwise-parallel prefill.
Introduces seven functional invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescaling, and alternative placements of decay and write factors.
Characterizes when these transformations preserve computation across linear, gated, and delta-rule recurrence families.
Extends the SSDi8 Mamba-2 low-precision prefill pipeline with applicable invariances.
Improves perplexity at matched latency across Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, 8B and Nemotron-H 8B models.

papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Boao Kong, Bing Liu
bullets: RoPE dependence varies across layers and models, motivating non-uniform allocation.

From-scratch experiments improve validation loss over budget-matched baselines, with favorable quality–storage–compute trade-offs for physical MLA.

papers.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
authors: Yipin Guo, Arun M George, Siddharth Joshi
bullets: Addresses KV-cache growth as a bottleneck for long-context LLM serving on memory- and bandwidth-constrained devices.
Uses adaptive base-plus-offset coding for BF16 exponent groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit.
Fused attention reconstructs compressed KV tiles on demand, supporting incremental updates and paged serving without full-cache decompression.
Across five models, achieves 1.405–1.407× BF16 KV compression, about 26% lower resident KV memory, and 13–29% higher serving throughput under comparable memory budgets.
Reports attention speedups on NVIDIA DGX Spark and Apple M4, including 1.19–1.27× at 64K-token context on DGX Spark and 1.02–1.25× on M4.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of GAAC. (a) GAAC exploits the concentration of BF16 exponent values in contiguous high-frequency regions. Each group of eight exponents shares a 2-bit tag indicating 3-bit, 4-bit, or raw mode. The sign and mantissa bits of each element are stored unchanged in a single byte. Each code is an offset from a calibrated per-channel base, ci = ei − bw,i. In the illustrated example, one exponent outside the 3-bit window causes the entire group g+1 to use 4-bit mode. Bits per element include the sign-mantissa byte and the mode tag. (b) Compared with standard attention, GAAC reduces KV loading time by reading fewer bytes from the compressed cache, with only a small computational overhead from on-the-fly decompression. o denotes the attention output. Example values and timelines are illustrative.

Figure 3: System design of GAAC. (a) New tokens are appended to an uncompressed BF16 tail until the block is full. (b) The full block is encoded once. If its compressed size S does not exceed the slot capacity C, it is stored in a compressed slot; otherwise, it remains in BF16 format. (c) The paged KV cache holds compressed and raw finalized blocks in block-table order, followed by the incomplete BF16 tail.

papers.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
papers.tldr: GAAC losslessly compresses LLM KV caches by exploiting exponent redundancy, reducing memory use and accelerating long-context inference on personal devices.

papers.abstract: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses the costly encoding of long, text-rich histories when each history typically supervises only one short semantic identifier.
Merge compresses each historical item’s SID and text into a few learned tokens; Branch predicts multiple target SIDs from the shared representation.
Uses a shallow, wide tree with tree FlashAttention to share history computation while keeping target branches independent.
A tree-structured key/value cache extends computation sharing to constrained decoding.
On public benchmarks, it outperforms strong baselines while improving training and decoding efficiency.

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.
Trains the memories and shared reader by behavioral distillation while keeping the backbone frozen.
Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SkillMem. Reusable textual skills are discovered from paired multi-agent trajectories. Each skill is compiled into a compact latent memory by matching the behavioral effect of skill injection. At inference time, the retrieved memory is shared across agents and consumed through a role-conditioned reader while inter-agent communication remains entirely latent.

Figure 3: Behavioral skill distillation. For each skill, agent role, and calibration task, the frozen backbone generates a teacher response with the textual skill included in the role prompt. We score the same response with and without the textual skill to measure its token-level effect. We then replace the skill text with its memory and train the memory and role-conditioned reader to reproduce the skill-supported behavior while preserving the base behavior at positions with limited skill support.

Figure 1: Accuracy and efficiency comparison. (a) Accuracy changes of SkillMem relative to TextMAS and LatentMAS using Qwen3-4B. (b) Total storage required by different skill representations as the skill library grows. (c) End-to-end inference speedup relative to TextMAS.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, David H. Yang, Parisa Shiravani, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Tejaswini Pedapati, Subhajit Chaudhury, Keerthiram Murugesan, Pin-Yu Chen
bullets: KV cache memory and decoding cost grow linearly with generation length, motivating compression for long reasoning outputs.
It replaces costly iterative sparse coding with one-shot Top-n screening followed by lightweight coefficient refinement.
The dictionary adapts during decoding by reusing inactive atoms rather than expanding indefinitely.
Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show a strong quality–efficiency trade-off while maintaining bounded dictionary size.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FAD-KV. Each incoming KV vector is first encoded through screening-based sparse coding. If reconstruction error is high, FAD-KV replaces an inactive atom with a context-relevant atom instead of appending a new one, keeping the dictionary size fixed throughout decoding.

Figure 3: Adaptive behavior and sensitivity analysis. (a) Normalized dictionary size during Qwen3-4BInstruct GSM8K decoding. (b) Reconstruction error on the same setting, averaged over K/V streams, layers, and active examples. (c) Sensitivity of MATH500 accuracy to τc and δ. (d) Sensitivity to dictionary size N and sparsity s.

Figure 1: Motivation for FAD-KV. Diagnostics are computed using Llama-3.2-3B on MATH-500 with 4096- atom key/value dictionaries and sparsity s = 8. (a)–(b) Decoding-time KV vectors have head-heavy dictionary correlations; we visualize value-vector scores as an example, and show that a small Top-n screened pool recalls most full-OMP atoms. (c)–(d) many atoms remain inactive after prefill, and inactive capacity is common across prompts. These observations motivate screening-based sparse coding and fixed-size dictionary adaptation.

papers.title: FAD-KV: Adaptive Dictionary KV Caching for Efficient Reasoning Decoding
papers.tldr: FAD-KV enables efficient long-context reasoning by combining fast sparse KV coding with fixed-size, adaptive dictionaries that avoid cache and dictionary growth.

papers.abstract: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.
authors: Miles Liao, Aaron Smieszek, Yuhao Ge
bullets: Efficient communication is a bottleneck in large language model multi-agent systems.
SelectKV selectively communicates KV-cache states while protecting inherited context, reducing communicated KV positions and payload by 9.7–9.9%.
HyLaMAS enables hybrid linear-attention agents to share both KV caches and recurrent states through a common workspace.
Across six benchmarks, SelectKV largely preserves accuracy, though it performs six points lower on HumanEval+.
HyLaMAS reduces decoded tokens by 53–80% and yields 1.16–2.78× speedups versus text-based communication across Qwen3.5 scales.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Boundary-protection ablation for SelectKV on MedQA. Removing protection permits greater compression but produces a larger observed accuracy loss. Boundary-aware SelectKV remains one accuracy point below full-cache LatentMAS while reducing communicated KV payload.

Figure 2: Matched-budget SelectKV selector ablation on MedQA. SelectKV outperforms random and recency-only selection at the same retained-KV budget, indicating that its selection criterion contributes beyond compression alone. The selector ablation was conducted as a separate experimental run from the main SelectKV evaluation in Table 1.

Figure 3: Hybrid-state channel ablation for HyLaMAS on MedQA. The right panel reports mean decoded tokens per completed problem and reports the logical state payload shared across agent boundaries in MiB.

Improve is HyLaMAS vs. TextMAS: accuracy in absolute points, token reduction (%), speed-up (TextMAS time / HyLaMAS time). Shaded Improve cells mark a change in the favorable direction.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models listen and speak at the same time, which makes them promising for natural, open-ended conversation. But can they sustain a coherent conversation for tens of minutes? Because they generate a token every frame, even while listening, they exhaust their context windows within minutes. Yet existing benchmarks evaluate only single turns or a few conversational rounds, too short to expose the long-horizon problem. We introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB), which tests five recent full-duplex models on long replayed conversations and in live conversation with an LLM partner. Every evaluated model eventually either degrades or exhausts its context. Models that keep the full history often degrade before their context runs out, while sliding-window models still fall into repetition, silence, and gibberish. For sliding-window models, we identify two contributing mechanisms. Gibberish and silence are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction, where the sliding window discards the first KV entry. Repetition is also reinforced by the model's own recent outputs. Guided by this diagnosis, we apply two simple fixes: Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps that first entry, and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages echoing while guarding against prolonged silence. Together, they support the diagnosis and, without retraining, substantially reduce conversational collapse in replays of up to an hour while running in real time.
bullets: Existing short-turn benchmarks miss failures that emerge over tens of minutes.
FD-LHB evaluates five full-duplex models on long replayed conversations and live conversations with an LLM partner.
All tested models eventually degrade or exhaust context; failures include repetition, silence, and gibberish.
Sliding-window failures are linked to evicting the initial KV entry and reinforcing the model’s own recent outputs.
Initialization-Anchor Pinning and Duplex Repetition Penalty reduce collapse without retraining, while preserving real-time operation.

papers.title: Why Full-Duplex Speech Models Collapse in Long Conversations
papers.tldr: Full-duplex speech models often collapse during long conversations, but simple inference-time fixes substantially improve stability for up to an hour.

papers.abstract: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill makes mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, but what it damages has not been measured. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions in four MoE families on short-answer question answering. At half the experts the F1 loss is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but no longer answers briefly. The loss is made at a few tokens: the two chat-template tokens before the answer in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and the first 8-32 tokens, where the instruction sits, in DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Keeping them at full experts removes most of the F1 loss and about half and a fifth of the increase in answer NLL. These tokens are not the familiar suspects: reduction leaves the first-token sink within 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most a quarter of the loss. On real prompts the localisation becomes a placement rule: with about 4% of tokens at full experts, putting them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while the same budget scattered in the documents is about 3 points worse in both prespecified primary tests of this comparison. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts.
bullets: At half the experts, models usually identify the answer but lose F1 because responses become less concise.
Damage concentrates on two chat-template tokens in Qwen3-30B-A3B and the first 8–32 instruction tokens in DeepSeek-V2-Lite.
Keeping these tokens at full experts removes most F1 loss and reduces roughly half to one-fifth of the answer-NLL increase.
Allocating full experts to about 4% of task-interface tokens keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model; scattering the budget in documents is about three points worse.
This placement rule reduces time to first token by about 14% on 11K-token prompts.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Why the last tokens matter in Qwen3. (a) The account. (b) Attention each token receives from the query that predicts the first answer token (log scale). (c) Increase in the loss of the model’s own answer when one attention path is blocked: the first answer token needs the last two prompt tokens to see the instruction and documents; the stop token needs the answer to see those two tokens. (d) Damage left after repairing one band of layers when the last eight tokens run two experts: the mean increase in the answer’s NLL as a share of the increase with no repair, over 300 prompts. A value above 100% means that the partial repair made the loss larger; the 95% prompt-bootstrap interval of this ratio excludes 100% for experts kept in layers 0–3 (120% [103, 141]) and 44–47 (113% [105, 121]) and for the clean state restored in layers 8–11 (126% [107, 148]). Repairing one band mixes repaired and reduced computation, a state the model sees under neither condition. The ratio is of means, which a few prompts dominate.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the impact of expert reduction in MoE models during prefill, identifying specific critical tokens (instruction, chat template) that cause performance loss and proposing a placement rule for efficient serving.
papers.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
papers.tldr: Reducing routed experts during MoE prefill mainly hurts short-answer F1 through a small set of task-interface tokens, and protecting those tokens preserves quality while retaining latency gains.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
bullets: Threshold calibration does not guarantee a fixed read budget: an intended 18% budget averaged only 12.9% reads in benchmarks.
Replacing thresholds with per-token top-k selection requires no calibration data and matched or outperformed threshold selection in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets.
Top-k selection avoided the repetition-loop collapse observed with calibrated thresholds on Gemma 4.
A weight-only reader uses a ternary sketch to screen channels and a low-rank map to recover skipped ones.
Across three post-trained MoE models, the reader retained 98.1% of full-model accuracy using 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with reported speedups up to 2.69×.

papers.selection_reason: Channel selection reduces routed-expert memory reads during MoE decoding, improving memory efficiency of inference.
papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
papers.tldr: Calibration-free top-k channel selection provides predictable MoE read budgets and preserves accuracy, while a weight-only reader achieves substantial decoding speedups with sparse expert reads.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization. CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations. On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.
authors: Zukang Xu, Zhixiong Zhao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Xin Si, Dawei Yang
bullets: Targets memory-efficient LLM deployment through low-bit weight quantization.
Uses multi-scale candidate probing and a tangent separable upper bound to enable joint index–scale updates efficiently.
Reduces candidate selection to lower envelopes of lines, avoiding exhaustive codeword-combination enumeration.
Outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks for Qwen3.8-27B.
Ablations indicate joint updates provide greater gains than scale-only refinement.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but this cache is still the part of a prompt's state that grows with the prompt and that must be stored or moved to reuse it. We present DCKV, a differentiable codec for the KV cache and the first KV-cache codec that is trained end to end. Its transform, its quantizer and its entropy models, which are conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized together against the frozen language model, both for the code length that the entropy models assign and for the change of the model's output. On Qwen3.5-2B, DCKV stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.
authors: Egor Maximov, Aleksei Merkelov, Vasiliy Alekseev, Ivan Krivorotov, Valentin Beliaev, Nikita Arsenin, Dmitry Bocharov, Aleksei Goncharov
bullets: Targets the growing, transferable KV cache used by full-attention layers in hybrid language models.
Jointly learns a transform, quantizer, and token-conditioned entropy models.
Optimizes both estimated code length and the frozen model’s output preservation.
On Qwen3.5-2B, achieves over 55× compression with at most a 1.8-point loss on three long-context benchmarks.
Exceeds 100× compression with at most a 3.6-point loss.

papers.selection_reason: Learned KV cache compression for efficient inference in hybrid LLMs.
papers.title: DCKV: Learned Transform Coding of the Prompt KV Cache in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: DCKV is an end-to-end learned codec that compresses hybrid language-model prompt KV caches by over 55× with limited benchmark degradation.

papers.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
bullets: Mamba-2 state energy is nearly rank-one, but the useful output-read content lies in a different low-dimensional, non-coordinate-aligned subspace.
The proposed post-training method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians, with an exact rotation enabled by Mamba-2’s scalar-identity transition.
HARP allocates layer-specific ranks from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers instead of using uniform budgets.
Using one-pass calibration, the method halves state dimension with a 0.3-point average WikiText-2 perplexity increase across 130M–2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points for GHOST.
The approach is evaluated for perplexity and retrieval; performance degradation increases at 25% retention.

papers.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression

papers.abstract: Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. Local administrations that hold these records typically lack GPUs, reliable connectivity, and the budget for external digitization services. We study whether a frugal pipeline, with consumer-grade capture and CPU-only inference, can make such registers machine-readable. We introduce a corpus of 1,568 smartphone images of handwritten birth, marriage, and death records from a municipal registry in Chad, with line-level transcriptions for 185 records. Our pipeline combines a fully classical preprocessing stage, running at about 2.6 images per second on a laptop CPU, with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned from a pretrained model in about four hours on a free-tier GPU. On manually corrected line segmentation and a single-registry test set whose writers also appear in training, fine-tuning reduces the character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and the word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%. On a six-core laptop CPU, the recognizer weighs 61 MiB, peaks below 2.6 GiB of RAM, and processes an image in under 6 s on average, excluding line segmentation. Finally, a downstream information-extraction task shows that residual recognition errors cost about 9 F1 points on role resolution, compared with a 36.7-point gap between the fine-tuned and pretrained recognizers. These results are evidence of feasibility within one registry, not of performance on unseen writers or sites; we discuss these limitations in detail.
authors: Ousmane Hamadou, Jean Louis Kedieng Ebongue Fendji
bullets: Targets digitization barriers in Sub-Saharan administrations lacking GPUs, reliable connectivity, and external-service budgets.
Introduces 1,568 smartphone images from 185 handwritten birth, marriage, and death records in a Chadian municipal registry, with line transcriptions.
Combines classical preprocessing with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned on a pretrained model; inference runs on a laptop CPU without a GPU.
On manually corrected segmentation and a same-writer test setting, fine-tuning reduces character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%.
Residual recognition errors reduce downstream role-resolution F1 by about 9 points; results demonstrate feasibility only within the studied registry.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a frugal pipeline for handwritten text recognition that optimizes for CPU-only inference and memory usage, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference
papers.tldr: A frugal smartphone-to-CPU pipeline can make handwritten civil-status records searchable within a single registry, but its strong accuracy has not been validated on unseen writers or sites.

papers.abstract: Attention Matching (AM) compacts a KV cache by keeping some keys per head, refitting their values and adding a bias to each kept key's logit. FlashAttention and vLLM's paged caches have no input for it. We fold the bias into the keys along one closed-form direction per head, fitted on context queries, giving a plain cache with AM's size and head dimension and the model's own query path; the output error is bounded by how far each query's projection on that direction is from 1. With equal per-head budgets, unmodified vLLM serves folded caches through a KV connector, matching Hugging Face's answers on all 51 Qwen3-4B questions and its greedy output on 180 of 200 Qwen3-14B LongBench samples. With equal budgets on QuALITY (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, Llama-3.1-8B) and LongHealth (three Qwen3 models), the fold is within noise of AM's accuracy in 13 of 14 settings, with lower KL to the full cache than dropping the bias in all 12 where both ran. Under the published per-head budgets, on Qwen3-4B, its Instruct-2507 variant and Llama-3.1-8B, it is within noise of AM in 9 of 10, no longer beats dropping the bias in KL, and the two each win once in accuracy.
bullets: AM compresses KV caches by retaining selected keys, refitting values, and adding per-key logit biases—but standard kernels cannot consume those biases.
The proposed closed-form, per-head key adjustment absorbs each bias along one fitted direction, preserving the model’s normal query path and cache dimensions.
Unmodified vLLM serves the folded caches through a KV connector; outputs closely match Hugging Face and retain most greedy generations in the reported tests.
Across equal-budget evaluations, folding matches AM within noise in 13 of 14 settings and generally produces lower KL divergence than omitting the bias.
Under published per-head budgets, folding remains comparable to AM in 9 of 10 settings, though its KL advantage disappears.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache compaction and memory-efficient inference by folding attention biases into keys.
papers.title: Folding Attention Biases into Keys Makes Compacted KV Caches Run on Standard Kernels
papers.tldr: Folding Attention Matching’s key biases into the keys enables compact KV caches to run on standard FlashAttention/vLLM kernels with nearly unchanged accuracy.

papers.abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.
bullets: Structured compression can change adversarial robustness without matching hardware gains.
S25-TRADES achieved the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models, while reducing parameters and MACs versus Full.
TRADES was the main driver of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy over clean recovery in matched controls.
On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%.
Native INT8 Q/DQ showed roughly twice the FP16 latency and energy despite 99.3% prediction agreement, highlighting hardware-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Robustness-constrained low-precision compression for edge inference, reducing memory, energy, and latency; relevant to efficient AI via memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
papers.tldr: ORBITAL jointly optimizes compressed EEG decoders for adversarial robustness and real edge-hardware efficiency, with FP16 compression offering the strongest practical trade-off.

papers.abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
authors: Suhas Kumar Morisetty, Vaibhavi Lokegaonkar, Sachin Mathew Varghese, Wesley Harris
bullets: Prefix caching benefits depend heavily on how KV-cache entries are evicted under limited memory.
Agentic requests favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations favor frequency.
No single eviction policy is consistently best across diverse workload mixes.
WAKMan selects an eviction policy from traffic behavior without identifying request types or reading prompts.
It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average and has the smallest mean and worst-case optimality gaps among evaluated policies.

papers.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
papers.tldr: WAKMan adapts KV-cache eviction to live workload patterns, improving prefix-cache hit rates over fixed policies.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.

papers.abstract: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
authors: Paul Raj, Simon Caldwell, Daniel Whitmore, Mutlu Mete
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of storing states during sparse MoE adaptation.
Uses trainable width bridges between two residual streams, with bridge warm-up before backbone adaptation and frozen router weights.
Analyzes convergence and replay conditions for reconstructing hidden states.
On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, reports 38.8 GB peak memory and 25.1 samples/s, versus 64.8 GB and 19.9 samples/s for checkpointed supervised fine-tuning.
Reports 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, while multilingual performance is weaker than the checkpointed baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient MoE LLM adaptation by replaying coupled hidden states, substantially reducing peak memory with moderate quality tradeoffs.
papers.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation
papers.tldr: DuplexTune reduces memory use for MoE adaptation by replaying coupled hidden states through frozen-routing pretrained modules, with higher throughput but some quality tradeoffs.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
authors: Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
bullets: Frequency-based precision allocation can hurt because frequent lookups often have small gates, while rare long-tail entity lookups have larger gates and greater quantization impact.
GateRQ stores each row as progressively refined 1-bit residual codes and uses an always-resident first level to estimate gates.
Deeper residual levels are fetched only for lookups ranked as most important by their gate values.
Without retraining, it reduces GPU table memory by 7.8× and improves vLLM throughput by 11%–31% over FP8 tables.
It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

papers.selection_reason: Gate-aware quantization of conditional LLM memory drastically cuts table memory and improves throughput while preserving long-tail fact recall.
papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.tldr: GateRQ improves quantized conditional memory by allocating extra precision per lookup based on the row’s gate value, preserving long-tail facts while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) impose substantial computation and memory costs as context sizes increase, motivating methods that compress a context into a shorter representation before inference. Existing soft-prompt compression methods typically use the same Transformer backbone as used in the target model, where producing the compressed representation leads to significant latency overheads. This restricts them to the offline setting where context is compressed once and then reused across many queries. We propose the Boa Compressor, a plug-and-play online context compressor built on a Mamba state-space model (SSM) that encodes arbitrary-length context in a single linear-time pass, producing a representation on which we condition a frozen target LLM. The SSM is trained by distillation, matching the next-token logit distribution from the LLM ingesting the full context (as teacher) to the same LLM ingesting the compressed representation (as the student). At equal compression ratios, Boa matches or surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art offline compression baselines, while being an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based implementations, thereby reducing end-to-end latency rather than adding compression time overhead. We demonstrate that Boa also scales well to longer contexts and to compression ratios as aggressive as 16x. By enabling effective compression that is cheap enough to run on every query at inference time, Boa becomes a practical and general tool for efficient long-context inference.
bullets: Addresses the latency and memory costs of long contexts and the overhead of Transformer-based compression.
Distills a state-space encoder to match the target LLM’s next-token distributions from full versus compressed context.
Matches or surpasses state-of-the-art offline compression at equal compression ratios.
Runs an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based compressors, reducing end-to-end latency.
Scales to longer contexts and compression ratios up to 16×, supporting per-query compression.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Boa Compressor, a linear-time context compression method using Mamba SSMs, directly addressing memory and latency in LLM inference.
papers.title: Linear-Time Context Compression with State-Space Encoding
papers.tldr: Boa Compressor uses a Mamba state-space model to compress arbitrary-length contexts in one linear-time pass, enabling fast online long-context inference with a frozen LLM.

papers.abstract: KV caching reduces the serving cost of large language models (LLMs), but the growing KV cache footprint is increasingly exceeds GPU and host-memory capacity. Therefore, people use SSD to expand the KV cache storage capacity with high I/O bandwidth. However, in production LLM workload, such as multi-round conversation and LLM agents, the total amount of KV cache writes significantly exceeds SSD capacity, shortening SSD lifetime from years to months. To improve SSD lifetime, a natural solution is to reduce the KV cache writes by gating the KV cache writes via historical access patterns. However, that significantly lowers the KV cache hit rate (and increase the LLM serving cost) since KV caches from different attention types might have identical historical access pattern but different future access patterns. Our insight is that, to reduce KV cache writes without hurting KV cache hit rate, one need to not only consider the access pattern, but also application-level information such as the attention type of KV cache. Leveraging this observation, we propose Gandalf , the first SSD KV cache offloading system with SSD life time awareness. Gandalf prioritize the admission of full-attention KV cache into SSD over the cache generated by other types of attention, which significantly increases SSD lifetime without sacrificing cache hit rate. Our evaluation shows that Gandalf extends the SSD lifetime by 7.3X on average, while having negligible impact on cache hit rate across multiple workload traces and wide range of hardware capacity. Gandalf design can be extended to other flash-based storage, such as High Bandwidth Flash (HBF).
bullets: LLM KV-cache writes can overwhelm SSD capacity in workloads such as multi-round conversations and LLM agents, reducing device lifetime from years to months.
Write gating based only on historical access patterns can lower cache hit rates because different attention types may share similar histories but have different future reuse.
Gandalf combines access patterns with application-level attention-type information to guide SSD cache admission.
It prioritizes full-attention KV caches over caches from other attention types, reducing writes while preserving cache effectiveness.
Across multiple workload traces and hardware capacities, Gandalf extends SSD lifetime by 7.3× on average with negligible cache-hit-rate impact; the design may also apply to high-bandwidth flash.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.
bullets: Addresses host-memory exhaustion and the model’s limited positional horizon during long interactive sessions.
Uses an analytical access model based on known camera poses to predict spill points and classify potential stalls.
Stores KV memory in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy, prefetches before computation, avoids waiting on misses, and writes back asynchronously.
Generates 37.5 minutes of continuous video at about 9.5 FPS with zero stalls and constant host memory on a single RTX 4090 system.
Reports no measurable quality loss with int4 storage on a sealed test set, but about a one-point MUSIQ drop for long-gap revisits.
papers.selection_reason: Presents tiered memory and zero-stall prefetching for interactive world model KV caches, relevant to efficient inference and world model deployment.
papers.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
papers.tldr: WorldPager enables continuous, zero-stall long-horizon world-model video by paging int4 KV memory across GPU, DRAM, and NVMe with pose-guided prefetching.

papers.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.
authors: Haolin Li, Haipeng Zhang, Mang Li, Zhaohui Xia, Xun Zhu, Miao Li, Yu Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses rising training and inference costs caused by long interaction histories and repeated item-text encoding.
Separates item semantic encoding from request-level modeling using learnable summary tokens and predictive REC tokens.
Composes cached, user- and query-independent item memories in interaction order, with an optional query for personalization.
Jointly trains cached memories with limited live re-encoding and periodic cache refreshes to maintain consistency.
Evaluations on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and LazSeq report state-of-the-art retrieval with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale.
papers.selection_reason: Cached item memories reduce repeated item-text encoding and inference cost in LLM-based retrieval, matching memory-efficient inference and LLM external-memory interests.
papers.title: CRIM: Composable and Reusable Item Memory for Efficient Personalized Retrieval
papers.tldr: CRIM makes personalized retrieval more efficient by caching compact, reusable item memories while preserving request-specific history modeling.

papers.abstract: Adaptive robot perception systems must balance detector accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption, particularly when high ambient temperatures cause processors to thermally throttle. We propose Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy that forecasts processor temperature using a closed-form RC thermal model and excludes detector configurations predicted to cross a throttling threshold. We evaluate THR with four YOLO11 configurations across seven real-world perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds, comparing it with latency-aware routing, fixed-threshold thermostats, duty caps, and a matched-compute-budget control. At ambient temperatures of 45-55 degrees C and a tight inference deadline, THR eliminates throttling in simulation, reduces deadline misses by 3.9-7.5 percentage points, and reduces energy per on-time frame by approximately 12-13% relative to a latency-belief router. A separate experiment using deadline-paced, nonoverlapping frame execution yields miss-rate reductions of 6.2-9.5 percentage points. A tuned thermostat or duty cap can match THR at a fixed operating point; predictive routing is most useful when ambient conditions or calibrated thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies. Measurements on an Apple M5 support the single-node heating approximation but do not validate hardware throttling. The results characterize the conditions under which thermal forecasting improves the efficiency and timeliness of resource-constrained robot perception.
authors: Sparsh Roy, Kevin Zhou, Arhaan Shah, Shreyan Garg, Vihaan Joshi-Apte, Maxim Kudryashov, Nanda Cheruvanthala
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between detection accuracy, latency, and energy when high temperatures cause processor throttling.
Uses a closed-form RC thermal model to predict temperature and avoids detector configurations likely to exceed a throttling threshold.
Evaluated four YOLO11 configurations across seven perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds against static and latency-aware baselines.
At 45–55°C with tight deadlines, it eliminates simulated throttling, lowers deadline misses, and cuts energy per on-time frame relative to a latency-belief router.
Predictive routing is most beneficial when operating conditions or thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies; hardware throttling itself was not validated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy for robot perception that forecasts processor temperature to avoid thermal throttling. This addresses efficiency and timeliness in resource-constrained AI systems.
papers.title: Thermal-Headroom Routing for Efficient Robot Perception in Extreme Heat
papers.tldr: Thermal-Headroom Routing uses thermal forecasting to select robot perception models, reducing throttling, deadline misses, and energy use in extreme heat.

papers.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training.
