We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.
authors: Junho Kim, CheHyun Lee, Donghun Kang, Youngho Cho, Dongwook Lee, Heeseung Kim, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Long sessions cause declines in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency.
A closed-loop evaluation framework measures stability, information retention, and efficiency over extended interactions.
Self-distillation with lightweight LoRA adaptation mitigates degradation across three architecturally distinct models.
Two-resolution context preserves recent exchanges in detail while compressing older history into key-value representations.
LoRA improves stability over ten-minute sessions, while TRC extends gains beyond training-session lengths and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.
papers.selection_reason: Two-resolution context compression reduces KV-cache growth by over 90% for long-session models.
papers.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
papers.tldr: The study diagnoses degradation in full-duplex speech models during extended conversations and improves stability using LoRA self-distillation plus compressed long-term context.

papers.abstract: GUI agents built on vision-language models interact with continuously evolving interfaces, yet conventional inference repeatedly recomputes representations of largely overlapping observations and histories. This mismatch makes multi-step interaction costly, while changes in context, interface content, and action arguments prevent straightforward cache reuse. We introduce GUIFlow, a framework for full-pipeline incremental inference in multi-image GUI interaction. Our central insight is that advancing a decision need not require rebuilding all supporting representations: each interaction step can instead selectively update computational states maintained across the trajectory. To support new decisions as the context evolves, GUIFlow adapts how past computation is reused: historical KV states are position-aligned and injected into the current context; change signals guide selective updates of current-observation states in the vision encoder and language model; and earlier action responses serve as speculative drafts verified by the target model. Together, these mechanisms enable cross-step reuse throughout visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training, a separate draft model, or changes to the model-visible inputs and action interface. Experiments demonstrate up to 3.39x geometric-mean speedup across offline multi-image benchmarks and up to 3.49x in online, closed-loop interaction on OSWorld, while maintaining task performance broadly comparable to the dense baseline.
authors: Ye Li, Haoran Ding, Huanan Liu, Yuan Meng, Yutian Shen, Yuansong Wang, Kangye Ji, Hanyun Cui, Hongbo Duan, Chen Tang, Jiawei Li, Shu-Tao Xia, Zhi Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of repeatedly recomputing overlapping observations and histories during GUI interaction.
Reuses position-aligned historical KV states and uses change signals to selectively update vision-encoder and language-model states.
Speculatively reuses prior action responses and verifies them with the target model.
Provides full-pipeline reuse across visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without a separate draft model or additional training.
Reports up to 3.39× offline and 3.49× online speedups, with task performance broadly comparable to dense inference.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental KV reuse and selective state updates for efficient vision-language model inference.
papers.title: GUIFlow: Temporal Redundancy-Aware Incremental Inference for GUI Agents
papers.tldr: GUIFlow accelerates multi-step GUI agents by selectively reusing and updating computations across changing visual and interaction contexts, achieving substantial speedups without retraining or changing the agent interface.

papers.abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
bullets: Targets the memory-bandwidth bottleneck of long-form reasoning by compressing model weights to roughly 2 bits.
Assigns ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit precision per layer using sensitivity, then searches quantization codewords block by block with Gumbel-softmax.
Recalibrates shared scales using knowledge distillation and applies short quantization-aware training to better match the base model’s output distribution.
Uses paired reasoning tests to select between recalibration and QAT checkpoints rather than relying only on perplexity or multiple-choice accuracy.
On Qwen3-1.7B, reports 46.7 MATH-500 after recalibration and 73.0 after QAT; a 3.74 GB model reaches 94.8 versus 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
papers.selection_reason: Two-bit weight quantization with bitwidth allocation and scale recalibration reduces LLM memory footprint while preserving reasoning.
papers.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning
papers.tldr: ThinkBit is a scalar 2-bit quantization framework that preserves challenging mathematical reasoning through sensitivity-based bit allocation, codeword search, scale recalibration, and reasoning-guided checkpoint selection.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
authors: Sooyoung Kwon, Carlee Joe-Wong, Kyunghan Lee
bullets: Targets onboard VLA inference, where processing hundreds of visual tokens causes high prefill latency.
Finds that reuse is effective for low-drift tokens, while pruning is preferable for high-drift tokens.
Uses a calibrated drift threshold and cache age to classify tokens as reusable, invalid-and-recompute, or prune.
A fixed recomputation budget directly controls latency.

On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, remains within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while reducing Jetson AGX Orin prefill latency by up to 48%; with 7% of tokens recomputed, it exceeds the strongest LIBERO-Object baseline by 24.4 points.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLA inference acceleration via joint token reuse and pruning with drift-based cache validity fits VLA and token/KV efficiency.
papers.title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
papers.tldr: TRIAGE combines token reuse and pruning based on cache drift to reduce VLA prefill latency while preserving near-full-recomputation robot performance.

papers.abstract: Typed decision-making tasks in agents, such as UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching, require models to choose from a set of discrete candidates. While prior work demonstrates that text-only System One models achieve four key properties including candidate-order invariance, scalability, and cache reuse via separate request-candidate encoding, extending them to multimodal settings where candidates are visual remains underexplored. We introduce Iris, a framework that accommodates image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving the core decision module. We prove that order invariance and exact cache reuse hold for any per-candidate encoder under Iris, and derive the closed-form latency reduction. We construct a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, deduplicated, order-shuffled, three generalization splits). Independent encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4 / 72.1 / 74.8 percent accuracy with zero-flip rate under candidate reordering. Joint encoding reaches 90.6 / 89.5 / 91.6 percent but suffers an 8 to 10 percent answer-flip rate when shuffled. To bridge this gap, we propose a design that encodes each candidate conditioned on the request state without inter-candidate cross-attention; it preserves strict order invariance, enables forked cache sharing, and attains 91.7 / 86.5 / 90.0 percent accuracy at one-third of OneJev latency with calibrated null probabilities (AUROC 0.93 to 0.97). Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. On MetaEncoder benchmarks, Iris-4B achieves 100 percent on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev. Finally, we resolve a systems bottleneck on Ampere GPUs: reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d into its exact matrix-product form accelerates processing by 350x. Code, data, and checkpoints: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris.
bullets: Targets typed-choice tasks such as UI selection, recommendation, and chart matching with visual candidates.
Uses per-candidate encoding, including request-conditioned encoding without inter-candidate cross-attention, to preserve strict order invariance and reusable caches.
The proposed design reaches 91.7/86.5/90.0% accuracy across three splits, with one-third of OneJev’s latency and AUROC 0.93–0.97 for calibrated null probabilities.
Reusing image candidates reduces latency by 37× at K=256 and 191× at K=2048.
An exact Conv3d-to-matrix-product reformulation accelerates Qwen3.5 patch embedding by 350× on Ampere GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal decision framework with order-invariant candidate encoding and reusable inference cache; relevant to memory-efficient inference and latency reduction.
papers.title: Seeing the Options: Typed Decisions over Visual Candidates with Reusable Option Memory
papers.tldr: Iris enables order-invariant, cacheable decisions over visual, textual, or hybrid candidates while achieving strong accuracy and major latency savings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. Ultra-low-bit quantization reduces this footprint, yet preserving task performance and controlling weight recovery costs remain challenging. We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7% task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5% success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5$^{*}$, uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves $6.10\times$ complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ
authors: Xuhong Qiu, Zhuoyu Wu, Qiawei Zheng, Wenhui Ou, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint of vision-language-action models on onboard, memory-constrained robots.
Allocates matrix bitwidths under storage budgets using action sensitivity and a proxy for weight recovery cost.
Uses per-channel calibration, matrix-uniform bitwidths, lossless coding, and block-wise recovery to reduce storage and recovery overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 92.7% success at W3 and 70.5% at W2.5; W3 exceeds AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points.
A W1.5* configuration with lossless coding provides 6.10× compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success.
papers.selection_reason: Ultra-low-bit quantization for VLA models; directly relevant to embodied VLA and memory-efficient deployment.
papers.title: AGQ: Action-Guided Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: AGQ enables memory-efficient VLA deployment by allocating ultra-low-bit weights according to action sensitivity and recovery cost while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer vision-language model that optimizes speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for local agentic workloads. Derived from the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B model family, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB combines Star Elastic compression with 2-bit Quantization-Aware Distillation for memory-constrained deployment. The model is optimized for reasoning, agentic tool use, and web & terminal interactions. We also trained a LiLiCorr speculative drafter that is released alongside the model to reach our target inference speed. The resulting model achieves a higher accuracy than leading models with similar memory footprints and speed across many benchmarks for general agentic capabilities (e.g., GDPVal v2), web browsing (e.g., BrowseComp), and terminal use (e.g., Terminal-Bench 2.1), with a relatively high TPS of 84 on RTX Spark that is comparable to models with much lower active parameter counts and more than sufficient for long-horizon agentic applications.
authors: Ganesh Ajjanagadde, Chris Alexiuk, Luke Alonso, Kumar Anshuman, Maor Ashkenazi, Nave Assaf, Gorkem Batmaz, Omer Belhasin, Shai Ben Nun, Akhiad Bercovich, Pritam Biswas, Caroline Blanco, Tijmen Blankevoort, Michael Boone, Christopher Borden, Kari Briski, Bryan Catanzaro, Zijia Chen, Aishwarya Chhabra, Hung-Yueh Chiang, Annamalai Chockalingam, Jonathan Cohen, Joey Conway, Olivier Delalleau, Gerardo Delgado Cabrera, Leon Derczynski, Li Ding, Will Efstratis, Michael Elad, Ellie Evans, Wes Feely, Michael Fukuyama, Gaurav Garg, Rishabh Garg, Arvind Gopalakrishnan, Shishir Goyal, Kartik Gulia, Hao Guo, Negar Habibi, Scott Hara, Ehsan Hosseini Asl, Rohit Jena, Udi Karpas, Bilal Kartal, Mayank Kaushik, Manoj Kilaru, Mackenzie Kosseim, Oleksii Kuchaiev, Matthieu Le, Raymond Lee, Jian Leong, Jonathan Li, Sheldon Liang, Mingjie Liu, Eileen Long, Katherine Luna, Chenjie Luo, Mingyuan Ma, Arsh Maknojia, Richard Mazzarese, Jessica Medina, Puhui Meng, Yoav Miron, Pavlo Molchanov, David Mosallanezhad, Chetan Mungekar, Marina Neseem, Oluwatobi Olabiyi, Jason Paul, Bhavesh Pawar, Seth Poulos, Anav Prasad, Meredith Price, Sweta Priyadarshi, Haifeng Qian, Vinay Raman, Kaustubh Rao, Hayley Ross, Matan Rusanovsky, Sudeep Sabnis, Karan Sapra, Micah Schaffer, Schmitty, Alex Settle, Ashton Sharabiani, Haran Kumar Shiv Kumar, Rameshwar Shivbhakta, Guillermo Siman, Barnaby Simkin, Oliver Simons, Andrii Skliar, Padmavathy Subramanian, Yoshi Suhara, Ali Taghibakhshi, Nima Tajbakhsh, Andrew Tao, Roy Uziel, Prasoon Varshney, Jose Vergara, Huy Vu, Mengru Wang, Rochelle Woods, Pinky Xu, Dina Yared, Chenhan Yu, Chaosen Zhang, Jian Zhang, Yiheng Zhang, Ran Zilberstein
bullets: Targets reasoning, tool use, web browsing, and terminal interactions for local deployment.
Combines a hybrid Mamba-Transformer architecture with Star Elastic compression and 2-bit Quantization-Aware Distillation.
Includes a LiLiCorr speculative drafter to improve inference speed.
Reports strong accuracy across agentic, web-browsing, and terminal-use benchmarks, with 84 TPS on RTX Spark.
Scope: optimized for memory-constrained local workloads rather than general-purpose deployment claims beyond the reported benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid vision-language model optimized for local memory-constrained deployment with compression and speculative decoding.
papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB: A Hybrid Vision-Language Model for Local AI
papers.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a compressed hybrid vision-language model designed for fast, capable local agentic AI under tight memory limits.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video-MemComp, a training-free and sensitivity-aware context management framework for memory-constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer-wise structural sensitivity via a first-order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre-RoPE safe zone with an attention-conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer-wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high-sensitivity layers. Video-MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full-cache and state-of-the-art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.
authors: Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
bullets: Targets memory bottlenecks and error accumulation in long-context streaming video understanding.
Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to separate local approximation error from layer-wise structural sensitivity.
Aggregates tokens in a pre-RoPE safe zone with attention-conserving logit bias to reduce geometric distortion.
Dynamically allocates KV-cache budgets using offline gradient priors and online context entropy.
Matches or exceeds full-cache and existing compression methods on MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema; Qwen2.5-VL-3B rises from 62.3% to 64.1% with over 90% KV-memory savings.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses streaming-video KV-cache and token compression for efficient MLLM inference.
papers.title: Video-MemComp: Taylor-Guided Sensitivity-Aware Memory Management for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Video-MemComp is a training-free method that compresses streaming-video KV memory by modeling sensitivity and approximation error, achieving over 90% memory savings with improved accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.
authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap caused by direct FP4 post-training quantization.
Stores low-rank factors as binary ±1 sign vectors, reducing storage per rank-one component by 16× versus high-precision corrections.
Runs the correction through additions/subtractions on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM.
On 4B–72B LLMs, matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ.
A fused B300 kernel is at most 11% slower than FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for ranks up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 through batch size 8.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces binary low-rank corrections (BiLoCo) for post-training quantization to reduce memory usage and latency in LLM inference, running efficiently on tensor cores.
papers.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: BiLoCo uses binary low-rank corrections to recover FP4-quantized LLM accuracy with far less storage and limited inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.
authors: Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
bullets: Reframes row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks.
Identifies GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent as hard, zero-temperature decisions that discard alternative codewords.
Uses vector approximate message passing for soft blockwise posteriors, followed by exact block coordinate descent for refinement.
Evaluated on 2-bit lattice and 3-/4-bit scalar quantization across Llama, Qwen, and Mistral models.
Reports improved perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over hard-decision baselines, with compatibility with activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization of LLMs directly reduces model memory requirements for efficient inference.
papers.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: MPQ improves post-training quantization by passing soft information between weight blocks before making final low-bit decisions.

papers.abstract: We present a surrogate-accelerated Bayesian history-matching framework, demonstrated on a realistic synthetic model ($N=100{,}188$ cells). The forward map $\mathcal{G}$ is replaced by a Fourier neural operator $\mathcal{G}_\theta$ trained in a closed loop, $\hat{x}_{n+1}=\mathcal{G}_\theta(u,\hat{x}_n)$, with the discrete black-oil residual $R(x_{n+1},x_n)$ as a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) penalty, truncated backpropagation and noise injection. We assimilate production data and 4-D seismic using adaptive regularised ensemble Kalman inversion (aREKI), and synthesise $\Delta V_p$ inside the rollout via a closed-form Gassmann transform of the surrogate, under a two-stage schedule (aREKI on production, then an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation, ES-MDA, on both). To temper the ill-posedness, we invert $(\log K,\phi)$ not in $\mathbb{R}^{2N}$, where $N_e\ll 2N$ leaves a rank-deficient covariance and a null space the data never inform, but on a chart $u=\Psi(\tilde m)$, $\tilde m\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d\ll 2N$, given by a Parseval-exact truncated cosine transform or a variational auto-encoder decoder. The ensemble then spans its own search space; the directions the data cannot constrain are cut to those the chart can express, and every member decodes to a geologically plausible field. For the rollout we prove an exposure bound $W_1\le\sum_j L^{\,n-1-j}\mathbb{E}e_j$, a physics-penalty contraction $\|D_x\mathcal{G}_\theta\|\le\alpha 0.999$ on pressure and saturation and rolls out in $0.579$ s, a $\sim2500\times$ speed-up, bringing an $N_e=190$-member, $N_a=10$-iteration joint inversion within one GPU-hour.
authors: Clement Etienam, David Blom, Hari Pattathil, Tsubasa Onishi, Harpreet Sethi, Lalson Vincent, Suraj Pawar, Kishan Ramesh Kumar, Pandu Devarakota, Faruk O. Alpak
bullets: Replaces the reservoir forward simulator with an autoregressive Fourier neural operator trained using black-oil residual penalties, truncated backpropagation, and noise injection.
Assimilates production and 4-D seismic data through a two-stage aREKI and ES-MDA workflow, with seismic changes synthesized using a Gassmann transform.
Restricts inversion of permeability and porosity to low-dimensional cosine-transform or variational-autoencoder charts to reduce unidentifiable directions and promote plausible fields.
Provides an exposure-bound analysis and reports stable rollouts, a roughly 2500× speed-up, and completion of the stated ensemble inversion within one GPU-hour on the synthetic model.
Demonstration is limited to a realistic synthetic model with 100,188 cells.
papers.selection_reason: Uses autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operators as surrogates for reservoir dynamics, acting as a fast predictor of environment states (world model) and improving computational efficiency.
papers.title: Autoregressive Physics-Informed Neural Operator Surrogates and Joint 4-D Seismic-Production Bayesian History Matching
papers.tldr: A physics-informed Fourier neural operator surrogate enables fast joint production–4-D seismic Bayesian history matching in a low-dimensional geological parameter space.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache growth caused by long chain-of-thought decoding.
Compresses completed text blocks into a few learned pause tokens, then frees the blocks’ original cache entries.
Uses in-block pause-token positions, layer-wise cache allocation based on entry value, and relatively large compression blocks.
On 446 competition problems with 32K-token generations, one-quarter of the generated cache matched an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length.
In vLLM, it reduced cache size 3.5× per sequence and improved saturated-H100 problem completion speed 3.2× versus full KV.
papers.selection_reason: Training learned pause tokens to compress long reasoning into a much smaller KV cache is a direct contribution to memory-efficient LLM inference and persistent memory.
papers.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
papers.tldr: AbridgeKV compresses long reasoning into learned pause-token KV entries, reducing cache use while preserving performance and speeding inference.

papers.abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
bullets: Existing Ouro Looped LMs require KV-cache storage for every loop depth, forcing all loop computations despite supporting dynamic computation.
The proposed “best-available” KV caching strategy enables up to 30% lower FLOPs and KV memory without losing full-depth performance.
Training with awareness of this caching strategy further improves efficiency and performance.
A revised early-exit objective produces heterogeneous token depths based on token difficulty rather than uniform shallow processing.
Results are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pretrained from scratch.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache strategy for looped language models enables dynamic computation with reduced memory and FLOPs, fitting efficient inference and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs
papers.tldr: A practical KV-cache strategy and improved early-exit training make Looped LMs dynamically allocate computation, reducing costs while preserving full-depth performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
bullets: Addresses text-based communication bottlenecks and downstream prefill latency in multi-agent systems.
Combines an upstream model’s KV cache with a downstream model through linear interpolation, without fusion-adapter training.
Evaluated across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
Reports up to 8.6 percentage-point accuracy gains over single-model baselines.
Achieves up to 12.2× faster time to first token than text-based multi-model communication.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV-cache sharing between language models reduces latency and enables efficient latent LLM communication.
papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.tldr: CacheFuse enables training-free latent communication between heterogeneous language models by linearly interpolating their KV caches, improving accuracy while reducing communication latency.

papers.abstract: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
authors: Hayden Prairie, Jacob M. Ryan, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Daniel Y. Fu
bullets: Looped architectures otherwise require separate KV-caches for each recurrence, causing memory usage to grow linearly with depth.
The method combines stochastic-depth pretraining with post-training that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache to earlier recurrences.
BeNice! achieves KV-shareability while matching standard fine-tuning’s unshared validation perplexity.
KV-sharing composes with sequence mixers and low-precision KV-cache quantization.
In simulated low-memory, long-context inference, it improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, throughput by up to 23.6%, and p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes KV-sharing to reduce inference memory in looped architectures, directly targeting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
papers.tldr: BeNice! enables looped models to share KV-caches across recurrences, reducing inference memory and latency without sacrificing validation quality.

papers.abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.
authors: Kyrylo Yemets, Andrii Yaroshevych, Victor Muryn, Ostap Khomenko, Pavlo Kryven, Maksym Kmet, Maksym Shamrai, Mariya Hirna
bullets: Evaluates KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization on four Apple machines under single-request decoding.
KV-cache pruning reaches up to 1.75× end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs.
All tested speculative decoding methods lower Apple throughput, contrasting with reported gains on server GPUs.
GPU-kernel portability is partial because Metal lacks asynchronous copy and batch-one decoding limits serving-oriented mechanisms; transferable components reach up to 1.20× decode throughput.
Quantization benefits vary across Apple machines, showing that optimization speedups are not portable properties of techniques alone.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic evaluation of LLM inference optimizations including KV-cache pruning and quantization on Apple Silicon; relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
papers.tldr: Inference optimizations developed for server GPUs do not transfer uniformly to Apple Silicon; their effectiveness depends on the technique, runtime, hardware, and workload.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually selects the visual tokens to keep once, at prefill, and reuses that selection for the whole generation. We show that this one-shot selection is severely limited on long-form generation: on detailed image description, even an oracle that selects with the attention of the uncompressed answer reaches only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L agreement with the uncompressed output, because the evidence the model reads moves as the description unfolds. Re-selecting whenever attention drifts out of the kept set is the natural remedy, but we find that a fixed drift threshold fails systematically: drift magnitudes are not comparable across samples, so low-drift samples are almost never refreshed although they benefit the most. We propose Rate-Controlled Refresh (RCR), which lets drift decide when and where to re-select while a per-sample controller regulates how often, combined with a low-rank drift detector, candidate-restricted re-selection, and a decision that stays on the GPU. With one setting for all models and tasks, RCR outperforms the per-step retrieval method InfiniGen by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L points on five of six model-task settings with no significant difference on the sixth, while staying within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection, with comparable estimated data movement per step and a 4x smaller GPU-resident detector. On DetailCaps, drift-chosen timing beats random timing at the same refresh rate and periodic timing even at a higher rate, by 2.0-5.0 points. On pre-registered video description, where drift is homogeneous across samples, RCR is on par with InfiniGen on Qwen2-VL and exceeds it on Qwen3-VL but no longer beats a fixed threshold at the nearest tested rates, consistent with the diagnosis; object-level evaluation shows that RCR achieves higher object F1 against the uncompressed output than InfiniGen on two of three models.
bullets: One-shot prefill-time token selection degrades on long descriptions because the model’s visual evidence shifts during generation.
Fixed drift thresholds refresh inconsistently: low-drift samples may rarely refresh despite benefiting most.
RCR combines drift-based timing and location selection with per-sample refresh-rate control, low-rank detection, candidate restriction, and GPU-resident decisions.
Across six model-task settings, RCR beats InfiniGen by 1.6–3.8 ROUGE-L points in five, matches it in one, and remains close to exact per-step re-selection with a smaller detector.
On image description, drift-based timing outperforms random or periodic refresh; on video description, performance aligns with the method’s assumption that drift varies across samples.
papers.selection_reason: Rate-controlled KV re-selection for long-form multimodal generation; a strong contribution to KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Drift Says When, Budget Says How Much: Rate-Controlled KV Re-selection for Long-Form Multimodal Generation
papers.tldr: Rate-Controlled Refresh dynamically re-selects visual KV tokens when attention drifts, improving long-form multimodal generation under a controlled refresh budget.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.
authors: Sebastian Loeschcke, Ivan Koryakovskiy, Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa, Riccardo Del Chiaro, Mart van Baalen, Paul N. Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding and scalability of VQ-QAT for billion-parameter LLMs.
Decomposes weights into normalized directions and gains, quantizing them with spherical-codebook and scalar quantizers.
Uses separate straight-through estimators that produce tangent-space updates, approximating spherical/Riemannian optimization.
Introduces distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8× and scaling training to 10B tokens.
Outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE across several LLaMA and Qwen models and achieves state-of-the-art VQ-QAT accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Spherical lattice vector quantization-aware training for low-bit LLM weights; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training
papers.tldr: SQuAT makes lattice-based vector quantization-aware training scalable and more accurate for low-bit LLMs by separately optimizing weight direction and magnitude.

papers.abstract: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
authors: Jiacheng Liu, Yaxin Luo, Xiaohan Zhao, Peng Sun, Xinyi Shang, Jiacheng Cui, Yonina C. Eldar, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Per-layer embeddings account for 35.2% of Gemma 4 E4B’s parameters, motivating extreme compression.
OPTIC stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at each layer using layer-specific affine decoders.
It fits codes and decoders to the model’s output path rather than directly to stored embedding vectors.
At about 100× BF16 PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% aggregate performance across seven benchmarks, versus 66.3% for the strongest conventional baseline.
At the same compression level, inference uses 29.7% less GPU memory and runs at most 0.40% slower; performance remains 84.1% at 1,002× compression.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces cross-layer latent vector quantization for extreme per-layer embedding compression, directly reducing LLM memory footprint.
papers.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
papers.tldr: OPTIC enables roughly 100× compression of per-layer embeddings while preserving most of the model’s benchmark performance and reducing inference memory with minimal slowdown.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular decode acceleration method. As such, it is particularly relevant to long-output generation, which requires an increasingly large KV cache. KV cache compression offers a way to constrain costs in long-context drafting. However, compression methods that focus on prefill information can lose relevance as the output length grows. We term this phenomenon decode staleness and show that it degrades draft model accuracy under selection-based KV cache compression. We introduce RIFT, a family of selection-based KV cache compression strategies that balance prefill information and recent generated tokens. We show that refreshing the KV cache selection during token generation significantly improves the drafter's quality at the cost of additional decode latency. To alleviate the refresh costs, we propose an adaptive KV refresh strategy that reduces the number of score calculations while retaining the drafter's quality. We further demonstrate how a compressibility-driven drafter training phase, based on sparse attention masks, can improve the drafter's quality under a compressed KV cache. Combined with compressibility training, RIFT enables Qwen3.5-4B, drafting for Qwen3.5-122B, to retain over 98% of its full-cache acceptance length on 32K-token inputs, 4K-token outputs, and an 8K-token KV cache budget.
authors: Dor Tsur, Maor Ashkenazi, Maximilian Golub, Peter Hicks, Yaniv Galron, Talor Abramovich, Yoav Miron, Tiyasa Mitra, Bita Darvish Rouhani, Ran Zilberstein
bullets: Identifies decode staleness: prompt-focused KV selection becomes less relevant during long generation and harms draft accuracy.
Balances prefill information with recently generated tokens through selection-based KV cache compression.
Uses adaptive KV refreshes to reduce score calculations and associated decode latency while preserving quality.
Adds sparse-attention, compressibility-driven drafter training to improve performance under compressed caches.
With training, Qwen3.5-4B drafting for Qwen3.5-122B retains over 98% of full-cache acceptance length under the stated 32K-input, 4K-output, and 8K-cache-budget setting.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression for draft models in speculative decoding fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: RIFT: KV Cache Compression for Draft Models with Complementary Compressibility Training
papers.tldr: RIFT improves speculative decoding with compressed KV caches by balancing prompt and recent-token information, adaptively refreshing selections, and training drafters for compressibility.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key-value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Discarding the tail biases the output, and sampling it as previous approaches do fails at reads of 5% and below, where the tail likely holds heavy hitters the selector missed. Our key observation is that the simplest possible proxy, one token that folds the entire tail into its count-aware mean, already yields lower output error than a sample at every read behind a practical selector. We further show in closed form that at low reads sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding while a single proxy stays below it. Building on these findings, we explore approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail. We propose OpenAttention, a pipeline of clustering, ErrorGate and top-k selection followed by a count-aware mean proxy. To implement clustering and selection both efficiently and effectively, we design training-free Query-Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query-Geometry Selector (QGS), which compress the keys while respecting the query directions. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, OpenAttention retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read. It also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across models, context lengths and datasets. Our customized attention kernel, OpenAttention.flash, runs the decode attention stage 10$\times$ faster than dense attention at a 1% read.
authors: Hyunwoo Yu, Jongbeom Lee, Hyunbin Kim, Sungjun Park, Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Seunghun Moon, Bongjoon Hyun, Kyomin Sohn, Kyeongbo Kong, Suk-Ju Kang
bullets: Sparse attention can be biased when unread tail tokens are discarded, while sampling performs poorly at very low read rates.
A single count-aware mean proxy for the entire tail reduces output and weight error more effectively than sampling.
The pipeline combines Query-Geometry Clustering, Query-Geometry Selection, ErrorGate, top-k selection, and tail proxies.
On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, it retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read.
OpenAttention.flash reports 10× faster decode attention than dense attention at a 1% read.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention with tail proxies and query-geometry clustering directly targets efficient KV-cache reading and attention acceleration.
papers.title: OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies
papers.tldr: OpenAttention uses query-aware clustering, error-guided selection, and a count-aware tail proxy to preserve 99% of dense-attention accuracy while reading only 1% of the key-value cache.

papers.abstract: In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained massive attention as an energy-efficient neural computing paradigm due to their event-driven and sparse computing capability. However, maintaining accuracy under low-precision constraints, necessary for practical deployment, has been largely unexplored for SNN models. In addition, existing Hessian-based approaches for quantization, such as HAWQ-V2, incur significant memory and computational overhead due to temporal unrolling across multiple SNN timesteps. We propose a spike-aware gradient-based mixed-precision quantization framework for SNNs that adaptively assigns bit-widths using first-order gradient information, avoiding costly second-order Hessian computations. We evaluate our method across various SNN-based architectures, including VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer models obtained from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training frameworks, on CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, on ResNet-34 evaluated on ImageNet, our method achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78$\times$ compression, which is comparable to that provided by HAWQ-V2, while reducing memory consumption by 2.31$\times$ and bit-allocation runtime by 100$\times$. We also present an energy analysis for mixed-precision SNNs showing that the proposed quantization strategy enables energy-efficient deployment without compromising performance.
authors: Rajshekhar Rakshit, Devgokul B. V, Rakshitha Kalkura, Gopalakrishnan Srinivasan
bullets: Targets accuracy degradation under the low-precision constraints needed for practical SNN deployment.
Uses first-order, spike-aware gradient information to adaptively assign layer bit-widths without costly Hessian computations.
Evaluated on VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer SNNs from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training across CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10.
On ImageNet ResNet-34, achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78× compression, comparable to HAWQ-V2, with 2.31× lower memory use and 100× faster bit allocation.
Includes an energy analysis indicating efficient mixed-precision SNN deployment without compromising performance.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization reduces memory and compute for SNN deployment; relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Spike-Aware Gradient-Based Mixed-Precision Quantization of Spiking Neural Networks for Vision Applications
papers.tldr: A spike-aware, gradient-based mixed-precision method compresses SNNs efficiently while preserving accuracy and avoiding the overhead of Hessian-based quantization.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory growth in long-context MoE inference, where eviction can alter expert selection and harm quality.
Scores context tokens using both attention weights and a Fisher-information-based measure of routing sensitivity.
Combines routing-aware eviction with complementary dense-model KV compression methods.
At 10% KV retention, improves over the prior state of the art by 24 points on LongBench and 20 points on RULER on average.
Demonstrates robust performance under aggressive compression across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces routing-aware KV cache compression for MoE LLMs, directly targeting memory-efficiency in inference.
papers.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoEZip compresses KV caches in sparse MoE LLMs while preserving expert-routing decisions, enabling strong long-context performance with only 10% KV retention.

papers.abstract: Lossless tensor compression could reduce memory usage during training, but training requires tensors to be repeatedly re-encoded. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT), a GPU execution framework designed for this repeated encode-decode regime. LCT exploits the natural redundancy in floating point data to reduce storage for weights, activations and optimizer states. Highly optimized GPU kernels implement Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks for low compression and decompression overhead, essential for training. Our analysis characterizes LCT's storage costs and adaptation to magnitude shifts. LCT achieves a compression ratio of up to $1.455\times$, and is demonstrated in training and finetuning settings. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, LCT reduces memory usage by $24.6\%$ for a $7.2\%$ step-time increase. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, LCT saves up to $23.8\%$ of peak memory, enabling a $3.5\times$ larger context length in training on the same GPU.
bullets: Targets repeated compression and decompression of weights, activations, and optimizer states during training.
Uses GPU-optimized Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks to keep encoding overhead low.
Achieves compression ratios of up to 1.455× and adapts to shifts in tensor magnitudes.
Reduces NanoGPT memory usage by 24.6% with a 7.2% step-time increase.
During Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, saves up to 23.8% peak memory and enables 3.5× longer context on the same GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a GPU-friendly framework for losslessly compressed tensors during training, reducing memory usage by 24.6% while maintaining acceptable step-time overhead, a significant contribution to memory efficiency.
papers.title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training
papers.tldr: LCT reduces training memory by losslessly compressing tensors with GPU-efficient encode/decode, trading modest runtime overhead for substantially larger context capacity.

papers.abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
bullets: Targets HBM bandwidth bottlenecks and large expert-storage footprints during autoregressive Sparse MoE decode.
Uses a Rotor Generation Unit to generate FFN weight tiles from compact rotor parameters instead of storing full expert tensors.
Replacing 30% of MoE FFN layers is estimated to improve system throughput by 1.3–2.8× and short-context per-user latency by 1.10–1.15×.
Expands KV-cache capacity by 1.2–2.6× and can compose with weight quantization.
The accuracy–efficiency tradeoff depends on the replacement ratio; accuracy decreases relative to fine-tuned models without rotor replacement.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a procedural weight generation system (FORGE) for Sparse MoE inference that reduces memory footprint and expands KV cache capacity, addressing key efficiency bottlenecks in large model deployment.
papers.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
papers.tldr: FORGE accelerates Sparse MoE decoding by regenerating approximate expert weights on-chip, reducing memory and communication demands at the cost of some accuracy.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces the cost of adapting foundation models by focusing training on a small parameter subset. Complementary to this idea, we introduce RoSA (Rotational Sparse Adaptation), which narrows adaptation to a subset of layers at a time. RoSA freezes lower layers close to the input throughout training and rotates a trainable block over later layers, progressively increasing the number of frozen layers close to the input. This design reduces optimizer-state memory, shortens backpropagation, and even forward propagation if activations at the last frozen layer are cached. Because RoSA is orthogonal to the choice of trainable parameterization, it can be combined with PEFT methods or sparse optimizers within each active block. Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks show that RoSA reduces peak memory while maintaining strong fine-tuning performance.
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of adapting foundation models.
Freezes lower, input-near layers and shifts the trainable block across later layers during training.
Can reduce optimizer-state memory, backpropagation cost, and—when activations are cached—forward-propagation cost.
Works alongside PEFT methods and sparse optimizers within each active block.
Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks report lower peak memory with strong fine-tuning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-efficient fine-tuning method (RoSA) that reduces optimizer-state memory and computation by freezing layers and rotating trainable blocks, directly addressing memory bottlenecks in LLM training.
papers.title: RoSA: Rotational Sparse Adaptation for Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: RoSA reduces fine-tuning memory and computation by rotating a trainable layer block through later layers while progressively freezing earlier ones.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks. We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.
authors: Shuncheng Jie, Desen Sun, Ri Hong, Yuyang Tian, Hong Zhang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Targets cloud-device image editing where request-specific inference stays on the phone for privacy, but reusable KV caches are too large to store locally.
Uses token-importance-aware cache compression to preserve image quality within a bandwidth budget.
Selects cache representations according to current network bandwidth and overlaps transfer, reconstruction, and on-device execution through pipelining.
Evaluated on three editing tasks and two diffusion models using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone.
Reports 1.82× and 3.27× lower latency than CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively, with 3.06× lower cache storage than uncompressed caches while preserving image quality.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses and transfers attention KV cache under bandwidth constraints, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SAKURA: Serving Attention Key-Value State Under Rate Adaptation for Private Image Editing on Phones
papers.tldr: SAKURA accelerates private, template-based diffusion image editing on phones by compressing and adaptively streaming reusable attention KV states under changing network bandwidth.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models keep their context in a recurrent state of fixed size, where an inference system stores one copy of this state for every sequence it decodes at the same time. Storing the state at lower precision therefore lets more sequences share an accelerator. Existing state quantizers round the state after every generated token and report that four bits lose accuracy unless the bit width is raised or the model is fine-tuned.\par We introduce PACE, a post-hoc four-bit state quantizer. PACE rounds the state only once every few generated tokens, as chunked kernels already do once per chunk during prefill, and keeps the tokens generated in between in a small buffer. Rounding less often reduces the error that accumulates in the state. Additionally, we find that the large entries of the gated-delta state gather in columns, because some channels of the update written at each token remain large across many tokens. PACE therefore shares each quantization scale within one column. It also keeps the heads that retain rounding error longest at eight bits. On four hybrid models from 4B to 35B parameters, PACE with mixed four- and eight-bit heads is competitive with eight-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two thirds of its memory, PACE with four-bit heads throughout scores higher than Q-Mamba at equal memory, and rounding every few tokens preserves the decoding speedup of the buffer.
authors: Patrick Haller, Filipe Laitenberger, Alan Akbik
bullets: Targets memory overhead in linear-attention language models, where each concurrent sequence stores a recurrent state.
Buffers several generated tokens and rounds the state once per chunk instead of after every token, reducing accumulated quantization error.
Shares quantization scales within state columns, exploiting channels whose update magnitudes remain large over time.
Keeps heads with persistent rounding error at eight bits while quantizing others at four bits.
Across four hybrid models, PACE matches eight-bit DAMP on larger models at roughly two-thirds the memory and outperforms Q-Mamba at equal memory; buffered rounding preserves decoding speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc quantization of recurrent states in linear-attention LLMs to reduce memory footprint during inference.
papers.title: PACE: Periodic and Channel-Aligned Encoding of Four-Bit Recurrent States
papers.tldr: PACE is a post-hoc recurrent-state quantizer that improves four-bit inference by rounding less often, aligning scales by channel, and selectively using eight-bit heads.

papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
authors: Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Zesen Zhao, Hei Ting Una Chan, Xueshen Liu, Zhen Zhang, Liyue Shen, Zechun Liu, Z. Morley Mao
bullets: Fixed-response QAT creates a training–generation trajectory mismatch that worsens for longer reasoning sequences.
The quantized student also miscalibrates next-token probabilities, especially at high-entropy prefixes.
OnQ combines block-wise calibration, on-policy distillation, and candidate-wise Dynamic KL to correct under- and overprediction.
Across Qwen3 1.7B–8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, it achieves the best nine-benchmark average, with particularly large long-horizon reasoning gains.
At 2 bits, it beats all baselines on every benchmark and produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitions.
papers.selection_reason: Recovers reasoning in low-bit quantized LLMs via on-policy distillation and dynamic KL, improving efficiency of deployed language models.
papers.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
papers.tldr: OnQ recovers long-horizon reasoning in low-bit LLMs by distilling teacher behavior on the quantized student’s own trajectories with adaptive KL correction.

papers.abstract: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
authors: Jia Deng, Zizhe Wang, Xin Lu, Yi Huang, Zehao Jia
bullets: Evaluates compression for space robots requiring a controlled, static artifact and behavioral fidelity to a BF16 reference.
Assigns each linear module among AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound variants using final next-token distribution scores.
A label-free fidelity mode accepts substitutions that reduce forward KL; an optional target-adapted mode uses labeled data.
Across three language models and 3-/4-bit settings, composed models achieve lower held-out perplexity than every single-family baseline.
Target adaptation improves pooled 3-bit accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points; evaluations remain limited to general-domain benchmarks on ground GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Composes low-bit quantized LLM checkpoints under a fidelity constraint for onboard deployment, directly targeting model memory efficiency.
papers.title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement
papers.tldr: QSelect composes compatible low-bit checkpoints into static onboard models that better preserve full-precision behavior under fixed storage constraints.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy.
