Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Sangyoon Lee, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Problem: Idle-time KV prefill must use restricted context, causing a mismatch because relevant query information is unavailable and irrelevant context may be included.
Method: At query time, re-prefill selected video tokens with query-relevant context and replace their cached KVs; no additional training is required.
Contribution: Enables shorter idle-time attention windows, lowering prefill computation while preserving or improving contextualization.
Results: Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy improves by up to 3.9 percentage points.
Efficiency: On RVS-Ego, per-frame prefill FLOPs decrease by over 20%, while total processing time drops by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Selective KV recomputation for streaming video LLMs; directly combines video understanding with cache-efficiency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameBlend improves streaming video understanding by selectively recomputing cached video-token representations with query-relevant context, reducing preprocessing cost while increasing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Disaggregated \textsc{LLM} serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textsc{KV}-cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present \textbf{KVLearn}, a learning-based framework for cost-aware \textsc{KV}-cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textsc{PRP}) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost-Aware Retention Score (\textsc{CARS}) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textsc{ATC}) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video-derived \textsc{KV} blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache, 38% versus LRU-Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake-style baselines, while cutting inter-node \textsc{KV} transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool. On MM-Session, throughput remains within ${\sim}5%$ of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.
authors: Dong Liu, Yanxuan Yu, Eric Jiang, Shu Wang, Ying Nian Wu
bullets: Disaggregation makes cache misses costly because they require both recomputation and network transfer; cache admission also consumes bandwidth.
A lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor estimates reuse from structural and temporal prefix features without changing model weights.
The Cost-Aware Retention Score balances reuse probability against recomputation, transfer, and storage costs.
An Adaptive Threshold Controller updates admission thresholds online using hit rates and memory pressure.
KVLearn reduces time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache and cuts inter-node KV transfer by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool; throughput stays within ~5% of an oracle on MM-Session.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware KV-cache retention for LLM serving directly targets KV-cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
papers.tldr: KVLearn learns cost-aware KV-cache retention decisions for disaggregated LLM serving, reducing latency and inter-node KV traffic across text and multimodal workloads.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from $3.8$ to $32$B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on \emph{generative} tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about $2.3$ effective bits per weight and retains $89$ to $97\%$ of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses $1.4$ to $30\times$ less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.
authors: Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Riccardo Grazzi, James Hensman, Pashmina Cameron
bullets: At 2 bits, scalar PTQ can collapse to chance-level accuracy, making representation, calibration data, and recovery data critical.
Vector codebook representations are the most important factor for restoring usable low-bit models.
Calibration and recovery data interact under limited recovery budgets and should be selected jointly, with task alignment.
Across six 3.8B–32B dense and mixture-of-experts models, the method retains 89–97% of full-precision QA accuracy using about 2.3 effective bits per weight.
Including recovery, it requires 1.4–30× less compute than the strongest QAT baseline; generative-task degradation remains model-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization reduces model memory footprint, directly fitting memory-efficient inference under Efficient AI.
papers.title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
papers.tldr: A data-centric 2-bit PTQ recipe using vector codebooks and jointly chosen calibration/recovery data preserves most QA accuracy at far lower compute than QAT.

papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
bullets: Combines joint autoregressive and block-causal training so one model supports both regular generation and multi-token drafting.
Offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding without separate draft and verifier models.
Uses accepted-prefix alignment, shared KV storage, and width-specialized CUDA Graph execution to reduce decoding overhead.
Reports 2.1–2.4× speedups on selected Bonsai models and up to 3.3× throughput on Jetson Orin across evaluated tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Co-design for multi-token prediction on low-bit LLMs, reducing decoding steps and KV/memory overhead in LLM inference.
papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.tldr: BitMTP co-designs multi-token prediction with ultra-low-bit LLM execution to accelerate generation while maintaining comparable task quality.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal
bullets: Targets KV-cache attention costs for long-context LLM inference, where sparse methods lose attention mass or suffer sampling variance.
Combines deterministic selection of high-scoring tokens with score-guided sampling of residual tokens and inclusion-probability correction.
Generalizes top-k, top-p, and hybrid top-k-plus-sampling methods.
Improves matched-sparsity performance across four benchmarks and five models, including stronger RULER-HARD accuracy at 50× sparsity.
With optimized CUDA kernels, reaches up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M-token context.
papers.selection_reason: Stratified sparse attention improves long-context efficiency by combining retrieval and sampling, directly relevant to efficient attention and KV cache.
papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.tldr: Stratified Sparse Attention narrows the accuracy gap between sparse and dense attention at extreme sparsity while enabling faster long-context inference.

papers.abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.
authors: Irene Tenison, Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Daniel Karl I. Weidele, Nima Dehmamy, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Targets head-dimension reduction while avoiding the decoding FLOPs overhead of reconstructing full-dimensional keys and values.
Uses a shared query-key projection derived from calibration activations and retains complete rotary pairs to preserve RoPE compatibility.
Selects rotary pairs by joint query-key activation energy, minimizing a separable upper bound on post-RoPE query-key approximation error.
The folded, post-training method requires no runtime reconstruction or specialized kernels and outperforms structured pruning across evaluated tasks.
At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, it reports 47.8% lower inference FLOPs, 1.79× higher throughput, 43.2% lower TTFT, and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory versus an uncompressed model.
papers.selection_reason: RoPE-compatible KV-cache compression reduces memory and inference FLOPs, fitting efficient attention and cache efficiency.
papers.title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
papers.tldr: RACE compresses attention heads by selecting RoPE-compatible rotary pairs using joint query-key activation energy, reducing KV-cache memory and inference computation without runtime reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.
bullets: Local inference can reduce serving costs and rate limits while improving privacy and user control.
The study analyzes multiple models across several GPU generations rather than focusing on one model-device pair.
Self-attention dominates runtime for long-context inference.
Self-attention underutilizes important GPU resources, with newer GPUs often receiving less effective utilization.
Key challenges include KV-cache paging, cache utilization, and GPU synchronization; the paper offers observations and recommendations for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of long-context LLM inference bottlenecks with focus on self-attention and KV-cache data management.
papers.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
papers.tldr: Long-context LLM inference on a single local GPU is constrained not only by memory capacity but also by substantial self-attention and data-management inefficiencies.

papers.abstract: Token merging is an effective approach to reducing KV-cache memory consumption in autoregressive video generation by clustering temporally redundant tokens and retaining only a small set of representatives. Existing methods, however, typically apply a uniform merging ratio across all attention layers and heads. We observe that different layers and heads exhibit substantially different yet jointly correlated sensitivities to token merging, and that these sensitivity patterns remain consistent across prompts. Based on this observation, we introduce CALM, a Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging that uses offline calibration to improve online cache compression. Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive. To enable efficient calibration, we show that attention-output error strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality and can therefore serve as a lightweight proxy for allocation risk assessment. We evaluate different allocation strategies using this proxy and construct a fixed layer-head risk map offline. Given a cache budget at inference time, CALM uses dynamic programming to determine the best allocation of merging ratios. Experiments across three different autoregressive video models demonstrate that CALM consistently outperforms uniform token merging under the same memory budget, by reducing the LPIPS to original videos by around 21% with higher video-quality scores.
authors: Zhen Wang, Ning Lai, Qingtao Yu
bullets: Uniform token-merging ratios overlook substantial, prompt-consistent sensitivity differences across attention layers and heads.
CALM uses attention-output error as a lightweight proxy for end-to-end video-quality risk during offline calibration.
It builds a fixed layer-head risk map, then selects merging ratios dynamically for a given cache budget.
Across three autoregressive video models, CALM outperforms uniform merging, reducing LPIPS to original videos by around 21% while achieving higher video-quality scores.
papers.selection_reason: Offline-calibrated layer-head token merging for KV-cache compression in autoregressive video generation.
papers.title: Offline Makes Online Better: Calibrated Cache Compression for Video Generation
papers.tldr: CALM uses offline layer-head sensitivity calibration and dynamic programming to allocate token merging, improving autoregressive video-generation quality at the same KV-cache budget.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
authors: Samkit Jain, Sai Kishan Pampana, Shlok Agarwal
bullets: Sparse attention still incurs costly full-prefix key searches at every layer.
A producer publishes a top-M candidate pool; each consumer independently selects its own top-K keys.
Implemented in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, sharing three consumer layers per producer improved serving efficiency across four long-context suites.
Single-run accuracy changes ranged from −1.49 to +0.29 percentage points; more aggressive sharing can reduce quality.
Recurring KV-position reuse motivates Top-G, an exploratory prefill method whose deployment and benefits remain open.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free sharing of sparse-attention candidate search improves long-context LLM serving efficiency and GPU energy.
papers.title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
papers.tldr: MLIPS accelerates sparse attention by sharing broad candidate-key pools across layers, achieving 1.14–1.40× speedups with 14.8–27.4% lower GPU energy but task-dependent quality trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.
authors: Hyojung Han, Ryangkyung Kang, Youngeun Kim, Seung-Hun Jeon
bullets: Across three embedders and 161 4-bit calibration runs, outcomes ranged from gains to severe degradation, largely tracking functional displacement from the uncalibrated model.
On EmbeddingGemma, the same learning-rate grid produced changes from +1.47 to −71.53 NDCG@10 points; a label-free cosine objective showed a similar collapse at the same dose.
Objective robustness varied by embedder: ranking calibration was more robust than cosine on e5, while BGE-M3 showed an unresolved opposite trend.
Functional displacement was the main risk axis but not sufficient: equal displacement reached through different paths differed by up to 1.61 points.
A validation rule made 0 harmful selections in 30 decisions, retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and incurred mean oracle regret of 1.52 points, including one missed 11.13-point gain.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training quantization calibration for text embedders, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
papers.tldr: PTQ calibration can greatly improve or catastrophically damage quantized text embedders, so validation-gated abstention offers a safer—but opportunity-costly—way to deploy it.

papers.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao
bullets: Addresses the repeated token-processing cost of passing shared context between LLMs.
Uses a frozen encoder to create a fixed-size latent packet and a different frozen receiver that reads it via prompt-conditioned cross-attention.
Combines compactness, cross-model readability, and reuse across multiple questions.
Improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points across 12 multiple-choice QA datasets.
On QuALITY, reduces receiver input by 57× and answers article questions 3× faster.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LatComm, a reusable context compression method for LLMs, which reduces memory requirements and processing time by compressing context into a fixed-size packet.
papers.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
papers.tldr: LatComm enables reusable, compact communication between LLMs by encoding context once and letting the receiver selectively read it per question.

papers.abstract: Smartphone GUI agents complete tasks in mobile apps by repeatedly reading the screen and asking a model for the next action. Mobile neural processing units (NPUs) enable local execution, keeping screen contents on the phone, but model latency accumulates with every action. Hybrid linear attention models reduce memory requirements, yet reusing their recurrent state requires checkpoints at the appropriate input positions. Agent requests retain instructions but rewrite recent history, so checkpoint policies designed for chat continuation can miss reusable prefixes. Retaining rollback states for speculative decoding can also move prompt processing off the NPU's matrix unit, adding overhead that outweighs decoding savings on short action outputs. A loaded model can further hold the NPU awake between tasks. We present Tandem, a runtime for hybrid GUI agents on mobile NPUs. Tandem saves recurrent state where consecutive prompts diverge, allowing later requests to reuse previously processed context. It keeps most prefill on the matrix unit and produces rollback states through a short per-token tail. Its verification kernel reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens. Between request bursts, Tandem releases NPU power votes without unloading the model. We implement Tandem in llama.cpp and evaluate it on recorded agent interactions across two Snapdragon generations. On a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Tandem reduces per-step latency by 30% for text-based screen descriptions and 16% for screenshots relative to llama.cpp's fastest NPU configuration, reduces energy per text step by 33%, and lowers standby power with the model loaded from 0.76 to 0.22 W.
authors: Zhuomin Chen, Jingchao Ni, Xu Zheng, Yong Chen, Mo Sha, Wei Cheng, Dongsheng Luo
bullets: Targets latency and energy overhead from repeatedly processing evolving GUI-agent prompts on smartphones.
Saves recurrent states at prompt-divergence points so later requests can reuse shared context.
Keeps most prompt processing on the NPU matrix unit and generates rollback states with a short per-token tail.
Uses a verification kernel that reads each weight block once for all proposed tokens, and releases NPU power votes between request bursts.
On Snapdragon 8 Elite, reduces per-step latency by 30% for text descriptions and 16% for screenshots, cuts text-step energy by 33%, and lowers loaded-model standby power from 0.76 to 0.22 W.
papers.selection_reason: Runtime for hybrid linear-attention GUI agents on mobile NPUs; reduces latency and energy via recurrent-state checkpoint reuse and efficient verification.
papers.title: Tandem: Serving Hybrid Linear-Attention GUI Agents on Mobile NPUs
papers.tldr: Tandem is a mobile-NPU runtime that accelerates hybrid linear-attention GUI agents by reusing prompt state efficiently while reducing energy and standby power.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Block diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by generating multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. However, each pass produces only a fixed-length block from a single target-generated anchor, limiting how far the draft can extend. Meanwhile, target verification computes hidden states even at positions beyond the first rejection, but these states are typically discarded rather than reused. We propose ReAnchor, a training-free method that reanchors a pretrained drafter at shifted positions using discarded verifier states to generate parallel draft blocks. These blocks improve predictions within the original block and extend coverage beyond its endpoint. At sampling temperature of T=0, ReAnchor achieves its largest average gains on Gemma 4-12B, improving acceptance length by 19.4% and decoding speed by 17.9% across eight benchmarks. Averaged equally over four target models and eight benchmarks, it improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4% with pretrained DFlash drafters.
authors: Sanghyun Lee, Wonjin Nam, Seungho Jang, Jaeho Lee, Jiho Park, Jaewoon Lee, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses fixed-length drafting and wasted verifier states beyond the first rejected token.
Reanchors pretrained drafters at shifted positions using verifier states to improve within-block predictions and extend draft coverage.
Training-free and compatible with pretrained DFlash drafters.
At T=0, reports average gains of up to 19.4% in acceptance length and 17.9% in decoding speed on Gemma 4-12B across eight benchmarks.
Across four target models and eight benchmarks, improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Reuses discarded verifier states to reanchor diffusion drafters, improving speculative decoding speed and memory efficiency.
papers.title: ReAnchor: Reusing Rejected Verifier States for Diffusion Drafting
papers.tldr: ReAnchor reuses discarded verifier hidden states to shift diffusion-drafter anchors, generating parallel blocks that improve speculative decoding acceptance and speed without training.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets efficient autoregressive video diffusion with sparse attention and KV cache compression, fitting efficient AI and video generation interests.
papers.title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: DASA makes autoregressive video diffusion more efficient by focusing computation and memory on regions with motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive video generation distillation with KV-cache efficiency improvements.
papers.title: TriTD: Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution Distillation for Real-Time Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: TriTD improves autoregressive video diffusion by jointly reducing rollout errors, enabling higher visual quality and real-time generation at 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
authors: Moritz Wagner, Christophe Roux, Max Zimmer, Sebastian Pokutta
bullets: Existing methods evaluate cache entries independently, overlooking how deleting one entry changes attention over all others.
KV-Surgeon uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate to jointly choose greedy deletions and compensate remaining entries.
It improves the cost–accuracy Pareto frontier across QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena for dense and mixture-of-experts models.
At 50× compaction, it improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching at comparable cost.
A faster variant also surpasses the prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets KV-cache compaction and memory-efficient LLM inference with compensation-aware offline pruning.
papers.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
papers.tldr: KV-Surgeon improves offline KV-cache compaction by modeling interactions caused by softmax renormalization, achieving better accuracy–cost tradeoffs than prior methods.

papers.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.
authors: Desheng Xu, Hanglin Li, Tianchen Song, Zhiyong Zhao, Kun Zhan
bullets: Addresses activation outliers and heterogeneous channel sensitivity in post-training quantization.
Uses a noise-weighted metric to identify sensitive channels.
Applies learnable rotations to sensitive channels and lightweight fixed rotations elsewhere.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across several LLM families under W4A4KV4.
For LLaMA-3-8B, calibration takes 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory; fused kernels provide up to 2.3× prefill speedup and 3.5× memory savings over FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LIRQuant, a sensitivity-aware quantization method for LLMs that reduces memory footprint and improves inference speed through selective learnable rotations and fused kernels.
papers.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: LIRQuant improves low-bit LLM quantization by applying stronger rotations only to sensitive channels, enabling accurate and efficient W4A4KV4 deployment.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose \textbf{PoSTCache} (\emph{Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache}), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality--efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.
authors: Liwei Lan, Hui Chen, Jungong Han, Guiguang Ding
bullets: Existing caching methods commit forward-only approximations that cannot incorporate later feedback.
PoSTCache uses an existing cache for forward proposals, then propagates discrepancy-based corrections backward from later full-computation steps.
Its PVR strategy selects full-computation anchors by estimated reduction in trajectory uncertainty using offline denoising trajectories.
Experiments on image and video generation models show consistent improvements over representative caching methods.
The framework is training-free and plug-and-play, with results scoped to the evaluated models and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a revisable trajectory cache for diffusion models that uses postdictive smoothing to correct previous steps, improving the efficiency-quality trade-off of inference.
papers.title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching
papers.tldr: PoSTCache makes diffusion caching revisable by using later full computations to correct earlier skipped-step predictions, improving the quality–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.
authors: Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Targets streaming video QA, where queries can arrive at any time and only a few preceding frames are typically relevant.
Encodes segments independently at varying representation levels, from inexpensive visual features to full KV caches.
Dynamically completes retrieved segments and pipelines computation across CPU and GPU resources using offline cost profiles.
Reports competitive accuracy with up to 10.4× lower time-to-first-token than prior methods and up to 5.9× lower than streaming systems.
Sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT below 0.5 s, or up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT below 2 s.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces StreamAhead for real-time streaming video QA, addressing video understanding and optimizing KV cache computation for efficiency.
papers.title: StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
papers.tldr: StreamAhead adaptively precomputes video representations to balance continuous processing with low-latency question answering.

papers.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.
bullets: Compaction replaces older agent turns with summaries to prevent long sessions from exhausting usable context.
On recall tasks, compaction improved accuracy for both 1.2B and 9B models versus truncation.
In 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, long-session resolution rose from 41% to 53%, with 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost.
Benefits appeared when compaction triggered early enough to preserve room for reasoning; short sessions did not benefit.
The gain disappeared under a 45-minute session budget because summaries took a median of 161 seconds; an 8B model often avoided compaction entirely.
papers.selection_reason: Context compaction for constrained windows addresses long-context processing and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
papers.tldr: Early context compaction improves long-session agent accuracy on constrained context windows, but its latency cost can erase the benefit under tight time budgets.

papers.abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.
authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
bullets: Adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev decision readout and continues generation from the existing KV cache when selected or when confidence is low.
On Qwen3-0.6B, JevBench accuracy was statistically unchanged, while expected calibration error decreased from 0.292 to 0.169 and Bitext routing accuracy reached 98.3%.
KV-cache reuse reduced latency by 15–37% on an Apple M4 Pro; copied-cache option scoring matched full-sequence scoring within 1.4e-6 probability.
System X v4 with Qwen3-1.7B increased JevBench accuracy from 55.0% to 61.0% versus its base model, without a significant IFEval change.
Failure modes include state conflicts and unsupported reply details; broader validation with multiple seeds, human raters, and real support data is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Reuses KV cache to avoid prompt prefill, reducing latency for LLM decision models.
papers.title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
papers.tldr: System X lets an LLM decision model generate replies directly from its decision KV cache, improving calibration and reducing latency while preserving roughly similar decision accuracy, though unsupported details remain a limitation.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning every transformer layer the same KV-cache budget despite differing token needs.
Uses multi-objective neural architecture search to find per-layer allocations compatible with existing eviction methods.
A single search captures the budget–task-score trade-off and transfers across target budgets; an optional constrained search further refines allocations.
Across four eviction methods and two LLMs, it outperforms uniform allocation in 146 of 154 evaluated settings and can match uniform performance with up to 75% less cache.
Allocations consistently concentrate cache on a small set of middle layers; compared with EvolKV, MOSAIC searches a much larger space with fewer evaluations and GPU-hours.
papers.selection_reason: Learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for token eviction methods, directly targeting efficient LLM inference and cache memory reduction.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
papers.tldr: MOSAIC learns layer-specific KV-cache budgets that substantially reduce LLM inference memory while preserving or improving task performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu, Miao Liu, Panwang Pan, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Visual token compression can harm reasoning by permanently deleting tokens that appear unimportant in early layers.
Layer-wise analysis reveals visual backtracking: stable visual pivots later retrieve context from previously low-saliency tokens.
ReTrace adds a dormant token state, caching non-pivot tokens outside expensive computation and restoring them during a backtracking window.
Tokens are pruned only after their information has been absorbed, preserving more visual context for reasoning.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 report nearly 90% lower FLOPs and KV-cache usage, a 2.83× prefilling speedup, and strong benchmark performance retention.
papers.selection_reason: Backtracking-aware visual token compression reduces FLOPs and KV cache in MLLMs.
papers.title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ReTrace accelerates MLLM inference by temporarily sidelining visual tokens while restoring them when later layers need their information.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading few keys of the KV cache, but existing methods do not control the error of a query, and on real KV caches their errors have heavy tails. We show that perturbing the score of every key with an independent Exp(1) variable turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys with probability proportional to their attention weights. Lowering the threshold along a geometric grid gives nested samples, a Horvitz--Thompson estimate of the output at every level, and confidence bounds that hold simultaneously over all levels, so each head stops at the first level whose certificate meets the target error $\varepsilon$. With fresh perturbations at every decoding step, each certificate fails with probability at most $\delta$ during generation. At a suitable threshold, the estimator reads $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ values regardless of the context length, and no adaptive method reads fewer, up to constants. A 4-bit scan with deterministic bounds, shared across a grouped-query-attention group, generates the candidates exactly but reads every key. On three LLMs and ten settings at 16K--128K tokens, no certificate is violated, and at equal keys read our 90th-percentile error is 4.6--7.9$\times$ lower than that of the best of 15 baseline families. At equal bytes, the best baselines have 0.6--1.6 times our 90th-percentile error and at least 4.9 times our largest. End to end, our method stays within one point of dense attention on tasks and within 0.1\% in PG-19 perplexity, and the strongest baselines at equal bytes score as well. On CPU, decoding steps at 32K--128K tokens run 1.1--1.4$\times$ faster than dense attention on the same 16-bit cache.
bullets: Perturbing key scores with independent Exp(1) noise converts threshold retrieval into sampling proportional to attention weights.
Nested samples across thresholds enable Horvitz–Thompson output estimates and simultaneous confidence certificates.
Each head stops when its estimated error is below ε; with fresh perturbations, certificate failure is bounded by δ during generation.
The estimator needs O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)) reads, independent of context length, and this read complexity is optimal up to constants.
Across 16K–128K contexts, certificates were never violated; decoding was 1.1–1.4× faster than dense attention on CPU while maintaining near-dense task quality.
papers.selection_reason: Certified sparse attention with perturbed retrieval reduces KV-cache reads for long-context decoding, fitting efficient attention and long-context model interests.
papers.title: Certified Sparse Attention via Perturbed Retrieval
papers.tldr: Certified Sparse Attention uses perturbed retrieval and adaptive sampling to provide high-probability error guarantees while reading far fewer KV-cache values during long-context decoding.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
authors: Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Targets high transient memory from full-prompt KV-cache construction, which limits long-context inference.
Processes prompt chunks layer by layer, retaining full-prompt KV only for the active layer before evicting it.
Preserves full-prompt-aware cache selection while reducing activation and temporary memory.
At 64K context, cuts construction-time transient memory by 83.89% on A100; on RTX 4090, TTFT increases only 1.06%.
Enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.
papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise delayed KV eviction reduces long-context LLM prefill memory; fits KV cache/memory efficiency and long-context inference.
papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TideKV reduces peak memory during long-context LLM prefill by delaying KV-cache eviction until each Transformer layer finishes processing the full prompt.

papers.abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.
authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Zhenyu Bi, Sirui Ding, Xuan Wang
bullets: Diagnoses context internalization through fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation.
Aggregates query-relevant evidence from a frozen document cache, then encodes only the query and memory-token suffix into LoRA updates.
Uses multi-style supervision to preserve evidence and better follow answer-format instructions.
Across 17 tasks, reaches 0.663 macro F1 versus 0.671 for full-context in-context learning, with 5.9× higher decoding throughput in the reported setting.
Generated LoRA is more robust than learned-KV under long intervening text and combines effectively with retained document KV.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Cache2LoRA to improve context internalization in LoRA methods, enhancing throughput and accuracy through memory-efficient techniques.
papers.title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
papers.tldr: Cache2LoRA improves context-to-LoRA by querying a reusable document cache before generating updates, nearing full-context accuracy while substantially increasing decoding throughput.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.
papers.selection_reason: Query-relevant frame selection for long-video VideoLLMs with streaming KV cache; fits video understanding and token/frame efficiency.
papers.title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameScout selects query-relevant frames from long videos using temporally contextualized streaming representations and contrastive frame-query alignment, improving VideoLLM long-video understanding.

papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
bullets: KV-cache memory grows with context length, while existing non-uniform head compression methods can be unstable across workloads.
The method finds that active-head composition shifts between prefill and decode but remains stable across later content tokens after filtering format tokens.
PeekKV performs a one-token peek to jointly score head groups and token importance, then allocates cache budgets and retains the highest-scoring tokens.
It applies directly to unseen workloads and models because it requires neither offline profiling nor additional training.
Across four benchmarks, it is closest to full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench; reported retention reaches 95.7% and 95.9% of full-cache accuracy at low memory budgets on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache budget allocation via one-token peek and token retention directly targets memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: PeekKV: The First Content Token Already Knows Which Heads Matter
papers.tldr: PeekKV uses the first content token after prefill to dynamically identify important attention heads and KV tokens, enabling accurate KV-cache compression without profiling or training.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.
authors: Jiaming Xu, Hanzhen Wang, Tianlang Zhao, Jiewen Xiao, Chengze Yuan, Jiayi Pan, Yongkang Zhou, Jiancai Ye, Yu Wang, Guohao Dai
bullets: Agentic workloads’ long, evolving histories reduce draft-model acceptance length and make historical KV-cache maintenance costly.
DLite reuses target-model hidden states for history-free, local speculative prediction.
A lightweight sequential head restores dependencies within each speculative block.
A two-stage training strategy supports the heterogeneous history-free architecture.
Across general-purpose, long-context, and agentic workloads, DLite achieves 2–6 acceptance length and up to 70% improvement over DSpark.
papers.selection_reason: History-free speculative decoding reduces KV cache and memory overhead; directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
papers.tldr: DLite accelerates speculative decoding for agentic AI by avoiding historical context while preserving effective local prediction.

papers.abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth.
