It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
authors: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko
bullets: Compiler regeneration often fails to realize predicted memory savings and can worsen memory use or alter GPU results.
Profiling generated code and reordering its statements exactly matches modeled peak memory and preserves bitwise-identical outputs on CPU.
Forward and reverse minimum-cut bounds certify optimal schedules for most tested graphs, including all studied microcontroller-class models.
Branching networks benefit most from reordering; compiled training saves up to 7.6%, while DeepLabV3 improves by 10.0%.
Selective recomputation is strongly NP-hard under fixed caps, but reduces peak memory by 5.2–6.1% on ReDimNet with under 0.4% extra MACs.
papers.selection_reason: Exact peak-memory scheduling and recomputation limits for inference directly target memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
papers.tldr: The paper presents a reliable, certifiably optimal operator-ordering approach for reducing inference peak memory, while showing when recomputation is useful or computationally hard.

papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
authors: Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jialin Liu, Dong Li
bullets: Addresses fixed-shape compilation constraints across varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and denoising-time caching decisions.
Uses one compilation backend for five pipelines, splits joint attention across cores by head, and fuses attention computation.
A host controller selectively reuses denoiser outputs, guided by a device-side probe that produces one caching signal per step.
Fused attention is 1.2–4.3× faster than PyTorch/XLA attention and is the only attention variant compiling at 32.8k visual tokens.
Resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation on four of five models.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Difflet, a fast inference engine for diffusion transformer models on AWS Trainium, optimizing attention computation and caching to improve serving efficiency.
papers.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
papers.tldr: Difflet speeds diffusion-transformer inference on AWS Trainium2 through shared compilation, fused attention, adaptive caching, and resident model serving.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$\kappa$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.
authors: Zhenxu Tian, Kebin Liu, Zhengwu Yang, Yi Su, Qingqing Dang, Yanlin Sha, Kaipeng Deng, Dianhai Yu, Yanjun Ma, Juntao Li, Min Zhang
bullets: Long-context decoding is bottlenecked by repeated attention over the growing KV cache.
Static cross-layer index sharing is efficient but can lose accuracy as attention patterns evolve across layers.
The method observes that salient-token changes are localized near the boundaries of previously selected regions.
Its coarse-to-fine proposal-refinement strategy preserves layer adaptability while reducing index recomputation.
It reports state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse-attention methods and a 3.4× decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention with cross-layer index sharing reduces KV-cache memory and decoding compute.
papers.title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
papers.tldr: Prism Attention accelerates long-context LLM decoding by refining shared sparse-attention indices across layers instead of rigidly reusing them.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman
bullets: Targets the computational and communication costs that hinder federated NLP and multimodal learning.
Processes text, images, and other modalities uniformly as byte sequences, without tokenization.
Uses lean linear attention to reduce memory and computational requirements.
Evaluated on multilingual and multimodal sentiment analysis using Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA.
The abstract reports higher accuracy than ByT5 and LSTM, alongside substantially lower memory and communication overheads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model for efficient federated learning, utilizing linear attention to reduce memory and computational footprint.
papers.title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
papers.tldr: FederatedBytes is a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model using linear attention to make multimodal federated learning more efficient while maintaining strong sentiment-analysis performance.

papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.
bullets: Problem: Determine whether calibration updates learned for one model representation can be reused by another representation.
Method: Extract positive group-wise gains and install them into recipient weights or native quantization scales while preserving quantized codes, zero points, and storage layout.
Main result: For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, transfer retained 76.9–90.5% of recipient-specific text-loss improvement on held-out WikiText and C4 cohorts.
Shuffling gain values within projections degraded both recipients, indicating that learned group assignments are important.
A Llama-3.2-3B control retained 98.6–99.3% of text-calibration benefit after cross-installation, with a small remaining preference for recipient-specific gains.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization calibration transfer improves memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
papers.tldr: Calibration gains learned for one representation can be transferred to another representation of the same pretrained model, preserving most of recipient-specific calibration benefits without recipient-side optimization.

papers.abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of monotonic decay mechanisms that cannot erase intermediate tokens selectively.
Uses path extrema: logits are penalized according to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field across the key–query span.
Includes the Forgetting Transformer as a special case; under a shared learned walk, unpenalized keys form a stack.
A constant-dimensional FPA head can realize arbitrary subsets of surviving keys, unlike comparable softmax-based mechanisms requiring dimension linear in key count.
In experiments, FPA converges to target key sets, matches FoX perplexity, and achieves perfect passkey retrieval at 8× training length with a cache compressed to about 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Novel attention mechanism with forget gates and KV cache compression, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory.
papers.title: First Passage Attention
papers.tldr: First Passage Attention enables selective forgetting of intermediate context while preserving older relevant tokens, outperforming comparable mechanisms on synthetic memory tasks and long-context passkey retrieval.

papers.abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
bullets: Learned embeddings improve validation loss by 0.20 nats but require 2.6× more trainable parameters.
The frozen-table model is better or tied on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, and PIQA; ARC-Easy favors learned embeddings.
Combined with a ternary BitNet b1.58 body, the model is 46 MB and generates 615–740 tokens/s on a laptop CPU.
The frozen table performs 1.7–2.3 nats better on rare words and supports 10,000 new words with only a 3% cost.
Scope: results target small Gemma-shaped and ternary models, with the table derived from a pretrained embedding via PCA and sign binarization.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces language model memory via frozen embedding table, relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.tldr: A frozen 16 MB binary vocabulary can replace a large learned embedding table in small and ternary language models with competitive evaluation performance and much lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. We offer this as a characterization on one probe, not a leaderboard claim. Our central contribution is a redirection: pursuing faithful substitute caches is the wrong target; adding a cache to what the reader already has is the promising one.
bullets: The study examines training-free KV-cache substitution between frozen LLMs as a less lossy alternative to text communication.
Readers only tolerate caches near those they would have produced themselves, but geometric similarity does not predict usability and failure is abrupt rather than gradual.
Competitive attention is offered as an explanation for why more faithful cache substitutes do not solve the problem.
Eight substitution methods perform at the uninformative-cache baseline, while a query-adaptation design that preserves the reader’s cache exceeds its own baseline in the reported probe.
The authors characterize this as a redirection from replacing reader caches to augmenting them with sender caches, not as a broad leaderboard claim.
papers.selection_reason: Studies KV cache substitution and cache-augmented inference in LLM systems, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
papers.tldr: Frozen readers cannot reliably use substituted sender KV caches, even when those caches are geometrically similar; retaining the reader’s cache and adding the sender’s as context is more promising.

papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
authors: Aozhong Zhang, Selcuk Gurses, Yanxia Deng, Naigang Wang, Chi-Chun Liu, Davis Wertheimer, Derrick Liu, Xin Li, Zi Yang, Felix X. -F. Ye, Penghang Yin
bullets: Targets the linear KV-cache memory growth that limits long-context LLM scaling.
Decouples residual-output perturbation into per-token scores, avoiding the underlying NP-hard combinatorial optimization.
Provides a provable constant-factor approximation under a cone condition empirically verified on three long-context LLMs.
Uses fused Triton kernels without materializing the full attention matrix, yielding a reported 19.8× scoring-kernel speedup and up to 9.9% end-to-end prefill speedup.
On RULER and LongBench, outperforms evaluated baselines at equal cache budgets and achieves the lowest reported inference latency among eviction methods.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a principled KV-cache eviction method with approximation guarantees and efficient kernels.
papers.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: DropKV enables fast, near-optimal KV-cache eviction for long-context LLMs by replacing an intractable joint optimization with independently scored token decisions.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained language models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision-language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block's output with the token representations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual instruction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pretrained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our experiments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline.
authors: Madhav Iyengar, Andreas Geiger, Hilde K\"uhne
bullets: Prunes the language backbone and repeatedly applies a subset of its layers, using linear adapters to merge representations across recurrences.
Uses three-stage recovery: language-backbone training, vision-language projector alignment, and visual instruction tuning.
Distills outputs from the original non-recurrent model during the first and final recovery stages.
On TinyLLaVA-1.4B, the retrofitted model outperforms an equally recovered unpruned baseline without adding vision-language data.
Improvements are strongest on reasoning benchmarks; basic visual understanding remains comparable to the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces VLM parameters via recurrence, fitting both multimodal foundation models and efficiency.
papers.title: Retrofitting Recurrent Vision-Language Models from Pretrained Backbones
papers.tldr: A pretrained vision-language model can be made recurrent and 23.3% smaller in language parameters while matching or improving performance through structured recovery training and distillation.

papers.abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma S\"oderberg, Christofer Rydenf\"alt
bullets: CodeHealth negatively predicted agentic review-and-fix token cost across all three tested LLMs, independent of PR footprint.
Each additional CodeHealth point corresponded to 3.5%–6.1% lower token cost.
The association appeared during review, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without producing more comments.
Adjusting for scored-file size removed the association, suggesting file size mediates the relationship.
Two registered code smells predicted fix cost, while batch fixing did not change median CodeHealth.
papers.selection_reason: Studies the token cost of agentic code review, providing empirical insights into the efficiency of LLM inference pipelines.
papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.tldr: In a pre-registered study of 465 agent-authored PRs, healthier code consistently required modestly fewer tokens for multi-agent review and fixing, largely because it involved smaller scored files.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Quantizes large LLM n-gram lookup tables with compressed reconstructable codes, drastically reducing model memory footprint while preserving output quality.
papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional Program compresses language-model lookup tables to two bits per value while reconstructing requested rows on demand, substantially reducing storage and quantization error.

papers.abstract: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.
authors: Johannes Knittel, Alec Helbling, Hanspeter Pfister
bullets: Targets sub-four-bit quantization, where memory savings often degrade factual knowledge and task accuracy.
Assigns scales by Transformer unit function: residual-stream readers use per-output-unit scales, while writers use per-input-unit scales.
Requires no search, calibration, or stored state, and converts existing checkpoints to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours.
In two model families from 0.6B to 14B parameters, ternary RoleQ reduces perplexity by up to half versus layout-based scaling; per-row scaling leaves MMLU near chance.
A sparse second ternary plane selected by Fisher saliency recovers about half of the lost 8B MMLU performance with a fraction of a bit.
papers.selection_reason: Ternary quantization of LLMs reduces model memory, fitting efficient AI memory-efficiency.
papers.title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
papers.tldr: RoleQ converts pretrained language models to ternary weights using role-aligned scaling, preserving knowledge and accuracy better than layout-based quantization at low memory cost.

papers.abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
bullets: A remote LMCache/Valkey tier increased 16k-token p99 latency from 3.96 s to 17.3 s, despite unchanged median time-to-first-token.
Remote hits initially took 0.88 s versus 0.31 s for prompt recomputation; synchronous loading caused severe queueing and 83.32 s p99 latency.
A cost model shows caching helps only above 2.53 GB/s and for prompts longer than roughly 17k tokens.
The proposed design shards MLA KV state and the remote tier across PCP ranks, adds asynchronous loading, and fixes three stalling client bugs.
The optimized system reduced hit-heavy p99 latency to 0.67 s, increased prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% with an upstream kernel fix.
papers.selection_reason: Scales remote KV cache tiers for context-parallel prefill; directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
papers.tldr: Remote KV caching can be slower than recomputing prompts, but sharding, bandwidth scaling, asynchronous loading, and client fixes make it effective for long-context PCP serving.

papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. We compute these statistics without materializing attention, by accumulation in the FlashAttention pass, sparse lookups after it, or a second tiled pass over the scores, and classify them by this path into nearly free and costlier ones. On an H100, the statistics of five published detectors add 16% to the latency of a Qwen3-8B forward at 2K tokens, falling to 1.4% at 35K, and store 22.5 KiB per response token. On three benchmarks, probes trained on frozen Qwen3 proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters prove strong detectors: a 4B proxy outperforms the strongest of nine zero-shot 4-9B LLM judges in F1 on two of the three, the proxies match or outperform specialized grounding checkers of up to 7B parameters, probing each proxy beats prompting it as a judge, and adding attention features significantly improves F1 in half of the 12 benchmark-proxy pairs, never significantly lowering it.
authors: Andrei Volodichev, Maksim Savichev, Nikita Sviridov, Artem Yuliy, Dmitry Simakov, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Targets unsupported but fluent LLM answers, including responses from proprietary generators.
Computes attention statistics during FlashAttention, via sparse lookups, or with a second tiled score pass, avoiding quadratic memory materialization.
On an H100, five detectors add 16% latency at 2K tokens and 1.4% at 35K, using 22.5 KiB per response token.
Across three benchmarks, frozen Qwen3 probes are strong detectors; a 4B proxy beats nine zero-shot LLM judges on two benchmarks and matches or exceeds specialized checkers.
Attention features significantly improve F1 in 6 of 12 benchmark–proxy pairs and never significantly reduce it.
papers.selection_reason: Computes attention statistics without materializing the attention matrix, reducing memory and latency for attention-based detectors.
papers.title: FlashAttention with Statistics: Low-Overhead Attention Features for Compact Hallucination Detectors
papers.tldr: FlashAttention-based computation makes attention features practical for compact, frozen-model hallucination detectors without storing the full attention matrix.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng, Ye Wang, Yongsheng Liang
bullets: Addresses redundant prefill computation when shared context moves between agents.
Orders KV blocks by model-side utility so the most valuable information is transmitted first.
Uses feedback-adaptive streaming FEC to schedule repairs before the receiver’s TTFT deadline.
Evaluations on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets show better task quality than compared transport schemes, especially under tight deadlines.
Scope: effectiveness depends on KV-utility estimation, link reliability, and available transmission time.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on deadline-aware KV-cache handoff and transport for edge multi-agent LLM systems, relevant to KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: PriorityFEC improves KV-cache handoff for edge multi-agent LLMs by prioritizing valuable cache blocks and adaptively protecting them under TTFT deadlines and unreliable links.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of repeatedly recomputing task context in VLA policies.
Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.
A lightweight actor combines current visual/proprioceptive feedback with learned time- and arm-indexed queries to predict action chunks.
Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action policy with fixed KV task memory for efficient closed-loop manipulation; strongly relevant to VLA and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Fast-VLA runs a 4B vision-language model once per episode, then enables efficient closed-loop robot control with a lightweight actor.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.
authors: Jaeyun Kim, Hoonki Lee, Susie Shin, Hyunmin Kim, Dahyun Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses the fixed-precision limitation of routed MoE experts.
Encodes expert FFN weights into prefix-decodable SharedScale AnyBCQ chunks and profiles reconstruction residuals offline.
Allocates precision at inference time using live router gate scores and per-expert residual profiles.
Outperforms uniform chunk allocation on KL divergence and downstream accuracy at matched weight budgets.
Evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in the prototype.
papers.selection_reason: Runtime precision allocation for MoE expert weights reduces inference memory; fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: DPA-MoE: A Runtime Precision Control Framework for MoE Inference
papers.tldr: DPA-MoE enables runtime, token-aware precision allocation for MoE experts from a single encoded checkpoint without retraining or re-encoding.

papers.abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.
bullets: Sparse KV caches retain selected states, but gaps from evicted tokens can distort RoPE query–key matching.
The method assigns compact, order-preserving coordinates and relocates cached key phases while synchronizing queries and generation.
It operates on a fixed selector-produced cache without renewed selection or historical re-prefill.
Across 36 comparisons, answer quality improved in 32 cases; one reported result rose from 23.6% to 35.4%.
Measured complete-request overhead was approximately 1%–3% in the evaluated configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Directly targets sparse KV cache compression and improves retained-state use through positional reorganization, fitting KV-cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
papers.tldr: RoPERelay improves sparse KV-cache use by reorganizing RoPE positions after token selection, boosting answer quality without selecting more tokens or increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
authors: Shiyu Ji, Peng Ling, Chen Lin, Shupeng Li, Yixuan Wang, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che
bullets: Targets errors in 2-bit MLA KV caches that affect both attention matching and value reconstruction.
Uses offline calibration with a learned shared rotation and coupled quantization thresholds and reconstruction gains.
Supervises calibration through prediction matching and attention-output matching while keeping model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest average accuracy among compared 2-bit methods across three MLA models and six benchmarks.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, delivers 3.96× BF16 KV capacity and 2.51× decode throughput at 256K-token inputs in SGLang.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces rotation and range calibration for 2-bit KV cache quantization in MLA, directly targeting memory-efficient long-context inference.
papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.tldr: RoLaQ improves 2-bit KV-cache quantization for multi-head latent attention by jointly calibrating rotations and quantization ranges, enabling higher accuracy and greater long-context capacity.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.
bullets: Long-context decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token accesses every layer’s KV cache.
MOIRA selects the smallest set of pages reaching a target attention-mass coverage per request, layer, KV head, and decoding step.
Its self-planning attention kernel handles variable page-list lengths without padding, imbalance, or host-side CUDA-graph breaks.
On an H200 with 128k-token contexts, it reads about 30% of pages at γ=0.99 and achieves 2.2–2.5× lower TPOT than dense FA3 while matching dense accuracy.
At γ=0.98, TPOT improves by 2.7× and serving throughput increases by up to 51%, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse adaptive-budget KV-cache decoding for long-context LLMs; strong efficiency contribution.
papers.title: MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: MOIRA enables fast, training-free long-context decoding by adaptively reading only the KV-cache pages needed by each layer and KV head while preserving dense-model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training compresses KV caches for long contexts; directly fits KV-cache efficiency and test-time learning.
papers.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Latent Compaction uses document-specific test-time training to compress KV caches while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
authors: Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang, Jianjin Li, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between target hidden features and the contextual needs of later draft positions.
Uses learned per-position queries and a lightweight state reader to retrieve and fuse supplementary context via residual updates.
Reduces overhead with low-rank state reads and fused operators, building on DSpark’s parallel backbone and sequential prediction head.
Across seven math, code, and dialogue benchmarks, reports a 3.16× average speedup over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms DSpark on all benchmarks, with average throughput and acceptance-length gains of 7.97% and 8.50%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding using recurrent states in hybrid linear attention LLMs; directly relevant to efficient attention, memory-efficient inference, and LLM architecture.
papers.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ReaDy accelerates speculative decoding in hybrid linear-attention LLMs by retrieving position-specific context from the target model’s recurrent states.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context speculative decoding with position-free far memory; fits KV-cache efficiency and long-context language modeling.
papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FOLD is a training-free long-context speculative-decoding method that improves drafting by combining exact local positions with sharpened, weight-controlled far-memory attention.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert's gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.
authors: Renjie Xie, Juncheng Yang, Aoting Hu, Yan Liang, Mingxi Zhang, Zheheng Hong, Wei Xu, Yanzhi Chen
bullets: MoE models require storing all expert weights, making quantization important despite sparse activation.
Expert sensitivity rankings do not indicate how strongly each expert’s errors should affect precision allocation.
NatScale applies a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based weights while preserving rankings.
It jointly evaluates experts’ gate, up, and down configurations, combining output errors with calibrated weights and prior statistics.
Across three models and nine settings, it achieved the lowest KL divergence and highest top-token agreement in every setting, plus the lowest perplexity in seven.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision quantization for MoE LLMs reduces model memory, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization
papers.tldr: NatScale improves mixed-precision MoE quantization by calibrating expert importance weights to better allocate precision under a storage budget.

papers.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Xiaobing Tu, Xiantao Zhang, Jinkui Ren, Yinggui Wang, Yue Ma, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high latency and non-causal processing of existing video object removal methods.
Transfers erasing capability from a text-to-video foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser.
Uses sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to maintain fixed-context, constant-speed generation.
Reports sub-second latency and up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
Introduces the LongErase benchmark and supports interactive, infinite-length video erasing with strong real-world generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video object removal with causal attention, attention sinks, and KV cache rolling directly targets video generation and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing
papers.tldr: StreamErase enables real-time, arbitrarily long video object removal by distilling bidirectional erasing quality into a causal streaming model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.
authors: Junlin Liao, Harshit Kondle, Di Liu, Zonghua Gu
bullets: Measures system energy, latency, and thermal behavior across Raspberry Pi 5 CPU/NPU and Jetson Orin Nano Super CPU/GPU deployments.
Separates fixed per-request energy from energy that scales with generated output length, while comparing deployment stacks rather than hardware alone.
Pi NPU offloading reduces energy per generated token by about two-thirds and prevents the thermal throttling seen with sustained CPU inference.
Image inputs increase both fixed and per-token energy, but answer generation typically dominates total energy at common response lengths.
Jetson GPU has lower fixed request cost; Pi NPU has lower per-token cost, with energy curves crossing near 40 output tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: Seeing at the Edge: Energy Characterization of Vision-Language Model Inference on Edge Platforms
papers.tldr: NPU acceleration makes Raspberry Pi 5 inference for a 2B vision-language model substantially more energy-efficient and thermally stable, while Jetson GPU is better for short responses.

papers.abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.
authors: Abdel-Rahim Mezidi, Jordan Patracone, Saverio Salzo, Amaury Habrard, Massimiliano Pontil, Remi Emonet, Marc Sebban
bullets: Recasts neural-operator layers as minimizers of Bregman-regularized problems on Banach function spaces.
Interprets activation operators as Bregman proximity operators mapping dual spaces to primal spaces.
Recovers classical neural operators and defines a new Bregman neural operator with an inverse activation operator.
The Bregman variant retains the expressivity of standard neural operators.
Experiments indicate improved training of deeper and more accurate Fourier neural operator models.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the energy efficiency, latency, and thermal behavior of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on edge hardware, directly addressing efficiency and multimodal deployment.
papers.title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators
papers.tldr: A Bregman-optimization perspective generalizes neural operators and introduces a Bregman variant that supports deeper, more accurate Fourier neural operator models.

papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, their energy consumption during inference has become a critical concern. While Autoregressive (AR) models are the industry standard, Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative capable of parallel token generation. In this paper, we perform a comparative energy benchmark of diffusion models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) against AR counterparts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B). We analyze the trade-offs between model architecture, KV-cache optimization, and Joules-per-token efficiency. Our results show that at longer sequences (200--600 tokens), diffusion models achieve 2.5--2.7 J/token, approximately 2$\times$ more efficient than AR models with KV-cache (5.3--5.7 J/token). KV-cache provides substantial benefits for AR models at longer sequences (50--70\% energy reduction).
bullets: Compares energy use during inference for diffusion models LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B with AR models Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B.
Analyzes architecture, KV-cache optimization, and joules-per-token efficiency.
For 200–600-token sequences, diffusion models use 2.5–2.7 J/token versus 5.3–5.7 J/token for AR models with KV-cache.
KV-cache reduces AR energy consumption by 50–70% at longer sequence lengths.
Scope is limited to the evaluated models and sequence lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks energy consumption and KV-cache efficiency of diffusion versus autoregressive language models, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Energy Consumption Analysis of Discrete Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion language models can use roughly half the inference energy per token of autoregressive models on longer sequences, while KV-cache substantially improves AR efficiency.

papers.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.
authors: Sifan Yang, Hongyi Tao, Dingzhi Yu, Haomin Bai, Wei Jiang, Silin Gao, Pi Bu, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses convergence degradation when gradient noise overwhelms the leading singular subspace late in training.
Introduces SMRC, which keeps optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to updates.
Extends SMRC to multi-stage basis refreshes using boundary correction to maintain consistency across stages.
Introduces PMRC for Muon by applying the matrix sign to projected momentum, with weighted momentum tracking analysis.
Theory gives O(T^{-1/4}) convergence for both SMRC and PMRC, matching their full-space counterparts; experiments support effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory-efficient subspace optimization for LLM training, directly relevant to reducing memory requirements in AI systems.
papers.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
papers.tldr: Residual correction makes subspace-based momentum SGD and Muon memory-efficient while preserving full-space convergence rates under fixed or refreshed subspaces.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.
bullets: Targets agent workloads whose multiple expert models cannot simultaneously fit in GPU memory.
Uses caller-output intent signals to prefetch models, partial k* residency for incremental switching, and bandwidth-aware transfer scheduling to protect live-session KV state.
Dynamically reallocates the unified memory budget between weights and KV blocks as workload demands change.
Reduces session completion time by 21.7% versus the strongest whole-model-swapping baseline and remains usable in crash scenarios where those baselines fail.
On SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, improves completion time by up to 49% and raises SLO attainment to 76.8–100%.
papers.selection_reason: Serving system optimizing weight/KV memory on constrained GPUs; directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
papers.tldr: JointServe accelerates multi-model LLM-agent serving on memory-constrained GPUs by jointly managing model weights and KV cache residency.

papers.abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-output LLM inference.
Uses RoPE channel-pair attention-logit perturbation analysis to identify salient pairs via query–key pair-norm products.
Assigns higher precision to salient key pairs once during prefill and reuses the allocation during decoding.
At 2.26-bit average precision, matches or outperforms prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32–2.39 bits across reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks.
Degrades more gracefully to 1.5 bits than compared baselines, which show sharper drops below 2.25 bits.
papers.selection_reason: Mixed-precision KV cache quantization for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
papers.tldr: PN-Mix improves low-bit KV-cache efficiency by assigning precision using query–key pair-norm saliency, enabling strong long-output LLM accuracy at very low bit rates.

papers.abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch.
