On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}
bullets: Addresses the tension between precise information retention and efficient long-context inference.
Uses hierarchical neural memory modules, blockwise attention, and full attention over recent tokens while compressing older context into fixed-size memory.
Replaces attention layers post-training, avoiding training a new language model from scratch.
On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, improves QuALITY and LongHealth accuracy over segmented attention windows and reports faster prefill/decode with lower steady-state decode memory.
Evaluated configurations show benefits at medium context lengths; broader scope beyond the reported model and tasks is not established by the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical memory architecture (NMMs) for retrofitting LLMs to improve long-context inference efficiency and memory usage, directly addressing LLM memory and efficiency.
papers.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
papers.tldr: Titan-Llama retrofits pretrained transformers with recurrent test-time neural memory to improve long-context accuracy while reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.
authors: Jiwon Song, Yoongon Kim, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses low-dimensional token-ranking errors and the latency cost of gathering scattered KV-cache tokens.
Learns a shared query–key subspace via a tractable spectral objective for token selection.
Introduces a gather-free indexed-attention kernel supporting distinct selections per KV head under GQA.
Remains close to full-KV accuracy across GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and MLA models.
Matches model-native DSA reasoning accuracy without training and reaches 96–99% of its decoding throughput at 700B scale.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse attention for efficient long-context decoding; directly relevant to efficient attention and KV-cache reduction.
papers.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: JSSA enables accurate, token-level sparse attention for long-context decoding while reducing KV-cache traffic and achieving up to 6.43× full-KV throughput at 128K context.

papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.
authors: OneRec Team, Chenglong Chu, Guohong Mu, Guowang Zhang, Hao Peng, Hui Wang, Jian Liang, Jiangxia Cao, Jiao Ou, Jiaxin Deng, Lu Ren, Muhao Wei, Ruiming Tang, Tianle Xu, Wenwu Ou, Xingmei Wang, Zhixin Ling, Zhiyuan Liang, Ziqi Wang, Chaoyi Ma, Haixiao Gao, Kuo Cai, Renpu Liu, Ruochen Yang, Wenlong Xu, Xinqi Jin, Yan Sun, Yifan Wang, Yingzhi He, Yiyu Wang, Yusen Huo, Zhaojie Liu, Zihan Zhou
bullets: Addresses fixed summary-compression windows across layers, which limit flexible KV-cache compression.
Reduces wasted computation in full-attention layers that previously ignored summary tokens while still incurring quadratic prefilling cost.
Uses summary tokens in two roles: compressed KV memory and sparse indexing.
Targets both more flexible KV-cache memory compression and lower full-attention computation cost.
papers.selection_reason: Summary-token attention with flexible KV cache compression and reduced full-attention cost; fits efficient AI and long-context LLM methods.
papers.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
papers.tldr: KSA V2 makes hybrid summary-token attention more flexible and efficient by separating summary tokens’ KV-memory and sparse-indexing roles.

papers.abstract: KV caches make long-context serving efficient by reusing past computation, but model switching breaks this reuse and forces the receiver to prefill the context again. We study \emph{zero-prefill cross-model context handoff}: translating a sender cache into a receiver-compatible state so that the receiver can continue directly without prefilling same context. Existing affine transport methods show that receiver KV states can be substantially reconstructed from sender caches. However, through extensive analyses, we find that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility. Similar K/V reconstruction errors can lead to substantially different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy, because conventional reconstruction objectives overlook the query-dependent functional importance of K and V in receiver attention. We thus introduce CACHELINK, which learns a coupled K/V correction through the receiver behavior directly. Across four independently trained sender--receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, CACHELINK improves the equal-weight mean over all methods for every pair. In matched diagnostics, CACHELINK changes K/V squared error by less than 0.4% while substantially changing receiver attention and next-token behavior. At 32K context, it reduces handoff latency by up to $7.27\times$ relative to receiver re-prefill. Our findings verify that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient and that preserving the receiver computation induced by the transported cache is important for effective cross-model KV transport.
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Zijia Song, Ruizi Han, Ziyue Qiao, Miao Zhang
bullets: Cross-model switching normally forces the receiver to re-prefill the shared context, reducing KV-cache reuse.
The work finds that similar K/V reconstruction errors can produce very different attention patterns, predictions, and downstream accuracy.
CacheLink learns a coupled K/V correction guided directly by receiver computation and behavior.
Across four sender–receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, it achieved the best equal-weight mean for every pair.
At 32K context, it reduced handoff latency by up to 7.27× versus receiver re-prefill.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes functional KV cache transport for zero-prefill cross-model handoff, directly targeting inference cache efficiency.
papers.title: CacheLink: Functional KV Transport for Zero-Prefill Cross-Model Context Handoff
papers.tldr: CacheLink transports KV caches between models by optimizing receiver behavior rather than reconstruction fidelity, enabling effective zero-prefill context handoff.

papers.abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.
authors: Xinmeng Liu, Xianglong Yan, Kaicheng Yang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high computational and memory costs that hinder ARVG deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
T-BGR uses a tail-aware reconstruction objective to better preserve important weight-distribution information during quantizer calibration.
CAPS allocates mixed activation precision across generation stages based on stage importance and computational cost under a bit budget.
Experiments across multiple ARVG backbones show improved robustness to aggressive low-bit quantization.
On Infinity, it achieves near full-precision quality at effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while W4A6 existing methods show degradation or inconsistency.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free quantization framework reducing memory and compute for autoregressive visual generation models.
papers.title: HGA-Quant: Heterogeneity-Aware Quantization for AutoRegressive Visual Generation Models
papers.tldr: HGA-Quant is a training-free PTQ framework that preserves ARVG image quality under aggressive low-bit quantization through heterogeneity-aware weight calibration and activation precision scheduling.

papers.abstract: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments, where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Prevailing solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. We argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it. To this end, we propose Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC), a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective, thereby eliminating redundant domain information under continual covariate shifts. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories and admits a theoretically grounded, tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor, making continual graph adaptation practical at scale.
bullets: Addresses the computational and scalability costs of synthesizing memory graphs during prolonged graph distribution shifts.
Uses a training-free, test-time framework with a closed-form distribution-matching objective to distill each incoming domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory.
Models inter-domain dependencies with state-evolving memories to balance generalizability and adaptability across target domains.
Provides a theoretically tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation.
Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory use by 92.4% relative to a recent competitor.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time framework for memory crystallization in graph learning, relevant to test-time adaptation and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Efficient Memory Crystallization for Graph Learning under Non-Stationary Distribution Shifts
papers.tldr: EMC enables efficient continual graph adaptation under non-stationary distribution shifts by crystallizing compact domain memories without training generative modules.

papers.abstract: Recent work on anchored diffusion language models improves denoising by shaping an intermediate latent space with supervised important-token targets. In this work, we introduce time-based (self-supervised) anchoring, which learns and reuses latent anchors without requiring such targets. Our key observation is that anchors encode persistent properties of the clean sequence, such as its semantic intent, global structure, or intermediate plan. Although their hidden representations become stale as the token canvas evolves, their semantic content remains useful across nearby diffusion times. This is implemented through a two-stage architecture consisting of a relatively expensive anchor network that generates the latent cache state and a lightweight denoising network that intelligently combines the cached latent state with the current state at each reverse step using a fusion module. This gives anchoring a latent-space caching interpretation: the anchor network is evaluated periodically, while its cached representation is reused across multiple reverse steps. We instantiate this framework as TADM:Post-train, which time-anchorizes pretrained DLMs, and TADM:Pretraining, which learns time-based anchors during pretraining. Applied to DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by approximately 49% to 79% on several math, code, and STEM benchmarks (GSM8K, AIME26, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench-v6, HumanEval, MMLU-Pro). TADM:Pretraining reduces Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% relative to a standard single-stage DLM, achieves up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.
bullets: Addresses the high per-step computation of diffusion language models and the need for supervised important-token targets in prior anchored approaches.
Uses a two-stage architecture: an expensive anchor network periodically creates a latent cache, while a lightweight denoiser fuses the cache with the current state across reverse steps.
Introduces TADM:Post-train for adapting pretrained DLMs and TADM:Pretraining for learning time-based anchors during pretraining.
On DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by about 49–79% across math, code, and STEM benchmarks.
TADM:Pretraining cuts Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% and reaches up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.
papers.selection_reason: Time-anchored diffusion language models with latent-space caching for faster generation, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architectures.
papers.title: Time-Anchored Diffusion Language Models: Latent-Space Caching for Fast Generation
papers.tldr: Time-based latent anchoring caches persistent sequence information across diffusion steps, substantially accelerating diffusion language model generation without supervised anchor targets.

papers.abstract: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
authors: David Gonz\'alez-Mart\'inez, Philipp Nazari, T. Konstantin Rusch, Shiwei Liu
bullets: Frames representation mixing across layers as storing and retrieving information through depth.
Unifies PreLN Transformers, mHC, and AttnRes as stream-based memory mechanisms.
Introduces LDM, using recursive least squares to retrieve information across depth.
LDM propagates residual, associative-memory, and inverse-covariance streams.
At 400M and 1.5B parameters, LDM reports the lowest perplexities among the compared baselines and competitive zero-shot accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified depth-memory framework and linear associative memory stream for transformer architectures, improving language modeling and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Depth Memory
papers.tldr: Depth Memory unifies residual-style depth aggregation as information storage and retrieval, and its Linear Depth Memory variant improves language-model perplexity with hardware-efficient execution.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
authors: Yangchengyu Zhou, Zhiping Wu, Runchang Jiang, Dongdong Ren, Youfang Han, Wei Zhao, Dongqi Cai, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context and reasoning-focused LLM inference.
Profiles layer sensitivity and token importance to guide adaptive precision allocation.
Balances layer-wise precision enhancement with token-wise preservation under a fixed budget.
Derives the allocation policy offline, avoiding online allocation search.
Shows consistent gains over existing single- and multi-granularity methods across diverse models and benchmarks at matched memory budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes budget-aware precision allocation for KV cache quantization, directly targeting memory-efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
papers.tldr: MultiAlloc improves KV-cache quantization by allocating a fixed memory budget between layer- and token-level precision preservation using offline profiling.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.
authors: Jophin John, Michael Hoffmann, Piroska Lendvai, Florent Dufour
bullets: Evaluates Bavarian, Standard German, and English with 14 open-weight 7B–10B instruction models on 206 aligned BAVGROUND questions.
8-bit GPTQ stays close to BF16 and mostly preserves the languages’ relative performance.
GPTQ-4 and AWQ-4 lower average accuracy by about 1.4–1.5 percentage points and alter 11.9–16.0% of BF16 decisions, mainly on uncertain examples.
4-bit compression does not consistently disadvantage Bavarian; the most affected language varies by model and quantisation method.
Free-form tests show greater 4-bit degradation than multiple-choice accuracy alone suggests, while calibration language particularly affects some AWQ-4 results.
papers.selection_reason: Studies post-training quantisation of LLMs, a memory-efficiency technique, with cross-language robustness analysis.
papers.title: Lightweight but Linguistically Fair? Quantisation Robustness across Bavarian, German, and English
papers.tldr: 8-bit quantisation largely preserves multilingual and dialect performance, but 4-bit methods are unstable and can degrade outputs in model-, calibration-, and evaluation-dependent ways.

papers.abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.
authors: Md Asiful Islam, Fahmida Alam, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of reasoning-based LLM guardrails.
Distills a frozen teacher’s safe/unsafe interpretations and comparisons into compact latent representations.
Jointly trains latent representations for safety prediction and on-demand reconstruction of human-readable reasoning traces.
Outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most reported in-domain and out-of-domain safety classification and explanation-extraction settings.
Achieves a 19.4× inference speedup at batch size one, with reconstructed traces showing high semantic similarity to the teacher’s reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LR-Guard, an efficient safety guardrail that achieves 19.4x inference speedup via latent reasoning and reconstruction, fitting both efficiency and LLM safety domains.
papers.title: Efficient Safety Guardrails through Latent Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning with On-Demand Trace Reconstruction
papers.tldr: LR-Guard delivers fast, explainable safety guardrails by replacing routine explicit reasoning with structured latent reasoning and reconstructing explanations only when needed.

papers.abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.
authors: Huihao Jing, Wenbin Hu, Shaojin Chen, Haochen Shi, Haoyu Huang, Sirui Zhang, Yuxuan Liu, Zhongwei Xie, Haoran Li
bullets: Prefix matching can fail when a hybrid-LLM consumer depends on state still being computed by a producer in the same round.
The native scheduler stops scanning at the blocked consumer, causing head-of-line blocking and idle batch slots.
RadixFlow decouples prefix matching from state readiness through state-ready traversal, turning a global scan barrier into a local wait.
Across five hybrid models, it reduces mean latency by 3%–24% and worker rounds by 11%–44% with nearly unchanged prefix reuse.
Traversal provides most gains on larger Qwen3.5 models; heavier rounds limit latency improvements, while full-attention workloads see little added benefit.
papers.selection_reason: Prefix-cached hybrid LLM serving with KV cache/recurrent state scheduling; fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
papers.tldr: RadixFlow reduces execution bubbles in prefix-cached hybrid LLM serving by letting independent requests run while blocked consumers await recurrent state.

papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.
authors: Jieyun Deng, Keming Hu, Yanghe Liu, Li Feng
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth that can exhaust single consumer GPUs during long-context decoding.
Combines query-aware key-block selection, dynamic retention budgets, and cost-aware local or full recomputation.
Requires no model-weight changes or offline training and integrates with FlexGen/FlexLLMGen.
On an RTX 3070 Ti laptop, it reduces latency by 31%–63% across 1k–4k prompts and achieves 1.4×–2.7× higher throughput.
Completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes, while the FlexGen baseline times out; cache retention remains strong across keep ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Runtime KV-cache recovery for memory-constrained LLM inference, directly fitting efficient AI and KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware
papers.tldr: SparPR reduces KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks for consumer-device LLM inference through runtime, training-free partial cache recovery.

papers.abstract: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.
authors: Yuechuan Chen, Yanda Guo, Xiaoxi Liu, Weilin Ruan, Huanbo Xu, Ruyi Wang, Wei Zhu
bullets: Addresses uniform or predefined per-head budgets that overlook input-dependent differences in attention demand.
Uses maximum aggregated observation-window attention as a proxy: dispersed heads receive larger budgets, while concentrated heads receive smaller ones.
Adds abnormal-head masking and a floor budget to improve robustness under weak attention responses.
Integrates with SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures.
Improves retained attention mass with negligible overhead, but does not consistently surpass Ada-KV; gains are mixed on tested 7B/8B models.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache compression with input-adaptive head-wise budget allocation, fitting the KV cache and memory efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: ChampionKV: Head-Wise Adaptive Budget Allocation for KV Cache Compression
papers.tldr: ChampionKV adaptively allocates KV-cache budgets across attention heads using attention concentration, improving long-context compression—especially for Llama3.1-70B-Instruct and tight budgets.

papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/kvreuse.
authors: Zhiwei Chen, Zhongtao Rao, Waikit Xiu, Yuxiang Zhang, Shuting Cui, Jian Chen, Tianxiang Zhao
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse improves inference efficiency but can cause up to a 90% performance drop when agents have conflicting tasks.
The method maps the target agent’s final prefix hidden state to a small set of latent tokens using an MLP.
These tokens are inserted after the reused KV block to help the target agent interpret shared context under its own instructions.
Full-prefill distillation trains the MLP to guide predictions toward the target task.
LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse remedies while keeping TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size increases.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces task-conditioned latent tokens to remedy non-prefix KV cache reuse, improving inference efficiency in multi-agent LLM systems.
papers.title: LatentRemedy: Efficient Remedy For Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: LatentRemedy restores performance in non-prefix KV cache reuse for conflicting multi-agent tasks by adding a few task-conditioned latent tokens instead of recomputing shared context.

papers.abstract: Long-running agents retain KV caches across turns and sessions for hours or days. Compressing these persistent caches requires reducing storage while controlling reconstruction error. We present AlignPred, a codec that combines local alignment with predictive coding under a configurable KV reconstruction-error budget. Local orthogonal transforms align related heads or layers into a common coordinate frame, allowing AlignPred to combine token-wise prediction with same-token prediction across heads or layers. Residuals are quantized on an error-bounded lattice and entropy-coded, without learned predictors, encoder-side mode search, or large joint transforms. Across three attention mechanisms, AlignPred requires less storage than the evaluated baselines at comparable measured reconstruction error. Against the evaluated CPU codec implementations, it decodes at least 1.6 times faster while matching or improving encode time. AlignPred achieves near-native task scores at substantially compressed operating points on LongBench-Pro at 128K context. AlignPred's SGLang HiCache integration reduces persistent target-KV storage by 42-72% relative to native HiCache, with comparable latency.
authors: Xu Yang, Jiapeng Zhang, Zhiwei Zuo, Yuxin Chen, Feiqiang Sun, Chengguang Xu, Feng Jin, Zhuo Tang
bullets: Targets long-running agents that retain KV caches across turns and sessions.
Combines local orthogonal alignment with token-wise and cross-head/layer predictive coding.
Uses error-bounded lattice quantization and entropy coding without learned predictors or large joint transforms.
Uses less storage than evaluated baselines at comparable reconstruction error and decodes at least 1.6× faster than evaluated CPU codecs.
Reduces SGLang HiCache persistent target-KV storage by 42–72% with comparable latency and near-native LongBench-Pro scores at 128K context.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an error-controlled KV cache compression codec, directly targeting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: AlignPred: Error-Controlled KV Cache Compression via Alignment and Predictive Coding
papers.tldr: AlignPred compresses persistent KV caches with bounded reconstruction error while reducing storage and maintaining fast decoding and near-native long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang, Jinguang Liu, Jinbao Xue, Hailong Yang, Ke Zhang, Yinjun Wu
bullets: Targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or logits, producing a quadratic objective with a closed-form low-rank solution.
Learns global top-k rank allocation using differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment.
Across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, achieves up to 70% low-rank KV-cache compression and up to 17.8× reduction with quantization.
Reports up to 23.3-point LongBench gains over the strongest baseline and up to 3.3× end-to-end decoding throughput.
Uses Triton GPU kernels and quantized caches to reach up to 2.7× attention-module speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank KV cache compression with learned rank allocation for long-context LLM inference, directly targeting KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
papers.tldr: BELT compresses long-context KV caches with behavior-aligned low-rank representations and learned rank allocation, improving memory efficiency and decoding speed while preserving quality.

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a linear attention variant that reduces KV cache size and training/prefill FLOPs for long-context LLMs, directly advancing efficient attention and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Virtual Head Attention
papers.tldr: Virtual Head Attention (VHA) reduces KV-cache and compute costs while maintaining or improving long-context language-model quality over standard attention alternatives.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinPrune uses spatial-density-aware token pruning separately for prefill merging and decode KV eviction, improving the compute–memory–accuracy trade-off while exposing pitfalls in phase-specific evaluation.

papers.abstract: Video language models represent a video as a long sequence of visual embeddings in a decoder's input. Every visual embedding is processed by every decoder layer during prefill, stored in the key value cache, and attended by every generated token, so a long video raises prefill, memory, and generation cost at once. We present WIRE (Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding), which reduces this recurring cost by moving part of the video conditioned computation of a frozen video language model from its input activations into a temporary low rank update of its weights. WIRE keeps a short explicit visual context, so the update acts as a correction rather than a replacement of the video. WIRE first compresses the full resolution embeddings of each frame into a small set of carrier tokens using a question conditioned bidirectional selective scan, and physically contracts the decoder input so every decoder layer, cache entry, and decoding step operates on the shorter sequence. Hypernetworks at selected decoder layers read the compressed forward pass together with a readout of the full resolution features removed by contraction and generate LoRA updates to the attention and feedforward projections. The updates are merged after prefill, so autoregressive decoding runs the unmodified frozen backbone. On Qwen3-VL-8B, WIRE with 16 carrier tokens per frame contracts the visual stream by $3.5\times$, reduces decoder prefill time by $3.35\times$ at 256 frames and $4.14\times$ at 1024 frames, shrinks the key value cache proportionally, and keeps per token decoding latency approximately constant. Across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames, it obtains the highest average accuracy among efficient video language models we evaluate under a common 256 frame budget.
authors: Ameen Ali, Tamim Zoabi, Lior Wolf, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Addresses the rising prefill, KV-cache, and attention costs caused by long video embedding sequences.
Compresses each frame into carrier tokens using a question-conditioned bidirectional selective scan, then contracts the decoder input.
Uses hypernetworks to generate LoRA updates from compressed features and removed full-resolution information at selected decoder layers.
Merges updates after prefill, allowing autoregressive decoding to use the unmodified frozen backbone.

On Qwen3-VL-8B with 16 carrier tokens per frame, achieves 3.5× visual-stream contraction, 3.35–4.14× faster prefill, proportional KV-cache reduction, and top average accuracy across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a method to compress visual tokens and reduce KV cache/prefill cost in frozen video LLMs, directly targeting efficiency in multimodal inference.
papers.title: WIRE: Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding of Frozen Video LLMs
papers.tldr: WIRE makes frozen video LLMs more efficient by replacing most long visual inputs with a short context plus temporary low-rank weight updates that preserve video information.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents revise their working context as information becomes obsolete, but deleting text does not erase its influence on cached computation. Later key-value (KV) states remain conditioned on the deleted content, while recomputing the entire retained suffix can be costly. We introduce budgeted KV-cache repair: recovering task performance by recomputing a user-chosen fraction of the retained suffix. Comparing repair allocations under identical relevance scores and token budgets, we find that refreshing coherent regions can substantially outperform refreshing isolated tokens. This finding motivates Semantic-Unit Refresh (SUR), which allocates the budget to query-relevant text regions using inexpensive embedding scores, without training or an auxiliary transformer forward. To execute these repairs efficiently, a layer-packed executor processes selected states together at each layer while preserving full causal cache access. Across five models, SUR achieves strong recovery in controlled deletion tasks while recomputing only 2-5% of the suffix. On four natural multi-hop QA datasets, it achieves near-full-recompute exact match at a 5% budget with lower post-edit latency. The executor accelerates fragmented refresh by up to 16.1x over interval-wise execution.
authors: Han Yu, Wenhui Zhu, Jincheng Cao, Rui Cai, Yuanda Xu, Zhengze Zhou, Xiwen Chen, Hao Wang, Xuanzhao Dong, Han Shi, Menglin Zhou, Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Lin Su, Mina Razghandi, Sayan Ghosh, Qing Lan, Rohit Jain, Alborz Geramifard
bullets: Deleting context leaves later KV states influenced by obsolete text, but fully recomputing the retained suffix is costly.
Budgeted KV-cache repair studies how to recover performance by recomputing only a chosen fraction of the suffix.
Semantic-Unit Refresh (SUR) uses inexpensive embedding relevance scores to refresh coherent regions without training or an auxiliary transformer pass.
A layer-packed executor efficiently processes selected cache states while preserving causal access, accelerating fragmented refresh by up to 16.1× over interval-wise execution.
Across five models and four natural multi-hop QA datasets, SUR uses 2–5% recomputation and reaches near-full-recompute exact match at a 5% budget.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache repair for evolving contexts directly targets cache memory efficiency and inference cost.
papers.title: Budgeted KV-Cache Repair for Evolving Contexts
papers.tldr: SUR repairs stale KV caches after context edits by refreshing only query-relevant text regions, achieving near-full-recompute quality with about 5% recomputation and lower latency.

papers.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.
authors: Zile Wang, Zhide Xie, Tao Ji
bullets: Addresses the limited compatibility and costly recovery of existing MHA-to-MLA methods, especially for QKNorm and MoE models.
Introduces calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization.
Preserves model performance across MHA and GQA models under substantial KV-cache compression.
Surpasses prior state of the art on commonsense and long-context benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, achieves up to 5.35× BF16 GQA serving throughput and reduces KV-cache footprint by 94.73% with 4-bit KV quantization.
papers.selection_reason: Converts modern LLMs to MLA with large KV-cache compression and throughput gains, directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
papers.tldr: MLAfication efficiently converts modern LLMs to high-fidelity MLA, supporting QKNorm and MoE architectures while sharply reducing KV-cache costs.

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM
bullets: Recovers about 99% of the frozen model’s multiple-choice accuracy using only two-thirds of its transformer layers.
Learns option probabilities via KL divergence, without correct-answer labels; one pass processes the question and all options together.
With 24 of Qwen3-8B’s 36 layers, FunDM reaches 75.0% mean accuracy across eight benchmarks versus 75.7% for the full model.
On MMLU-Pro, it provides 1.56–1.57× batched throughput and about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory.
Label-free agent heads select passing runs on 74.4–74.6 of 100 held-out tasks, outperforming a CLM-shaped action-trained head.
papers.selection_reason: Frozen-LLM decision heads reduce compute and memory while preserving accuracy, fitting efficient inference interests.
papers.title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: FunDM distills a frozen language model into a cheap, label-free decision head that nearly preserves accuracy while reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.
authors: Xuanlin Yang, Jia Li, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Targets the high memory cost of backpropagation and optimizer states in large-language-model fine-tuning.
Uses large-query zeroth-order estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace, then spectrally controls and maps updates back to the full parameter space.

Theoretical analysis reduces the effective estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$ when optimization-relevant directions are concentrated; projection error depends on the activation Gram matrix’s spectral tail.
Across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B downstream tasks, it improves over existing ZO baselines by up to 8.7% on average and 26.9% on individual tasks, while staying within 1.5% of FO-Adam on average.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient fine-tuning method using structured zeroth-order optimization, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLMs.
papers.title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: StructZO narrows the gap between memory-efficient zeroth-order and Adam fine-tuning by estimating updates in a compact, activation-informed subspace with spectral control.

papers.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].
authors: Zhixiong Zhao, Zukang Xu, Xing Hu, Lifeng Liu, Guangyu Sun, Dawei Yang
bullets: Addresses activation shifts, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation that undermine standard PTQ methods.
Uses Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization to learn a shared quantization-friendly representation while preserving parameter sharing.
Allocates activation precision through interaction-aware, loop-wise sensitivity modeling under a fixed bit budget.
Applies lightweight loop-conditioned task calibration to align quantized inference with low-bit recursive trajectories.
On Ouro-2.6B, W4A4 surpasses W4A8 baselines, cuts memory by 65.3%, and achieves 1.7× BF16 decoding speed with 3.4% storage overhead over naive INT4.
papers.selection_reason: Loop-aware quantization for efficient LLM inference; fits efficient AI and language models.
papers.title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopQuant enables accurate, efficient low-bit post-training quantization for recursively computed LoopLMs by modeling cross-loop dynamics and sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.
bullets: Targets efficient KV-cache compression for attention via approximate inner-product preservation.
Replaces dense Gaussian projections with compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms and Gaussian diagonals.
Gaussian dithering smooths quantization in the first construction; a random permutation regularizes measurement covariance in the second.
Both methods run in O(d log d) time.
Embedding dimensions are O(ε⁻² log²(d/δ)) for the first and O(ε⁻² log(d/δ)) for the second, with a restriction on m for the latter.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces structured quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms for KV cache compression, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
papers.tldr: Two fast structured constructions make 1-bit Quantized Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms computable in near-linear time while preserving theoretical embedding guarantees.

papers.abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
bullets: Mamba’s selective scan creates token-dependent activation ranges, making one layer-wise clipping range ineffective.
A lightweight pre-scan predictor assigns tokens to groups using offline-calibrated, group-wise clipping bounds—without runtime statistics or post-scan grouping.
Pseudo-labels come from clustering post-scan activation descriptors with similar clipping and rounding behavior.
Frequency-Preserving Refinement aligns teacher and quantized outputs in Fourier amplitude and phase to retain high-frequency details.
The method reportedly improves over prior PTQ baselines across settings, transfers beyond Mamba SR, and reaches 2.23× FP16 speed on Jetson Orin Nano.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-friendly activation quantization for efficient low-bit inference; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: Token-Group Quantization enables hardware-friendly low-bit post-training quantization for Mamba super-resolution by predicting token-specific clipping groups before scanning and preserving image frequencies during calibration.

papers.abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.
authors: Muntaser Syed (Florida Institute of Technology), Ameerah Alsulami (Florida Institute of Technology), Marius Silaghi (Florida Institute of Technology)
bullets: Targets incremental editing, branching/snapshotting, KV-cache prefix reuse, and repeated-segment encoding.
Stores a polynomial subtree hash over a Mersenne prime in every rope node to support content-identity checks.
Uses persistent structure sharing for logarithmic updates and queries across evolving contexts.
Validated through pre-registered, replicated experiments against Ropey, a PagedAttention copy-on-write table, and SGLang’s radix matcher.
Reported 369.7× advantage over Ropey at one million characters and 1.20× faster exact detection of a one-million-token shared prefix than the radix matcher in a live vLLM setup.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent data structure for LLM context and KV-cache management; directly relevant to efficient serving and long-context handling.
papers.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
papers.tldr: Hashrope unifies four LLM context-management mechanisms in one persistent, hash-augmented weight-balanced rope with logarithmic edits and verified identity queries.

papers.abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.
authors: Sejun Park, Haocheng Xia, Yongjoo Park
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning.
The Reader processes the full context, while the Reasoner receives only the question and generated sequence.
Combines Reader and Reasoner logits at each token to form a single next-token prediction; fine-tuning improves performance.
On HotpotQA, a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of full-context accuracy while using about one quarter of the KV memory.
At 45.7K-token contexts, throughput improves by up to 3.2×, with gains generalizing across three model families.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a memory-efficient inference method for LLM QA by fusing reader and reasoner logits, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: PAIR: Memory-Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
papers.tldr: PAIR combines a small full-context Reader with a larger context-free Reasoner to deliver near-full-context QA accuracy with substantially lower memory use and higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.
authors: Cameron Barker, Andreas Paraskeva, Jan N. van Rijn, Elliot J. Crowley, Henry Gouk
bullets: Existing pruning methods often optimize retained weight count without accounting for hardware-specific storage and processing costs.
HSP searches over dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head/channel pruning options.
A global solver selects one structure per projection by minimizing proxy pruning loss under a resource budget.
Evaluations on OPT and LLaMA models using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super show improved quality–resource frontiers over training-free baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-aware heterogeneous structured pruning reduces LLM memory and latency, fitting the efficient-AI theme of memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
papers.tldr: HSP enables hardware-aware, training-free pruning by assigning different sparsity structures and densities to each sublayer under latency and memory constraints.

papers.abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.
authors: Zhiwei Lin, Jiahao Liu, Yan Liu, Chengpeng Wang
bullets: Safety incompatibility varies with the sender–receiver model pair and cache-reuse configuration.
Reusing value tensors causes larger safety deviations than reusing key tensors.
VReparo learns offline per-layer, per-KV-head affine maps to align sender values with receiver-native values.
Across evaluated settings, VReparo lowers average HarmBench ASR from 57.28% to 39.21% and StrongREJECT from 0.4215 to 0.2163.
It retains an average 85.62% reduction in time to first token.
papers.selection_reason: Studies cross-model KV cache reuse and proposes a mitigation for safety incompatibility, relevant to KV-cache-based efficient inference.
papers.title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
papers.tldr: Cross-model KV-cache reuse can substantially alter safety behavior, but VReparo mitigates these deviations while preserving most of the latency benefit.

papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability.
