We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
authors: Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yilan Zhang, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Yimeng Chen, Liangyu Wang, Yifan Xu, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, Wenyi Wang, Yanning Dai, Yuhui Wang, J\"{u}rgen Schmidhuber
bullets: Linear attention’s fixed recurrent state must handle both computation and long-term storage, limiting context retention.
NoteBank archives selected text before queries are known, addresses it using native backbone features, and replays retrieved evidence through the model’s forward computation.
The training-free, plug-and-play method requires no external embedder, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader.
On one-million-token RULER retrieval tasks, Gated DeltaNet’s mean accuracy improves from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens.
The approach adds at most 0.025% analytical FLOPs and uses far less persistent storage than a Transformer KV cache; evaluations cover multiple recurrent backbones and long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse episodic memory and native replay expand long-context capability of linear attention, directly relevant to memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.tldr: NoteBank substantially extends linear-attention models’ long-context memory by sparsely storing and natively replaying past evidence without retraining or external retrieval components.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.
authors: Haotian Li, Liran Dong, Kaicheng Xiao, Guoliang Xing
bullets: Recurrent states are requantized after every update, causing coherent errors that accumulate over time.
Low-Rank Bypass (LRB) stores small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges them into the state.
Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR) rounds reversed state updates toward their intended direction without extra storage.
Evaluated across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, the method outperforms INT4, cuts state memory by up to 5.3×, and speeds decoding by up to 1.9× versus FP32 states.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes low-bit recurrent state quantization with update-preserving techniques, directly targeting memory and decoding efficiency for recurrent/linear-attention models.
papers.title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
papers.tldr: A training-free low-bit recurrent-state quantization method preserves small update directions, substantially improving INT4 state performance while reducing memory and accelerating decoding.

papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Targets on-device SLM agents whose accuracy–latency tradeoff changes as context grows.
Calibrates execution-time costs across precisions and context lengths, then combines them with tensor sensitivities to allocate precision under latency or accuracy budgets.
Accounts for the fact that lower-bit weights are not always faster by predicting latency from measured execution costs rather than weight size alone.
Adjusts weight precision as the KV cache grows or becomes quantized, with schedules prepared before execution and followed while preserving the session cache.
Laptop-GPU and tool-use experiments identify cases where context-aware scheduling helps, while showing that accuracy recovery remains limited.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware mixed-precision scheduling for on-device SLMs, directly targeting KV-cache and inference memory/latency efficiency.
papers.title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A context-aware mixed-precision scheduler adapts SLM weight precision to changing context lengths, balancing latency and accuracy while retaining the KV cache.

papers.abstract: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Serving speed depends on phase, batch size, context length, and the resource that becomes limiting.
The model predicts latency from a configuration and operating point using hardware- and stack-specific calibrated constants.
A dynamic-programming allocator combines modeled latency costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs.
The approach is evaluated across three hardware classes and compared with byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.
Scope: performance depends on calibration for the target model, GPU, and serving stack.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses mixed-precision LLM serving efficiency, including KV-cache access and memory/latency trade-offs.
papers.title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
papers.tldr: A calibrated cost model improves mixed-precision LLM serving by accounting for compute, weight loading, and KV-cache bottlenecks instead of relying on bit-width or memory alone.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host-to-device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per-layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3-30B-A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE-3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE-3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.
authors: Hongliang Cao, Xiuyu Li, Siqi Wang, Ziming Wang, Jingmin Zhu, Hailong Yang
bullets: Offloaded MoE inference makes host-to-device expert transfers a decoding bottleneck, so longer drafts are not always faster.
SpecFit predicts committed tokens from draft-path probabilities and cycle time from subtree size and the experts activated across layers.
It searches ancestor-closed draft subtrees using a monotone submodular expert-coverage cost and also determines when to stop drafting.
With Qwen3-30B-A3B, it decodes 21.6% faster on CNN/DailyMail and 7.0% faster on a GSM8K subset than EAGLE-3, using the same expert cache.
Scope: results are reported for the stated summarization and math benchmarks with an offloaded MoE model.
papers.selection_reason: Improves MoE inference efficiency via speculative decoding and expert offloading, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: SpecFit: Not All Draft Tokens Cost the Same in Offloaded MoE Inference
papers.tldr: SpecFit speeds up speculative decoding for offloaded MoE models by selecting draft subtrees that maximize throughput while accounting for expert-transfer costs.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Targets the difficulty of preserving generative performance under low-rank LLM compression.
Uses Generation-Aware Weight Whitening based on gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation.
Employs evolutionary search to optimize layer-wise rank allocation for a target global compression ratio.
Evaluated on Mistral-7B, Qwen3, and Llama-3.3 across multiple-choice and generative benchmarks.
Reports consistent gains over existing SVD-based baselines and scalability to models up to 70B parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank LLM compression reduces model memory and inference cost.
papers.title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
papers.tldr: GA-SVD improves one-shot SVD-based LLM compression by allocating ranks and whitening weights with generation quality in mind.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Structured pruning performance depends on the coordinate basis used for deletion.
The method selects a basis by minimizing local linear reconstruction loss caused by pruning.
Under positive-definite second moments, WUS jointly diagonalizes and balances activation and weight statistics, making deletion error spectrally separable.
A scalable implementation uses blockwise WUS transforms and compact input projections.
Experiments on 8B–72B Llama and Qwen models report consistent gains over pruning baselines across diverse benchmarks, with reduced latency and memory usage.
papers.selection_reason: Structured pruning of LLMs directly targets memory and inference efficiency.
papers.title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
papers.tldr: WUSPruner chooses an optimal pruning basis using activation and weight second moments, enabling principled structured pruning with improved quality and lower inference cost.

papers.abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.
authors: Sasho Nedelkoski, Alexander Acker, Soeren Becker, Dominik Scheinert, Odej Kao
bullets: Addresses the quality instability of 2-bit KV-cache quantization and the memory cost of using 3-bit keys.
Uses E8-lattice vector quantization for keys to exploit correlations across adjacent dimensions and improve quantization efficiency.
Applies table-based asymmetric attention scoring to avoid explicit codebook dequantization.
Across five LLM families, E8 k2v2 is about 20% smaller than scalar k3v2 and improves perplexity in 80% of evaluated settings.
Provides a structured, low-overhead primitive for improving the quality–memory trade-off in long-context inference.
papers.selection_reason: E8 lattice vector quantization for low-bit KV-cache compression in long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: E8 Lattice Key Quantization for Low-Bit KV-Cache Compression
papers.tldr: E8-lattice vector quantization enables 2-bit keys and values to compress LLM KV caches by about 6× while retaining near-baseline long-context quality and scalar-baseline decode throughput.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models enable streaming generation of long videos but suffer from significant memory overhead due to the rapidly growing KV cache. Existing KV cache quantization methods are primarily designed for LLMs and transfer poorly to video models, where activations exhibit different statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy. We observe that the video KV cache is largely predictable over time, with a clear asymmetry. Keys are highly predictable from their temporal history, while values depend primarily on the current key and need a short history of preceding values. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{\method}, a training-free predictive KV cache quantization framework for AR video generation. \method predicts keys and values according to their distinct dependencies and stores only the residuals at low precision. Both predictors are lightweight, calibrated once offline by linear regression on a small set of BF16 samples, and remain fixed across prompts and generation runs. Experiments on Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B show that \method consistently achieves higher generation quality than existing KV cache quantization methods at comparable or higher compression ratios, reaching up to $6.71\times$ KV cache compression with the best overall quality--efficiency tradeoff. Our code will be released on GitHub.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Weile Mo, Peiliang Cai, Jiacheng Liu, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Xiaobing Tu, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: AR video diffusion models face rapidly growing KV-cache memory overhead during long-video streaming generation.
Existing LLM-oriented KV quantization methods transfer poorly because video activations have distinct statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy.
TempoKV predicts keys from temporal history and values from the current key plus a short value history, then stores residuals at low precision.
Predictors are calibrated once offline with linear regression on a small BF16 sample set and remain fixed across prompts and runs.
Across Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B, it reports better quality than existing methods at comparable or higher compression, with up to 6.71× compression.
papers.selection_reason: Predictive KV cache quantization for autoregressive video generation directly targets memory efficiency in inference.
papers.title: TempoKV: Predictive KV Cache Quantization for Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: TempoKV uses lightweight, training-free predictors to compress autoregressive video-generation KV caches by quantizing only prediction residuals, achieving up to 6.71× compression while preserving generation quality.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. Even when this context is retained, cache reconstruction error alone does not capture how quantization errors affect subsequent attention. We present RECAP, a post-training quantization method that calibrates reasoning models on the history they read. Dynamic-prefix calibration separates long historical context from short-block reconstruction. It regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the active block to supervise every position along the trajectory. Prefix read geometry further supervises historical cache errors according to their effects on attention outputs, weighting key and value errors asymmetrically. With both components applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple reasoning models and quantization settings. Under W4A4KV4, RECAP improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 percentage points on MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 15.8 points on AIME-120 with Qwen3-4B. These results highlight the importance of preserving historical dependencies during calibration for low-bit reasoning.
authors: Chi Ruan, Yujie Chen, Zixiang Zhao, Jingcai Guo, Haotong Qin
bullets: Low-bit quantization can degrade long-chain reasoning as cache errors accumulate across thousands of historical tokens.
RECAP uses dynamic-prefix calibration to reconstruct long prefixes and supervise each position along the reasoning trajectory.
Prefix read geometry weights historical key and value errors by their effects on attention outputs.
Applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple models and quantization settings.
Under W4A4KV4, it improves accuracy by 13.3 points on MATH500 and 15.8 points on AIME-120 in the reported settings.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization method for reasoning models that calibrates on cached historical context, directly targeting KV cache error accumulation and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
papers.tldr: RECAP improves low-bit quantization of reasoning models by calibrating on the long histories their attention actually reads.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse is difficult because cached states depend on the prompt prefix, positions, and preceding documents.
SAFE-KV selects a repair start document using risk-guided K2 selection and re-encodes the causal suffix.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, recovery reached 99.8%/98.4% on HotpotQA-500/2Wiki-500 with donor-copy repair and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding.
Unrepaired composition degraded from exact behavior at four documents to substantially worse behavior at sixteen; document-only and fixed-window repairs were less effective.
Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, and in the reported single-request L40S study full prefill remained the operating choice.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache reuse and memory-efficient inference in RAG, fitting the KV cache and memory efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
papers.tldr: SAFE-KV repairs non-prefix KV-cache compositions by re-encoding a causal suffix, restoring behavior close to exact full-prefill generation.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-guided layer fusion compresses LLMs, reducing memory and improving inference throughput.
papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FCM compresses LLM depth by grouping functionally similar non-adjacent layers, achieving strong perplexity and efficiency improvements at up to 3× compression.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.
bullets: Quantization errors compound because the recurrent state is rewritten at every decoding step.
Tying the quantizer scale to a full-precision reference eliminates norm explosion but recovers only part of the lost performance, separating instability from resolution limits.
Outlier-aware quantization does not resolve the remaining degradation; persistent scaling performs better in the reported comparisons.
Learned bit allocation helps mainly by protecting the first few layers, and group-wise INT4 provides little value at 32K context.
Quantization claims should report the decode horizon over which a bit-width is validated.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent-state quantization for linear-attention and SSM LLMs directly targets memory-efficient long-decode inference.
papers.title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
papers.tldr: Recurrent-state INT4 quantization in linear-attention and SSM LLMs fails over long decoding because scale feedback causes instability, while preventing scale explosion does not fully restore functionality.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi-view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed-forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per-scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long-horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk-then-align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block-wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block-wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence-aware re-anchoring further mitigates long-range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re-initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state-of-the-art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT-2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point-cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.
authors: Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses GPU-memory and quadratic-attention limits in continuous multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Uses block-wise causal attention to retain local future context while scaling beyond full bidirectional attention.
Detects unreliable streaming states, re-initializes the KV cache, and stitches refreshed segments with SE(3) alignment to reduce drift and trajectory discontinuities.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo; on nuScenes, it improves AbsRel, point-cloud Accuracy, and ATE over DVGT-2.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming geometric foundation model for multi-view 3D reconstruction, with block-wise attention and KV cache re-anchoring for long-horizon driving.
papers.title: Drive3R: Block-wise Streaming Geometric Foundation Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: Drive3R enables scalable, drift-resistant 3D reconstruction for long-horizon autonomous-driving sequences through block-wise streaming attention and confidence-aware re-anchoring.

papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses the bandwidth, redundant-compute, and context limitations of text-only communication between agents.
Transfers KV caches across model families without requiring the receiver to prefill the communicated text.
Combined with KV-cache compaction, it reports 40% higher mean accuracy and 4× faster mean wall-clock time than text-to-text communication.
Evaluated across 17 benchmarks, 12 LLMs, and 6 model families.
Can transfer a sender VLM’s vision capabilities to a text-only receiver, while keeping both models frozen.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-family KV-cache transfer for prefill-free multi-agent LLM communication; directly targets KV-cache efficiency and LLM systems.
papers.title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
papers.tldr: SwaT enables fast, prefill-free KV-cache communication between different LLM families, outperforming text-based agent communication in accuracy and speed.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
bullets: Analyzes 600 coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models.
Median observations are small (118–286 tokens); large build logs are uncommon, appearing near the 99th percentile.
Prefix caching serves 98.6% of input tokens, making flat input pricing overestimate loop cost by about 7× on average.
Turn count explains 84% of variance in log trajectory cost, versus 4% for mean observation size.
Delegation raises cost in half of evaluated settings, and the study does not show that reducing turns preserves task success.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes coding agents and focuses on cache efficiency (prefix cache) and loop engineering, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLM agents.
papers.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: Coding-agent cost is driven far more by the number of turns than by typical observation size, especially when prefix caching is accounted for.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.
authors: Yujie Chen, Weiyan Zheng, Yiwu Yao, Tianchi Hu, Bo Wang, Jiyu Guo, Wenzhan Li, Jingcai Guo, Michele Magno, Haotong Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining predictive behavior when weights use only a few quantization levels.
Introduces Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC): randomized Hadamard mixing and a symmetric four-level quantizer with lookup-free sign-basis decoding.
Introduces Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC), which selects high-divergence calibration sequences and updates only quantization levels and scales while freezing pretrained weights.

Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen show effectiveness for weight-only and joint quantization; on LLaMA-2-7B, it reports 6.62 WikiText2 perplexity at W2A16 and improves W2A4KV4 perplexity from 8.31 to 6.96.
Reduces linear-layer weight memory by 8× versus FP16.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FidelityQ, a quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity while reducing model memory requirements, directly addressing memory efficiency.
papers.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
papers.tldr: FidelityQ enables accurate 2-bit language-model quantization by combining source-adaptive weight coding with targeted calibration that preserves teacher-like predictions.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
authors: Junjie Li, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
bullets: GDN prefill signals—write gate, decay, and write magnitude—anticipate future KV-entry utility before attention queries are available.
Lightweight per-head nonlinear predictors estimate utility without using attention scores.
The model’s native attention output gate determines the retention budget separately for each attention layer.
After one post-prefill scoring pass, discarded KV entries are physically released for serving.

At one-tenth of the KV cache, GateSight leads KVzip across all four model-benchmark pairs and is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three; scope covers Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next up to 262K tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes query-agnostic KV eviction for hybrid LLMs to reduce attention cache memory, directly targeting inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
papers.tldr: GateSight uses recurrent Gated DeltaNet signals to predict which attention KV-cache entries will matter, enabling query-agnostic cache eviction with substantially lower memory and little scoring overhead.

papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
authors: Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang, Kaicheng Yang, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation in sub-3-bit weight-only quantization, especially on real-world tasks.
Energy-Stratified Grouping mixes channels across energy tiers and uses activation-weighted fitting to protect sensitive channels.
Adaptive Bit Split assigns the fixed bit budget between direction and radius for each weight matrix based on reconstruction error.
Achieves state-of-the-art 2-bit quantization performance across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following, and tool-use benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, retains 95.3% of BF16 average benchmark score and reaches up to 2.55× non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16 with a custom CUDA kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Extreme low-bit weight quantization reduces LLM memory and deployment cost, fitting efficient AI and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
papers.tldr: SAGE improves the accuracy and deployment efficiency of 2-bit vector-quantized LLMs through energy-aware channel grouping and adaptive bit allocation.

papers.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
authors: Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao
bullets: Targets prefix-heavy workflows where multiple models share long contexts such as schemas, tools, histories, and intermediate results.
Combines partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads to enable accurate cross-model reuse.
Uses block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel to make attention-map reuse practical for long contexts.
Experiments report lower prefilling latency and better end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous models and multi-turn workloads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents cross-model attention map reuse for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
papers.tldr: MapFlow accelerates heterogeneous LLM serving by reusing transferable attention maps instead of model-specific KV states.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.
authors: Hao Wu, Tianyu Shao, Shengju Qian, Yizhou Zhao, Fan Zhang, Penghao Zhao, Weiyan Wang, Yufei Huang, Fan Xu, Kun Wang, Xin Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Yuxuan Liang
bullets: Full-context decoding can make persistent scene information, recent states, and stale generated history compete for attention.
ReCAP is a training-free context schedule that freezes the tokenizer, world model, and decoder.
It preserves temporal order and complete recent visual-action blocks while bounding active context growth independently of rollout length.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN, it improves visual fidelity, action consistency, and robot-structure preservation over Full Context.
On BridgeV2, LPIPS falls 63.3%; at H=64, logical KV footprint falls 73.3% and p50 latency falls 6.51%. The memory-conflict explanation remains confounded by context-length and positional effects.
papers.selection_reason: Context scheduling for long-horizon robot video world models; fits video world models and inference memory efficiency.
papers.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: ReCAP improves long-horizon robot video prediction by retaining the initial scene and recent visual-action context while evicting stale history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: In autoregressive video generation, retaining all historical key-value (KV) states increases memory usage and per-step attention costs as videos grow longer. A fixed cache budget bounds these costs but raises the challenge of preserving historical content that supports consistent, high-quality generation. Existing methods control cache size through history selection or consolidation, yet deciding what to retain and how to limit the loss of useful content remains a shared challenge. Our analysis shows that spatial queries depend on different historical content and that higher current attention coverage does not necessarily yield better long-video quality. We introduce FrameFold, a training-free KV cache consolidation method that compares the content retrieved by the same recent historical queries before and after merging to guide both representative construction and merge selection. Exploiting temporal redundancy between adjacent historical entries, FrameFold merges their KV states into shared representatives while retaining complete spatial grids. It fits value-merging coefficients in closed form by matching conditional attention responses, then selects the merge with the lowest remaining response distortion. Under matched KV cache budgets, experiments on Self Forcing and Causal Forcing at 30 and 60 seconds and on LongLive at 120 seconds demonstrate improved consistency and visual quality. Continuous eight-minute Self Forcing rollouts further show less quality degradation than the baselines.
authors: Muyu Liu, Mingming Liu, Hong Gu, Yuyao Zhang, Qin Lu
bullets: Fixed-size KV caches reduce memory and attention costs but risk discarding content needed for temporal consistency.
FrameFold uses recent historical queries to compare attention responses before and after candidate merges.
It merges temporally redundant adjacent KV entries into shared representatives while preserving complete spatial grids.
Value-merging coefficients are solved in closed form, and merges are selected to minimize response distortion.
Experiments across 30-second to eight-minute rollouts show better consistency, visual quality, and slower degradation than baselines under matched cache budgets.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache consolidation for autoregressive video generation.
papers.title: FrameFold: Response-Guided KV Cache Consolidation for Autoregressive Long Video Generation
papers.tldr: FrameFold is a training-free method that consolidates historical KV caches for long video generation while preserving attention responses and improving long-horizon quality under fixed memory budgets.

papers.abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.
authors: S M Mahbub Murshed, Hayden Bright, Rezaul Karim, Ali Shiri Sichani
bullets: Audits KV-cache compression on an 8.39M-parameter, 33.6 MB decoder-only LM with end-to-end edge measurements.
Finds polar-guided key-cache quantization performs poorly; RTN causes roughly an order of magnitude less damage.
Finds consistency-anchored progressive pruning is no better than one-shot magnitude pruning.
Introduces Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF), which uses teacher-forced, token-level log-losses and distinguishes compression backends missed by perplexity.
On a Raspberry Pi 5, tested compression backends use more energy per token than uncompressed FP16; KIVI is close to lossless by LCDF.
papers.selection_reason: Audits KV-cache compression methods for edge deployment, introducing a new evaluation metric (LCDF) to assess fidelity.
papers.title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
papers.tldr: EdgeLLM-Nano finds that several KV-cache compression methods underperform on-device, while LCDF reveals quality losses that perplexity misses.

papers.abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
authors: Sihwan Park, Sung-Yub Kim, Doohyuk Jang, Eunho Yang
bullets: Asynchronous rollouts increase KV-cache workload per decode step, making KV quantization especially impactful.
KV4-RL uses calibration-free INT4 KV quantization and protects attention sinks plus recent context in INT8.
The selective protection reduces sampler mismatch and mitigates learning degradation from fully INT4 rollouts.
Across 400 GRPO iterations, it achieves 1.80× cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27× full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout.
Final accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training on six benchmarks for Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
papers.selection_reason: INT4 KV cache quantization for faster asynchronous RLVR rollouts, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
papers.tldr: KV4-RL accelerates asynchronous RLVR rollouts with INT4 KV-cache quantization while preserving nearly BF16-level training accuracy through selective INT8 protection.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
authors: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du
bullets: Addresses memory challenges from the large parameter footprint of MoE models.
Jointly optimizes prune-and-merge assignments with global Integer Linear Programming rather than separate greedy decisions.
Uses expert-usage frequency in a surrogate objective to favor frequently used experts as merge representatives and improve routing stability.
Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B show strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks.
Serving benchmarks with vLLM quantify memory and throughput benefits after compression.
papers.selection_reason: MoE LLM compression via expert pruning and merging for memory and throughput, relevant to efficient AI and large language models.
papers.title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
papers.tldr: PRIME unifies frequency-aware expert pruning and merging for MoE compression, preserving accuracy while reducing deployment costs.

papers.abstract: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a naming of an input and output layout and a copy or reduction operation. In the middle, we introduce a shared orchestration protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives coordination from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.
bullets: Existing collective systems tightly couple what data moves, when and where it moves, and how movement is implemented, limiting customization and hardware adoption.
Purlin specifies collectives through input/output layouts and copy or reduction operations.
Its SNAC protocol provides reusable orchestration, while the Atom layer implements hardware-specific copy and reduce primitives.
Evaluated on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs across seven collectives, Purlin achieves up to 5.14× lower latency and 4.50× higher bandwidth than baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves LLM serving throughput and interactivity and reduces diffusion-generation latency, with gains varying by workload and load.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes GPU collective communication for distributed LLM inference by separating orchestration from the datapath, significantly reducing latency and improving throughput.
papers.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
papers.tldr: Purlin improves GPU collective communication by separating collective semantics, orchestration, and hardware-specific data movement, delivering substantial gains across GPUs and inference workloads.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models maintain fixed-size recurrent states, but existing quantizers typically use eight bits or more. Quantization errors persist according to channel decay rates. We derive distortion weights from the observability Gramian and combine them with normalized state ranges for mixed-precision bit allocation, without calibration data, rotation, or training. We also quantize decay rates logarithmically. With per-token state quantization, a four-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3--27.9 relative to the best of seven baselines across three hybrid models; metadata costs vary. At six bits, negative log-likelihood differs from the FP32-state baseline by less than 0.005 nats. Ablations separate gains from variable bit widths, decay weighting, and range normalization. With less frequent write-backs, gains diminish and depend on the model and budget.
bullets: Existing recurrent-state quantizers generally use at least eight bits, while persistent errors depend on channel decay rates.
The method allocates bits using observability-Gramian distortion weights and normalized state ranges, and logarithmically quantizes decay rates.
It requires no calibration data, rotations, or retraining, and supports per-token state quantization.
Across three hybrid models, four-bit mean payloads reduce excess negative log-likelihood by 3.3–27.9× versus seven baselines; metadata costs vary.
At six bits, negative log-likelihood is within 0.005 nats of the FP32-state baseline; benefits diminish with less frequent write-backs and depend on model and budget.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization of recurrent states in hybrid language models reduces memory footprint; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Low-Bit Recurrent States in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: A calibration-free mixed-precision quantizer enables accurate low-bit recurrent states in hybrid language models, with four-bit states substantially reducing quantization error and six-bit states nearly matching FP32 performance.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
authors: Ze-Wei Liou, Harris Nover, Amey Naik, Andrii Skliar, Igor Shovkun, Ido Shahaf, Tri Dao
bullets: SSM state I/O can bottleneck decoding because each step reads and writes a fixed-size recurrent state.
ReplaySSM represents state with a periodic checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, avoiding most state writes and roughly halving dominant state-memory traffic.
Input buffering makes speculative rollback a pointer operation and supports output-only verification without materializing intermediate states.
Separate low-precision output and high-precision update checkpoints prevent rounding errors from propagating through recurrent updates.
In vLLM implementations for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, standard decoding reaches 1.20–1.47× speedup, while speculative decoding reaches about 1.8× throughput on two 120B-class models.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces state memory traffic and improves inference throughput for SSM-based hybrid models, directly targeting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
papers.tldr: ReplaySSM accelerates hybrid SSM decoding by caching recent inputs instead of updating recurrent state every step, while enabling cheap speculative rollback and safer state quantization.

papers.abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.
bullets: Addresses KV-memory exhaustion and fixed cache budgets in long-context serving, including compatibility with DSpark and DFlash2.
Protects the required working set, uses spare GPU memory for extra history, and exactly retrieves missing entries from host memory under pressure.
Reuses speculative-decoding mechanisms such as shared missing-row retrieval, window-bounded draft-KV caching, and verification staging across layers.

At 100K context and concurrency 128, achieves 793 output tokens/s per GPU with GLM-5.3 and DFlash2; the abstract reports higher throughput and concurrency than HiSparse and non-speculative adaptive serving.
At low load, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows, while memory is released as load increases.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes load-adaptive hierarchical KV cache management with speculative decoding for long-context LLM serving, directly fitting efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
papers.tldr: Adaptive DHiSparse combines load-adaptive hierarchical sparse KV caching with speculative decoding to improve long-context serving throughput while preserving latency bounds.

papers.abstract: Speech recognition on low-cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present O\'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). O\'ido executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other the on-device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two-core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1-11.1 s after clips of 3.6-10.6 s (7.2-22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34-60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.
authors: Daniel Varela S\'anchez, Guillermo Mart\'in-Coello Ju\'arez
bullets: Addresses the limitations of low-cost microcontrollers, which typically support only keyword spotting or fixed commands.
Runs a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model using int8 quantization, SIMD-optimized attention, and flash/PSRAM-aware scheduling.
Achieves 3.70%/8.23% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other, with improved results from language-model and transducer variants.
On a physical board, runs at 1.97× audio duration on one core; streaming provides partial transcripts but still has multi-second latency.
Code and models are released; the two-core schedule is disabled because it produces incorrect results on silicon.
papers.selection_reason: On-device ASR with int8/int4 memory-efficient inference; fits efficient AI.
papers.title: O\'ido: Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator
papers.tldr: O’ido brings open-vocabulary English speech recognition to a $5 ESP32-S3 microcontroller without a neural accelerator, achieving strong accuracy but not yet real-time performance.

papers.abstract: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution.
