Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.
authors: Yuhang He, Hongyu Ge, Zihan Lin, Siyi Liu, Yongqi Zhang
bullets: Direct sparse sampling can bias group-relative policy updates because each response’s advantage depends on other group members’ rewards.
S$^3$R uses the same policy for sparse drafting and full-attention verification, avoiding a separately trained drafter.
A KV-aware scheduler reduces repeated KV-cache offloading and restoration while preserving rollout parallelism.
Aggressive sparse drafting remained stable in training, unlike direct sparse sampling with training-side correction.
On long-context mathematical reasoning, it reports 1.35–1.39× end-to-end training throughput with comparable task performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R) to reduce KV-cache traffic in RL rollouts using sparse attention and verification. A strong technical contribution to Efficient AI.
papers.title: S$^3$R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: S$^3$R accelerates long-context RLVR rollouts by using sparse attention for proposals and exact full-attention speculative verification, preserving dense-policy response distributions and training quality.

papers.abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.
authors: Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, Jun Deguchi
bullets: Addresses the inability of exact-prefix caching to reuse repeated documents across varying prompts and metadata.
Provides an open-source, vLLM-based testbed with segment scheduling, prompt construction, cache management, workload generation, and monitoring.
Naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document QA and summarization.
At 30 GB cache capacity, token-level hit rate reaches 63.9% versus 3.3% for prefix caching under a Zipfian RAG workload, with lower TTFT.
Cross-document reasoning remains a clear limitation; source code is Apache-2.0 licensed.
papers.selection_reason: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse for efficient serving.
papers.title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
papers.tldr: KV-Repurpose evaluates segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prompt prefixes, substantially improving cache hits and reducing time to first token in RAG-style workloads while revealing cross-document reasoning limitations.

papers.abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.
authors: Bahareh Nikpour, Hossein Rajabzadeh, Maryam Dialameh, Vahid Partovi Nia, Parsa Omidi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth with sequence length, batch size, and model depth.
Represents key/value activations as sums of Kronecker products, strictly generalizing Tensor Product Attention.
Introduces a matched structured rotary embedding that preserves RoPE’s relative-position property without a separate positional branch.
Matches or exceeds several attention baselines across four model scales and nine benchmarks, with up to 10× KV-cache compression.
A tunable Kronecker head split controls the compression–accuracy trade-off without architectural changes.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression via structured Kronecker factorization, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Kronecker Product Attention: Memory-Efficient KV Compression via Structured Factorization
papers.tldr: Kronecker Product Attention compresses autoregressive KV caches by factorizing keys and values into compact, token-dependent Kronecker factors while preserving positional information and attention expressivity.

papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Euijin Hong, Sheng Cao, Zechun Liu, Shuowei Jin, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Zhenyu Shi, Priyanka Nigam, Beidi Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and data demands of pretraining sparse architectures, especially limitations of MoE upcycling.
Retains pretrained FFN up-projections and adds STEM-based token-indexed embeddings as complementary residual information.
Performance improves with static memory capacity and transfers to both 1B and 7B OLMo-2 backbones.
Outperforms dense continued training and static sparse baselines across coding, math, and question-answering benchmarks.
Compared with an MoE upcycling baseline, achieves higher average performance while decoding 2× faster and using less GPU memory; throughput stays close to dense training and generation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Static sparse memory upcycling improves LLM capacity and inference efficiency.
papers.title: STAPLE: Static Sparse Upcycling of Pretrained Checkpoints via Embedding Modules
papers.tldr: STAPLE efficiently expands pretrained LLMs by adding token-indexed static sparse embeddings as a residual pathway, improving task performance with minimal training and decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
authors: Faisal Ladhak, Shantanu Acharya, Santiago Akle Serano, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg, Krishna C Puvvada
bullets: Addresses the one-loop accuracy tax that often makes recurrent models unattractive under latency constraints.
Uses gated state updates with learned step sizes, mixed loop counts during training, and loop-index/budget conditioning.
Late mixed-depth training can reduce added training cost; reusing MoE expert routes cuts update time by 11.7% without measurable accuracy loss.
Retaining only the final loop’s attention KV cache keeps KV memory at the one-loop level while preserving most multi-loop gains.

On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE models, four loops improve ten-task averages by 7.25 and 4.75 points, respectively; the post-trained Koi-4B reaches estimated Intelligence Index scores of 18 at one loop and 29 at four.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic latent recurrence for looped LLMs with one-loop tax removal and KV-cache memory savings; strong architectural and efficiency contribution.
papers.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
papers.tldr: Elastic Latent Recurrence trains one language-model checkpoint to match non-recurrent accuracy at one loop while gaining accuracy as additional loops increase inference compute.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. However, when later frames attend to the compressed history, small reconstruction errors can compound as the video grows. Beyond the within-layer similarity exploited by clustering, we find strong dependencies across cache layers in video models. This motivates Coral-KV - Calibrated Offline, Residual-coded, and Adapted Locally - a KV-cache compression framework that uses cache states in each layer to predict keys and values in subsequent layers, then quantizes the remaining prediction residuals. We construct compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank (block-DPLR) predictors: block-diagonal components model channel relationships within each attention head, while a global low-rank term models dependencies between heads. Coral-KV exposes a flexible fidelity-memory trade-off: it can reuse its predictors across videos or refit lightweight block-diagonal predictors to the current video for higher fidelity. Across extensive evaluations on both HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1, our reusable configuration improves PSNR over QVG-4 by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB, respectively, while using 48% and 37% less cache memory. Against QVG-Pro, our video-adapted configuration improves MAGI-1 PSNR by 3.77 dB while using 33.7% less cache memory. Coral-KV also maintains higher reconstruction fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities while retaining comparable generation latency.
authors: Albert Ge, Akash Haridas, Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Ian Colbert, Frederic Sala, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and error accumulation in long video diffusion generation.
Uses block-diagonal-plus-low-rank predictors to capture within-head channel and across-head dependencies.
Supports reusable predictors for efficiency or lightweight video-specific refitting for higher fidelity.
Improves PSNR while reducing cache memory versus QVG-4 and QVG-Pro across HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1.
Maintains fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities with comparable latency.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache compression for autoregressive video diffusion models; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference and video generation.
papers.title: CORAL-KV: Compact Cross-Layer Prediction and Residual Coding for Autoregressive Video KV Caches
papers.tldr: Coral-KV compresses autoregressive video KV caches by predicting later-layer states from earlier layers and quantizing only the residuals, reducing memory while preserving video quality.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) can clone a voice from seconds of audio. Yet the quality comes from billion-parameter diffusion transformers whose size and multi-step sampling put them out of reach of the on-device, assistive, and real-time applications that need them most. Post-training quantization (PTQ) shrinks such models without retraining, but it has been built for language and vision, not speech. At 4 bits, a strong quantizer leaves intelligibility close to full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre, so error rates stay low while the voice drifts from the target speaker. We ask why quantization hurts speech, where the damage lives, and whether it can be repaired without retraining. To find out, we run the first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B. The timbre cost comes from both the weight and the activation quantization, but only the activation part has the timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. We therefore introduce TTS-Q, which selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that assigns higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations. TTS-Q recovers timbre best at both scales, at no cost to intelligibility. Separately, the deployed calibrated-W4A4 reference reduces peak memory on GPU, providing a practical reference for resource-constrained TTS deployment.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Weilun Feng, Yi-Cheng Lin, Kai Li, Xianglong Wang, Kuo Yang, Chuanguang Yang, Yingli Tian, Wei Li, Zhongwei Cheng, Lin Chen
bullets: Targets the memory and latency barriers of billion-parameter, multi-step zero-shot TTS models for on-device and real-time use.
A W4A4 study at 1B and 3.5B shows that quantization damages timbre through both weights and activations, while intelligibility remains relatively robust.
Only activation quantization has timestep-dependent structure that can be addressed with a precision schedule.
TTS-Q uses task-matched calibration candidates and budget-balanced mixed precision, assigning higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations.
It achieves the best timbre recovery at both model scales without reducing intelligibility; the calibrated-W4A4 reference also lowers peak GPU memory.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient AI by proposing a post-training quantization method for large diffusion transformers, reducing model memory requirements and compute.
papers.title: TTS-Q: Perception-Guided Post-Training Quantization of Text-to-Speech Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: TTS-Q improves 4-bit post-training quantization of TTS diffusion transformers by preserving speaker timbre without sacrificing intelligibility.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve remarkable performance in video synthesis, but their iterative denoising process suffers from high inference latency. To address this, caching has emerged as an effective acceleration strategy by capitalizing on inter-step redundancy during denoising. Existing dynamic caching methods typically estimate the error that cache reuse would introduce at each denoising step (step error) to guide cache decisions, whereas our concern is how much quality loss cache reuse would cause in the final generated video (terminal error). We show that step error does not directly correspond to terminal error and that latent information helps capture their relationship, thereby informing cache decisions. Moreover, existing threshold-based methods cannot provide precise speedup control, making it difficult to meet practical requirements for user-specified acceleration targets. To address these limitations, we introduce MORCA, a cache scheduling framework trained through offline-to-online reinforcement learning to make latent-aware reuse/recompute decisions under user-specified acceleration targets. Extensive experiments on different video generation models across multiple target acceleration ratios demonstrate that MORCA achieves better generation fidelity than state-of-the-art caching methods under comparable computational budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/x10ngyx/MORCA.
bullets: Existing caching methods optimize per-step error, which does not reliably reflect final video quality loss.
MORCA learns the relationship between latent information, cache decisions, and terminal generation error.
Its policy makes reuse-versus-recompute decisions under explicit acceleration targets, offering finer speedup control than threshold-based methods.
Experiments across multiple video generation models and acceleration ratios show better fidelity than prior caching methods at comparable computational budgets.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based cache reuse to accelerate video diffusion; fits efficient inference and video diffusion.
papers.title: MORCA: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Cache Reuse in Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: MORCA uses latent-aware offline-to-online reinforcement learning to adaptively schedule cache reuse in video diffusion, improving fidelity while meeting user-specified acceleration targets.

papers.abstract: Mid-prefill pruning can reduce the sequence processed by deeper transformer layers, but attention concentration alone does not certify that discarded context is dispensable. We formulate EntroPrefill as a Renyi-guided proposal mechanism coupled to explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. Sink-isolated, regularized head pooling respects grouped-query attention while exposing a quantitative trade-off between specialization and worst-head coverage. We derive a mixture-to-head deletion envelope, a computable upper bound on feasible token removal, and a finite-sample observer guarantee that remains valid when the pruning layer is selected adaptively. We then establish a conditional transformer perturbation bound with explicit sufficient Lipschitz constants and a first-token decision-margin corollary. A counterexample shows why shallow observations alone cannot imply an unconditional future-output guarantee. The systems analysis distinguishes query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload, and gives an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. This manuscript is theoretical in scope: it defines the procedure, its assumptions, and its formal limits, but does not report measured acceleration or task-accuracy preservation. Experiments are reserved for subsequent validation of the assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs.
bullets: Addresses the lack of formal guarantees that low-attention context tokens are safely dispensable.
Uses Rényi-guided proposals, sink-isolated regularized head pooling, and constraints on discarded attention mass.
Derives deletion bounds, adaptive finite-sample observer guarantees, and conditional transformer perturbation and decision-margin bounds.
Separates attention-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payloads, yielding an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning.
Theoretical only: no measured speedup or task-accuracy results are reported, and guarantees depend on stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Context pruning with guarantees for RAG; directly fits token pruning and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: EntroPrefill: Renyi-Guided Context Pruning with Conditional Stability Guarantees for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: EntroPrefill provides a theoretically bounded method for pruning RAG context during prefill while clarifying when output stability and systems-level savings can—and cannot—be guaranteed.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models through bidirectional diffusion-based token generation. However, their growing model sizes and high inference costs make efficient deployment challenging: full-sequence denoising repeatedly invokes compute-intensive forward passes, while block-diffusion models additionally introduce a memory-intensive KV-cache. Low-bit weight-activation quantization is therefore attractive, yet existing dLLM post-training quantization methods rely on calibration data despite activation distributions shifting across masking states and denoising steps. We present SoloQ, a calibration-free quantization framework that maps weights and activations into a normalized rotated basis with a predictable marginal distribution, enabling data-independent quantization. SoloQ combines a structured K-RPBH rotation with a lightweight rescaling correction for calibration-free quantization. Its predictable post-rotation distribution supports both distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4. For block-diffusion models, SoloQ further applies commit-time KV-cache quantization to compress persistent states without perturbing the actively denoised block. Across full-sequence dLLMs (LLaDA and Dream) and block-diffusion dLLMs(Fast-dLLM v2 and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion), SoloQ retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and outperforms calibration-based baselines on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks. With NVFP4, SoloQ reduces peak memory by up to 2.61X and accelerates end-to-end inference by up to 2.24X.
bullets: Addresses the high compute and memory costs of repeated denoising and KV-caches in diffusion language models.
Normalizes a rotated weight-activation basis using structured K-RPBH rotation and lightweight rescaling, avoiding calibration data.
Supports distribution-matched codebooks and hardware-native NVFP4 quantization.
Adds commit-time KV-cache quantization for block-diffusion models without perturbing the actively denoised block.
Across four dLLM families, retains accuracy under 4-bit quantization and achieves up to 2.61× lower peak memory and 2.24× faster inference with NVFP4.
papers.selection_reason: Calibration-free quantization for diffusion LLMs with KV-cache compression and inference memory/latency reduction, fitting efficient AI and KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: SoloQ: Calibration-Free Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: SoloQ enables calibration-free 4-bit quantization for diffusion language models, preserving accuracy while substantially reducing memory use and inference time.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on KV caching to reduce repeated prefill computation in long context and interactive applications. As lightweight adapters evolve, cached states reflect earlier versions, so stale reuse distorts current model outputs, while complete affected suffix recomputation restores fidelity at substantial cost. We seek minimal recomputation that recovers current adapter behavior. Existing systems track token, context, or stable adapter identity, but neither represent caches from earlier adapter versions nor distinguish update propagation from the recomputation required for behavioral recovery. To address these gaps, we introduce CacheReforge, which represents stale KV caches as layerwise mixed-version objects. It combines per-layer adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, accumulated drift, and executable restart boundaries to select direct reuse, bounded recomputation, or complete affected-suffix recovery. We distinguish dependency depth from the functional recomputation horizon and use cumulative tail influence to characterize when bounded recovery preserves current-model behavior. We evaluate CacheReforge on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B with continual LoRA updates, including 16K HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA workloads. CacheReforge reduces mean KL divergence by 92.4% relative to stale reuse, while recomputing only 5.44% of layers and reducing cache-maintenance time by 93.2% relative to fresh full prefill. These results show that version-aware recovery preserves model fidelity and most KV caching gains.
bullets: Represents stale caches as layerwise mixed-version objects rather than assuming a single stable adapter version.
Uses adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, accumulated drift, and restart boundaries to choose reuse, bounded recomputation, or full suffix recovery.
Separates dependency depth from the functional recomputation horizon and uses cumulative tail influence to assess recovery fidelity.
On Qwen2.5 models with continual LoRA updates, it reduces mean KL divergence by 92.4% versus stale reuse while recomputing 5.44% of layers.
Reduces cache-maintenance time by 93.2% versus fresh full prefill, preserving most KV-caching benefits.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded recovery of stale KV caches under evolving adapters for efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: CacheReforge: Bounded Recovery for Stale KV Caches under Evolving Adapters
papers.tldr: CacheReforge restores current-model behavior from stale KV caches under evolving LoRA adapters while recomputing only a small portion of affected layers.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process long contexts, including long documents and lengthy conversations, but face token-level memory usage that increases proportionally to input length. Although model optimization and lossy prompt compression are widely used, these methods still fail to solve the long-context recall problem beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows. This paper proposes a long-context recall method that maintains near-constant GPU memory usage as context length increases, without additional training. The main idea is to reconstruct facts using parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors representing facts from the source document. Utilizing residual vectors allows the LLM to deterministically reconstruct query relevant facts without referencing the original document, preserving high fidelity and reducing memory usage without fine-tuning weights. Experimental results show that the proposed method enables answering single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where previous methods fail.
bullets: Targets long-context recall while avoiding memory growth proportional to input length.
Stores source-document facts in residual vectors from the LLM’s feed-forward layers.
Reconstructs query-relevant facts deterministically without rereading the original context or fine-tuning weights.
Answers single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts, where prior methods fail.
Scope: demonstrated for single-fact question answering in long story contexts.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context recall via residual vectors with near-constant memory; fits long-context and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Residual Vector-based Reconstruction as Long-Context Recall Regardless of Context Window Size
papers.tldr: A training-free method uses feed-forward residual vectors to recall facts from contexts far beyond standard context-window limits with near-constant GPU memory.

papers.abstract: While caching key-value (KV) states accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) decoding, this cache can dominate memory usage at long context lengths. One solution is to compress this memory by exploiting inter-layer cache similarities. However, most existing techniques necessitate architectural changes to LLMs and incur substantial overhead. In this work, we propose a symmetry-aware value cache merging strategy that reduces cache memory while avoiding both harmful performance degradation and architectural overhead during decoding. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be exploited alongside existing cache compression techniques, composing with high-ratio quantization or key cache pruning to reach compression ratios that neither method reaches alone, with minimal additional cost. Ultimately, our findings reveal a major source of underutilized capacity in the value cache, offering a simple yet highly effective direction for scaling context windows under memory constraints.
authors: Neha Verma, Sungwon Kim, Kenton Murray, Kevin Duh
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory growth at long context lengths, especially underused capacity in value caches.
Uses a symmetry-aware cross-layer value-cache merging strategy during decoding.
Designed to avoid harmful performance degradation and substantial architectural modifications.
Composes with high-ratio quantization and key-cache pruning for additional compression.
Supports scaling context windows under memory constraints with minimal extra cost.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes symmetry-aware cross-layer value cache compression to reduce memory usage in LLMs, directly targeting KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression
papers.tldr: VFold compresses LLM value caches by merging symmetry-aware representations across layers, reducing memory use without architectural changes or major decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: The memory-bound nature of the decoding stage of large language model (LLM) inference incurs significant latency. Layer-wise training-free network pruning approaches guided by the Hessian have been a prominent solution to this problem, as pruning reduces the number of nonzero parameters read from memory during decoding. Nevertheless, typical methods in this line compute the Hessian using pre-collected natural sequences, whereas the model is fed self-generated tokens during decoding, creating a distribution shift between the two sequences. The Hessian calculated on the natural sequence is different from that calculated on the generated sequence. We observe that this discrepancy causes the activation distribution during generation to deviate from that used for pruning, further hurting the pruned model performance. Moreover, most existing LLM pruning methods that bring actual speedup primarily target the sparse matrix-matrix (SpMM) multiplication, providing limited support for the sparse matrix-vector (SpMV) operations, which dominate decoding. To solve these problems, we introduce SparseDecoding, a principled decoding-aware pruning framework tailored for accurate and efficient LLM decoding. Specifically, at the algorithmic axis, SparseDecoding constructs calibration matrices from layer-wise activations collected during the dense-model autoregressive generation, excluding prefill, thereby aligning the pruning objective with the decoding activations. At the system axis, we develop an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel with bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal. Substantial empirical results on representative LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-14B / 32B) demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on the long-form generation benchmarks while achieving up to 1.48x end-to-end wall-clock decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
authors: Qitong Wang, Xinwei Niu, Mingluo Su, Shanwei Zhao, Shiai Zhu, Huan Wang
bullets: Addresses distribution shift between natural-text calibration and autoregressive decoding, which can degrade pruned-model quality.
Collects layer-wise activations during dense-model generation, excluding the prefill stage, to make pruning decoding-aware.
Introduces an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel using bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal.
Outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on long-form generation benchmarks across several representative LLMs.
Achieves up to 1.48× end-to-end decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces decoding-aware pruning for LLM inference to improve efficiency and accuracy.
papers.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
papers.tldr: SparseDecoding improves LLM decoding accuracy and efficiency by calibrating pruning on generated-token activations and accelerating sparse matrix-vector operations.

papers.abstract: Many key-value (KV) caches are compressed before anyone knows what will be asked of them: a document cached for retrieval, a prompt prefix shared across requests, the memory of a long conversation. The prevailing approach scores KV entries by rehearsal: the model rereads the context and keeps the entries it attends to, assuming that the more completely a cache rehearses its context, the better it remembers it. We show that under tight budgets this assumption backfires: rehearse everything, remember nothing. At a 3% keep ratio, rereading the whole context keeps 31.5 of 96.5 points on RULER, and on LongBench's natural-text tasks it falls below methods that rehearse nothing at all. The cause is that a cache keeps what it rehearses: rereading spreads the budget across the whole context, so the answer's own entries survive at little more than chance. Like a student before an exam, a cache remembers more by testing itself than by rereading. Two principles follow: rehearse what will be read, and rehearse as much as there is. We instantiate them as Attic-KV (Attic for short), a training-free rehearsal in which the model quizzes itself with question-answer pairs that quote the context, alongside anchor tokens in a content-adaptive amount. Changing only the rehearsal lifts three hosts that score it in three different ways: Attic alone is the best training-free method in all eight settings we test on RULER and LongBench's natural-text tasks, and plugged into the gradient-based KVgrad and the trained RestoreKV+, it raises them by up to 17.1 and 28.1 points. Its advantage grows as the budget shrinks, reaching 41.9 points over full rereading at a 3% keep ratio, and it compresses faster than rereading the whole context.
bullets: Full-context rereading spreads a tiny cache budget too broadly, causing important answer-related entries to be lost.
Attic-KV uses context-quoting question–answer pairs plus content-adaptive anchor tokens for training-free rehearsal.
Its benefit increases as the keep budget shrinks, including a reported 41.9-point gain over full rereading at a 3% keep ratio.
Attic is reported as the best training-free method across eight RULER and LongBench natural-text settings.
Adding Attic’s rehearsal to KVgrad and RestoreKV+ improves them by up to 17.1 and 28.1 points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV cache compression method for LLM long-context tasks, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference and long-context processing.
papers.title: Rehearse Everything, Remember Nothing: Attic-KV Rehearses What Will Be Read
papers.tldr: Attic-KV improves ultra-low-budget KV-cache compression by rehearsing likely future reads with self-generated question–answer probes instead of rereading the entire context.

papers.abstract: Tabular in-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a training-free and accurate paradigm for tabular prediction, but current approaches to compressing its in-context examples face an accuracy-throughput tradeoff: fixed subsets can sacrifice accuracy, while query-specific retrieval limits cache reuse and batching across queries, reducing throughput. We propose QCOC (Query-Calibrated Operator Compression), which exploits the exchangeability and repeated use of in-context examples by compiling their full KV cache once into compact memory shared across subsequent queries. Instead of retaining raw examples, QCOC clusters their states into joint-KV prototypes, preserves per-cluster multiplicities and the original example count, and calibrates prototype values against attention query vectors produced by the in-context examples through an anchored closed-form solution. Prototype compression drives the speedup, while value fitting helps preserve accuracy. On 64 held-out OpenML-CC18 datasets, QCOC achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared compression and retrieval methods at both retained counts. Across 12 configurations on seven long tables, it ranks first among compressed methods in ten and averages 0.23 percentage points below full context. Compressing 8,192 in-context examples to 512 memory slots yields a 10.5x cache compression ratio; excluding one-time compilation, in a single-core CPU online-serving comparison over 1,000 queries, QCOC is up to 508x faster than dynamic retrieval baselines and 1.98x faster than full-context inference. These results show that QCOC enables compact-memory reuse and efficient inference across queries while retaining accuracy close to full context.
authors: Xu Zhao, Jiaming Zhao, Bin Zhao, Yong Yang
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–throughput tradeoff between fixed example subsets and query-specific retrieval in tabular ICL.
Clusters example states into joint-KV prototypes while preserving cluster multiplicities and the original example count.
Fits prototype values to attention queries using an anchored closed-form calibration.
Across the reported benchmarks, QCOC has the strongest average accuracy among compared compression methods and stays 0.23 percentage points below full context on long tables.
Compressing 8,192 examples to 512 slots gives 10.5× cache compression and up to 508× faster serving than dynamic retrieval, excluding compilation time.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache compression for tabular in-context learning; directly fits memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Compile the Table: Query-Calibrated Operator Compression for Tabular In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: QCOC compiles tabular ICL examples into query-calibrated prototype memory, substantially improving inference throughput while preserving accuracy close to full context.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion enables causal video streaming without a bidirectional pass over the full clip, but existing few-step systems usually retain only the opening and most recent frames in a fixed-size KV cache. Once an event leaves this window, later frames can no longer attend to it, a failure we term mid-horizon forgetting. We present Memory Forcing, a few-step streaming method that preserves this missing history without increasing the cache size. Its Archive \& Working Banks partition the cache into sink, archive, and working regions, retaining diverse intermediate events alongside recent motion under fixed memory. Because absolute temporal indices drift outside the training range, Bank-aware RoPE reassigns indices at attention time so each bank remains distinguishable. At 1.3B, Memory Forcing leads on longer clips, shows the smallest drop from 5s to 60s among methods reporting all four lengths, and preserves subjects and scenes through leave-and-return. The same design scales to Wan2.2 5B, producing more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos and, to our knowledge, the first public 5B model on this forcing line.
authors: Jiaming Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Huafeng Shi, Gangshan Wu, Limin Wang
bullets: Existing streaming systems typically retain only initial and recent frames, so intermediate events become inaccessible over long clips.
Archive and Working Banks divide the cache into sink, archive, and working regions to retain both past events and recent motion without increasing memory.
Bank-aware RoPE remaps temporal indices at attention time so the separate memory banks remain distinguishable beyond the training range.
At 1.3B, the method performs strongly on longer clips, with the smallest reported 5s-to-60s degradation among comparable methods.
Scaling to Wan2.2 5B yields more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos, including subject and scene continuity through leave-and-return events.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video generation with cache partitioning and RoPE addressing; directly relevant to video diffusion, autoregressive video, and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Memory Forcing: Attendable Mid-Horizon History for Streaming Video Generation
papers.tldr: Memory Forcing prevents mid-horizon forgetting in few-step streaming video generation by preserving diverse past events within a fixed-size attention cache.

papers.abstract: AI research progress can be viewed as the interaction between two processes: benchmark creation and method discovery. Historically, both were driven by human intelligence. However, recent advances in AI have accelerated automated method discovery, while automated benchmark creation has received comparatively less attention. To enable self-advancing systems, we propose Generative Adversarial Loop (GAL), a generator-discriminator framework alternating between two agentic searches: (1) a discriminator that generates adversarial data to expose weaknesses in current systems, and (2) a generator that discovers algorithms to overcome them. We apply this framework to approximation algorithms for efficient inference. Unlike existing auto research systems, which primarily focus on algorithm discovery, GAL introduces a discriminator agent that automates goalpost setting by continually searching for weaknesses in the current algorithm. We demonstrate adversarial data generation across four tasks: KV compression, sparse video generation, sparse attention, and context extension, where the discriminator identifies weaknesses in state of the art techniques. We further show that GAL enables autonomous improvement, with newly discovered algorithms improving not only on adversarially generated data, but also on established benchmarks. Specifically, GAL improves CompactorPress on KV compression with Qwen3-4B at 4x, raising performance on the discriminator dataset from 0.35 to 0.97, while also outperforming RULER-HARD (+0.77 pts). For context extension, GAL boosts Dual Chunk Attention from 0.20 to 0.90 on the discriminator dataset, while yielding gains on standard benchmarks(ScienceFiction (+6 pts) and PG19 32K (-0.33 PPL)). GAL thus provides a path toward autonomous goalpost setting and algorithmic improvement, where AI systems continually discover their own weaknesses and develop methods to overcome them.
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Nidhi Jain, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Priyanka Jayaswal, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Aditya Desai
bullets: Targets the imbalance between increasingly automated method discovery and comparatively limited automated benchmark creation.
Alternates a discriminator that generates adversarial data with a generator that discovers algorithms addressing the exposed weaknesses.
Applied to KV compression, sparse video generation, sparse attention, and context extension.
Demonstrated autonomous improvement on adversarial datasets and established benchmarks, including KV compression and context extension.
Scope is approximation algorithms for efficient inference; the framework depends on agentic searches that can generate meaningful weaknesses and solutions.
papers.selection_reason: Adversarial loop framework for automated algorithm discovery, demonstrated on KV compression, sparse attention, and context extension.
papers.title: Generative Adversarial Loops
papers.tldr: Generative Adversarial Loops automate both benchmark creation and algorithm discovery by having agents expose system weaknesses and develop methods to overcome them.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) enable generalist robot manipulation by conditioning an action expert on representations from a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT). In closed-loop control, the video DiT runs at every chunk to encode the current observation into layerwise key-value (KV) pairs that the action expert queries. This prefill dominates the per-chunk computational cost, yet existing training-free accelerations leave it fully dense. We present WAM-Cache, a training-free framework that retains layerwise key-value representations across chunks and recomputes only a sparse refresh set of tokens. Crucially, we find that the intuitive heuristic of refreshing visually drifted tokens plateaus far below the dense baseline, even with an oracle predicting ground-truth KV drift. Downstream action accuracy is instead governed by where the action expert attends, not by what moved. WAM-Cache therefore selects the refresh set by uniting the action expert's cross-attention with visual latent surprise, complemented by a strict age bound that suppresses compounding error. On Fast-WAM, WAM-Cache cuts video DiT prefill FLOPs by 32-42% across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-world experiments, while staying within 0.7-1.8 percentage points of the dense policy in simulation and 2.5 points on a real robot.
authors: Kai Ding, Yang He, Ruijie Quan, Yi Yang
bullets: Video DiT KV prefill dominates per-chunk computation in WAM-based robot control.
Refreshing tokens solely by visual drift performs poorly, even with oracle KV-drift information.
The method combines action-expert cross-attention with visual latent surprise to choose refresh tokens.
A strict age bound limits error accumulation from stale representations.
It reduces video DiT prefill FLOPs by 32–42%, with small accuracy gaps in simulation and real-robot tests.
papers.selection_reason: KV reuse for video DiT in robot world action models directly targets efficient inference and embodied manipulation.
papers.title: WAM-Cache: Staleness-Bounded KV Reuse for Efficient World Action Models
papers.tldr: WAM-Cache accelerates closed-loop World Action Models by reusing KV representations and selectively refreshing tokens while maintaining near-dense-policy action accuracy.

papers.abstract: JEV models make multimodal decisions by directly scoring candidates. Although the common context is encoded once, candidate evaluation can still repeat matching token histories, duplicate inference states, and execute the full backbone. In this paper, we study these sources of redundancy and present FastJEV for compact candidate evaluation. We jointly organize history reuse and state storage, since sharing computation requires preserving states for later branches. We first introduce shared context anchoring to reuse recurrent initial states and omit unused final recurrent caches. We extend this reuse through candidate prefix sharing, retaining the intermediate states needed by subsequent branches. To further reduce the depth of these paths, we apply decision guided pruning based on relative score changes measured on a small unlabeled set. Our method retains full context encoding and all candidates without additional training. We evaluate FastJEV across three OmniJev model sizes on five public benchmarks and reconstructed LIBERO-10 offline questions. At the selected pruning budgets, the complete method reduces candidate depth by 43.75% to 45.83%, while retaining 93.66% to 97.52% of the original task scores on average across the six evaluation sets. Through controlled experiments, we show how candidate overlap and branching structure affect the execution cost of history reuse. In our implementation, candidate prefix sharing can reduce repeated computation while increasing latency. These findings motivate designing sharing granularity and execution schedules together for efficient JEV inference.
authors: Jie Ma, Jie Gao, Yihang Liu, Zhike Qiu, Junle Li, Chongyi Zhuang, Jiayi Ji, Xiaoshuai Sun
bullets: Targets redundancy from repeated token histories, duplicate inference states, and full-backbone execution during candidate scoring.
Reuses recurrent states through shared context anchoring and candidate prefix sharing, while retaining states needed by later branches.
Uses decision-guided pruning based on relative score changes from a small unlabeled set, without additional training.
Evaluated across three OmniJev sizes and six evaluation sets; reduces candidate depth by 43.75%–45.83% while retaining 93.66%–97.52% of original scores on average.
Finds that prefix sharing may reduce repeated computation yet increase latency, highlighting the need to co-design sharing granularity and execution schedules.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant computation and reuses recurrent states/caches for compact multimodal JEV inference, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: FastJEV: Understanding Redundancy for Compact JEV Inference
papers.tldr: FastJEV speeds up compact JEV candidate evaluation by reusing shared computation and pruning low-value decision paths while preserving most task performance.

papers.abstract: Cross-model KV-cache reuse remains a key challenge in modern LLM serving. Coding agents and multi-model systems increasingly route a shared context across models: a user may switch models mid-session, or a cascade may escalate a difficult query. Because KV caches contain model-specific representations, each switch typically forces the receiving model to prefill the entire context from scratch. Recent work shows that closed-form linear maps can translate KV caches between models in the same family, but transfer accuracy degrades as the model-size gap widens. In this paper, we establish that these transfer failures are concentrated in a small subset of information-dense tokens. To bridge this gap, we introduce RaReCache, a framework that enables a large target model to decode accurately from a cache prefilled by a much smaller source via selective recomputation. RaReCache identifies these critical positions using a novel rank disagreement metric, scoring each token by the energy of its mapped KV in output directions weakly supported by the calibration data. Across two model families and five benchmarks, on a 23x parameter gap (Qwen3-0.6B to 14B) recomputing just 30% of positions retains 95-99% of the target accuracy, whereas on a 8.8x gap (Llama3-8B to 70B), recomputing 40% retains 96.5% of the target accuracy. RaReCache largely removes sensitivity to source-model size, and achieves up to a 3.04x prefill speedup. For online serving, it handles 1.8x the request throughput of target prefill on a single GPU, and at the target's saturation load, reduces median and 99th-percentile time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 5.0x and 6.4x respectively, with a 30% recompute budget. RaReCache establishes an efficient serving paradigm where small models prefill on behalf of massive targets, enabling large models to recompute only critical tokens, drastically reducing prefill latency.
authors: Sreetama Sarkar, Saptarshi Mitra, Sitao Huang, Souvik Kundu, Peter A. Beerel
bullets: Cross-model KV transfer can fail when source and target model sizes differ substantially, especially for information-dense tokens.
RaReCache ranks token positions using a rank disagreement metric based on mapped KV energy in weakly supported output directions.
Recomputing 30–40% of positions retains 95–99% of target accuracy across two model families and five benchmarks, including gaps up to 23×.
The framework provides up to 3.04× prefill speedup and improves serving throughput and TTFT under the reported settings.
Its scope is selective recomputation for cross-model cache reuse, with performance depending on the chosen recompute budget and model pair.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-model KV cache reuse with selective recomputation for efficient LLM serving.
papers.title: RaReCache: Bridging the Gap in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse via Rank disagreement-based Selective Recomputation
papers.tldr: RaReCache accelerates cross-model KV-cache reuse by selectively recomputing only tokens whose transferred representations are most likely to be inaccurate.

papers.abstract: KV-cache entries are stored before their future queries are known, but each decoding query needs precision in different places. We study this mismatch using separate budgets for retained bits and bits fetched per query. ReadKV stores each key and value in a progressive code whose prefixes support different reconstruction precisions. For each query, it allocates key-channel prefixes using the query, computes attention from the reconstructed keys, and then allocates value-token prefixes using that attention. Stored entries remain unchanged. Each stage optimizes a calibrated distortion objective under a fixed budget; we prove exact allocation under diminishing refinement gains and relate these objectives to attention-output error. We also exhibit a finite-dimensional attention family where query-dependent access strictly outperforms every query-independent reader at the same read budget, even with unrestricted competing encoders and decoders. Across six base models, reading four bits on average from an eight-bit cache increases C4 perplexity by at most 0.66%, using about one quarter of the logical reads and half the retained capacity of a 16-bit cache. It is consistently more accurate than storing and fully reading four bits at the same payload-read budget. Retaining more bits than each query fetches is aimed at long-context decoding, where the cache bytes moved per step, rather than the weights, dominate cost. Long-context question answering and retrieval on two instruction-tuned models provide additional quality evidence. On the tested 8K-token, batch-one, single-layer workload on an NVIDIA A10G, a restricted eight-bit ReadKV reader with a two-bit mean payload-read budget has 39% lower latency than the tested TurboQuant codec.
authors: Siddharth Bhandari, Lucas Gretta, Krishna Balasubramanian, Shiva Kasiviswanathan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed KV-cache storage and query-dependent precision needs.
Uses progressive key/value codes: queries select key precision first, then attention-guided value precision, without modifying stored entries.
Provides allocation guarantees under diminishing refinement gains and proves query-dependent reading can outperform query-independent readers at equal read budgets.
Across six base models, four average read bits from an eight-bit cache increase C4 perplexity by at most 0.66% while reducing logical reads and retained capacity versus a 16-bit cache.
On a tested 8K-token, batch-one A10G workload, a restricted reader achieves 39% lower latency than the tested TurboQuant codec.
papers.selection_reason: Query-adaptive progressive KV-cache quantization with theoretical guarantees, directly improving cache memory and attention read efficiency.
papers.title: Read What Matters: Query-Adaptive Quantization for KV Caches
papers.tldr: ReadKV makes KV-cache reads query-adaptive, improving long-context decoding efficiency by fetching precision only where each query needs it.

papers.abstract: Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) relies heavily on reconstruction loss minimization to preserve model quality at low precision. We show that the weights favored by minimizing this loss need not yield better model performance on new tasks. In fact, we find that lower reconstruction loss can even degrade model performance on the same calibration data. Our analysis further shows that weights with lower reconstruction loss on calibration data can have higher loss than other weights when the distribution of input activations changes. Motivated by these observations and our analysis, we propose Distributionally Robust Quantization (DRQ), a post-hoc refinement process that minimizes worst-case reconstruction loss over a constrained set of input activation distributions. DRQ refines the integer codes representing quantized weights within the existing quantization grid, keeping quantization parameters and inference operators unchanged. Extensive experiments show that DRQ improves models quantized by six representative PTQ methods, including AWQ, GPTQ, and ParoQuant, and delivers gains across both dense and mixture-of-experts large language models. These results establish DRQ as a general post-hoc refinement framework for weight-only PTQ, achieving better downstream performance without adding inference overhead.
authors: Yanlong Zhao, Xiaoyuan Cheng, Huihang Liu, Baihua He, Xinyu Zhang, Harrison Bo Hua Zhu, Wenlong Chen, Li Zeng, Zhuo Sun
bullets: Weight-only PTQ can select weights with lower calibration reconstruction loss yet worse same-data or new-task performance.
Distribution shifts in input activations can make calibration-based reconstruction loss unreliable.
DRQ minimizes worst-case reconstruction loss over a constrained set of activation distributions.
It refines integer weight codes within the existing quantization grid, leaving quantization parameters and inference operators unchanged.
Experiments report improvements across six PTQ methods, including AWQ, GPTQ, and ParoQuant, for dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a refinement method for low-bit LLM quantization, a memory-efficiency technique for inference.
papers.title: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
papers.tldr: Lower reconstruction loss does not always improve quantized LLMs, so DRQ robustly refines quantized weights across possible activation distributions to improve downstream performance without inference overhead.

papers.abstract: KV-cache quantization and linear attention are two representative approaches to tackling the storage and computational costs of Transformers. KV-cache quantization compresses individual KV entries into discrete codes but retains all entries, whereas linear attention recurrently aggregates multiple historical KV contributions into a fixed-size continuous state but can introduce interference. This contrast raises the question of whether per-KV compression and multi-KV aggregation can be bridged within a single mechanism for efficient attention. We identify RAM-Net as such a bridge through soft assignments over a discrete address space. These assignments determine recurrent updates to the continuous slot state associated with each address. Under a restricted RAM-Net construction, we prove that soft address assignments extend hard quantized matching to a separable read-write overlap that locally approximates full-attention similarity and supports recurrent aggregation. These connections further enable Transformer-to-RAM-Net weight migration through a new path based on a soft-quantized intermediate construction. Across nine pretrained Transformer models from 0.3B to 7B parameters, RAM-Net recovers an average of 87.1% of the teachers' accuracy gains over random guessing across six commonsense and knowledge tasks using only a 500M-token budget per model.
authors: Kaicheng Xiao, Liran Dong, Haotian Li, Guoliang Xing
bullets: KV-cache quantization compresses individual KV entries, while linear attention aggregates history into a fixed-size state but may cause interference.
RAM-Net connects both approaches through soft assignments to a discrete address space and recurrent continuous slot updates.
A restricted construction theoretically links soft assignments to separable read-write overlap, locally approximating full-attention similarity while supporting aggregation.
A soft-quantized intermediate enables migration of pretrained Transformer weights to RAM-Net.
Across nine 0.3B–7B models and six tasks, RAM-Net retained an average of 87.1% of teachers’ accuracy gains over random guessing using 500M tokens per model.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies KV-cache quantization and linear attention via RAM-Net, directly targeting efficient attention and cache memory.
papers.title: Bridging KV-Cache Quantization and Linear Attention: From Theory to Pretrained Weight Migration
papers.tldr: RAM-Net bridges KV-cache quantization and linear attention by using soft discrete addressing to recurrently aggregate KV information, enabling pretrained Transformer weight migration with substantial accuracy retention.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context attention, but existing kernels typically process queries independently, repeatedly loading and dequantizing KV entries shared across queries. We observe substantial overlap in the KV entries selected by neighboring queries, creating opportunities for cross-query reuse. We present QUILT, a workload-aware sparse-attention execution mechanism that jointly processes neighboring queries and reuses shared KV entries to reduce redundant memory traffic and computation. QUILT introduces Shift-and-Compare Set Decomposition (SCSD), which transforms irregular set operations into regular data-parallel primitives suitable for modern accelerators, and pipelines SCSD with attention computation to hide its overhead. Cascaded sharing captures reuse hierarchically at multiple granularities. A tile-aware execution strategy balances sharing granularity with hardware tile utilization and selectively removes low-importance query-specific tails to eliminate underutilized tiles. We evaluate QUILT on LongBench using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-3.2 under both tensor and sequence parallelism. Compared with the state-of-the-art sparse-attention kernel, QUILT reduces average kernel latency by up to 55.1% and processed KV data by up to 55.9%, while reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency by up to 36.8% with negligible accuracy degradation.
authors: Zhenduo Zhao, Qihui Zhou, Mingcong Song, Zhiyi Chen, Chuangguan Ye, Fengfan Hou, Zequn Gong, Jing Li, Hongjie Si, Guoping Long
bullets: Targets redundant KV loading and dequantization caused by independently processed queries.
Uses SCSD to convert irregular set operations into accelerator-friendly data-parallel operations and pipelines them with attention computation.
Combines hierarchical cascaded sharing, tile-aware execution, and selective removal of low-importance query tails.
On LongBench with GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-3.2, reduces kernel latency by up to 55.1%, processed KV data by up to 55.9%, and TTFT by up to 36.8%.
Scope: evaluated under tensor and sequence parallelism, with negligible accuracy degradation.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse-attention execution with shared query reuse directly targets efficient attention and memory traffic reduction.
papers.title: QUILT: Rethinking Sparse-Attention Prefill through Shared Query Execution
papers.tldr: QUILT accelerates sparse-attention prefill by jointly processing neighboring queries and reusing their shared KV entries, reducing kernel latency and KV traffic with negligible accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) offer a single architecture for both image generation and multimodal understanding, but their iterative decoding requires tens to hundreds of forward passes. Existing few-step distillation methods largely focus on either image generation or text generation, making it unclear how to compress a fully discrete multimodal dLLM into a single efficient student while preserving both generation and understanding. We introduce Omni-Diffusion-Distill, a unified two-stage distillation framework that retains strong generation and understanding capabilities while substantially reducing the inference cost of a unified multimodal dLLM. Omni-Diffusion-Distill aligns the distillation of both generation and understanding, for both images and text, in the discrete token space. In the first stage, the student is trained to skip decoding steps by replaying cached teacher trajectories, and in the second stage the student is refined on intermediate states along its own rollouts. We further remedy two sources of degradation in unified distillation with a pairwise collision penalty that reduces repetition under parallel text decoding, and entropy-matched guidance that prevents entropy collapse caused by fitting the sharpened teacher distribution in image generation. Omni-Diffusion-Distill achieves state-of-the-art trade-offs between decoding efficiency and generation and understanding performance for multimodal dLLMs, reducing image generation from 128 to 8 decoding steps and multimodal understanding from 512 to 64, giving 18.2x and 21.2x wall-clock speedups. Under these budgets, it scores 0.828 on GenEval and 83.0 on DPG-Bench for text-to-image generation, while reaching GPT judge scores of 20.0 on MM-Vet and 57.2 on COCO captioning (twice the teacher's 28.4 at the same steps) for multimodal understanding.
authors: Hong Huang, Chenhongyi Yang, Junzhe Sun, Animesh Sinha, Wuyang Chen, Yifan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of unified multimodal diffusion LLMs, whose iterative decoding can require hundreds of passes.
Uses two-stage discrete-token distillation: teacher-trajectory replay followed by refinement on the student’s own rollouts.
Adds pairwise collision penalties to reduce repetition in parallel text decoding and entropy-matched guidance to avoid image-generation entropy collapse.
Reduces image generation from 128 to 8 steps and multimodal understanding from 512 to 64, yielding 18.2× and 21.2× wall-clock speedups.
Reports strong results at these budgets, including 0.828 GenEval, 83.0 DPG-Bench, 20.0 MM-Vet, and 57.2 COCO captioning.
papers.selection_reason: Few-step distillation of unified multimodal diffusion LLMs for efficient generation and understanding; relevant to multimodal foundation models and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Omni-Diffusion-Distill: Few-Step Distillation of Unified Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Omni-Diffusion-Distill compresses a unified multimodal diffusion LLM to 8 image or 64 understanding steps while retaining strong performance and achieving substantial speedups.

papers.abstract: A large language model can only use the text that fits in its context window, and it recomputes its internal key-value (KV) state for a prompt every time the prompt is sent. We test a memory layer, the public package galahad-kv, that saves the KV state of each block of about 16,000 tokens to encrypted local NVMe disk and loads it back later, byte-exact, without recomputing it. We ran it on 50,000,000 tokens of real public text, served through vLLM on one NVIDIA H100, with Gemma 4 12B and Gemma 4 31B. Every block we probed was loaded back from the encrypted store with no recompute (100 of 100, at depths from 0 to 50M tokens) on both models. Loading a block was 2.8x to 4.3x faster than recomputing it and used 8.8x to 12.3x less GPU energy, and GPU memory stayed flat over the whole 50M-token stream. Asked about facts planted millions of tokens earlier, the 12B model gave the right answer 82 times out of 100 and the 31B model 98 times out of 100. Neither model made up an answer. The limits are as follows. This is reuse of stored state, not a wider attention window: one block is loaded at a time, and how well a question is answered depends on the model. Writing the memory is a one-time cost, and the store takes terabytes of local NVMe disk. We describe the test protocol, which is built to resist common ways of gaming long-context benchmarks, and give a single-GPU reproduction that uses public software and a free licence for the package.
bullets: Motivation: standard long-context inference recomputes a prompt’s KV state and is constrained by GPU context capacity.
Method: galahad-kv stores roughly 16K-token KV blocks on encrypted local NVMe and reloads them byte-exactly through vLLM.
Evaluation: tested on 50M tokens of public text with Gemma 4 12B and 31B on one NVIDIA H100.
Results: all 100 probed blocks loaded without recomputation; loading was 2.8–4.3× faster and used 8.8–12.3× less GPU energy than recompute.
Scope: this reuses stored state rather than expanding attention; only one block is loaded at a time, with a one-time write cost and terabytes of disk storage required.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent KV-state memory layer for long-context LLM inference; directly relevant to KV cache/memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: Real Long-Term Memory for AI: A 50-Million-Token Window That Is Faster and Cheaper Than Recompute
papers.tldr: A disk-backed KV-cache memory layer enables exact reuse of context across up to 50M tokens, reducing retrieval latency and GPU energy versus recomputation while preserving flat GPU memory use.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably internalize substantial amounts of sensitive or private information during pre-training, while LLM unlearning aims to selectively erase specific knowledge to prevent privacy leakage with minimal loss of model utility. However, existing methods struggle to balance forget quality with utility, and typically incur substantial computational costs due to parameter fine-tuning. To address this, we propose Nullify, a training-free, non-destructive activation steering method for LLM unlearning. Nullify employs steering vectors during inference to redirect privacy-related activations away from their memorized answers, while satisfying a null-space constraint that leaves retained-query activations essentially unaffected to maintain utility. Evaluations on TOFU and MUSE show that Nullify matches or surpasses established baselines in forget quality while achieving near-lossless preservation of model utility. By avoiding weight updates entirely, Nullify serves as an efficient, plug-and-play inference-time intervention framework.
authors: Wei Zhai, Xiang Liu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Lemao Liu, Ziwei Li, Ziqi Wang, Zhitao Huang, Dejing Dou
bullets: Targets selective removal of sensitive or private knowledge with minimal impact on retained capabilities.
Uses inference-time steering vectors to redirect privacy-related activations away from memorized answers.
Applies a null-space constraint so retained-query activations remain essentially unchanged.
On TOFU and MUSE, matches or surpasses established baselines in forget quality with near-lossless utility preservation.
Avoids parameter updates, making it a plug-and-play, non-destructive intervention.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free inference-time activation steering for LLM unlearning with null-space constraints; relevant to test-time intervention and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Nullify: Null-Space Activation Steering for Training-Free LLM Unlearning
papers.tldr: Nullify enables training-free LLM unlearning by steering privacy-related activations into a null space, reducing memorized answers while preserving model utility.

papers.abstract: Training a compact model often needs far more memory than storing it, because the optimizer keeps its own records of past gradients. For a hyperdimensional classifier whose learned parameters are low-bit angles, which we call a \emph{phase memory}, these records take several times more memory than the model itself. We ask whether such a model can be trained while storing nothing but the model. The proposed method, Phase-HDC, turns each stored angle by at most one step per update, against the sign of its current gradient, and only when that gradient is large enough. We show that this simple rule is the exact solution of a first-order loss model in which every changed parameter pays a fixed cost. When everything except the update rule is held fixed, Phase-HDC matches the accuracy of Adam with 6-bit moments while storing three times less. Across eleven image, tabular, and text datasets, it stores 16--23$\times$ less than standard float32 Adam and 4--6$\times$ less than 8-bit Adam. The price is an average loss of about five accuracy points against float32 Adam, while Phase-HDC is more accurate than 8-bit Adam on six of the eleven datasets, including byte-level text prediction, where 8-bit Adam collapses. Instrumented training runs explain these outcomes. Once parameters must sit on a discrete grid, Adam's moments mainly decide whether a parameter moves at all, a decision that a threshold on the current gradient can make without memory, and coarse quantization of the moments breaks this decision for inputs that the data rarely contain. The storage savings are logical state rather than measured hardware memory.
bullets: Addresses the memory overhead of optimizer state, which can greatly exceed the compact model itself.
Updates each discrete angle by at most one grid step, in the opposite gradient direction, only when the gradient exceeds a threshold.
Matches 6-bit-moment Adam accuracy while using three times less storage; across 11 datasets, it uses 16–23× less than float32 Adam and 4–6× less than 8-bit Adam.
It loses about five accuracy points on average versus float32 Adam but outperforms 8-bit Adam on 6 of 11 datasets, including byte-level text prediction.
The method targets logical state savings; hardware memory reduction is not directly measured.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient training method that eliminates optimizer state, directly relevant to reducing memory requirements in model training.
papers.title: Phase-HDC: Replacing Optimizer History with Gradient Thresholds in Discrete Phase Learning
papers.tldr: Phase-HDC trains low-bit phase-based hyperdimensional classifiers using only the model by replacing optimizer history with thresholded, one-step gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Comparing parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes under a single, shared learning rate is a common but flawed practice: when the arms being compared have very different trainable-parameter counts, a shared rate can simultaneously depress the larger arms' means and inflate their variance, manufacturing a large, seemingly multi-seed-significant advantage for the smallest arm that is not a real effect. We document this confound in a concrete setting: post-hoc SVD-based KV-cache compression, where an already-pretrained model is converted to a low-rank (multi-head-latent-attention-style) cache by factorizing its key/value weights into a down-projection ("encoder") and an up-projection ("decoder"), after which a short fine-tune ("healing") recovers the accuracy lost to truncation. Under a shared learning rate, freezing the decoder and healing only the encoder looks like a clear win over healing the decoder or both factors; once every arm is given its own tuned learning rate, that apparent advantage disappears, and encoder-only healing instead reaches parity with the alternatives, at a real, measured saving of 3x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less optimizer-state memory. We verify this parity with per-arm learning-rate tuning and three seeds per configuration on a vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct), at the one compression ratio this protocol covers, and replicate it on a text-only testbed across two backbones. Encoder-only healing is therefore a lower-memory drop-in recipe for retrofitting low-rank KV-cache compression at training time, and the shared-learning-rate pitfall we document and correct is a cautionary result for comparing any fine-tuning recipes whose arms differ in trainable-parameter count.
bullets: A shared learning rate can unfairly favor smaller adaptation methods by depressing larger methods’ means and increasing their variance.
For low-rank KV-cache compression, the study compares healing the encoder, decoder, or both factor matrices after SVD truncation.
With per-arm learning-rate tuning, encoder-only healing reaches parity rather than showing a genuine accuracy advantage.
The result is verified with three seeds on a vision-language model and replicated on two text-only backbones.
Scope is limited to the tested compression ratio and evaluated model configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient healing for SVD-based KV-cache compression, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Freeze the Decoder, Heal the Encoder: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for SVD-Based KV-Cache Compression
papers.tldr: Encoder-only healing matches decoder or full-factor healing for SVD-based KV-cache compression while using 3× fewer trainable parameters and optimizer-state memory, provided learning rates are tuned per method.

papers.abstract: Gradient observations promise more accurate Gaussian process (GP) surrogates, but the cost of incorporating them has long stood in the way of realizing that promise. We propose a derivative GP with a budget of just two directions per observed gradient. One direction focuses on each gradient's direct contribution to target prediction, while the other aggregates its indirect contributions through correlations with the conditioning function values.
